Wash Your Hands Song for Kids - Good Habits Nursery Rhymes For Childre

weeks.theme: Every day and right now: a zoo keeper's day
weeks.obj: contrast present simple (routine) and present continuous (now): A zoo keeper feeds the lions at nine. Right now he is feeding them.; use time markers every day, usually, at the moment, now; ask What does he do? What is he doing?; write 6 sentences about a person's routine and what they are doing now
weeks.lang: feed, clean, check, give, wash, carry, watch; lions, monkeys, elephants, penguins, zoo; He feeds the lions at nine. / He is feeding them now.; What does she do every day? What is she doing now?; every day, usually, at the moment, now, right now; Does he...? Is he...?
weeks.res: Present continuous disappearing words (PPT); What are they doing? Hidden picture game (PPT)
weeks.act: A day in the life of a zoo keeper: describe a routine and then a picture of what is happening now; spot-the-difference game
weeks.hw: Write about a family member: 3 sentences about what they do every day and 3 about what they are doing right now.

skills.L: Listen to a routine and a now description and tick which is which
skills.S: Ask What does he do? What is he doing? and describe both
skills.R: Read a short text with both tenses and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write 6 sentences contrasting routine and now

lp.wu: Now and usually mime: the teacher says 'Every day I brush my teeth... Right now I'm brushing my teeth!' and children mime both; then children make their own pair of sentences.
wuAlt: Stand up if it is true: 'Right now we are sitting.' 'Every day we eat lunch.'
Which tense? hold a card for simple or continuous
lp.pres: Present the contrast on a two-column board: every day/usually (present simple, Does he feed...?) vs now/at the moment (present continuous, Is he feeding...?). Use zoo pictures: a keeper's timetable and a scene with the keeper in action. Model 'He feeds the lions at nine. Right now he is feeding them.' Highlight the time markers.
presAlt: Sort the sentences into 'every day' and 'right now' columns
Picture match: timetable line and scene picture
lp.prac: Timetable and scene in pairs: Child A has the keeper's timetable (8:00 feed the monkeys, 9:00 clean the pool) and Child B has a picture of what the keeper is doing at 9:00. They ask and answer 'What does he do at nine? What is he doing now?' and write 6 sentences contrasting the two.
pracAlt: Spot the difference: two zoo scenes, find 5 differences with present continuous
Interview a keeper: one child is the zoo keeper, the other asks 5 questions
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'Every day Mr Khalid feeds the lions at nine o'clock. He cleans the cages at ten. Right now he is feeding the monkeys. He is smiling.' Children tick routine or now for 6 sentences and number pictures. Read twice.
lp.re: Tense flash: the teacher reads a sentence with a time marker and children show a card (simple or continuous); then correct wrong sentences ('Right now he feeds the lions.').
lp.prod: Class zoo poster: groups draw a zoo keeper's day (4 times) and a scene of 'right now', then write 6 sentences contrasting both ('The keeper usually... At the moment he is...'). Present as tour guides.
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence text about a keeper's day and answer 5 questions. Then write 6 sentences contrasting routine and now for a person you know. Fast finishers add a negative (He isn't sleeping now).
lp.st: Video 'Interesting Facts about Cats' or a short animal video from Videos/Videos for Children/Animals; children say what the animals do usually and what they are doing now. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Mime and say a routine and a now sentence.
Show a card for the right tense.
Ask questions to a child playing the keeper.
Correct sentences with the wrong tense.
diff: Fast finishers: write a longer text about a day at a farm or airport with both tenses.
Support: sentence frames with 'Every day' and 'Right now' in two colours.
hw: Write 3 routine and 3 'now' sentences about a family member.
Take a photo or draw what people at home are doing now and write sentences.
Make a timetable of someone's day with 5 times.
lp.tip: The contrast is the point: always use the time markers as clues. Use pictures for 'right now'. Present simple vs continuous is a central A2 skill and a common Movers task. Avoid mixing with the past in this lesson.

kit.l: What are they doing? Hidden picture game (PPT)
Cambridge Global English 3 Learner's Book (Unit 1: Working together, present continuous)
What are you usually doing at...? (worksheet)
Animal facts: interesting facts about cats (video)
A day in the life of a football player (worksheet)

weeks.obj: name the planets and 10 space words; compare planets (Jupiter is the biggest planet. Mars is smaller than Earth.); say how things move and how long they take (The Moon goes around the Earth. It takes 28 days.); write a 6-sentence fact file about a planet
weeks.lang: Sun, Moon, Earth, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, star, planet, rocket, astronaut; The Earth goes around the Sun. It takes 365 days.; Jupiter is the biggest planet. Mercury is the closest to the Sun.; hot, cold, big, small, far from, close to; Is there life on Mars? No, there isn't.
weeks.res: Space flashcards; Space reveal game (PPT); Solar system (PPT game)
weeks.act: Planet fact cards and a solar system model; 'Which planet am I?' guessing game
weeks.hw: Write 6 sentences about your favourite planet or the Moon using comparatives and superlatives.

skills.L: Listen to planet facts and match them to the planets
skills.S: Describe and compare planets and ask Which planet is...?
skills.R: Read a short fact text and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write a 6-sentence fact file about a planet

lp.wu: Order the planets: 9 children hold planet cards and put themselves in order from the Sun; the class says 'Mercury is the closest to the Sun.' Teacher models, the class repeats.
wuAlt: Planet song: sing along to the planet names
Space word hunt: find words in a word search
lp.pres: Present the planets and space words with the Solar System PPT, the Planets song and the Planets of the Solar System video. Model fact sentences with comparatives and superlatives (Jupiter is the biggest. Mars is colder than Earth.). Show 'goes around' and 'takes ... days' with a physical model of Sun and Earth.
presAlt: Planet and fact match: cards and pictures
Sentence strips: build sentences about planets
lp.prac: Planet fact cards in groups: each group receives a planet card (size, temperature, moons, distance) and prepares 4 sentences to introduce it. Groups swap cards and write 2 comparisons ('Venus is hotter than Mars.'). Then they play 'Which planet am I?' with 3 clues.
pracAlt: Solar system model: arrange planets by size and say the order
Information gap: partners have different tables of planet facts and ask Which planet is...?
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Earth is the third planet. Jupiter is the biggest planet. It has many moons.' Children match facts to planets in a table and tick true/false statements. Read twice.
lp.re: Planet quiz: teams answer 10 questions (Which planet is the biggest? Is Mars bigger than Earth?). Then rocket countdown where children say a sentence per number (10 - 1).
lp.prod: Solar system poster: groups draw the planets, label them and write 6 sentences with comparatives and superlatives. Present as space guides: 'Welcome to Mars. It is red and cold.'
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence fact text about the Moon and the Earth and answer 5 questions. Then write 6 sentences about a planet. Fast finishers add 'I would like to visit...' (optional).
lp.st: Planet song from Videos/Videos for Children/Space/Astronomy (planets song) with actions. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Stand in the order of the planets from the Sun.
Say a space sentence for each number from 10 to 1.
Find space words in a word search.
diff: Fast finishers: write 8 sentences about a space trip to Mars.
Support: planet cards with pictures and sentence frames The ___ is ___.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your favourite planet.
Look at the night sky and write 3 sentences about what you see.
Make a fact card for the Moon with 5 facts.
lp.tip: Planet order is a good chant: 'My Very Easy Method...' works in any language. The language is comparatives, superlatives and present simple for facts. Keep numbers simple (days, not millions).

kit.l: Cambridge Global English 4 Learner's Book (Unit 3: Day and night, the solar system)
The Sun, Earth and Moon: solar system for kids (video)
The Earth, the Moon and the Sun lesson game (PPT)
Wordsearch: Earth, Moon, Sun and stars

weeks.theme: Extreme weather and natural disasters: what should we do?
weeks.obj: name 8 natural events (storm, flood, earthquake, volcano, drought, hurricane, snowstorm, heatwave); describe a past event with was/were and the weather; use should/shouldn't and must for safety advice; write 6 sentences about what to do
weeks.lang: storm, flood, earthquake, volcano, drought, hurricane, heatwave, snowstorm; The storm was big. The wind was very strong. It wasn't safe.; What should we do? We should stay calm. We shouldn't use the lift. We must leave the building.; because, so; safe, dangerous, strong
weeks.res: Modal verbs: necessity (worksheets); 7 ways to survive natural disasters (video); Natural disasters interactive games (PPT)
weeks.act: Disaster safety poster and a role play: a safety announcement with should/shouldn't
weeks.hw: Make a safety rule list for one event (earthquake or flood) with 5 sentences using should/shouldn't.

skills.L: Listen to safety advice and tick the right pictures
skills.S: Say what we should and shouldn't do in a disaster
skills.R: Read a short text with safety tips and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write 6 sentences of safety advice

lp.wu: Weather and disaster mime: children mime a storm (wind and rain), an earthquake (shake) and a heatwave (fanning) and the class names it. Then 'What was the weather like yesterday? It was...' recycles was/were.
wuAlt: Picture predict: guess the event from a close-up photo
Word association: say a word you think of for 'storm'
lp.pres: Present the natural events with the Seven tips to survive natural disasters text, the survival video and pictures. Model 'What should we do in an earthquake? We should get under a table. We shouldn't run outside.' Teach must for strong rules (We must leave the building) and 'It was a big storm' in the past.
presAlt: Sort advice cards: should or shouldn't for each event
Match: event pictures to safety tips
lp.prac: Safety announcement in groups: each group chooses an event and prepares a 5-sentence announcement ('Attention, please! There is a storm. You should stay inside. You shouldn't use the lift.'). They perform it as a news reporter and the class says whether the advice is right.
pracAlt: Pair debate: 'Which is more dangerous, a flood or a fire?'
Dialogue: A reports a problem, B gives advice
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'There is an earthquake. Stay calm. Get under a strong table. Don't use the lift. When it stops, go outside.' Children tick the correct actions on picture cards. Then 'Last night there was a big storm. The wind was strong.' Read twice.
lp.re: Safety actions race: the teacher says an event and teams run to the right advice card and hold it up with a sentence. Then 'should or shouldn't?' quick-fire.
lp.prod: Make a safety poster for one event: draw pictures with labels and write 5 sentences using should/shouldn't. Present to another group, who ask 'What should we do if...?'
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence text about staying safe in a storm and answer 5 questions. Then write 6 sentences of advice for an earthquake or flood. Fast finishers add what happened in a real event in the past.
lp.st: Video '7 Ways to Survive Natural Disasters' from Videos/Videos for Children/Nature. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Mime a natural event for the class to name.
Present a safety message as a news reporter.
Sort advice cards for each event.
Run to the right advice card and say a sentence.
Guess the event from a close-up photo.
diff: Fast finishers: write a news report of a past storm (6 sentences) with was/were.
Support: advice cards with pictures and sentence frames We should ___. We shouldn't ___.
hw: Make a safety rule list for an earthquake or flood with 5 sentences.
Check your home: where is the safe place in an earthquake? Draw it.
Tell someone at home 3 safety tips in English.
lp.tip: Sensitive topic: keep the focus on safety and preparation, not on fear. Use drills (calm, practical) and respect children who have experienced events like the 2023 earthquake. Ramadan is an optional overlay.

kit.l: Seven tips on how to survive natural disasters (reading)
What is an earthquake? The Dr. Binocs show (video)
Cambridge Global English 4 Learner's Book (Unit 7: Australia, extreme weather)
Weather and seasons: games and videos (PPT)
Blast the aliens: modal verbs (PPT game)
Stop the zombies: modal verbs (PPT game)
Is the weather getting more extreme? (reading)
Weather vs. climate: Crash Course Kids (video)

occ.act: Ramadan (expected around 8 Feb 2027, depends on the moon): optional 10-minute link: talk about the evening weather ('It was cold last night. It is clear tonight.') and write a Ramadan greeting card. Respect fasting children.
occ.hw: Optional: write a greeting card with 2 sentences.

weeks.theme: Oceans and sea life: why we protect them
weeks.obj: name 10 sea animals and 4 ocean zones; say why we protect the sea with because and so; use have to / mustn't for rules about rubbish; write a 6-sentence paragraph about an ocean animal
weeks.lang: whale, shark, dolphin, turtle, octopus, jellyfish, crab, seahorse, coral, fish; surface, deep sea, coral reef, beach; Whales are mammals. They breathe air.; Turtles eat jellyfish but plastic bags are dangerous.; We have to protect the sea because... We mustn't throw rubbish in the sea.; It's in danger.
weeks.res: Sea animals vocabulary (video); Sea animals flashcards (PPT)
weeks.act: Ocean fact cards, 'Sea or land?' sorting game and a 'Protect the sea' poster
weeks.hw: Write 6 sentences about a sea animal: where it lives, what it eats and why we must protect it.

skills.L: Listen to facts about sea animals and tick true or false
skills.S: Say why we protect the sea with because and have to
skills.R: Read a short text about the ocean and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about a sea animal

lp.wu: Sea animal mime and sound: children move like a jellyfish, a crab or a shark; the class guesses and says 'It lives in the sea.' Then 'Fish or mammal?' with a few quick clues.
wuAlt: Dive deep: stand up for the surface, crouch for the deep sea and say an animal for each
Animal bingo with sea animal pictures
lp.pres: Present sea animals and zones with the Sea animals PPT and the video 'Sea animals vocabulary'. Model facts: 'The turtle lives in warm water. It eats jellyfish.' Present danger with because and have to: 'We have to protect turtles because plastic is dangerous. We mustn't throw rubbish.' Use What if all oceans dried up video as a hook.
presAlt: Sort animals into zones: surface, deep sea, reef
Match: animal - danger - solution cards
lp.prac: Ocean fact cards in groups: each group receives an animal card (home, food, danger) and writes 5 sentences with because. They present to another group and the audience answers 'How can we help?' with a rule ('We mustn't throw plastic into the sea.').
pracAlt: Information gap: partners have different animal tables and ask Where does it live? What does it eat?
Debate: 'Which animal is the most important? Why?'
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'The blue whale is the biggest animal in the world. It lives in the ocean. It eats very small animals. It is in danger because of plastic and ships.' Children mark 6 true/false statements. Read twice.
lp.re: Sea or land? game: the teacher calls a fact ('It breathes air. It lives in the sea.') and children move to 'whale' or 'fish' cards; then a quick-fire quiz on dangers and solutions.
lp.prod: Protect the sea poster: groups draw a sea scene and write 6 sentences ('Sea turtles live in warm water. They are in danger because...'). Present to another group, who suggest a rule with 'We have to...'
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence text about coral reefs and answer 5 questions. Then write a 6-sentence paragraph about a sea animal with at least 2 because sentences. Fast finishers add 'We should / We mustn't' advice.
lp.st: Video 'Sea animals vocabulary' from Videos/Videos for Children/Animals. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Move like a sea animal and say where it lives.
Show the zone with your body and say an animal.
Answer questions about dangers and solutions.
diff: Fast finishers: write a mini report on a sea animal's life cycle (8 sentences).
Support: animal cards with pictures and sentence frames It lives in ___. It eats ___.
hw: Write 6 sentences about a sea animal and why we protect it.
Find 3 ways to reduce plastic at home and write them with have to.
Draw a sea scene and label 6 animals.
lp.tip: CLIL: keep science facts simple and visual. Link to the Atlantic and Mediterranean for local relevance (dolphins, turtles). The environment message should be hopeful: what we can do.

kit.l: Hide and seek: sea animals (PPT game)
What if all the world's oceans dried up? (video)
Seven continents and oceans: Our planet Earth (video)

weeks.theme: Rules, signs and safety: must, mustn't, have to
weeks.obj: use must, mustn't, have to and don't have to for rules; read 10 common signs; ask and answer Do I have to...? Must I...?; write a set of 6 rules for a place
weeks.lang: must, mustn't, have to, don't have to; Don't run. No phones. Keep quiet. Danger! Exit.; You must wear a helmet. You mustn't swim here. We have to wear a uniform. We don't have to wear a tie.; Do we have to...? Yes, we do. / No, we don't.; at school, at home, on the road, at the pool
weeks.res: Class rules reveal game (PPT); Class contracts (worksheet)
weeks.act: Design a set of signs and rules for school, the road or the swimming pool; 'Rules or not?' debate
weeks.hw: Write 6 rules for your home or classroom with must/mustn't/have to and draw 2 signs.

skills.L: Listen to rules and match them to signs
skills.S: Ask and answer Do we have to...? and give rules
skills.R: Read a rules poster and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write 6 rules with must/mustn't/have to

lp.wu: Sign guess: show road and school signs without words and ask 'What does it mean?' Children answer 'You mustn't run.' 'You must stop.' Add gestures: a hand up for 'must', a cross for 'mustn't'.
wuAlt: Sign matching: signs and sentences
Simon says with rules: 'You must stand up!'
lp.pres: Present must/mustn't with signs and a 'Rules at the swimming pool' poster. Contrast mustn't (it is forbidden) with don't have to (it is not necessary) with a visual of a tie at school. Practise questions 'Do we have to...?' with short answers. Show negative and affirmative in a table.
presAlt: Rule sort: must, mustn't, don't have to on three posters
Sign jigsaw: match sign to the rule
lp.prac: Design a rules poster in groups: choose a place (school, pool, road, library) and write 6 rules with must/mustn't/have to and draw 3 signs. Then groups play 'Rules or not?': one group says a rule, the others say if it is a real rule or not and why.
pracAlt: Pair role play: a safety officer explains rules to a visitor
Survey: 'Do you have to wear a uniform? Do you have to do homework?'
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'At the pool you must wear a swimming hat. You mustn't run. You have to shower first. You don't have to bring a towel, because they give one.' Children tick the matching sign pictures and mark must/mustn't/don't have to. Read twice.
lp.re: Rules statues: the teacher says a rule ('You mustn't run!') and children freeze or move accordingly, then correct a wrong rule. Next, 'real or silly rules?' quick-fire.
lp.prod: Present your rules poster to another class (or group) in a safety talk: 'At the library you must keep quiet. You mustn't eat.' The audience asks 'Do we have to...?' and the presenters answer.
lp.rw: Read a rules poster (8 lines) and answer 5 questions. Then write 6 rules for your home or school with must/mustn't/have to. Fast finishers add a rule for the future (You must... next year).
lp.st: Video 'Road Safety video: Traffic Rules And Signs For Kids' from Videos/Videos for Children/Machines/Vehicles. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Say what a sign means with must/mustn't.
Decide if a rule is real or silly.
Sort must, mustn't and don't have to.
Move or freeze according to the rule.
diff: Fast finishers: write a rulebook for an imaginary school (8 rules).
Support: sentence frames with must/mustn't in colour and sign pictures.
hw: Write 6 rules for your home with must/mustn't/have to.
Find 3 signs near your home and draw them with their meaning.
Ask someone at home what rules they had at school.
lp.tip: Contrast mustn't and don't have to with visuals; it is a common error. Link to safety: road, pool and online (see Week 27). Keep rules positive and fair.

weeks.theme: Life in the future: will and won't
weeks.obj: make predictions with will/won't and maybe/probably; ask and answer Will we...? What will you do?; talk about the future of transport, school and homes; write a 6-sentence prediction paragraph and a time capsule note
weeks.lang: will, won't, maybe, probably, in 2050, in the future, next year; Robots will clean our homes. We won't use paper books. Cars will fly.; Will people live on Mars? Yes, they will. / No, they won't.; What will you be? I will be a doctor.; I think..., I hope...

weeks.hw: Write 6 predictions about life in 2050 and a time capsule note to yourself in 10 years.

skills.L: Listen to predictions and tick the ones you agree with
skills.S: Make predictions with will/won't and ask Will we...?
skills.R: Read a short text about the future and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Write 6 predictions and a note to my future self

lp.wu: Crystal ball: a child holds a pretend crystal ball and predicts something about a classmate ('You will be a doctor.') and the class says 'Yes, you will!' or 'No, you won't!'
wuAlt: Agree or disagree: stand on the line for a prediction
Mime the future: act a job in 2050
lp.pres: Present will/won't with a timeline (now - tomorrow - 2050). Show affirmative, negative and question forms in a table. Teach maybe and probably and 'I think'. Use pictures of the future (flying cars, robots in school) to elicit predictions and write them on a prediction wall.
presAlt: Prediction cards: say a sentence for each picture
Will or won't? sort sentences about the future
lp.prac: Future city in groups: draw a city of 2050 and write 6 predictions ('There will be flying cars. People won't use plastic bags.'). Then each group presents and the class votes 'Maybe' or 'No way' and says why. Class survey: 'Will we live on Mars?'
pracAlt: Prediction survey: ask 6 classmates 'Will robots teach us? Will cars fly?' and graph the answers
Fortune teller: one child predicts the future of a partner with 3 sentences
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'In 2050 people will live in cities with flying cars. Robots will clean the houses. We won't use paper money.' Children tick 6 predictions in a table and say if they agree. Read twice.
lp.re: Will or won't? relay: teams race to complete sentences ('In 2050 we ___ walk to school') with will/won't and justify with a reason. Then a 'crystal ball' final round.
lp.prod: Future city presentation: each group presents its city with 6 predictions and one 'good' and one 'bad' change. Then write a note to yourself for the time capsule: 'Dear me, in 2037 you will be...'
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence text 'Life in 2050' and answer 5 questions. Then write 6 predictions and a short time capsule note. Fast finishers add maybe/probably and a reason.
lp.st: Song or video 'What are you going to do? Simple Future Tense' from Videos/Videos for Children/Grammar vids for kids/Tenses/Future Tense. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Predict a classmate's future with will.
Stand on a line for each prediction.
Complete sentences with will or won't.
Predict a partner's future with 3 sentences.
Ask classmates and graph the answers.
diff: Fast finishers: write a story of a day in 2050 (8 sentences) with will.
Support: prediction frames with will/won't in colour and picture prompts.
hw: Write 6 predictions about life in 2050.
Ask a family member what they think life will be like in 2050.
Write a note to yourself for the time capsule.
lp.tip: Will is easy to use for predictions: do not over-explain the difference with going to. Keep topics positive and fun. Starts of 'Next week I will...' can recycle weekend vocabulary.

weeks.theme: Writing workshop 1: a paragraph with linking words
weeks.obj: write a paragraph of 6 sentences with a topic sentence and linking words (and, but, because, so, first, then, finally); use capital letters and full stops correctly; check and improve my own paragraph
weeks.lang: topic sentence, detail, ending; and, but, because, so, first, then, finally; My favourite day is Friday because...; I like football but I don't like swimming.; capital letter, full stop, comma, question mark
weeks.res: Writing simple sentences (worksheet); Paragraph writing: from sentence to paragraph
weeks.act: Paragraph building: sentence cards into a paragraph, 'Fix the paragraph' and an own paragraph about my favourite day
weeks.hw: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about your favourite place, with a topic sentence and 3 linking words.

skills.L: Listen to a paragraph and order the sentences
skills.S: Explain my ideas for a paragraph to a partner
skills.R: Read a paragraph and find the linking words
skills.W: Write a 6-sentence paragraph with a topic sentence and linking words

lp.wu: Sentence stretch: the teacher says a short sentence ('I like football.') and children add 'and', 'but', 'because' to make it longer ('I like football because it is fun.'). Chain the answers.
wuAlt: Join the sentences: two short sentences become one
Punctuation mime: act capital letter, full stop, comma
lp.pres: Show a model paragraph on the board with the structure (topic sentence, 3 details, ending) coloured. Teach the linking words in three groups: adding (and), contrast (but), reason (because, so), order (first, then, finally). Show before/after: five short sentences vs one connected paragraph.
presAlt: Sort the linking words by function
Fix the paragraph: add linking words to a flat text
lp.prac: Paragraph building in pairs: sentence cards are mixed. Pairs order them to make a clear paragraph (topic, details, ending) and underline the linking words. Then they write a new paragraph from a picture prompt (a beach, a market) with 6 sentences and 3 linking words.
pracAlt: Planning: use a spider diagram to plan a paragraph
Peer check: swap paragraphs and tick a checklist (capital letters, full stops, linking words)
lp.ls: Teacher reads a paragraph aloud (no recording needed): 'My favourite day is Friday because I play football with my friends. First we go to the park. Then we have a picnic. I like it but I don't like going home!' Children number 6 sentence strips in order and circle the linking words. Read twice.
lp.re: Linking word race: teams run to fill in gaps with and, but, because, so, first, then; the first correct team keeps the card. Then a quick 'fix the full stops' game.
lp.prod: Write and share a paragraph: children write a 6-sentence paragraph about their favourite day, check with a checklist and read it aloud to a partner, who gives one compliment and one suggestion.
lp.rw: Read a model paragraph, underline the linking words and answer 4 questions. Then write your paragraph of 6 sentences and check it with the checklist. Fast finishers write a second paragraph about their worst day.
lp.st: Short poem or rhyme from Kids English resources (read and rhyme) read aloud together. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Make a short sentence longer with and, but, because.
Fill gaps with the correct linking word.
Swap paragraphs and tick a checklist.
Order sentence cards into a paragraph.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph of 8 sentences with at least 5 different linking words.
Support: paragraph frame with the linking words printed and a picture prompt.
hw: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about your favourite place with linking words.
Find 5 linking words in a text at home and underline them.
Read your paragraph to someone and ask for one suggestion.
lp.tip: Writing is a process: plan, draft, check. Give a short checklist (capital letters, full stops, linking words). Praise good ideas first. Eid is an optional overlay this week.

weeks.theme: Writing workshop 2: describing a place and writing an email

weeks.res: Giving directions (worksheets); Spot the difference sheets; Describe it (worksheet); Your neighbourhood (worksheet)

skills.L: Listen to a short email and tick true or false
skills.S: Describe a place and ask a pen-pal questions
skills.R: Read an email and answer 4 questions
skills.W: Write an email of 6 sentences with greeting and closing

lp.wu: Describe my street: children close their eyes and the teacher describes a known place ('There is a big tree. There are two cafes.') and the class guesses. Then pairs describe a place and the partner guesses.
wuAlt: Picture description: say 3 sentences about a picture
Adjective race: write 5 adjectives for a place in 30 seconds
lp.pres: Show a model email with parts (greeting, opening, body, closing, name) and a place description. Present phrases for starting and ending an email, and adjectives for places. Revise there is/there are and present simple. Show good and weak emails side by side for comparison.
presAlt: Parts of an email: label the parts on a model
Order the lines of an email
lp.prac: Write an email in pairs: each child writes an email to a pen-pal (partner) describing their neighbourhood in 6 sentences with 2 adjectives and one question. Swap and reply with a short answer (3 sentences). Use a checklist.
pracAlt: Information gap: partner has a different town map, ask and describe
Peer review: check an email for the 5 parts
lp.ls: Teacher reads an email aloud (no recording needed): 'Dear Sara, I live in a small town near the mountains. There is a big market and a beautiful park. Please write back. Best wishes, Amina.' Children tick true/false statements and underline the greeting and the closing. Read twice.
lp.re: Email jigsaw: teams put cut-up sentences of an email in order and read it aloud. Then 'spot the mistake' with capital letters and polite phrases.
lp.prod: Email exchange: children exchange emails with another group (on paper) and write a reply, then read the reply aloud. Display the best pairs on a 'post office' wall.
lp.rw: Read an email (7 lines) and answer 4 questions. Then write your email of 6 sentences to a pen-pal and check it. Fast finishers add a P.S. with a question.
lp.st: Song of choice from Music/Songs, then children write one 'thank you' line to a partner. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Guess the place from the teacher's description.
Label the five parts of a model email.
Order cut-up lines of an email.
Deliver and reply to an email on paper.
Write adjectives for a place in 30 seconds.
diff: Fast finishers: write a longer email (8 sentences) describing your best day.
Support: email frame with the five parts printed and a word bank.
hw: Write an email of 6 sentences to a pen-pal about your neighbourhood.
Read an email on a phone with a parent and say who wrote it.
Draw a map of your neighbourhood and label 5 places.
lp.tip: Real audience helps: children write to a partner class or a pen-pal if possible. Keep the format simple. Emails on paper are enough; no devices needed. Check privacy: no addresses or phone numbers in emails.

skills.L: Listen to the story and order 6 pictures

wuAlt: Story prediction: look at the cover and guess what happens

lp.pres: Tell the story twice with pictures and gestures (use the story pack text and the animated video). Introduce the story elements on a chart: characters, setting, problem, ending, moral. Teach key words and sequence words and ask comprehension questions in the past ('What did the boy do? Why did nobody come?').
presAlt: Story chart: fill in the 5 elements with the class
Picture sequence: order 6 pictures
lp.prac: Story elements in groups: each group completes a chart for the story (characters, setting, problem, ending, moral) and then retells it in 6 sentences using the sequence words. They swap and check each other's retellings. Then they prepare a mini play of the key scenes.
pracAlt: Hot seat: be the boy, the wolf or a villager and answer questions
Mini play: act the story with simple lines
lp.ls: Teacher tells the story aloud (use the Boy Who Cried Wolf story pack text or video from Comprehension/Fiction comprehension/Story packs): 8 short sentences. Children number 6 pictures in order and answer 5 true/false questions. Read once more with pauses.
lp.re: Story relay: teams order 8 sentence strips to make the story, read it aloud and add a connecting word from the board. Then 'what would you do?' quick-fire about trust and honesty.
lp.prod: Write a new ending or a modern version: groups write 4 sentences to change the story ('The boy told the truth...') and perform it. The class says what the moral is now.
lp.rw: Read the 8-sentence story and answer 5 questions (Who? Where? What happened? Why? What is the moral?). Then write a retelling of 6 sentences and a new ending. Fast finishers write the story from the wolf's point of view.
lp.st: Aesop's fables audio (track fables_01_03) from Audiobooks/Young readers/Aesop's fables. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Say which story is a lie and why.
Fill in characters, setting, problem, ending, moral.
Answer questions as a story character.
Order sentence strips to build the story.
Act the key scenes of the story.
diff: Fast finishers: write the story in a different setting (a village in Morocco) in 8 sentences.
Support: picture sequence with sentence strips and a past simple verb bank.
hw: Write a retelling of the story in 6 sentences and draw 3 pictures.
Tell the story to someone at home and ask them what the moral is.
Write a new ending in 4 sentences.
lp.tip: Story weeks are a break from grammar: let children enjoy performing. Use the 3-level comprehension sheets (Lower, Middle, Higher) to differentiate. Easter is an optional overlay; the story is the main lesson.

wuAlt: City names chant
Word map: write words for a city on the board

Sentence strips: build facts about a city

pracAlt: Tourist and guide role play: a visitor asks 'What is Fes famous for? What should I buy?'
Information gap: two partners have different city fact cards
lp.ls: Teacher reads aloud (no recording needed): 'Chefchaouen is a small town in the mountains. Many houses are blue. Visitors take photos in the narrow streets. You should walk in the old town.' Children match facts to pictures and tick true/false statements. Read twice.
lp.re: Where is it? quiz: the teacher says clues ('It's famous for blue houses. It's in the north.') and teams write the city; then a 'craft or food?' sort.
lp.prod: Present your guide page like a tour guide: 'Welcome to Fes. It is famous for leather. You should visit the medina.' The audience asks 2 questions and the group answers. Display the guide pages as a class Morocco guide.
lp.rw: Read a 7-sentence guide about Essaouira and answer 5 questions. Then write your own 6-sentence guide page. Fast finishers write a short list of 'Top 5 things to do' in Oujda.
lp.st: Video 'Cultures of the World' from Videos/Videos for Children/Countries/Culture, or a calm song from Music/Songs. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Guess the place from a picture and say what you see.
Name the city from the clues.
Role play asking and giving advice.
Sort Moroccan things into crafts, food and places.

Support: guide frame with pictures and sentence starters (___ is famous for ___).
hw: Write a 6-sentence guide to a place or tradition in Morocco.
Ask a grandparent about a tradition and write 3 sentences about it.
Draw a postcard of a Moroccan place with a caption.
lp.tip: Use the children's own knowledge and families as experts. Library resources on Morocco are limited, so rely on photos, children's stories and the Countries and cultures PPT. Avoid stereotypes: include modern and everyday life as well as tradition.

Safe or unsafe? sort picture cards

Ask an adult at home what they do to stay safe online.

skills.S: Present my favourite piece of work to a partner
skills.R: Read a short text and answer questions
skills.W: Write a self-assessment (3 sentences) and a portfolio page

lp.wu: Year in a minute: teams write on the board 10 words from different topics (space, sea, recipes, rules, technology...) in 60 seconds and use each in a sentence.
wuAlt: Chain story: each child adds a sentence from a topic
Review quiz with true/false cards
lp.pres: Introduce the carousel: 8 stations (Past simple, Superlatives and comparatives, Present simple vs continuous, Should/must/have to, Will and predictions, Reading and spelling, Recipes and maps, Writing). Show the portfolio page with 3 sections (my best work, what I learned, my goals).
presAlt: Review board game: roll a dice and answer a question from a topic
Topic bingo: cover topics based on a sentence
lp.prac: Carousel rotations (8 minutes each): each station has a game from a previous week (Alibi, Records quiz, Zoo spot the difference, Safety announcement, Crystal ball, Spelling bee). Teams collect a stamp per station.
pracAlt: Swap in any favourite from the game bank
Mixed review dominoes: match sentences with pictures
lp.ls: Listening station: the teacher reads 6 short items (no recording needed) across topics ('Yesterday I walked to the park.' 'Jupiter is the biggest planet.') and children tick pictures. Optional stretch: Cambridge Movers Test 2 audio from the Tests folder.
lp.re: Review games: 'Four corners' with topic names, 'Fast flash' with flashcards from weeks 2-28, and 'Hot seat' questions.
lp.prod: Portfolio: each child chooses 3 pieces from the year (a biography, a recipe, the magazine page), adds a self-assessment ('I can... I need to improve...') and presents one piece to a partner.
lp.rw: Read a model self-assessment and portfolio page and answer 4 questions. Then write 3 sentences of self-assessment and a title for each piece. Fast finishers add a goal for next year.
lp.st: Review song of choice from Music/Songs. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Add a sentence from a topic in turn.
Roll and answer a topic question.
Move to the topic corner and say a sentence.
Answer questions as a famous character.
diff: Fast finishers: write a longer self-assessment (6 sentences) and a goal for next year.
Support: portfolio frames with pre-printed sentence starters and a picture word bank.
hw: Finish your portfolio and choose your favourite piece.
Practise the week 30 questions with a family member.
Make a poster of 10 new words you know.
lp.tip: Tick the observation checklist for weeks 29 and 30 during the carousel; pre-fill it before Week 30. A portfolio makes progress visible to children and parents. Earth Day is an optional overlay this week.

kit.l: Cambridge Global English 4 Learner's Book (Review units 1-5 (review pages))
YouTube Happy Music Pack - Upbeat Instrumental Background Music for Vi

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April): optional 10-minute recycling sort and instructions game ('We must put the bottle in the blue bin. We mustn't waste paper.'); plant a seed with 'First... Then...'.
occ.hw: Optional: find 3 things at home to recycle and name them in English.

weeks.obj: show everything I can do in a game-based final assessment in Movers style and a short quiz; celebrate the year with my portfolio
weeks.lang: all year outcomes: present simple and frequency; was/were and past simple; superlatives; present simple vs continuous; should/must; will; paragraphs, emails and recipes; CLIL topics
weeks.res: Classic childhood games; Tests: general tests (Cambridge Movers Test 2); Question games; Mover Speaking 5 (PPT); Mover Speaking 6 (PPT)
weeks.act: Assessment carousel with 6 stations (speaking, listening, reading, writing, spelling, game), then a celebration and certificate ceremony
weeks.hw: Show your portfolio and certificate to your family and tell them 5 things you can say in English.

skills.L: Listen-and-tick final quiz in Movers style (teacher reads, no recording needed)
skills.S: Picture talk and a one-minute talk about my year
skills.R: Read a short text and answer 5 questions
skills.W: Guided writing: a paragraph of 6 sentences

lp.wu: Quick-fire warm-up: 'Stand up if...' statements across topics, then a team sprint to write 10 words in 60 seconds.
wuAlt: Pass the ball with question cards
Whisper chain with a sentence from the year
lp.pres: Explain the stations: 6 games, a stamp for each, and the teacher with the checklist. Remind them of the sentence frames on the wall and the Movers-style tasks (listen and tick, read and complete, picture talk).
presAlt: Olympics framing: teams, medals and a closing parade
Spin and play: the spinner chooses the game
lp.prac: Station 1 Speaking: a Movers-style picture talk (6 sentences) and answering 5 questions (What did you do last weekend? What will you do tomorrow?). The teacher records accuracy and range.
pracAlt: Pair interview: ask each other about last weekend, routines and plans
Role play: interview a famous person
lp.ls: Station 2 Listening: the teacher reads 6 items (no recording needed): 'Yesterday I visited my grandma.' 'Jupiter is the biggest planet.' 'You mustn't run.' Children tick pictures and number items. Optional stretch: Cambridge Movers Test 2 audio from the Tests folder.
lp.re: Station 3 Spelling and reading: dictate 8 words (-ed, -ing, plurals) and read a short text with skim and scan questions. The teacher records accuracy.
lp.prod: Station 4 Presentation: present a portfolio piece in 5 sentences and answer 2 questions from a partner. Then the celebration: show portfolios on a gallery walk.
lp.rw: Station 5 Reading and Station 6 Writing: read a 7-sentence text and answer 5 questions, then write a 6-sentence paragraph about last year or my plans. Fast finishers write a letter to next year's class (4 sentences).
lp.st: Closing ceremony: certificates, a class photo and the 'You are English speakers' cheer. Preview the next level. Goodbye: exit ticket, each child says one sentence about today's lesson at the door.
g: Six game-style stations with a checklist.
Walk around the portfolios and name 5 pieces.
The spinner chooses the next review game.
diff: All: the checklist records each child at their own level; no one fails a game.
Second adult if available: one runs stations while you observe and tick.
hw: Show your portfolio and certificate to your family.
Tell your family 5 things you can say in English.
Plan one English activity for the summer (read, song, game).
lp.tip: End on identity: 'You are confident English users.' Send the final report cards and hand out the certificates at the ceremony. Labour Day is an optional overlay; do not replace the assessment.
checklist: Talks about routines, last weekend and plans with correct tenses
Uses was/were and the past simple (regular and irregular)
Compares and uses superlatives
Gives rules and advice with must/should/have to
Reads short texts and finds the main idea and details
Writes a 6-sentence paragraph with linking words
Spells common words and verb endings correctly

occ.hw: Optional: draw a worker you know and write 'He works in...'.

levels.desc: For children aged 9-11 who write full sentences. The year moves from A1+ to A2: past simple, superlatives, present simple and continuous, must, should and will. Children write paragraphs and emails, meet CLIL topics and practise Movers-style tasks.

levels.label: Teens · Beginners

weeks.theme: Welcome and getting to know you
weeks.obj: introduce themselves, spell their name, count to 20, ask 5 get-to-know-you questions and complete a partner profile
weeks.lang: be (am/is/are); Wh- questions (what, where, how old); my/your/his/her; alphabet and spelling; numbers 0-20
weeks.res: Games/Downloadable games (icebreakers); Worksheets
weeks.act: Human bingo; name toss with questions; partner profile poster; class rules negotiation
weeks.hw: write a 5-sentence profile of your partner

skills.L: Listen to partner profiles and complete the grid
skills.S: Ask and answer 5 get-to-know-you questions
skills.R: Read sample profiles and underline the question words (Worksheets)
skills.W: Complete a partner-profile card in full sentences

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students walk around with a bingo grid containing prompts like 'likes football', 'has a brother', 'lives near school'. They ask 'Do you like football?' and mark 'BINGO' when they find someone who says 'Yes, I do'.
wuAlt: Name Toss: Students stand in a circle and toss a soft ball, saying their name and one hobby, e.g., 'I'm Ali and I like football'.
Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about themselves, two true and one false, and others guess the lie.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'be' verbs with flashcards showing people with names, ages, and hometowns. Model sentences: 'I am 14', 'She is from Oujda', 'They are students'. Check understanding by asking 'How old are you?' and 'Where are you from?' to students. Then teach my/your/his/her with the same flashcards ('my name', 'her name') and the alphabet chant so students can spell their names.
presAlt: Realia Introduction: Teacher shows personal items (a book, a photo, a key) and says 'This is my book. I am a teacher. It is blue'.
Animated GIFs: Display GIFs of teens with captions like 'He is 13', 'They are friends' to illustrate 'be' + adjectives.
lp.prac: Pair drill: students practise 'What's your name? How do you spell it? How old are you? Where are you from?' with a partner. The teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation. Then they play 'Find Someone Who...' with a worksheet where students write names next to prompts like 'is 13', 'is from Oujda', 'has a brother'.
pracAlt: Question Chain: Students sit in a circle and take turns asking the person next to them a question, e.g., 'What's your name?', and that person answers and asks the next student.
Flashcard Match: Match name cards with age/hometown cards, e.g., 'Lina' + 'is 14' + 'is from Berkane'.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short profiles of Moroccan teens aloud. Students listen and fill in a grid with names, ages, and hometowns. Check answers as a class, e.g., 'Is Amina 13 or 14?'
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: teacher says a sentence like 'If you are 13, stand up' or 'If you are from Oujda, sit down'. Students move quickly to practise 'be'.
lp.prod: Partner Profile Poster: Students work in pairs to create a poster with their partner's name, age, hometown, and hobbies. They use full sentences like 'He is 14', 'She is from Oujda', 'His hobby is football'. Present posters to the class.
lp.rw: Read three sample profiles and underline the question words (What, Where, How old). Then, write 3 questions about a new profile using the underlined words, e.g., 'What's his name?', 'Where is she from?'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write your name and spell it aloud to the teacher at the door, then say one fact about your partner ("He is 14. He is from Nador.").
g: Students ask 'Do you like football?' to fill their grid.
Students toss a ball and say name + hobby.
Students write names next to prompts like 'is 13'.
Students move based on 'be' + adjective sentences.
Students ask and answer questions in a circle.
diff: Fast finishers: Add a hobby and a favorite color to their partner's profile.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'He is ___', 'She lives in ___' on the worksheet.
hw: Write a 5-sentence profile of your partner.
Draw a picture of your partner and label 3 things (e.g., 'football', 'book').
Record a 30-second video introducing your partner.
lp.tip: Use local references (e.g., 'Are you from Oujda?') to make the language relevant. Pair stronger and weaker learners to boost confidence.

weeks.obj: describe 4 family members or friends with simple details
weeks.lang: possessive 's; have got; adjectives (tall, kind, funny)
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Family; Flashcards/Family
weeks.act: Family tree project; guess who descriptions; adjective matching relay
weeks.hw: family tree + 3 description sentences

skills.L: Listen to family descriptions and identify who is who
skills.S: Describe 4 family members with have got + adjectives
skills.R: Read short family profiles and match the details (Lesson Plans/Family)
skills.W: Write 3 sentences about my family or friend

lp.wu: Family Charades: Teacher acts out a family member (e.g., cooking, playing football) and students shout the word in English. Students then take turns in pairs acting out a family member while their partner guesses.
wuAlt: Family Bingo: Teacher calls out family words (mother, father, sister, brother) and students cross them off their bingo cards. First to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Family Chain: Students sit in a circle. Student 1 says 'I have a mother.' Student 2 says 'Student 1 has a mother. I have a father.' and so on, building a chain.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of family members (mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, cousin). Model: 'This is my mother. Her name is Amina. She is kind.' Then possessive 's with names: 'Karim is Amina's brother.' Model have got: 'I've got one brother and two sisters. He's got a car.' Check understanding: 'Whose brother is Karim?' 'Has Karim got a car?'
presAlt: Family Photo Story: Teacher brings a real photo of her family and tells a short story using the target language: 'This is my sister. She is tall and funny. She has got a dog.' Students ask questions.
Photo pairs: students bring or draw a family photo and describe two people to a partner ('This is my cousin. He is tall. He has got a bike.').
lp.prac: Adjective Matching Relay: Students line up in two teams. At the front, there are two sets of cards: family member pictures and adjective cards (tall, kind, funny). The first student runs to match a family member with an adjective (e.g., 'My father is tall.'), runs back, and tags the next student. The first team to match all cards wins.
pracAlt: Find Your Partner: Each student gets a card with either a family member or an adjective. They walk around asking 'Who has got...?' or 'What are you?' to find their match and form a complete sentence.
Sentence Building Race: In pairs, students get jumbled sentence cards (e.g., 'my / brother / is / funny'). They race to arrange them correctly and read the sentence aloud.
lp.ls: Listen and Draw: Teacher describes a family member: 'This is my sister. She is tall. She has got long hair. She is kind.' Students draw the person. Teacher then shows a picture to check. This checks comprehension of listening for details. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher says 'Stand up if you have got a brother.' 'Stand up if your mother is kind.' Students stand up or sit down.
lp.prod: Guess Who?: In pairs, Student A thinks of a family member. Student B asks questions: 'Is he tall? Is she funny? Has he got a car?' Student A answers: 'Yes, he is. No, she isn't. Yes, he has.' Student B guesses who it is. This encourages freer use of the language.
lp.rw: Read and Match: Students read 3 short family profiles (e.g., 'My name is Amina. I have a brother. His name is Karim. He is tall and funny.'). They match each profile to a picture. Then, they write 3 sentences about their own family using 'have got' and adjectives.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about a family member with has got or an adjective ("My sister has got long hair.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students act out a family member (e.g., cooking, playing football) and their partner guesses the word.
Teams race to match family member pictures with adjective cards to make sentences.
Students with family member and adjective cards find their match to form a sentence.
Students ask yes/no questions to guess which family member their partner is thinking of.
Teacher gives clues about family members and students stand up if it applies to them.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a description of a famous Moroccan celebrity or athlete.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My _______ is _______ and _______. He/She has got _______.'
hw: Draw your family tree and write 3 sentences: 'My _______ is _______. He/She has got _______. He/She is _______.'
Interview a family member in Arabic and write 3 simple facts in English about them.
Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) about your best friend using 'have got' and adjectives.
lp.tip: Use realia like family photos to make the lesson personal and relatable. For Moroccan learners, connect the theme to local family values, like respect for elders, which are universal but can be highlighted in English.

weeks.obj: describe their school day using present simple I/you/we/they
weeks.lang: present simple; time expressions (at 7 o'clock, in the morning)
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Time; Flashcards/Daily Routine
weeks.act: Routine survey mingle; daily timeline drawing; verb drill tennis
weeks.hw: write your real school day in 6 sentences

skills.L: Listen to a student's day and order the events
skills.S: Describe my school day with present simple + time
skills.R: Read a routine text and find the time expressions
skills.W: Write my daily routine paragraph (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Routine Charades: Teacher mimes waking up, eating breakfast, going to school. Students shout the verbs (wake up, eat, go). Teacher writes them on the board.
wuAlt: Verb Tennis: Teacher says 'wake up', student says 'eat breakfast', teacher says 'go to school', student says 'study English'.
Quick Survey: Teacher asks 'What time do you wake up?' to 3 students, writes answers on the board.
lp.pres: Teacher shows flashcards of a school day (7:00 wake up, 8:00 go to school, 10:00 have a break, 1:00 eat lunch, 4:00 go home). Models 'I wake up at 7 o'clock' and 'You wake up at 7 o'clock'. Checks understanding by asking 'What time do you wake up?' to a student. Teach o'clock and half past (7:30) with a clock face.
presAlt: Storytime: Teacher tells a simple story about 'Ali's School Day' using the flashcards and gestures.
Realia: Teacher shows a real alarm clock and says 'I wake up at 7 o'clock'.
lp.prac: Verb Drill Tennis: Students stand in two lines. Teacher says 'I wake up at...', student in the other line says 'You wake up at...'. Continue with 'go to school', 'have a break', 'eat lunch', 'go home'.
pracAlt: Routine Survey Mingle: Students walk around asking 'What time do you...?' for 3 routines, write answers on a grid.
Daily Timeline Drawing: Students draw a timeline of their school day and label times with 'at...'.
lp.ls: Listen and Order: Teacher reads a short script about 'Leila's School Day' (e.g., 'I wake up at 7. I go to school at 8. I have a break at 10. I eat lunch at 1. I go home at 4.'). Students cut and paste 5 picture cards in the correct order.
lp.re: Routine Relay: Two lines of students. Teacher says a routine (e.g., 'wake up'), first student runs to the board, writes the verb, runs back. Next student does the next one. Fastest team wins.
lp.prod: My School Day Presentation: Students work in pairs. They draw 4 pictures of their school day and write a sentence for each (e.g., 'I wake up at 7 o'clock. I go to school at 8 o'clock. I eat lunch at 1 o'clock. I go home at 4 o'clock.'). They present to the class.
lp.rw: Read and Find: students read a short text 'My Day' written in the first person ('I wake up at 7 o'clock. I go to school at 8 o'clock. I have a break at 10 o'clock. I eat lunch at 1 o'clock. I go home at 4 o'clock.'). They underline all the time expressions (at 7 o'clock, etc.).
lp.st: Exit ticket: say your wake-up time to the teacher at the door ("I wake up at 7 o'clock.") or write it on a slip.
g: Students volley present simple sentences back and forth in pairs.
Students ask 'What time do you...?' to classmates and write answers.
Students draw a timeline of their school day with time expressions.
Students listen to a script and order picture cards of a daily routine.
Teams race to write present simple verbs on the board.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about their ideal school day.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'I ______ at ______ o'clock.' for 4 routines.
hw: Write your real school day in 6 sentences (e.g., 'I wake up at 6:30. I eat breakfast at 7:00. I go to school at 7:30. I have a break at 10:00. I eat lunch at 1:00. I go home at 4:00.')
Draw a picture of your school day and label 3 activities with time expressions.
Ask a family member about their daily routine and write 3 sentences about it.
lp.tip: Use gestures for all verbs to support visual and kinesthetic learners. For the American Space Oujda context, connect the topic to local school schedules (e.g., 'In Morocco, we have a long lunch break at 1 o'clock').

weeks.obj: talk about school subjects and timetables using present simple he/she/it, and say what they like
weeks.lang: school subjects; days of the week; present simple he/she/it (-s, -es); does/doesn't; like/don't like + noun; bonus: because
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Worksheets/Print outs
weeks.act: Timetable swap pairs; Does he/she...? question game; subject popularity graph; reading about a student's school week
weeks.hw: write 5 sentences about your best friend's school day

skills.L: Listen to a student describe a school week and complete the timetable
skills.S: Ask and answer about school days with Do you...? and Does he/she...?
skills.R: Read a short text about a student's school week and answer questions
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about a friend's school day (he/she + -s)

lp.wu: Wake-up line: without speaking, students line up by the time they wake up (7:00 to 9:00). They then check the order by asking "What time do you wake up?" and answering "I wake up at 7:30." This recycles Week 3.
wuAlt: Mime and guess: students mime a school activity (read, write, draw, run, sing) and the class says "You read!"
Pair quiz: students ask each other three "What time do you...?" questions and report one answer to the class.
lp.pres: Show a school timetable on the board (Monday: Math, English, Art; Tuesday: Science, PE, English...). Teach the school subjects with picture cards and the days of the week. Model present simple with a named student: "Sara studies Math on Monday. She likes Art because it is fun. She doesn't like Science." Mark the -s / -es endings in colour (studies, watches, goes). Check understanding: "Does Sara study Math on Monday? Yes, she does. Does she like Science? No, she doesn't."
presAlt: Use a real timetable from a Moroccan school and ask "What does Karim study on Tuesday?"
Put a short text about a teacher's day on the board with the he/she verbs underlined; students find the -s forms.
lp.prac: Timetable swap: Student A and Student B each hold half of a student's timetable with different gaps. They ask "What does Sara study on Monday?" and "Does she study Art on Tuesday?" to complete the grid. The teacher monitors the -s ending and does/doesn't.
pracAlt: Add-the-s race: teams add -s/-es to ten verbs on cards (go, watch, study, play, do, have) and say a sentence with each.
Find someone who likes Art / hates PE... then report: "Amina likes Art."
lp.ls: Teacher reads this text twice: "Yassine goes to school from Monday to Friday. On Monday he has Math and English. On Tuesday he has Art and PE. He likes PE because it is fun. He doesn't like Math because it is difficult." Students complete Yassine's timetable and tick or cross his likes. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Subject jump: the teacher calls a subject; students step forward if they like it and step back if they don't, then tell a neighbour "I like Art because it is fun." Round two: they report about the neighbour: "She likes Art."
lp.prod: Interview and report: in pairs, students ask "What is your favourite subject? Why? What do you study on Monday?" and note the answers. They then form new pairs and report: "Fatima studies Science on Monday. She likes Art." Fast finishers add because.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a student's school week (6 to 8 lines) and answer four questions in full sentences ("What does he study on Monday?"). Then write five sentences about a friend's school day using he/she + -s.
lp.st: Exit ticket: on a slip, write one sentence about a classmate's favourite subject ("Omar likes Science because it is interesting.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students fill a grid with subjects; the teacher says "She studies Art on Monday" and they cross out the matching box.
Describe a subject without saying its name or the three taboo words.
Teams add -s/-es to verbs on cards and say a sentence; one point per correct sentence.
Subjects in the four corners; students go to their favourite and say why.
One student describes a day ("He studies Art and PE") and the others guess which timetable column it is.
diff: Fast finishers: write about a teacher's day (6 sentences with he/she).
Support: sentence frame "He/She studies ___ on ___. He/She likes ___ because it is ___." and a verb list with the -s forms.
hw: Write 5 sentences about your best friend's school day (he/she + -s).
Make your own weekly timetable in English and add one reason for your favourite subject.
Ask a family member about their school days and write 2 sentences.
lp.tip: Present simple he/she is the main grammar hurdle of the term: say the -s slowly, mark it in colour, and correct it gently every time. Pair strong and weaker students for the timetable swap.

weeks.obj: talk about hobbies with like/love/hate + -ing and adverbs of frequency, and ask Do you...? questions
weeks.lang: like/love/hate + -ing; always, usually, sometimes, never; Do you...? and short answers; bonus: Does he/she...?
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Games/Game ideas
weeks.act: Find someone who... mingle; hobby poster pairs; frequency line-up game
weeks.hw: write 5 sentences about your free time

skills.L: Listen to teens describing their free time and tick the hobbies and adverbs
skills.S: Ask and answer Do you...? / Does he...? about hobbies
skills.R: Read short hobby profiles and match them to pictures
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about my free time with like/love/hate + -ing and an adverb

lp.wu: Hobby charades: students draw a hobby card (play football, read, cook, draw, listen to music, watch TV, play video games, swim) and mime it. The class guesses "You play football!" and then describes the mimer: "She plays football." (recycles Week 4).
wuAlt: Hobby line-up: students stand in a line by how many hobbies they have, checking with "How many hobbies have you got?"
Pair talk: two minutes to find three things you both do after school.
lp.pres: Show hobby flashcards. Model: "I like playing football. I love listening to music. I don't like cooking. I hate getting up early." Draw a scale on the board with faces (love, like, don't like, hate). Then add adverbs on a line: always, usually, sometimes, never. Model: "I always play football on Fridays. I never watch TV in the morning." Teach the questions: "Do you like swimming? Yes, I do. / No, I don't." and "Does he play video games? Yes, he does." Check with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Teacher shares a real weekly hobby diary and students tick which sentences are true for them.
Show a short video clip of teens doing hobbies and elicit sentences with like + -ing.
lp.prac: Find someone who...: students mingle with a grid ("likes swimming", "never watches TV", "always reads at night", "plays video games on Sunday"). They ask "Do you like swimming?" or "Do you always read at night?" and write the name when the answer is yes. The teacher monitors -ing after like and the short answers.
pracAlt: Hobby survey in groups of four: tally the class's favourite hobbies on the board.
Sentence dice: roll two dice (hobby and adverb) and make a sentence.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short descriptions twice (for example: "My name is Salma. I love drawing. I usually draw after school. I never play football."). Students tick the hobbies and circle the adverbs on a grid. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Frequency line-up: four cards (always, usually, sometimes, never) are displayed on the wall. The teacher reads a hobby ("watch TV") and students stand under the card that is true for them and tell the person next to them: "I usually watch TV."
lp.prod: Hobby poster pairs: students interview each other ("Do you like...? Do you usually...? What do you love doing?") and make a poster "All about ___'s free time" with five sentences using like/love/hate + -ing and an adverb ("Amina loves drawing. She usually draws after school."). Pairs present the poster to another pair.
lp.rw: Read three short hobby profiles ("I am Amina. I love reading. I never play sports.") and match each to a picture. Then write five sentences about your own free time using like/love/hate + -ing and an adverb.
lp.st: Exit ticket: on a slip, write two true sentences about your free time (one with love or hate + -ing, one with an adverb) and give it to the teacher at the door.
g: Students fill a grid with hobbies; the teacher mimes or describes and they cross out the match.
Mingle and ask Do you...? questions to complete a grid of names.
Stand under always, usually, sometimes or never for each hobby and say a sentence.
One student mimes a hobby; the next says "She plays football" and mimes a new one.
A student sits with a hobby card behind them; the class gives clues until they guess it.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph about a family member's free time (he/she + -s) with three adverbs.
Support: sentence frame "I like ___ing. I usually ___ on ___." and a word bank with the -ing forms.
hw: Write 5 sentences about your free time (like/love/hate + -ing, with one adverb).
Ask someone at home "Do you like...?" three times and write their answers.
Make a hobby survey of 5 friends (name + hobby) and be ready to report.
lp.tip: Insist on -ing after like/love/hate and on the short answers (Yes, I do / No, I don't) from the start. Keep the love-hate scale and the frequency line on the wall for the next few weeks.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute reading in the present simple: "Every year Moroccans celebrate the Green March on 6 November. People hang flags and families watch the speech." Students underline the verbs and tell a partner what their family does that day.
occ.hw: Write 3 sentences about what your family does on a national day.

weeks.obj: say what they can and can't do; hold a short can-can't interview
weeks.lang: can/can't for ability; adverbs (well, fast)
weeks.res: Worksheets/'Can / Can't'; Lesson Plans/Sports
weeks.act: Class olympics quiz; talent show circle; can-can't guessing game with teams
weeks.hw: Interview a family member: 'Can you cook? Can you drive?' Write 3 sentences.

skills.L: Listen to can/can't mini-interviews
skills.S: Hold a can-can't interview with a partner
skills.R: Read ability profiles and complete the grid (Worksheets)
skills.W: Write 3 can / can't sentences about me

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Stand if You Can' game. Teacher calls out sports (e.g., 'Run!'), students stand if they can do it. Teacher models: 'I can run.' Students repeat. Teacher calls 'Swim!', students sit if they can't. Teacher models: 'I can't swim.'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Simon Says' with can/cant commands (e.g., 'Simon says: You can jump!')
Alternative 2: Quick survey: 'Ask 3 classmates: Can you play football?'. Tally results on board.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of sports (football, swim, run). Teacher models: 'I can play football.' Point to self. Then shows a sport they can't do (e.g., ice skate). Models: 'I can't ice skate.' Students repeat sentences chorally. Check: 'Can I play football?' (Yes!) 'Can I ice skate?' (No!)
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a story about a character who can/can't do sports. Draw stick figures on board.
Alternative 2: Bring in a real football. Teacher demonstrates 'I can kick the ball.' Then tries to juggle and says 'I can't juggle.'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Can-Can't Relay' in teams. Teams race to write sentences on board: 'I can swim.' 'I can't play tennis.' Teacher monitors for accuracy. Support: Give sentence starters on board.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Matching Pairs' worksheet. Match sports to can/cant sentences.
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill'. Student 1: 'I can run.' Student 2: 'He can run. I can swim.'
lp.ls: Listening slot: Students listen to 3 short interviews (audio recording) about sports. They complete a grid: 'Name / Can do / Can't do'. Check answers as class.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Freeze Dance'. Play music, students dance. When music stops, teacher calls: 'Freeze! Can you jump?' Students jump if they can. If not, freeze.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Talent Show Circle'. Students stand in a circle. Each student says: 'My name is [name]. I can [skill]. I can't [skill].' (e.g., 'I can sing. I can't dance.')
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read 3 short ability profiles (e.g., 'Fatima: She can cook. She can't swim.'). They complete a grid with names and skills. Then write 3 sentences about themselves: 'I can... I can't...'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you can do and one thing you can't do and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams answer quiz questions: 'Who can swim? A) Ali B) Sara'
One student acts a sport, others guess: 'Can you play football?'
Student mimes a sport, others guess: 'Can you run?'
Students walk around asking: 'Can you play basketball?' and write names
Students write 9 abilities in grid. Teacher calls: 'Can you swim?' Students mark if they can.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 can/cant sentences about a famous athlete.
Support: Use picture prompts for writing sentences (e.g., a picture of a football for 'I can play football.')
hw: Interview a family member: 'Can you cook? Can you drive?' Write 3 sentences.
Draw 3 things you can do and 3 you can't. Label them in English.
Complete the worksheet: 'My Sports Skills'.
lp.tip: Use local sports like football and athletics to make it relevant. Encourage peer correction gently during the talent show to build confidence. Plan a short written check for next week.

weeks.obj: say and write the date, use months and ordinal numbers, and say when festivals and birthdays are
weeks.lang: months; ordinal numbers (1st to 31st); What is the date? / When is...? It's on the...; in/on with months and dates
weeks.res: Worksheets (dates and months); Games (calendar and ordinal games); festival pictures
weeks.act: Birthday line-up; festivals calendar poster; When is...? pair quiz
weeks.hw: write the dates of 5 festivals or birthdays in your family

skills.L: Listen to dates in a short dialogue and write them in numbers
skills.S: Ask and answer When is your birthday? and When is...?
skills.R: Read a short text about festivals and underline the dates
skills.W: Write the date and 4 sentences about important dates

lp.wu: Birthday line-up: without speaking, students line up in order of their birthdays (January to December). They then check by asking "When is your birthday?" and answering "It's on the 5th of March." This recycles numbers and be.
wuAlt: Number bingo 1 to 31: the teacher calls numbers and students mark them.
Alphabet race: teams spell a name or month on the board, letter by letter.
lp.pres: Teach the months with a calendar poster and repeat chorally, marking the stress (Jan-u-ary, Feb-ru-ary). Teach ordinal numbers: 1st, 2nd, 3rd are irregular, then 4th to 31st with -th. Model the date: "Today is Monday, the 16th of November. My birthday is on the 3rd of May." Show festival cards: "Independence Day is on the 18th of November. Halloween is on the 31st of October. Valentine's Day is on the 14th of February." Check understanding: "When is Independence Day? Is Halloween in November?"
presAlt: Class calendar on the wall: students stick a birthday star on the right date and read it aloud.
Photo quiz: show festival pictures and students say the month.
lp.prac: Date dictation in pairs: A reads six dates ("the 5th of March") and B writes them in numbers (5/3); then swap. Then a When is...? chain with fact cards: Throne Day 30 July, New Year 1 January, Labour Day 1 May, Green March 6 November, Independence Day 18 November, Earth Day 22 April.
pracAlt: Ordinal number steps: students step on numbered floor cards and say the ordinal.
Month memory game: pairs match month names to the season picture.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short dialogue twice: "When is your birthday?" "It's on the 12th of June." "And your brother?" "On the 30th of September." Students write the dates they hear on a form with four names. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Month relay: teams race to write the months in order on the board; then the teacher calls a month and one student from each team writes a festival or birthday that happens in it.
lp.prod: Class festivals calendar: groups get a blank 12-month calendar and a set of fact cards. They place each festival or birthday on the correct date and write one sentence for each ("Independence Day is on the 18th of November."). Groups present the calendar and quiz another group: "When is...?"
lp.rw: Read a short text "Festivals in Morocco" (six sentences with dates: Throne Day 30 July, Green March 6 November, Independence Day 18 November, New Year 1 January). Underline the dates, then write four sentences about important dates in your own family.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the date of your birthday and one festival in words (for example "the 3rd of May") and hand it in at the door.
g: Line up in birthday order without speaking, then check with When is your birthday?
Bingo with dates written in numbers and words.
Pairs dictate dates to each other and race to write them correctly.
Teams answer festival date questions from fact cards; one point per correct sentence.
Match each festival picture to its date and month.
diff: Fast finishers: add the weekday of each date for this year.
Support: months word wall with first letters and an ordinal number chart from 1st to 31st.
hw: Write the dates of 5 festivals or birthdays in your family.
Ask a family member "When is your birthday?" and write the date in words.
Make a mini calendar of this month with 3 important dates.
lp.tip: Ordinals and month spelling need repeated recycling: keep the class calendar on the wall for the rest of the year and ask students to write the date at the top of every page.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute timeline: students put national days (6 Nov, 18 Nov) on a class calendar and say "Independence Day is on the 18th of November." Halloween (31 Oct) has passed: use it as an example of a festival date.
occ.hw: Write one sentence: "My favourite festival is ___. It is in/on ___."
