weeks.obj: name common foods and drinks, use some/any and ask How much/How many
weeks.lang: countable/uncountable nouns; a/an and plurals; some/any; How much...? How many...?; Moroccan dishes
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Food; Flashcards/Food
weeks.act: Food categories team race; shopping list relay; Kim's game; some/any pair dialogue
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about what you eat and drink on a normal day

skills.L: Listen to a dialogue about cooking and circle some/any and the quantities
skills.S: Ask and answer How much...? and How many...? about food
skills.R: Read a short text about breakfast and sort countable and uncountable nouns
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about what I eat and drink using some/any

lp.wu: Food categories race: teams take turns running to the board to write one food word per column (fruit, vegetables, drinks, other). The fastest team with correct spelling wins.
wuAlt: Alphabet food chain: each student says a food that starts with the next letter of the alphabet.
Food mime: students mime eating or drinking something and the class guesses.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of Moroccan and international foods (tagine, couscous, harira, bread, olives, chicken, eggs, tomatoes, potatoes, apples, milk, mint tea, water, rice). Sort them into two hoops: countable (an egg, two eggs) and uncountable (rice, milk, bread, water). Teach a/an and the plural endings (tomatoes, potatoes). Model: "I've got some rice. I haven't got any eggs. Have you got any milk?" and the questions "How many eggs? How much milk?" Check understanding: "Is bread countable?" (thumbs up or down).
presAlt: Use real items (bread, an apple, a glass of water) to show countable and uncountable.
Show a picture of a fridge and elicit what it has and has not got.
lp.prac: Shopping list relay: teams get a list with gaps ("___ eggs", "___ milk", "___ olives"). A runner writes some or any and the food in a sentence ("We haven't got any eggs."), then the next runner continues. The teacher monitors some/any and countable/uncountable errors.
pracAlt: Pair dialogue: A has a fridge picture and B asks "Have you got any...?" to find what is inside.
Container match: students match foods to containers (a bottle of, a kilo of, a glass of).
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short dialogue twice (two friends making a tagine): "Have we got any potatoes?" "Yes, we've got some. How many do we need?" "Three. And we've got some rice." "How much rice?" "A kilo." Students circle some or any and write the quantities they hear. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Kim's game: the teacher shows ten food flashcards for 20 seconds and hides them. Teams write what they remember and make sentences ("We've got some rice. We haven't got any eggs.").
lp.prod: Moroccan meal survey: pairs interview three classmates ("What do you eat for breakfast? How many eggs do you eat? How much tea do you drink?"), record the answers in a table and report: "Karim eats two eggs and drinks some milk."
lp.rw: Read a short text "A typical Moroccan breakfast" (six sentences) and underline the countable nouns in one colour and the uncountable nouns in another. Then write five sentences about what you eat and drink on a normal day using some/any.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one countable and one uncountable food you have at home, then write one question with How many or How much and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams run to the board to write food words in the right column.
Remember the foods on the flashcards after 20 seconds and say what is there.
Fill in some/any and the food in a sentence, one runner at a time.
Describe a dish with "It's got some... It hasn't got any..." and the class guesses.
Quick fire: the teacher says a food and students call out "countable" or "uncountable".
diff: Fast finishers: write a recipe list for a dish with quantities (a kilo of, a glass of).
Support: word bank with food words in two columns (countable / uncountable) and a some/any sentence frame.
hw: Write 6 sentences about what you eat and drink on a normal day (use some/any).
Make a shopping list for a family meal with quantities.
Ask a family member "What do you eat for breakfast?" and write 2 sentences.
lp.tip: Teach some/any through real or pictured containers (full and empty) so the idea is concrete. Use Moroccan dishes first, then compare with other cuisines. Check for food allergies if you bring real food.

occ.act: Thanksgiving (26 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute comparison: a Thanksgiving meal (turkey, potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie) and a Moroccan family meal. Students count the countable and uncountable foods in each.
occ.hw: Ask one person at home what they are thankful for and write it in one sentence.

weeks.obj: order food and drink politely in a roleplay
weeks.lang: Would you like...? I'd like...; Can I have...?
weeks.res: Listening (graded cafe dialogues mp3); Lesson Plans/Food
weeks.act: Cafe roleplay with menus made in class; waiter rotation; dialogue listening gap-fill
weeks.hw: write your ideal menu

skills.L: Listening folder: cafe dialogues - order and confirm
skills.S: Cafe roleplay: order, ask and pay politely
skills.R: Read a cafe menu and match dishes to sections
skills.W: Write my own cafe dialogue (6 lines)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who...' with food/drinks cards. Students mingle, ask 'Do you like...?' and collect signatures. Teacher models: 'Do you like tea? Yes, I do / No, I don't.'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Flashcard Race' - two teams race to match food/drink pictures to words on the board.
Alternative 2: 'I Spy' - teacher says 'I spy something sweet' and students guess 'Is it cake?'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a cafe menu flashcard. Model dialogue: 'Would you like coffee?' 'No, thanks. I'd like tea, please.' 'Can I have a sandwich?' 'Certainly.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Would you like cake?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a story about a boy at a cafe, acting out the key phrases.
Alternative 2: Realia - hold up a cup, ask 'Would you like a cup of tea?'
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Menu Match' - pairs match food/drink pictures to words. Then 'Dialogue Drill' - students repeat after teacher, then practice in pairs. Support: sentence frames on the board.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Order Relay' - teams take turns saying 'I'd like...' for items on the board.
Alternative 2: 'Gap-fill' - complete simple dialogues with 'Would you like...?' or 'I'd like...'
lp.ls: Listening slot: Play a KET-style cafe dialogue audio. Students listen and circle the correct order (e.g., 'tea or coffee?'). Check answers as a class. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up, Sit Down' - teacher says 'Would you like coffee?' students stand, 'I'd like tea' students sit.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Cafe Roleplay' - students use menus they made earlier. One is waiter, one is customer. Waiter asks 'Would you like...?', customer orders 'I'd like... / Can I have...'. Rotate roles.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a simple cafe menu and match dishes to sections (Drinks, Food, Desserts). Then write 3 sentences: 'I'd like...', 'Would you like...?', 'Can I have...?'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one polite sentence you would say in a cafe ("I'd like a tea, please.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students mark off food/drinks called out; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students pass a toy; when music stops, holder says 'I'd like...' and class repeats.
Teams race to write 'I'd like coffee' on the board correctly.
Teacher removes 2 items from the menu; students guess 'Is it cake?'
Pairs perform their dialogue; best pair gets 'Waiter of the Day' badge.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a 'Dream Cafe' poster with 5 items and prices.
Support: Use picture-based menus with words written in Arabic script below.
hw: Write your ideal cafe menu with 5 items and prices.
Write a 6-line dialogue ordering food at a cafe.
Interview a family member about their favorite drink and write 2 sentences.
lp.tip: Tip: Use local cafe names (e.g., 'Café de France') to make it culturally relevant. Praise polite language use heavily to reinforce the objective.

weeks.obj: give simple directions and describe their neighborhood with there is/are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; prepositions of place; imperatives (turn, go)
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Directions; Flashcards/Directions
weeks.act: Map of Oujda pair task; treasure hunt directions; describe-and-draw neighborhoods
weeks.hw: Draw a map of your route from home to school. Write 3 sentences using 'there is/are' and 'turn/go'.

skills.L: Listen to directions audio and follow the map
skills.S: Give directions from school to 3 places
skills.R: Read direction phrases and sequence them on a map
skills.W: Write directions from home to school

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Find Someone Who' with neighborhood questions. Students mingle with a handout asking 'Find someone who lives near a mosque/school/market'. They ask 'Do you live near...?' and write names. Teacher reviews answers on the board.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Neighborhood Bingo' - Students have bingo cards with places like 'bakery', 'park', 'library'. They ask classmates 'Is there a... near your home?' and mark off answers.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Draw' - Teacher calls out places (e.g., 'mosque'), students draw it on mini-whiteboards and hold up.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a large map of Oujda with landmarks marked. Model sentences: 'There is a mosque near my school.' 'There are shops on the main street.' Use gestures for 'near', 'on', 'next to'. Check understanding by asking 'Where is the hospital?' and having students point.
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a story about 'Ali's neighborhood' with flashcards of places. Ask 'Is there a park in Ali's neighborhood?' to model 'there is/are'.
Alternative 2: Bring realia (toy buildings, toy cars) to create a 3D neighborhood on the table. Students describe it using 'there is/are'.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Map Directions' pair task. Students have a simple Oujda map with missing places. They ask and answer: 'Is there a cinema near the station?' 'Yes, there is. It's next to the post office.' Teacher monitors and corrects prepositions.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Place the Flashcards' - Students work in pairs to place flashcards of places on a blank map, then describe using 'there is/are'.
Alternative 2: 'Preposition Race' - Teacher calls out 'Put the book on the chair', students race to follow the imperative.
lp.ls: Listening slot: Students listen to an audio of someone giving directions from school to the American Space. They follow along on a map and circle the route. Then they listen again and write down 3 landmarks mentioned (e.g., 'turn left at the mosque'). If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Simon Says' with direction imperatives. Teacher says 'Simon says turn left', 'Simon says go straight'. Students who make a mistake sit down. Last student standing wins.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Treasure Hunt' groups. Groups create a simple treasure map of the classroom with 3 clues (e.g., 'Go to the door. Turn right. There is a book under the chair'). They trade maps with another group and follow the clues to find the 'treasure' (a small prize).
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read 4 simple direction phrases (e.g., 'Turn left at the park', 'Go straight to the market'). They cut and paste them in the correct order on a map from home to school. Then they write 2 directions for their own route.
lp.st: Exit ticket: draw a mini map with three places and write one direction sentence ("Turn left at the mosque.").
g: Students match picture cards of places to their names on a worksheet.
Students act out directions (e.g., 'turn left') for others to guess.
Students draw a place (e.g., 'bakery') and others guess using 'Is there a...?'
Students hop to different spots in the room as teacher calls 'on the chair', 'next to the door'.
Students trace a route on a map with a crayon as teacher gives oral directions.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a dream neighborhood and label 5 places using 'there is/are'.
Support: Use a partially completed map with word banks for directions.
hw: Draw a map of your route from home to school. Write 3 sentences using 'there is/are' and 'turn/go'.
Interview a family member about places near their home and write 2 sentences.
Write 5 direction phrases (e.g., 'Turn left at the mosque') for a classmate.
lp.tip: Use local landmarks (e.g., King Mohammed VI Avenue, Sidi Yahia) to make directions relevant and boost engagement. Teens respond better when learning connects to their daily lives. Keep the participation checklist this week.

weeks.obj: handle a simple shop exchange: sizes, colors, prices
weeks.lang: clothes vocabulary; How much is/are...? this/that/these/those
weeks.res: Flashcards/Clothes; Listening (shopping dialogues)
weeks.act: Shop roleplay rotation with price lists; this/that auction game; dialogue reconstruction
weeks.hw: dialogue writing (shop exchange, 6 lines)

skills.L: Listening folder: shopping dialogues (sizes, prices)
skills.S: Shop roleplay: sizes, colours and prices
skills.R: Read a shop ad and answer price questions
skills.W: Write a shop conversation (6 lines)

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Clothes Line' · Students form a line, teacher calls out a clothing item, students race to grab a flashcard and line up holding it. Teacher asks 'What is this?' and students reply 'It's a T-shirt'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'I Spy' · Teacher says 'I spy something blue', students guess clothing items.
Alternative 2: 'Mime the Item' · Student mimes a clothing item, classmates guess 'Are you a jacket?'
lp.pres: Presentation: Use real clothes (T-shirt, jeans, dress) and flashcards. Teacher holds up items and says 'This is a red T-shirt. That is a blue dress'. Drill 'this/that/these/those' with students pointing. Ask 'What color is this?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Alternative 1: 'Fashion Show' · Teacher models clothes with exaggerated poses, students repeat vocabulary.
Alternative 2: 'Price Tag Game' · Stick price tags on items, teach 'How much is this?' with fake coins.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'This/That Auction' · Students in pairs bid on flashcards using 'This/That is... dirhams'. Teacher gives fake money, highest bidder wins. Support with price lists and sentence frames.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Color Match' · Students match clothing flashcards to color cards, saying 'This is a green shirt'.
Alternative 2: 'Size Drill' · Hold up size flashcards (S/M/L), students repeat 'This is small'.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short shop dialogue twice: 'Can I help you?' 'Yes, I'd like a T-shirt.' 'What size?' 'Medium.' 'Here you are. It's 100 dirhams.' Students circle the correct size and write the price. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Clothes Relay' · Two lines of students race to dress a mannequin with paper clothes, shouting 'This is a hat!' as they run.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Shop Roleplay Rotation' · Students rotate as shopkeeper/ customer using price lists. Shopkeeper asks 'Can I help you?' Customer replies 'How much are these jeans?' and 'I'll take this'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Read a simple shop ad with prices (e.g., 'T-shirts: 100 dirhams'). Students answer 'How much is the T-shirt?' in notebooks. Then write a 6-line dialogue for homework.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one question and one answer about a price ("How much is this T-shirt? It's 100 dirhams.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students bid on flashcards using 'This/That is... dollars'
Race to dress a mannequin with paper clothes
Rotate as shopkeeper/customer with price lists
Match clothes flashcards to color cards
Hold up size flashcards and repeat 'This is small'
diff: Fast finishers: Design a dream outfit and write prices.
Support: Use sentence frames for dialogue (e.g., 'How much is ___?')
hw: Write a 6-line shop dialogue (customer/shopkeeper)
Draw 5 clothes items and label them in English
Ask family about clothes prices and write 3 sentences
lp.tip: Use realia (clothes) to make shopping vocabulary tangible for Moroccan teens, linking to local markets like souks.

weeks.theme: Weather and what is happening now
weeks.obj: describe the weather, say what people are doing right now, and make a simple suggestion
weeks.lang: present continuous (I am / he is + -ing; Is he...? Yes, he is); What's the weather like?; Let's... / Shall we...?
weeks.res: Flashcards/Seasons-Weather; Lesson Plans/Weather-Seasons
weeks.act: Weather report mini-presentations; spot the difference; phone call roleplay cards
weeks.hw: write a weather report for your city and 5 sentences about what people are doing now

skills.L: Listen to short weather phone calls and tick what each person is doing
skills.S: Ask and answer What are you doing? and What's the weather like?
skills.R: Read short postcards and underline the -ing verbs
skills.W: Write a postcard of 5 sentences with the weather and what I am doing

lp.wu: Weather charades: students act out the weather (sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, snowy, hot, cold) while the others guess "Is it rainy?" The winner mimes next.
wuAlt: Weather bingo with picture cards.
Quick poll: stand up if it is sunny today / if you like rain.
lp.pres: Show a picture of a busy park in different weather. Teach the weather words, then the present continuous with the picture: "It's raining. A boy is playing football. Two girls are running. They aren't swimming." Write the form on the board: am/is/are + verb + -ing (spelling: run, running; make, making). Ask "What is he doing? Is she reading? Are they swimming?" with short answers. Then add suggestions: "It's sunny. Let's go to the park!" "Shall we play football?" "Good idea! / Sorry, I can't."
presAlt: Mime a verb and ask the class "What am I doing?" (You are...).
Show two short video clips with the sound off and ask what people are doing.
lp.prac: Spot the difference: pairs have two park pictures with six differences. They ask "What is he doing?" and "Is she wearing a hat?" to find them ("In picture A he is reading. In picture B he is eating."). The teacher monitors the -ing form and the short answers.
pracAlt: Action chain: each student mimes and says "I'm swimming." The next says "He's swimming. I'm reading."
Sentence cards: put the words in order (is / the boy / playing / football).
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short phone calls twice (for example: "Hi Sara, it's raining in Oujda. I'm watching TV. What are you doing?" "It's sunny in Agadir. I'm swimming!"). Students tick the right weather picture and write what each speaker is doing. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Mime and guess: one student mimes an action and the class asks "Are you eating? Are you swimming?" until they guess. The guesser mimes next.
lp.prod: Phone call roleplay: pairs get a weather card and an activity card. They phone each other: "Hi! What are you doing?" "I'm watching TV. It's raining here. What's the weather like there?" "It's sunny. Shall we go to the park tomorrow?" Students swap cards and repeat with a new partner.
lp.rw: Read three short postcards from different cities (the weather and what the writer is doing). Underline the -ing verbs. Then write a postcard of five sentences to a friend using the frame: "Hello! I'm in ___. It's ___. I'm ___ing."
lp.st: Exit ticket: look out of the window and write two sentences on a slip: the weather and what one person is doing now. Hand it in at the door.
g: Act out the weather; the class guesses with Is it...?
Pairs find differences between two pictures with What is he doing?
Mime an action and the class asks Are you...?
Roleplay a weather and activity phone call with a partner.
Bingo with weather pictures called out by the teacher.
diff: Fast finishers: write a weather report for three Moroccan cities (the weather and what people are doing).
Support: sentence frame "It's ___. He/She is ___ing." and a picture dictionary of -ing verbs.
hw: Write a weather report for your city and 5 sentences about what people are doing now.
Look out of the window and write what 4 people are doing right now.
Write a postcard to a friend (5 sentences).
lp.tip: The present continuous is the first tense for "now": keep every example visual and physical. Check the spelling rules (run, running; make, making) with a quick mini-whiteboard round.

occ.act: Christmas week (25 December). Optional 10-minute winter party task: pairs invite a friend with Let's/Shall we ("Shall we have a party on Friday?") and read two short facts about how people celebrate Christmas and Eid.
occ.hw: Write a short invitation (4 lines) to a winter party.

weeks.obj: talk about yesterday and childhood with was/were
weeks.lang: was/were (positive, negative, questions); time expressions (yesterday, last year, last week)
weeks.res: Worksheets/'Was' vs 'Were'
weeks.act: Childhood memories board; was/were human sentence; when-was-it quiz
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about your last weekend (part 1)

skills.L: Listen to teens talking about yesterday and tick what they did
skills.S: Ask and answer Where were you yesterday? Was it...?
skills.R: Read a short diary and underline was/were
skills.W: Write 3 to 6 sentences about last weekend with was/were

lp.wu: Stand in a circle and throw a soft ball. The student who catches it says "Yesterday I was happy" (or tired, hungry, busy) and throws the ball to someone else. Continue until everyone has spoken.
wuAlt: Feelings cards: students pick a card and say "Yesterday I was tired."
Pairs ask each other "Are you happy today?" and then report "Yesterday he was tired."
lp.pres: Display a photo of a child's birthday party. Ask "Who was happy?" and elicit "The boy was happy." Point to the cake: "The cake was big." Model was/were in positive sentences, then negatives ("The girl wasn't sad. The balloons weren't blue.") and questions ("Was the girl sad? No, she wasn't. Were the children happy? Yes, they were."). Check understanding with thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Show two pictures of the same street in the past and now and say "The shop was small. The street was quiet."
Teacher tells a short story about last weekend with was/were and students raise a hand when they hear was or were.
lp.prac: Give each pair a set of was/were sentence cards. They race to match them to picture cards (for example "The cat was black" with a black cat). The teacher monitors pronunciation and the choice of was or were.
pracAlt: Question chain: "Where were you yesterday?" "I was at school." around the circle.
Gap-fill cards: choose was or were for six sentences.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short text twice: "Last Saturday I was at my cousin's house. It was a hot day. My cousin and his brother were in the garden. We were very happy." Students tick the true/false sentences on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Freeze: play music; students dance. When it stops, the teacher asks one student "Where were you yesterday at 5 o'clock?" and the student answers "I was at home."
lp.prod: In groups, students make a Childhood Memories poster. They draw pictures of when they were younger and write sentences: "When I was five, I was small. My toy was red." Groups present the poster to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short diary entry about a boy's New Year's Eve (six lines) and underline every was/were. Then write three sentences about your last weekend using was/were.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about yesterday with was or were and one question with Were you...? and hand it in at the door.
g: Throw the ball and say how you were yesterday.
Match sentence cards to pictures and read them aloud.
Students hold word cards and stand in order to make a was/were sentence.
Question chain around the circle with places and times.
Teams answer quick questions about the past (When was your birthday?).
diff: Fast finishers: write a short description of your childhood home (5 sentences with was/were).
Support: sentence frame "Yesterday I was ___. My ___ was/were ___." and a was/were chart.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your last weekend using was and were.
Ask a family member "Where were you when you were ten?" and write 2 sentences.
Draw a picture of your favourite place from last year and label it with was/were sentences.
lp.tip: Use personal, real examples from your own life so was/were feels useful. Keep the time words (yesterday, last year, last week) on the board all lesson.

occ.act: New Year week. Optional "last year" memories: students write three sentences about last year with was/were ("Last year I was in Year 8. My teacher was kind.") and share them with a partner.

weeks.obj: tell a simple story about last weekend with regular past verbs, in statements, negatives and questions
weeks.lang: past simple regular (-ed and spelling); didn't + verb; Did you...? Yes, I did / No, I didn't; yesterday, last weekend
weeks.res: Worksheets (past simple regular verbs); Games (past tense)
weeks.act: Did-you bingo; verb auction; story chain about last weekend
weeks.hw: finish your weekend story (6 sentences, one negative)

skills.L: Listen to a short text about a weekend and tick what the person did
skills.S: Ask and answer Did you...? about last weekend
skills.R: Read a weekend text and underline the -ed verbs
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about my last weekend with regular verbs

lp.wu: Did-you bingo: students get a 3 by 3 grid with past activities (watch TV, visit family, play football, cook, study English...). They ask "Did you watch TV last weekend?" and write the name when the answer is "Yes, I did."
wuAlt: Pair talk: tell your partner two things you did yesterday (use the words you already know).
Picture flash: show five activity pictures for 10 seconds and students say what they did last weekend.
lp.pres: Write a short story on the board: "Last Saturday I visited my grandmother. We cooked lunch and watched TV. I didn't study." Underline the -ed verbs. Teach the three endings by sorting (walked /t/, played /d/, visited /id/). Show the spelling rules in a table (visit, visited; live, lived; study, studied; stop, stopped). Teach "didn't + verb" and "Did you...? Yes, I did / No, I didn't." Check: "Did I study? No, you didn't."
presAlt: Write ten verbs on the board and ask students to add the -ed in pairs, then check the spelling rules.
Teacher mimes five actions ("I cooked.") and the class says what the teacher did.
lp.prac: Verb auction: teams "buy" correct sentences from a list of twelve (some contain mistakes such as "I visit my uncle yesterday" or "I didn't watched TV"). They then correct the wrong ones. A team that buys a correct sentence wins a point.
pracAlt: Spelling sort: students sort verbs by the -ed rule (add -ed, add -d, change y to i, double the consonant).
Sentence building: reorder jumbled words into a past simple sentence.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short text twice: "Last weekend I visited my cousin in Nador. We played football and watched a film. I didn't do my homework! My cousin cooked dinner." Students tick the activities and answer "Did he play football? Yes or no?" If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Past verb relay: the teacher calls a verb (play, visit, cook...) and one student per team writes the -ed form on the board with correct spelling. The first team with all correct wins.
lp.prod: Weekend story chain: groups of four build a story about a weekend, each adding one sentence in the past (the first sentence comes from a card: "On Saturday morning I..."). Then pairs interview each other "Did you...? last weekend" and write three sentences about their partner.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a student's weekend (six sentences) and underline all the -ed verbs. Then write five sentences about your own last weekend using regular verbs and one negative.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you did last weekend and one thing you didn't do ("I played football. I didn't study.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Ask Did you...? to find a classmate for each box.
Buy the correct past sentences and fix the wrong ones.
Sort verbs by the -ed spelling rule.
Add one past sentence each to build a weekend story.
A student sits with a verb card behind them; the class gives past sentences until they guess it.
diff: Fast finishers: add two irregular verbs you already know (went, had) to the story.
Support: -ed spelling table and a sentence frame "Last weekend I ___ed. I didn't ___."
hw: Finish your weekend story (6 sentences, one negative).
Interview a family member: "What did you do last weekend?" and write 3 sentences.
Find 5 regular verbs in a text and write their -ed forms.
lp.tip: Teach the -ed sounds by listening and sorting, not by rules alone. Keep irregular verbs for Week 21: mixing them in now overloads beginners.

occ.act: New Year recap (4 January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year ("I visited my cousins. I watched football. I played games.") and report one thing to the class.

weeks.obj: complete the written paper and the paired speaking task
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes
weeks.res: Tests (teacher-selected level items); assessment kit
weeks.act: Written paper (35 min); paired speaking tasks while others work on review pack
weeks.hw: Review S1 vocabulary flashcards (15 mins).

skills.L: Listening paper across S1 topics (Tests)
skills.S: Paired speaking task (assessment kit)
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing task (5-6 sentences)

lp.wu: Students play 'Stand Up If...' with teacher calling out S1 review prompts: 'Stand up if you like pizza', 'Stand up if you can swim', 'Stand up if you have a brother'. Students stand and say 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of S1 verbs (like, play, have, can) and mingle to find classmates who match.
Students play 'Quick Quiz' with flashcards showing S1 vocabulary (food, school items, free time activities) and race to name them.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a sample KET-style writing task prompt on the board: 'Write about your best friend. Name, age, what you like to do together'. Models 2-3 sentences: 'My best friend is Ali. He is 13. We like football'. Checks understanding by asking 'What do you write about?'
presAlt: Teacher distributes a guided writing worksheet with sentence starters: 'My name is... I am... I like... I can...' and students complete it.
Teacher shows a model speaking task video and highlights key phrases: 'This is my friend. He/She is... We like...'
lp.prac: Students complete a 35-minute written paper with 4 parts: matching, sentence completion, short email, and guided writing. Teacher circulates to clarify instructions but not help with answers.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs to practice a speaking task from the assessment kit: 'Describe your family' using prompts (mother, father, brother, sister).
Students do a peer review of each other's guided writing tasks using a simple checklist (name, age, activity).
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio about a boy's daily routine (S1 topic) and number the pictures in order (wake up, eat breakfast, go to school, play football, do homework). Teacher pauses to check comprehension. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with S1 action verbs: 'Simon says stand up', 'Simon says jump', 'Simon says touch your nose'.
lp.prod: Students take turns in pairs doing the KET-style speaking task: 'Describe your best friend' using the prompt card. They ask and answer 3-4 questions each (What's his/her name? How old is he/she? What do you like to do?). Teacher uses a checklist to assess.
lp.rw: Students read a short text about a girl's free time (S1 topic) and answer 3 multiple-choice questions. Then, they write 5 sentences about their own free time using the text as a model.
lp.st: Closing circle: students tell a partner one thing they did well in the assessment and one thing they want to practise. Collect the papers and say goodbye.
g: Students write 6 S1 words on a grid and listen as teacher calls them out; first to cross all 3 in a row wins.
Students get a flashcard with a S1 question, quiz a partner, trade cards, and repeat.
Students sit in a circle and say 'I like...' adding one new word each turn (e.g., 'I like football', 'I like football and pizza').
Teacher calls out S1 verbs; students race to write them on the board.
Students use word cards to make correct sentences about S1 topics.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 3 more sentences about their best friend including 'He/She can...' and 'He/She has got...'.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My best friend is ___. He/She is ___. We like ___.'
hw: Review S1 vocabulary flashcards (15 mins).
Write 5 sentences about your family using 'have got' and 'can'.
Practice the speaking task prompt with a family member.
lp.tip: Tell students the assessment shows what they can do now and what to practise next. Use the checklist during the speaking task and give feedback on strengths first. Record the semester marks and issue the report cards this week.
checklist: I can write 5-6 sentences about myself or a friend.
I can understand a short audio about daily routines.
I can read a short text and answer simple questions.
I can ask and answer questions about family and friends.
I can use 'have got', 'can', and 'like' correctly.
I can follow instructions for a KET-style task.
I can work with a partner to complete a speaking task.

weeks.obj: talk about learning goals and review semester 1 language
weeks.lang: review structures; goal language (I want to... I'd like to...)
weeks.res: Worksheets (review sets)
weeks.act: Goal-setting one-pager; semester 1 team quiz; error correction auction (gentle)
weeks.hw: goals paragraph

skills.L: Listen to goal statements and match them to people
skills.S: Talk about my goals: I want to... I will try...
skills.R: Read S1 review texts and self-check can-dos
skills.W: Write 3 learning goals for the year

lp.wu: Goal Bingo: Students get a bingo grid with 9 simple semester 1 words (e.g., 'school', 'friend', 'pizza'). Teacher calls out definitions or shows pictures, students mark the word and say it aloud when they get a line.
wuAlt: Word Chain: Students say a word from S1, next student says a word starting with the last letter, e.g., 'book' → 'kite' → 'elephant'.
Flashcard Race: Two lines of students race to slap the flashcard the teacher names (e.g., 'Show me red!')
lp.pres: Teacher shows a New Year's resolution poster with 'I want to...' and 'I'd like to...' (e.g., 'I want to learn English', 'I'd like to read more'). Models 3 examples, asks students to repeat. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Do you want to learn English?'
presAlt: Goal Charades: Teacher acts out a goal (e.g., 'running'), students guess and complete the sentence: 'You want to...'.
Story Time: Show a short comic strip of a teen making a resolution, students identify the goal language.
lp.prac: Goal-Setting One-Pager: Students fold a paper into 4 sections. In each, they draw/write one S1 topic (e.g., food, school) and a goal using 'I want to... I'd like to...'. Teacher monitors, helps with spelling.
pracAlt: Goal Match-Up: Cards with 'I want to...' on one side and activities (e.g., 'do homework') on the other. Students match pairs and make sentences.
Pair Drill: Student A says a goal, Student B asks 'Why?', Student A answers 'Because I want to...'
lp.ls: Listen and Match: Audio of 4 teens saying goals (e.g., 'I want to play football'). Students match each voice to a picture of the activity on their worksheet. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher calls out goals (e.g., 'Stand up if you want to learn English!'), students stand and repeat the sentence.
lp.prod: Goal Survey: Students walk around asking 3 peers 'What do you want to learn this year?' and write down their answers. Report back: 'Fatima wants to...'
lp.rw: S1 Review Paragraph: Students read a short text about a teen's semester (e.g., 'I go to school. I have friends. I can play football'). Circle 3 things they can do. Then write 3 sentences about their own semester.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one goal for this semester with I want to... and stick it on the goals wall.
g: Students mark S1 words on a grid as teacher calls them.
Two lines race to slap the correct S1 flashcard.
Match 'I want to...' cards to activity pictures.
Stand and repeat goal sentences when called.
Ask peers about goals and report back.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a comic strip of someone achieving their goal.
Support: Trace or copy goal sentences from the board.
hw: Write 3 learning goals for the year: 'I want to... I'd like to...'
Draw a picture of one goal and write a sentence under it.
Ask a family member their goal and write it down.
lp.tip: Use students' own goals (learning, school, hobbies) and keep them on the wall to revisit at the end of the year.

weeks.obj: name jobs and workplaces, say what people do, and talk about their dream job
weeks.lang: jobs and places of work; he/she works in...; Does he...? Yes, he does; What does she do?; I want to be a...
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Jobs-Careers; Reading tasks/Famous people
weeks.act: Job charades; What does he do? guessing game; dream job pairs; job profile reading
weeks.hw: write about your dream job (5 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to short job descriptions and write the job
skills.S: Ask and answer What does he do? and What is your dream job?
skills.R: Read a short job profile and complete a fact file
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about my dream job

lp.wu: Job charades: the teacher mimes a job (doctor, teacher, chef) and students say "You're a doctor!" Then students draw a job card, mime it and the class guesses.
wuAlt: Picture pairs: match job pictures to words in two minutes.
Chain: "I want to be a ___" around the circle, each student repeating the one before.
lp.pres: Show job flashcards with workplaces (doctor and hospital, teacher and school, chef and restaurant, driver, nurse, mechanic, engineer, farmer, police officer). Model: "What does a doctor do? A doctor works in a hospital. She helps sick people." Ask "Does a chef work in a school? No, he doesn't. He works in a restaurant." Teach "I want to be a ___ because I like ___ing." as a chunk. Check understanding: "Where does a nurse work?"
presAlt: Show a short video clip about a job and ask what the person does.
Bring real objects (stethoscope, chalk, spoon) and students say the job.
lp.prac: What does he do? In pairs, A has a job card and B asks yes/no questions ("Does he work in a hospital? Does he wear a uniform?") to guess the job within six questions. Swap roles.
pracAlt: Job matching cards: match the job, the place and the action ("teacher, school, teaches children").
Sentence building: reorder words to make "She works in a hospital."
lp.ls: Teacher reads three job descriptions twice (for example: "She works in a school. She teaches children. She likes talking to people."). Students write the job next to each description. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Job relay: the teacher reads a clue ("He cooks food in a restaurant.") and one student per team writes the job on the board. The fastest correct team scores.
lp.prod: Dream job pairs: Student A asks "What is your dream job? Why?" and Student B answers "I want to be an engineer because I like building things." Then each student tells another pair about their partner: "Salma wants to be a doctor because she likes helping people."
lp.rw: Read a short job profile (video game tester, five sentences) and complete a fact file (job, place, what he does). Then write five sentences about your dream job using the frame "I want to be ___. I want to work in ___."
lp.st: Exit ticket: write your dream job on a slip with one reason ("I want to be a pilot because I like travelling.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Mime a job; the class guesses You're a...
Guess the job with yes/no questions (Does he work in...?).
Read a clue and race to write the job on the board.
Match job, place and action cards.
Ask classmates about their dream job and report one answer.
diff: Fast finishers: write a job advert for a dream job (4 lines).
Support: word bank with jobs, places and verbs (help, teach, cook, drive, build).
hw: Write about your dream job (5 sentences).
Interview a family member about their job and write 3 sentences.
Find 5 job words around your town (signs, shops) and bring them.
lp.tip: Keep the target at present simple he/she (works, helps) and the chunk "I want to be". Use local jobs students know (shopkeeper, farmer, tour guide) and avoid have to, which belongs to the next level.

weeks.obj: compare two cities, foods, or teams with comparative adjectives
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more... than)
weeks.res: Worksheets/Adjectives; Lesson Plans/Countries
weeks.act: City debate teams; compare-and-write pairs; adjective duel game
weeks.hw: 5 comparisons about Oujda vs another city

skills.L: Listen to city comparisons and note the -er forms
skills.S: Compare two cities, foods or teams with comparatives
skills.R: Read a comparison text and find the comparatives
skills.W: Write 4 comparison sentences

lp.wu: City Bingo: Students get bingo cards with city names (Oujda, Casablanca, Paris, London, New York). Teacher says clues like 'This city is bigger than Oujda' or 'This city is more modern than Rabat'. Students mark the city and shout 'Bingo!' when they have a line.
wuAlt: Adjective Race: Students line up. Teacher shows flashcards of adjectives (big, small, old, new, tall, short). Students race to say the comparative form (bigger, smaller, older, newer, taller, shorter).
Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Is your city bigger than your friend's city?' and write names of people who say yes.
lp.pres: Teacher shows two city flashcards (Oujda and Paris). Models sentences: 'Oujda is smaller than Paris. Paris is bigger than Oujda.' Uses gestures for 'small' and 'big'. Asks students to repeat chorally. Checks understanding by pointing to flashcards and asking 'Which city is bigger?'
presAlt: Realia Comparison: Teacher holds two objects (a small Moroccan tagine and a big American coffee mug). Models: 'The tagine is smaller than the mug. The mug is bigger than the tagine.' Students repeat.
Picture Story: Shows a simple comic strip with two characters comparing their cities. Reads aloud: 'My city is older than yours. Your city is newer than mine.'
lp.prac: Adjective Duel Game: Students in pairs get a set of adjective cards (big, small, old, new, tall, short). Teacher says two cities (e.g., 'Oujda and Rabat'). Students race to flip the card for the correct comparative ('Oujda is smaller than Rabat'). First pair to get 3 points wins.
pracAlt: Comparative Pairs: Students work in pairs. Each pair gets two city cards. They take turns making one comparative sentence about the cities (e.g., 'Casablanca is more modern than Fes'). Teacher monitors and corrects.
Flashcard Line-Up: Students get flashcards of cities. They line up in order from smallest to biggest, saying sentences as they move: 'Oujda is smaller than Tangier.'
lp.ls: City Comparison Audio: Students listen to a short audio where two teens compare their cities (Oujda and Agadir). They have a worksheet with two columns: 'Agadir' and 'Oujda'. They write down the comparatives they hear (e.g., 'Agadir is more modern. Oujda is older.')
lp.re: Comparative Charades: One student comes to the front. Teacher whispers a comparative sentence (e.g., 'Tall'). The student acts being 'tall' and then 'taller' by stretching up. Class guesses the comparative word.
lp.prod: City Debate Teams: Divide class into two teams (Team Oujda vs Team Rabat). Each team has 5 minutes to prepare 3 comparative sentences to argue why their city is better (e.g., 'Oujda is more beautiful than Rabat. Rabat is noisier than Oujda.'). Teams take turns presenting their sentences. Class votes for the most convincing team.
lp.rw: Read and Compare: Students read a short text comparing two Moroccan cities (Marrakech and Chefchaouen). The text has gaps with comparatives (e.g., 'Marrakech is _____ (big) than Chefchaouen. Chefchaouen is _____ (old) than Marrakech.'). Students fill in the gaps with -er or more. Then they write 2 sentences comparing their own city to another.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one comparison about two cities or two things in your bag ("Oujda is smaller than Casablanca.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students race to flip the correct comparative card for two cities.
Students mark cities on bingo cards based on comparative clues.
Students act out comparatives for the class to guess.
Students line up city cards and say comparative sentences.
Teams argue why their city is better using comparatives.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 5 comparisons between Oujda and a city of their choice (e.g., 'Oujda is sunnier than London.')
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'Oujda is _____ (adjective) than _____ (city).' with a word bank of adjectives (big, small, old, new).
hw: Write 5 comparisons about Oujda vs another city (e.g., 'Oujda is smaller than Casablanca.')
Draw two pictures of your city and another city. Label 3 things in each picture and write 1 comparative sentence (e.g., 'The mosque in Oujda is older than the one in Tangier.')
Interview a family member: 'Is Oujda bigger than your hometown? Write down their answer and 1 more comparison.'
lp.tip: Use local cities (Oujda, Rabat, Casablanca, Tangier) to make the comparisons relevant and engaging. Teens are more motivated to talk about places they know.

weeks.obj: use superlatives to nominate classmates for fun awards
weeks.lang: superlatives (the -est, the most...)
weeks.res: Worksheets/Adjectives; Games
weeks.act: Class awards ceremony planning; superlative survey; the-best-of presentations
weeks.hw: Write 3 superlative sentences about your family.

skills.L: Listen to award nominations and identify the winner
skills.S: Nominate classmates with superlatives
skills.R: Read class-award texts and find the superlatives
skills.W: Write 3 superlative award sentences

lp.wu: Awards Nomination Relay: Students stand in two lines. The first student in each line runs to the board, writes a superlative about a classmate (e.g., 'Fatima is the kindest'), and runs back. The next student does the same with a different classmate and superlative.
wuAlt: Superlative Bingo: Each student writes 5 superlatives (e.g., 'the tallest', 'the funniest') on a grid. The teacher calls out classmates' names with superlatives; students mark if they match.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Who is the most...?' (e.g., 'Who is the most helpful?') and write names.
lp.pres: Show 3 flashcards: a student helping (kind), a student running (fast), a student laughing (funny). Model sentences: 'Amina is the kindest. Youssef is the fastest. Omar is the funniest.' Ask 'Who is the kindest?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Realia Awards: Bring in a trophy or medal. Hold it up and say 'This is for the best student in class. Who is the best?' Elicit responses with superlatives.
Class Photo Awards: Show a class photo. Point to students and say 'He is the tallest. She is the prettiest.'
lp.prac: Superlative Survey: In pairs, students ask 3 classmates 'Who is the most...?' (e.g., 'Who is the most creative?') and write names. Teacher monitors and corrects errors. Then, groups share their findings.
pracAlt: Superlative Memory Game: Students sit in a circle. Each student adds a superlative about the previous student (e.g., 'You are the tallest. He is the funniest.').
Superlative Chain Drill: Teacher starts with 'I am the oldest.' Each student says a superlative about themselves or the previous student.
lp.ls: Listen to Award Nominations: Teacher reads 5 award nominations (e.g., 'Karim is the most helpful because he always helps with homework.'). Students write down the winner for each award (e.g., 'Karim').
lp.re: Superlative Charades: One student acts out a superlative (e.g., 'the tallest' by standing on tiptoes), others guess and say the full sentence.
lp.prod: Class Awards Ceremony: In groups, students plan 3 awards (e.g., 'The Best Artist', 'The Funniest Joke') with superlatives. Each group presents their awards and winners to the class.
lp.rw: Read the class awards poster (five nominations such as 'Karim is the funniest. Amina is the kindest.'). Then write five sentences about classmates' awards using superlatives and the word bank (the best, the most, the -est).
lp.st: Exit ticket: nominate a classmate for an award with a superlative ("Karim is the funniest.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students rotate in pairs, asking 'Who is the most...?' and writing answers.
Students draw a superlative (e.g., 'the fastest') and others guess.
Two teams race to write superlatives about the teacher on the board.
Groups add one sentence with a superlative to a story about Ramadan.
Students throw a ball and say a superlative about the person who catches it.
diff: Fast finishers: Design a trophy for their award winner with a superlative caption.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame '______ is the most ______ because ______.'
hw: Write 3 superlative sentences about your family.
Make a Best of list for your town (the best cafe, the biggest shop...) with 5 sentences.
Draw a trophy for a friend and write a superlative caption.
lp.tip: Use peer nominations to build rapport: teens respond well to positive recognition from classmates. Keep nominations kind and specific. Keep a participation checklist this week.

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students share 'the best thing about Ramadan' with a superlative ('The best part is iftar with my family.') and write one sentence.

weeks.obj: describe weekend and holiday plans with going to
weeks.lang: going to (plans); time expressions
weeks.res: Worksheets/'will'/'going to'
weeks.act: Plan grid mingle; going-to fortune teller (paper craft); plan swap listening
weeks.hw: 6 sentences about next weekend

skills.L: Listen to weekend plans with going to
skills.S: Describe my weekend and holiday plans
skills.R: Read plan texts and underline going to
skills.W: Write my weekend plan (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Weekend Plans Bingo: Students write 5 weekend activities on a bingo grid. Teacher calls out activities (e.g., 'play football', 'visit family'). Students mark off and shout 'Bingo!' when complete, then share one plan.
wuAlt: Two Stars and a Wish: Students share one good thing and one wish for the weekend, then guess a partner's plans.
Quick Poll: Teacher asks 'What are you going to do this weekend?' Students raise hands for options like 'study', 'play games', 'go out'.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of weekend activities (e.g., 'visit grandma', 'study English', 'play football'). Model sentences: 'I'm going to visit grandma on Saturday.' Elicit time expressions ('on Saturday', 'in the evening'). Check understanding by asking 'What are YOU going to do?'
presAlt: Plan Grid Poster: Draw a 3x3 grid on the board with 'Saturday morning', 'Saturday afternoon', etc. Fill in plans with 'going to' and elicit from students.
Dialogue Roleplay: Teacher and a student act out a conversation about weekend plans using 'going to' and time expressions.
lp.prac: Plan Grid Mingle: Students receive a half-filled grid with time slots (e.g., 'Saturday morning'). They mingle, ask 'What are you going to do [time]?', and write partners' answers. Swap grids and repeat.
pracAlt: Going-To Fortune Teller: Students fold paper into a fortune teller, write activities inside. They ask partners 'What are you going to do?' and lift flaps to reveal 'predictions'.
Sentence Relay: Teams race to write correct 'going to' sentences on the board for prompts like 'Sunday / clean room'.
lp.ls: Plan Swap Listening: Students listen to 3 audio clips of teens talking about weekend plans. They match each speaker to a time slot on a handout (e.g., 'Speaker 1: Saturday afternoon / Speaker 2: Sunday morning').
lp.re: Action Charades: Teacher mimes an activity (e.g., 'swimming'). Students shout 'You're going to swim!' and mime the action. Fast-paced to re-energize.
lp.prod: Holiday Plans Survey: Students interview 3 partners using 'What are you going to do during the next holiday?'. They tally responses (e.g., '2 students: visit family') and share findings with the class.
lp.rw: Read and Underline: Students read a short text about a teen's holiday plans (e.g., 'I'm going to travel to Agadir with my family. We're going to swim and eat seafood.'). They underline all 'going to' phrases and write 1 new sentence about their own holiday.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one plan for this weekend with going to and hand it in at the door.
g: Students swap written weekend plans and correct errors using 'going to'.
Match activity cards to time expression cards (e.g., 'watch a movie' + 'Saturday evening').
Students sit in a circle and build a sentence: 'I'm going to play football on Saturday. What are YOU going to do?'
Cut up a 'going to' sentence and students reassemble it correctly.
Students draw emojis for activities and write sentences: 'I'm going to 😊 on Sunday.'
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 'going to' sentences about a dream holiday.
Support: Use sentence frames: 'I'm going to ___ on ___.' with word bank.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your next weekend using 'going to' and time expressions.
Draw a picture of your weekend plans and label 3 activities with 'going to' sentences.
Interview a family member about their weekend plans and write 2 sentences about them.
lp.tip: Use real plans from students' weekends and holidays. Remind them that going to is for plans already decided.

weeks.obj: use common irregular past verbs to say what happened yesterday and last week
weeks.lang: irregular past (go-went, have-had, see-saw, eat-ate, buy-bought, make-made, get-got, do-did, take-took, come-came); did/didn't + verb; yesterday, last week
weeks.res: Worksheets (irregular verbs); Flashcards (verbs); Games (past tense)
weeks.act: Irregular verb memory cards; What did you do yesterday? mingle; strip story order
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about yesterday

skills.L: Listen to a short diary text and put pictures in order
skills.S: Ask and answer What did you do yesterday?
skills.R: Read a short diary and underline the irregular verbs
skills.W: Write 6 sentences about yesterday with irregular verbs

lp.wu: Past verb memory: in groups of three, students play Memory with cards that match the base form and the past form (go and went). They say both verbs aloud when they find a pair. This recycles the regular -ed verbs from Week 14.
wuAlt: Quick quiz: the teacher says a regular verb and students give the past form.
Pair talk: tell your partner two things you did yesterday.
lp.pres: Write a short diary on the board: "Yesterday I got up at 7. I had breakfast and went to school. I saw my friend and we ate lunch together. I didn't make dinner." Underline the irregular verbs and explain they change completely, with no -ed. Show a wall chart of ten core irregulars with pictures: go-went, have-had, see-saw, eat-ate, buy-bought, make-made, get-got, do-did, take-took, come-came. Drill "What did you do yesterday? I went to..." Check: "Did I eat breakfast? Yes, you did."
presAlt: Act out ten verbs and students say the past form ("You ate").
Song or chant for five irregular verbs, spoken with a clapping rhythm.
lp.prac: Irregular verb tennis: in pairs, A says the base verb and B says the past form. Then A says a sentence start ("Yesterday I...") and B completes it with an irregular verb. Finally, pairs reorder jumbled diary sentences ("went / I / to / school / yesterday").
pracAlt: Mini-whiteboard race: the teacher says a base verb and students write the past form.
Gap fill: complete ten sentences with the correct past verb from a box.
lp.ls: Teacher reads "Layla's yesterday" twice: "Yesterday Layla got up at 6. She had a big breakfast and went to school by bus. At lunch she saw her cousin. They ate pizza. After school she bought a book." Students number five pictures in order and tick true/false statements. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Past verb flash: the teacher shows a picture (eat) and the first student to say the past form and a sentence ("I ate couscous on Friday") scores a point for the team.
lp.prod: Yesterday mingle: each student has a card with five prompts (get up, have breakfast, go to school, eat lunch, see friends). They ask classmates "What time did you get up yesterday? What did you eat?" and record the answers. Then pairs write "Yesterday of ___" in six sentences and read it to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short diary entry about a teen's Saturday (six to eight sentences with regular and irregular verbs). Underline the irregular verbs in one colour and the regular verbs in another. Write your own diary of yesterday: six sentences using the frame "Yesterday I ___."
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the past form of three irregular verbs and one sentence with one of them, and hand it in at the door.
g: Match base forms and past forms in a Memory game.
Say the base verb and your partner gives the past form.
Race to say the past form and a sentence from a picture.
Put jumbled diary sentences in order.
Bingo with past sentences (She went to school).
diff: Fast finishers: add five more irregular verbs (write, read, give, tell, run) and make sentences.
Support: wall chart of base/past pairs with pictures and a sentence frame "Yesterday I ___ and I ___."
hw: Write 6 sentences about yesterday using at least 4 irregular verbs.
Learn 10 irregular past forms with flashcards.
Ask a family member "What did you do yesterday?" and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Irregular verbs need frequent, short recycling: finish each of the next three lessons with a two-minute verb flash. Teach the ten core verbs first and no more.

weeks.obj: give simple health advice with should
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; body and illness vocabulary
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Emergency; Flashcards/Body
weeks.act: Doctor-patient roleplay; advice column pairs; problem page writing
weeks.hw: write advice for 3 problems

skills.L: Listen to doctor-patient dialogues
skills.S: Give health advice with should / shouldn't
skills.R: Read a health leaflet and find the advice (Lesson Plans/Emergency)
skills.W: Write advice for 3 health problems

lp.wu: Play 'Simon Says' with body parts and health actions (e.g., 'Simon says touch your head', 'Simon says pretend to cough'). Students stand up and follow commands. Teacher models and corrects pronunciation.
wuAlt: Play 'Charades' with body parts and illness actions (e.g., 'sneeze', 'stomach ache') for students to guess.
Use flashcards of body parts/illnesses for a quick 'What's missing?' game.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of common illnesses (headache, cold, stomach ache) and model advice: 'You should drink water' or 'You shouldn't eat ice cream'. Demonstrate with a short doctor-patient dialogue acted by the teacher and a volunteer. Check understanding with 'What should I do if I have a headache?'
presAlt: Read a simple health leaflet (the Emergency folder in Lesson Plans has material) and highlight the should/shouldn't sentences.
Use a story about a character with a cold and elicit advice from students.
lp.prac: Play 'Doctor Says' in pairs: one student pretends to have an illness, the other gives advice using 'should/shouldn't'. Teacher circulates to correct and model. Use sentence frames on the board for support.
pracAlt: Complete a gap-fill worksheet with 'should/shouldn't' and health vocabulary.
Play 'Advice Race': teams write correct advice for illnesses on the board.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short doctor-patient dialogue twice (for example: 'I have a headache.' 'You should rest and drink water. You shouldn't play football today.') and students circle the correct advice on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Play 'Pass the Action': students pass a ball and say a health advice sentence (e.g., 'You should sleep') while doing an action (yawn, stretch).
lp.prod: Roleplay 'Advice Column' in pairs: one student writes a problem (e.g., 'I have a stomach ache'), the other gives advice. Swap roles. Teacher monitors for correct language use.
lp.rw: Read a short 'Problem Page' with three letters ('I have a cold.', 'I can't sleep.', 'I have a stomach ache.') and write advice for each with should/shouldn't. Share the answers with a partner.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one health problem and one piece of advice with should ("I have a headache. You should drink water.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students follow commands with 'should/shouldn't' (e.g., 'You shouldn't run').
Act out illnesses for others to guess and give advice.
Teams write advice for illnesses on the board.
Pass a ball and say advice with an action.
Read and write advice for health problems.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dialogue for a doctor-patient scenario.
Support: use sentence frames with 'should/shouldn't' and vocabulary lists.
hw: Write advice for 3 health problems (e.g., 'My friend has a cold').
Draw a comic strip showing someone giving advice.
Record a voice message giving advice for an illness.
lp.tip: Use real-life examples from students' experiences (e.g., 'What should you do if you eat too much couscous?') to make the language relevant.

weeks.obj: tell a simple story about a past trip and ask simple travel questions
weeks.lang: past simple (regular and irregular); Where did you go? Who did you go with? How did you travel?; travel words
weeks.res: Reading tasks (travel-themed); Listening (travel dialogues)
weeks.act: Holiday brochure corner; travel buddy interview; reading and questions
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about your last holiday

skills.L: Listen to two friends comparing holidays and fill a grid
skills.S: Ask and answer Where did you go? How did you travel?
skills.R: Read a short text about a trip and answer questions
skills.W: Write 6 sentences about a past trip

lp.wu: Travel bingo: students get bingo cards with travel pictures (plane, hotel, beach, bus, train, tent, ticket, suitcase). The teacher calls the words; students mark them and shout "Bingo!"
wuAlt: Picture quiz: show a place and ask "Is it a beach or a city?"
Pair talk: tell your partner one place you went to last year.
lp.pres: Show three holiday photos (beach, mountains, old city) with sentences: "Last summer I went to Agadir with my family. We travelled by bus. We swam in the sea and ate fish. I didn't go to the mountains." Teach the questions "Where did you go? Who did you go with? How did you travel? What did you do?" with short answers. Recycle the irregular verbs from Week 21 (went, ate, saw, bought). Check: "Did I go by plane? No, you didn't. You went by bus."
presAlt: Teacher shows a map of Morocco and tells a short trip story, pointing to the places.
Show a boarding pass and a hotel booking and ask what they tell you about a trip.
lp.prac: Travel buddy interview: pairs ask "Where did you go last holiday? How did you travel? What did you see?" and write the answers in a table. The teacher monitors did + base verb and the irregular forms.
pracAlt: Question cards: pick a card (Where? Who? How?) and ask the class.
Sentence building: put words in order to make a past sentence about a trip.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short dialogue twice: "Where did you go?" "I went to Chefchaouen with my cousins." "How did you travel?" "By bus." "What did you do?" "We took photos and ate in a cafe." Students fill a grid (Name, Place, Transport, Activity). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Holiday chain: student 1 says "Last summer I went to Marrakech." Student 2 repeats and adds "and I ate..." and so on in groups of six.
lp.prod: Holiday brochure corner: groups design a brochure for a real place in Morocco (Chefchaouen, Essaouira, Merzouga) with three pictures and four sentences in the past ("Last year we visited the blue streets. We took many photos."). They present it to another group, who ask "Did you...?"
lp.rw: Read a short text about a girl's trip to Chefchaouen (about eight sentences with regular and irregular verbs) and answer four questions. Then write six sentences about your last holiday or trip using the frame "Last ___ I went to ___. I travelled by ___."
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one question about a trip ("Where did you go?") and one answer, and hand it in at the door.
g: Bingo with travel pictures called out by the teacher.
Repeat and add a past sentence about a holiday.
The class asks yes/no questions to guess a place the teacher visited.
Groups quiz each other about their brochure places.
Race to write the past form of travel verbs on the board.
diff: Fast finishers: write an email to a friend about the trip (six to eight sentences).
Support: sentence frame "Last ___ I went to ___. I travelled by ___. I ___ed / ate / saw ___." and the verb chart.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your last holiday.
Interview a family member about their best trip and write 3 sentences.
Find 5 travel words in English around town (signs, tickets) and bring them.
lp.tip: This is the first free past simple lesson: let students talk about real trips, accept simple sentences and correct only the target forms (did/didn't and the irregular verbs).

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: pairs ask "Where did you go on Eid? What did you eat?" and write three sentences about their last Eid.
occ.hw: Write 5 sentences about your best Eid memory.

weeks.obj: express and justify opinions about music
weeks.lang: I think... because; opinion adjectives
weeks.res: Music/Songs; Listening
weeks.act: Lyric listening gap-fill (clean song); top-5 band discussions; opinion line-up
weeks.hw: 5-line opinion paragraph

skills.L: Listen to song excerpts and catch the opinion words
skills.S: Express and justify opinions about music
skills.R: Read a short music review and find the opinions
skills.W: Write a 3-sentence song review

lp.wu: Music Opinions Relay: Write 'I think... because' on the board. Students line up in two teams. Each student runs to the board, writes one word (e.g., 'think', 'because', an adjective like 'good'), and runs back. The team with the correct sentence first wins.
wuAlt: Quick Poll: Ask 'Do you like pop music?' Students stand if yes, sit if no. Ask follow-ups: 'Why?'
Word Association: Say 'music'. Students say one word (e.g., 'fun', 'loud', 'singing')
lp.pres: Show flashcards of music genres (pop, rock, rap). Model sentences: 'I think pop is good because it's fun.' Ask students to repeat. Check understanding by asking: 'Is pop good or bad? Why?'
presAlt: Realia: Bring a phone with music. Play a song and say: 'I think this song is great because it's happy.'
Story: Draw a simple comic of a boy saying 'I think rock is cool because the drums are strong.'
lp.prac: Lyric gap-fill: give students the lyrics of a clean song the class likes (the teacher prints them) with the opinion adjectives removed (for example good, nice). Students listen and fill the gaps in pairs, then check answers as a class.
pracAlt: Matching Game: Cards with opinion adjectives (good, bad, fun, boring) and reasons (because it's fast, because it's slow). Students match them.
Sentence Builders: Give students word cards to build 'I think... because...' sentences.
lp.ls: Opinion Listening: Play a 1-minute clip of a teen saying: 'I think rap is exciting because the words are strong.' Students write down the opinion and the reason. Check answers together. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Opinion Line-Up: Call out an opinion (e.g., 'I think music is boring'). Students line up on one side if they agree, the other if they disagree. Quick discussion: 'Why?'
lp.prod: Top-5 Band Discussion: Groups of 3. Each group writes their top 3 music genres. They use 'I think... because...' to justify. Groups present their choices to the class.
lp.rw: Music Review Reading: Give a short review of a song (e.g., 'This song is great because it's happy and easy to sing.'). Students underline the opinion and the reason. Then write 3 sentences about their favorite song using 'I think... because...'.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one opinion about a song or singer with because ("I think ___ is great because ___.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students write 5 opinion adjectives (good, bad, fun, boring, loud). Teacher calls out reasons (e.g., 'because it's fast'). Students cross off if they have a matching adjective.
Play music. When it stops, students say an opinion about the last song (e.g., 'I think it's loud!').
Student 1: 'I think pop is good.' Student 2: 'Because it's fun.' Student 3: 'I think rock is cool.' Continue the chain.
Teacher describes a genre (e.g., 'This music is fast and has strong drums'). Students guess: 'Rock!'
Two teams. Each student runs to the board, writes one word to complete 'I think... because...'. First correct team wins.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about music they don't like.
Support: Use sentence frames: 'I think ____ is ____ because ____.'
hw: Write a 5-line paragraph about your favorite song: 'My favorite song is ___. I think it is ___. because ___. It is ___. I like it.'
Draw a picture of your favorite song and write 2 sentences about it using 'I think... because...'.
Interview a family member: 'Do you like music? Why?' Write their answers.
lp.tip: Use Moroccan music examples (e.g., Gnawa) to connect the theme to students' culture, making the language more relevant and memorable.

weeks.obj: talk about devices, say what they usually do and what they are doing now
weeks.lang: tech words; present simple (usually, every day) and present continuous (now); like/love/hate + -ing
weeks.res: Worksheets; Lesson Plans/Technology
weeks.act: Tech charades; now-or-usually sorting game; class tech survey
weeks.hw: write about your tech habits (5 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to phone calls and tick what people usually do and what they are doing now
skills.S: Ask and answer Do you usually...? and What are you doing?
skills.R: Read a short text about a day with a phone and sort the verbs
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about my tech habits (3 usual, 2 now)

lp.wu: Tech charades: students draw a word from a hat (phone, laptop, tablet, game console, headphones, camera, smartwatch) and mime using it. The class guesses "Are you using a phone?"
wuAlt: Picture bingo with devices.
Pair talk: tell your partner two things you do on your phone.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of devices. Contrast the present simple (habit) and the present continuous (now): "I usually listen to music on my phone. Right now I'm using a laptop." Draw two columns on the board: Usually (always, usually, never, every day) and Now (now, at the moment, today). Model with pictures: "Amina usually plays games after school. Today she is doing homework." Check: "Do you usually use a laptop? Are you using a laptop now?"
presAlt: Students stand up if the sentence is a habit and sit if it is now.
Show two short clips and ask "Is it a habit or now?"
lp.prac: Now or usually? Teams get cards with twelve sentences ("She plays football on Fridays", "He is watching a video now") and sort them into the two columns. Then they complete sentence gaps with the correct form (plays or is playing).
pracAlt: Mini-whiteboard quiz: the teacher says a time word and students write a sentence.
Sentence building: reorder words to make a habit or now sentence.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short phone conversations twice ("I usually text my friends after school, but now I'm watching a film."). Students tick a grid for what each person usually does and what they are doing now. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Device freeze: the teacher calls a device ("laptop") and students mime using it. When the teacher says "Freeze!" they ask one student "What are you doing?" and the student answers "I'm using a laptop."
lp.prod: Tech habits survey: groups of three write a four-question survey ("Do you usually play video games? How often do you use your phone?"), ask five classmates and report: "Four students usually use their phones every day. Today Sara is using a tablet." They show the results on a simple bar graph.
lp.rw: Read a short text "A day with my phone" (usual habits and what the writer is doing now, about eight sentences). Underline the present simple in one colour and the present continuous in another. Write five sentences: three about your usual tech habits and two about what you are doing now.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence that is a habit and one that is happening now, and hand it in at the door.
g: Mime a device and the class guesses with Are you using...?
Sort sentence cards into habit and now columns.
Mime a device, freeze, and answer What are you doing?
Ask classmates tech habit questions and note the answers.
Find the odd word out in lists of devices and verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short paragraph comparing your usual week and today.
Support: two-column board (Usually / Now) with a sentence frame for each.
hw: Write 5 sentences about your tech habits (3 usual, 2 now).
Ask a family member what they usually do on their phone and write 2 sentences.
List five apps you use and say how often (always, usually, sometimes, never).
lp.tip: Present simple and present continuous is a classic confusion: keep the time words (usually and now) on the board and ask "Is it a habit or is it now?" before every answer. Local examples like WhatsApp or TikTok make the topic real.

weeks.theme: Stories: telling a story in the past
weeks.obj: tell a short story in the past using sequence words and regular and irregular verbs
weeks.lang: past simple (regular and irregular); first, then, after that, finally; was/were
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Stories; Reading tasks/Fables
weeks.act: Story from pictures; story strips; group story; simple fable reading
weeks.hw: write a picture story (8 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to a short story and put pictures in order
skills.S: Tell a short story from pictures to another group
skills.R: Read a simple fable and underline the past verbs and sequence words
skills.W: Write a story of 6 to 8 sentences with sequence words

lp.wu: Mime and guess: students take turns miming a past action (lost a phone, missed the bus, found a wallet) while the others guess "You lost your phone!"
wuAlt: Verb quiz: the teacher says a base verb and students give the past form.
Pair talk: tell your partner what you did first this morning.
lp.pres: Show a four-picture comic strip about a boy who loses his phone. Tell the story with sequence words: "First he went to the park. Then he lost his phone. After that he asked a man. Finally he found it." Underline the sequence words and past verbs and ask students to sort the verbs (regular or irregular). Check understanding with a picture-ordering question: "What happened first?"
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story with gaps and students supply the sequence word.
Show a story in four pictures and ask students to number them.
lp.prac: Story strips: pairs get six jumbled sentences of a short story and put them in order using the sequence words, then read it aloud to another pair.
pracAlt: Sentence building: reorder words to make a past sentence.
Tell the picture story in pairs, one sentence each.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short story twice: "Last Friday Omar went to the market. First he bought some bread. Then he saw his friend. After that they ate an ice cream. Finally Omar went home." Students order five pictures and answer three questions. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Sequence relay: the teacher reads a jumbled story sentence by sentence; teams race to put the sentence strips in order on the wall.
lp.prod: Group story: each group gets six picture cards in a sequence (for example getting lost in a city). They write six sentences with sequence words and past verbs, then tell the story to another group, who ask "What happened next?"
lp.rw: Read a simplified fable (The Hare and the Tortoise, about ten short lines). Underline the past verbs and the sequence words. Then write a new ending of three sentences.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the first two sentences of a story with First and Then, and hand it in at the door.
g: Mime a past action and the class guesses.
Put jumbled story sentences in order.
Each student adds one past sentence to a picture story.
Race to order story sentences on the wall.
Tell a story and the listeners guess what comes next.
diff: Fast finishers: write the story with extra detail (where, when, who).
Support: sentence frame "First ___. Then ___. After that ___. Finally ___." and the verb chart.
hw: Write a picture story (8 sentences) with First, Then, After that, Finally.
Tell a family member a short story from your week and write 3 sentences.
Find a short story in English online and underline 5 past verbs.
lp.tip: Beginners tell stories best from pictures. Give the sequence words as a frame and accept simple sentences: the goal is order and past verbs, not long stories.
