weeks.obj: complete sample A2 Key reading tasks and understand the format
weeks.lang: KET reading part formats; skimming and scanning
weeks.res: KET folder (sample papers)
weeks.act: Guided KET reading part 1-2 practice; strategy notes; team question hunt
weeks.hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet from the KET folder.

skills.L: KET listening part 1 samples - format tour
skills.S: KET-style personal questions in pairs
skills.R: Complete KET reading parts 1-2 (skimming) (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style sentence writing (part 6 style)

lp.wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with KET reading task prompts. Teacher hands out a grid with 'Find someone who can read a short text quickly' and 'Find someone who knows what skimming means'. Students mingle, ask questions, and mark names. They report back to the class: 'Youssef can read a short text quickly!'
wuAlt: Students play 'Quiz Quiz Trade' with KET reading terms. Each student gets a card with a term like 'skimming' or 'scanning', they quiz a partner, trade cards, and find a new partner.
Students do a 'Picture Prompt' game. Teacher shows a KET reading part 1 image, students shout out what they see in English to build vocabulary.
lp.pres: Teacher uses a PowerPoint slide to show the KET reading part 1 format (multiple-choice matching). Teacher models skimming by reading a short text aloud quickly, then asks 'What is this text about?'. Students repeat the process with a new text. Teacher checks understanding by asking 'Do we read every word for skimming?' and students answer 'No!'.
presAlt: Teacher uses flashcards with KET reading task numbers (1, 2, 3) and describes each part: 'Part 1 is matching pictures to words'. Students repeat the task numbers and descriptions.
Teacher draws a simple KET reading part 2 (multiple-choice) on the board and explains 'We choose A, B, or C'. Students practice saying the options.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs on a guided KET reading part 1 worksheet. Teacher circulates and helps with skimming strategies. They then play 'Reading Race' where they time each other to complete the task. Teacher gives support by highlighting key words in the text.
pracAlt: Students play 'Team Question Hunt' in groups of three. Teacher hides KET reading questions around the room. Groups race to find and answer them, writing answers on a whiteboard.
Students do 'Sentence Match-Up' with KET reading part 2. Teacher cuts up sentences and options, students work in pairs to match them correctly.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short text aloud twice with five words missing. Students fill the gaps on a worksheet to practise text completion, then check with the teacher.
lp.re: Students play 'Simon Says' with KET reading actions. Teacher says 'Simon says skim the text!' or 'Simon says scan for names!'. Students move around the room to stay active.
lp.prod: Students work in groups of four to create their own KET reading part 1 quiz. They draw four simple pictures and write matching descriptions. Each group quizzes another group, and the class votes on the best quiz.
lp.rw: Students complete a short KET reading part 2 (multiple-choice) text about a school trip. They read the text and choose the correct answers (A, B, or C). Then, they write two simple sentences about their own school trip using 'I went to...' or 'I saw...'.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one reading strategy you will use in an exam (skim, scan, check the options) and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams race to match KET reading questions to the correct answers on the board.
Students toss a ball and name a KET reading word when they catch it.
Teacher calls out a word from the text, students find it in their books and point.
One student is the quiz master, others answer KET reading questions.
Students search a text for specific words and raise their hands when found.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a short paragraph about their favorite book using KET reading vocabulary.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with key vocabulary from the texts to complete the reading tasks.
hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet from the KET folder.
Write three sentences about what you read today in English.
Find a short English text online (like a menu or sign) and practice skimming it.
lp.tip: Use short, familiar texts (a message, a menu, a notice) so students learn the exam format without extra difficulty. Teach one strategy at a time: skim first, then scan for the answer.

weeks.obj: complete a KET-style paired speaking task confidently
weeks.lang: KET speaking part 1-2 frames
weeks.res: KET folder; Speaking tests folder
weeks.act: Mock KET speaking in pairs with observer rubric; feedback circles; retry
weeks.hw: Record yourself answering 'What do you like doing in your free time?' and send to teacher.

skills.L: KET listening part 2 samples
skills.S: KET speaking parts 1-2 with frames
skills.R: KET reading part 3 practice (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style short message writing

lp.wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three sentences about their free time (e.g., 'I play football', 'I watch TV', 'I speak Spanish'), then share with a partner who guesses the lie. Teacher models first with own sentences.
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking 'Do you...?' questions (e.g., 'Do you play video games?') and tally responses on a bingo sheet.
Free Time Charades: Students act out free time activities (e.g., 'swimming', 'reading') while classmates guess the verb phrase.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of free time activities (e.g., football, cinema, music). Model KET Part 1 frames: 'What do you like doing in your free time?' and 'I like...' with answers. Elicit responses from students and check understanding with thumbs up/down for correct/incorrect answers.
presAlt: Realia Display: Bring in props (e.g., football, book, headphones) and ask 'What do you do with this?' to elicit activity vocabulary.
Dialogue Modeling: Teacher and student role-play a short conversation using KET frames, then students repeat in pairs.
lp.prac: KET Part 1 Drill: Students practice asking and answering 'What do you like doing?' with a partner using flashcards. Teacher circulates to correct pronunciation and provide sentence starters like 'I like...' or 'I don't like...'. Use the Movers Speaking PowerPoints in the Speaking materials folder for picture-description practice.
pracAlt: Matching Game: Students match activity pictures to verb phrases (e.g., 'play football') and then use them in sentences.
Chain Reaction: One student says 'I like...', the next repeats it and adds their own, building a chain.
lp.ls: Listening practice: students listen to two friends talking about free time and tick the activities they hear (swimming, cinema...) on a worksheet. The teacher reads the script twice if no recording is available.
lp.re: Free Time Relay: Divide class into two teams. One student runs to the board, writes an activity verb (e.g., 'play'), and returns to tag the next, who adds the noun (e.g., 'football'). Fastest team wins.
lp.prod: Mock KET Speaking Part 2: Students work in pairs. Student A describes their free time preferences using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'. Student B asks follow-up questions like 'Why?' or 'When do you...?'. Teacher uses a rubric to observe and note strengths/areas for improvement.
lp.rw: KET Reading Part 3 Practice: Students read a short text about a teenager's free time (e.g., 'My name is Sam. I like football and music.') and answer multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'What does Sam like?') by circling A, B, or C.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two questions you would like an examiner to ask you in a speaking test and hand it in at the door.
g: One student mimes an activity (e.g., 'swimming') while others guess using 'Do you...?'
Students listen to teacher call out activities and mark them on their bingo cards
Students match activity pictures to verb phrases on cards
Students ask 'What do you like doing?' to three classmates in 2 minutes each
Pairs practise the KET Part 1 questions and swap examiner and candidate roles.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 sentences about a friend's free time using 'He/She likes...'.
Support: Use sentence frames ('I like...') and picture prompts during the mock speaking task.
hw: Record yourself answering 'What do you like doing in your free time?' and send to teacher.
Write 5 questions to ask a friend about their free time.
Draw 3 free time activities and label them in English.
lp.tip: Encourage students to use 'I like...' and 'I don't like...' naturally, not just memorized answers. Pair stronger students with weaker ones to build confidence during mock exams. Use the speaking rubric notes this week.

weeks.obj: review the year across stations with accuracy and speed
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.res: Games; Tests/Grammar tests (selected)
weeks.act: 5 stations with a passport; team challenge quiz; error auction
weeks.hw: make a revision card for each grammar point (one example sentence each)

skills.L: Listen to two short texts and answer questions at the listening station
skills.S: Ask and answer review questions at the speaking station
skills.R: Read short texts and correct mistakes at the grammar stations
skills.W: Write a 6-sentence paragraph about myself using three tenses

lp.wu: Station passports: hand out a passport to each team of four and explain that they stamp each station when they reach 80 percent. Warm-up: the teacher shows five flashcards from across the year and students say a sentence for each.
wuAlt: Quick quiz with questions from every term (name, routine, food, past).
Pair talk: tell your partner one thing you can do now that you could not do in October.
lp.pres: Explain the five stations (grammar 1, grammar 2, listening, vocabulary, speaking) and the rules. Run a quick class poll on the grammar the class found hardest (present simple he/she, past irregulars, present continuous) and re-teach one of them for three minutes.
presAlt: Show a year-in-pictures poster and ask students to say what they did in each term.
Pairs write three questions they would like the class to answer.
lp.prac: Stations 1 and 2 (grammar): error correction cards (present simple he/she, past simple regular and irregular, present continuous) and a verb-form quiz. Teams correct the mistakes and stamp the passport.
pracAlt: Mini-whiteboard grammar race.
Error auction: teams bid on correct sentences from a mixed list.
lp.ls: Station 3 (listening): the teacher reads two short texts twice (a daily routine and a holiday story). Students tick or number the answers. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Station 4 (vocabulary): Pictionary and Taboo with the year's topics (food, clothes, places, jobs, travel).
lp.prod: Station 5 (speaking): interview cards with eight questions from the year ("What time do you get up? What did you do yesterday? What are you going to do this weekend?"). Pairs ask and answer; the teacher stamps the passports.
lp.rw: Final round: each student writes a six-sentence paragraph about themselves using the frame "My name is ___. I usually ___. Yesterday I ___. Next weekend I'm going to ___."
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one grammar point you feel sure about and one you want to practise again, and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams collect stamps at each station.
Bid on the correct sentences and fix the wrong ones.
Draw a word from the year and the team guesses.
Describe a word without saying the taboo words.
Ask and answer review questions in pairs.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short story that uses all three tenses.
Support: grammar summary card with one example for each tense.
hw: Make a revision card for each grammar point (one example sentence each).
Practise the interview questions with a family member.
Choose the three words you found hardest this year and write a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Photograph the stations for your records. Tick the checklist during the speaking station and note which grammar points need more work before the final assessment.

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls this week. Optional eco poster: groups design a poster for the American Space with five rules using imperatives and should ("Don't litter." "You should turn off the lights."). Both forms are already taught.
occ.hw: Write 3 sentences about what you should do to help the planet.

weeks.obj: complete the final written and speaking assessments and celebrate the year
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.res: Tests; program certificates pack
weeks.act: Final papers; speaking slots; awards and thank-you circle
weeks.hw: choose one thing you will do this summer to practise English and write it in a sentence

skills.L: Listen to a short text and answer six questions
skills.S: Take part in a short paired speaking test
skills.R: Read short texts and answer questions
skills.W: Write a short email and a picture story

lp.wu: Find someone who...: students mingle with year-review prompts ("can swim", "went to a new place last year", "usually wakes up at 7") and ask classmates the questions to find a name for each prompt.
wuAlt: Quick quiz from the year (teams, five questions).
Pair talk: tell your partner your favourite lesson of the year.
lp.pres: Explain the assessment: Part 1 is a written paper of about 35 minutes with four tasks (vocabulary gap fill, matching short dialogues, a short email of about 30 words, a five-sentence picture story). Part 2 is a short paired speaking test. Go through one example of each task type before starting.
presAlt: Show a model answer for the email task and discuss why it is a good answer.
Students list the tasks they feel confident about.
lp.prac: Part 1 written paper: students complete four tasks. Task 1: gap fill with ten items. Task 2: match questions to answers. Task 3: a short email (about 30 words) about a trip. Task 4: a five-sentence picture story. The teacher circulates only to clarify instructions. Build the paper from the Tests folder or use the task types above.
pracAlt: Use the Semester 1 paper as a model and write new items for the second half.
Split the class into two halves: half do the paper while half do the speaking test.
lp.ls: Listening task: the teacher reads a short text twice about a girl's weekend ("Last Saturday Sara got up at 8. She went to the market with her mother...") and students answer six questions (true/false and short answers). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: While pairs wait for their speaking slot, students play a quiet year-review quiz (teams, five questions) or complete a puzzle sheet.
lp.prod: Paired speaking test: in pairs, students take turns for about five minutes. Part A: personal questions (name, family, routine). Part B: a picture description. Part C: a short roleplay (order food or ask directions). The teacher scores communication, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation (1 to 3 each).
lp.rw: Self-assessment: students complete "I can..." statements (colour in each) and write one goal for the next level.
lp.st: Awards circle: each student receives one positive comment from the teacher and nominates a classmate for a class award (best helper, funniest, most improved). Students write thank-you notes on sticky notes.
g: Teams answer review questions from the whole year.
Order and tell a picture story as a team.
Nominate classmates for fun awards using superlatives.
Write short thank-you notes to classmates and the teacher.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second picture story or a longer email.
Support: frame sentences on the board and a verb chart during the written paper.
hw: Choose one thing you will do this summer to practise English and write it in a sentence.
Write a thank-you message to a classmate or the teacher (3 sentences).
Read one short English text and note 5 new words.
lp.tip: Keep the tone celebratory and use the checklist for the speaking test. Send the final reports home and hand out the certificates at the closing ceremony.

I can celebrate my progress

levels.desc: A first English class for teens aged 12-16. Thirty weeks build a strong A1 base · present simple, be, have got, can, daily routines, food, directions · through teen-relevant themes (identity, friends, school, free time), with pair and group work every week and the first KET-style tasks appearing from mid-S1.

levels.label: Teens · Intermediate

weeks.theme: Welcome back and getting to know you
weeks.obj: ask and answer questions with the correct word order, keep a conversation going with follow-up questions, and introduce a partner to the class
weeks.lang: question forms and word order (wh- word + do/does/did/be/can + subject + verb); who as subject (Who lives here?); follow-up questions (Really? Why? What about you?); spelling and numbers review
weeks.res: First day games; Question words and structure worksheets
weeks.act: Two truths and a lie mingle; question builder race; partner interviews with follow-up questions; class facts wall
weeks.hw: write a six-sentence profile of your partner from your interview notes

skills.L: Listen to two teens meeting on the first day and complete a profile card
skills.S: Ask and answer eight questions with at least three follow-ups
skills.R: Read a short teen profile and answer five questions
skills.W: Write a six-sentence profile of a partner

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie: each student writes three statements about themselves on a slip (two true, one false) and mingles, reading them to three partners. Partners guess the lie and ask one follow-up question. The teacher listens for missing auxiliaries to use in the presentation.
wuAlt: Speed introductions: inside-outside circle, 30 seconds per partner, one new fact each time.
Phone photo: students show one photo from their phone (or draw one) and the partner asks three questions about it.
lp.pres: Write six answers on the board ("Karim", "In Oujda", "Because I love football", "Twice a week", "My cousin", "At 7:30") and elicit a question for each. Build the word-order table together: question word, auxiliary (do, does, did, is, are, can), subject, main verb. Contrast "Where do you live?" with "Where does she live?" and show that who as subject needs no auxiliary ("Who lives here?"). Check with five wrong questions on the board ("Where you live?") that students correct in pairs.
presAlt: Error hunt: six incorrect questions go on the board and pairs fix them, then compare with another pair.
Cut-up cards: groups rebuild eight questions from jumbled words and then sort them by auxiliary.
lp.prac: Question builder race: teams of four receive jumbled word cards and race to build and read aloud ten questions (What time does the lesson start? Where did you go yesterday?). Then pairs interview each other with eight prompt cards (name, home, free time, brothers and sisters, favourite subject, last weekend, something you can do, plans for Friday) and must ask at least one follow-up each time ("Really? Why?"). The teacher monitors the word order.
pracAlt: Quiz Quiz Trade: each student has a question card, asks a partner, swaps cards and moves on.
Find someone who: a grid of eight prompts ("has been to Spain", "plays an instrument") turned into questions by the students.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short dialogue twice. Nora: "Hi, I'm Nora. Are you new?" Adam: "Yes, I moved here from Casablanca last month." Nora: "Why did you move?" Adam: "My dad has a new job. I play basketball and I'm learning the guitar." Nora: "Me too! I play in a band on Saturdays." Students complete a profile card for Adam (from, reason, hobbies) and write the three questions Nora asked. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Hot seat: one student sits with a secret identity card (a famous athlete, singer or YouTuber) behind them. The class asks wh- questions in the correct word order and the student answers in role until the identity is guessed. Teams score a point for every correct question.
lp.prod: Class profile project: in pairs, students interview each other for four minutes with at least eight questions, three of them follow-ups. They then join another pair and introduce their partner in six sentences ("This is Hamza. He is 15 and he lives near the stadium."). The class adds the facts to a class facts wall (the most common hobby, the most common birthday month).
lp.rw: Read a short profile of a teen (about 60 words) and answer five questions in full sentences. Then write a six-sentence profile of the partner using the interview notes, checking each sentence for the verb form.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one question you still want to ask a classmate, then ask it at the door and listen to the answer.
g: Students read three statements and the class guesses the lie by asking questions.
A student answers questions in role as a secret famous person.
Teams rebuild jumbled questions and read them aloud for points.
Students turn grid prompts into questions and collect names.
The class asks yes/no questions to find a secret object or person.
diff: Fast finishers: write five questions to ask a famous person and answer them as that person.
Support: give a question-word table with the auxiliary and one model question for each prompt card.
hw: Write a six-sentence profile of your partner from your interview notes.
Write five questions you would ask a new student, in the correct word order.
Choose a famous teen athlete or artist and write five questions you would like to ask them.
lp.tip: Use this week as a diagnostic: note who still drops the auxiliary ("Where you live?") and who can keep a conversation going with follow-ups. Use the notes to set pairs for the next weeks and to decide who needs extra support.

weeks.obj: describe people's appearance and personality with present simple, have got and look like, and ask What is she like?
weeks.lang: present simple he/she/it; have got / has got; What does he look like? vs What is he like?; appearance (curly hair, tall, slim) and personality adjectives (shy, confident, funny, lazy, generous); and / but / because
weeks.res: Describing people, places and things worksheets; Describing games
weeks.act: Guess who with photo cards; two question types sorting game; describe your best friend pair talk; character profile writing
weeks.hw: write six to eight sentences describing a friend or family member (looks and personality)

skills.L: Listen to teens describing a friend or cousin and match them to photos
skills.S: Describe a person's looks and personality and ask What is he like?
skills.R: Read a short profile of a famous person and decide which adjectives fit
skills.W: Write a description of a friend or family member (looks and personality)

lp.wu: Guess who: the teacher puts five photos of well-known people (athletes, actors, singers) on the board and describes one ("She is tall, she has long dark hair and she plays tennis"). Students guess, then take turns describing a photo in pairs.
wuAlt: Adjective line-up: students stand in a line from "very shy" to "very confident" by their own opinion and explain their position to a neighbour.
Draw and describe: one student describes a face while the partner draws it without looking at the original.
lp.pres: Show two questions on the board: "What does he look like?" and "What is he like?" and elicit answers using photos ("He is tall and slim. He has short black hair." and "He is funny and a bit lazy."). Sort appearance and personality adjectives into two columns and teach have got / has got for features. Practise third person -s with "She likes", "He has got". Check understanding with a quick sort: "Is shy an appearance or a personality word? Which question do we ask for it?"
presAlt: Show a short text about a famous person and ask students to underline appearance in one colour and personality in another.
Use a family tree on the board and describe two relatives, then ask students to describe a third.
lp.prac: Two questions pairs: Student A asks "What does your best friend look like?" and Student B answers, then they swap roles with "What is your best friend like?". Then they play Describe it with cards of well-known people: one student describes without naming, the other guesses, and the describer must use at least one have got sentence and one personality adjective. The teacher notes -s errors on the board.
pracAlt: Matchmaker: students read short profiles and match them with the right photos.
Character traits cards: groups sort adjectives into positive and negative and make a sentence for each.
lp.ls: The teacher reads three short descriptions twice. For example: "My cousin Sara is 16. She is quite tall and she has curly hair. She is very funny but she is sometimes late." Students match each description to one of five photos and note one personality word for each person. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Hot seat with personalities: a student sits with a card describing a character ("kind, shy, loves animals") behind them and the class gives clues using He/She is... and He/She has got... until the student guesses who they are.
lp.prod: Describe your best friend: in pairs, students prepare a one-minute talk about a friend or family member covering looks, personality, one thing the person likes and one reason they like them ("I like Yassine because he is generous"). They present the talk to another pair, who ask two follow-up questions.
lp.rw: Read a short profile of a famous person (about 80 words) and underline the appearance and personality words. Then write a description of a friend or family member (six to eight sentences) using have got, look like and at least three adjectives.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about the person sitting next to you using has got and one personality adjective, and hand it in at the door.
g: One student describes a photo card and the class guesses the person.
One student describes a face while the partner draws it.
Groups sort adjectives into positive and negative and add example sentences.
Students match short profiles with photos.
Students stand along a line of adjectives and justify their place.
diff: Fast finishers: write a profile of a fictional character using five different adjectives and two because clauses.
Support: give a table of appearance and personality words with pictures and a sentence frame.
hw: Write six to eight sentences describing a friend or family member (looks and personality).
Choose a famous person and write five sentences with has got and is.
Ask a family member What are you like? and write their answer in two sentences.
lp.tip: Teens enjoy describing famous people but avoid negative comments about classmates or real people: keep the language of personality kind and use adjective pairs (shy but friendly). Correct the -s on has and likes gently every time.

weeks.obj: compare weekday and weekend routines and say how often they do things with adverbs of frequency and time expressions
weeks.lang: present simple (statements, negatives, questions); adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never) and their position; How often...? once, twice, three times a week; every day / on weekdays / at weekends; prepositions of time (at, in, on)
weeks.res: Adverbs of frequency worksheets; Present simple questions worksheets
weeks.act: Class routine survey with graph; weekday vs weekend comparison; frequency line-up; routine blog post
weeks.hw: write six to eight sentences comparing your weekdays and your weekends

skills.L: Listen to two teens talk about their week and complete a timetable
skills.S: Ask and answer How often do you...? and compare weekdays and weekends
skills.R: Read a short blog post about a teen's routine and answer questions
skills.W: Write six to eight sentences about my routine with adverbs of frequency

lp.wu: Frequency line-up: the teacher calls out an activity (check my phone, do homework, help at home, play football) and students stand along a line from "always" to "never". They tell a neighbour why: "I usually check my phone in the morning."
wuAlt: Two sentences, one lie: students say two sentences about their routine and the partner guesses which one is false.
Mime a routine action and let the class say what you do and how often.
lp.pres: Show a weekly timetable of a teen (Amina) with ticks for each day and elicit "How often does she go to the gym?" "She goes twice a week." Teach the frequency scale (always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never) and its position (before the main verb, after be). Review questions and negatives with do/does ("She doesn't usually have breakfast"). Add the time prepositions at, in, on (at 7, in the morning, on Fridays, at the weekend). Check understanding with true/false statements about Amina's timetable.
presAlt: Use a pie chart of how a class spends the week and ask students to describe it with percentages and frequency words.
Give a jumbled paragraph about a routine and ask students to order the sentences by time.
lp.prac: Class routine survey: students receive a grid with eight activities (go to bed after midnight, eat breakfast, walk to school, play video games, read for pleasure, help at home, exercise, study). They ask classmates "How often do you...?", record answers and then report in groups: "Most of us hardly ever...". Then pairs compare weekdays and weekends: "On weekdays I get up at 6:30 but at the weekend I sleep until 10."
pracAlt: Find someone who with how often questions ("never eats breakfast", "always walks to school").
Board game How often do you...? in groups of four.
lp.ls: The teacher reads two short monologues twice (Leila: "I usually get up at 6:30 on weekdays. I always take the bus. At the weekend I never set an alarm." Omar: "I train three times a week and I hardly ever watch TV."). Students complete a grid with times and frequencies. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Truth or lie routine: one student at a time says a sentence about their routine with a frequency adverb. The class votes true or false and the speaker answers "Yes, I do" or "No, I don't. I hardly ever...". Two points for a convincing lie.
lp.prod: Weekday vs weekend report: in pairs, students interview each other about both parts of the week and prepare a short report comparing their routines with three differences. Each pair presents to another pair, who write one question to ask after the report.
lp.rw: Read a short blog post "A day in my life" (about 80 words) and answer five questions. Then write six to eight sentences about your own routine using at least four adverbs of frequency and two time expressions.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you always do and one thing you never do, and hand it to the teacher at the door.
g: Students place themselves on a line from always to never and justify their choice.
A student states a routine sentence and the class guesses true or false.
Groups move round a board answering how often questions.
Students ask how often questions to find a name for each prompt.
A student mimes a routine action and the class says what they do and how often.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph about a classmate's routine from your interview notes (he/she verbs).
Support: give a frequency ladder with the five adverbs and a sentence frame "I usually ___ at ___."
hw: Write six to eight sentences comparing your weekdays and your weekends.
Make a one-week chart of your routine with ticks and write three How often questions about it.
Ask a family member How often do you...? about two activities and write their answers.
lp.tip: Many teens put the adverb in the wrong place ("I go always"). Show the rule on the board in colour and give a short correction round at the end of the lesson. Use survey results as real data for the report.

weeks.obj: contrast present simple (habits) with present continuous (now and these days) and describe what is happening in a picture
weeks.lang: present simple vs present continuous; time expressions (usually, every day vs now, at the moment, today, this week); state verbs (want, like, know, need) are not used with -ing; school subjects and activities
weeks.res: Present continuous worksheets; Present continuous questions worksheets
weeks.act: Spot the difference (usually vs today); mime and guess; school week text; sentence sort
weeks.hw: write six sentences about what you usually do at school and what is happening in your school this week

skills.L: Listen to a phone call between two friends and tick what each is doing now
skills.S: Describe what people usually do and what they are doing now
skills.R: Read a short text about a school's special week and underline both tenses
skills.W: Write six sentences contrasting a usual day and today

lp.wu: Mime and guess: students draw a card with a school activity (take notes, copy from the board, whisper, sleep in class, text under the desk) and mime it. The class says "You are taking notes!" and then "Do you usually take notes?"
wuAlt: Pair photo guess: one student describes what a person in a photo is doing, the partner finds the photo.
What am I doing? Students ask yes/no questions about a mimed action ("Are you holding something?").
lp.pres: Draw two columns on the board: "Every day" and "Right now". Use a student: "Sara usually sits at the front, but today she is sitting at the back." Elicit the form (am/is/are + -ing) and the time words for each column. Show the state verbs (want, like, know, need, have for possession) that stay in the simple form: "I want a drink" not "I am wanting". Check understanding with sentences on the board: "She usually wears glasses. Today she is wearing contact lenses." Students decide which tense fits.
presAlt: Show two pictures of the same classroom (a normal day and an exam day) and describe the differences.
Teach with a short phone-call script: "Where are you? I'm walking to school. I usually take the bus but it's late."
lp.prac: Spot the difference: pairs receive Picture A (a normal class) and Picture B (the same class today, with changes). They ask and answer "What does Sara usually do?" and "What is she doing today?" to find eight differences. Then they write four sentences contrasting usual and today ("Mr Ali usually sits at his desk but today he is standing at the board."). The teacher monitors the -ing spelling (running, writing) and the state verbs.
pracAlt: Present tense sort: groups sort 16 sentences into present simple and present continuous and correct the wrong ones.
Chain sentences: one student says what they usually do, the next says what they are doing this week.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short phone call twice. Hamza: "Where are you? I'm at the school gate. I usually walk with Youssef but he isn't here today. He is studying for a test." Students tick what each person is doing now and circle what they usually do. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Silent action chain: one student mimes an action and the next must say "You are ___ing" and then mime something new, no repeats. After five rounds, the class says what each person usually does at school.
lp.prod: This week at school: pairs invent a "school week report" for a school with unusual activities (a sports week, an exam week). They prepare six sentences: three about what students usually do and three about what is happening this week. Pairs present as news reporters, using "Right now..." and "Every day...".
lp.rw: Read a short text about a school's special week (about 80 words) and underline the present simple in one colour and the present continuous in another. Then write six sentences contrasting your usual school day and today.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence with usually and one with right now about yourself and hand it in at the door.
g: Pairs find differences between two pictures using both tenses.
One student mimes an action and the class says what they are doing.
Groups sort sentences into present simple and present continuous.
Pairs report on a school event live.
Teams correct wrong sentences with state verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short conversation on the phone with three present continuous and three present simple sentences.
Support: give two sentence frames (Every day I ___. Right now I am ___ing.) and a list of -ing spellings.
hw: Write six sentences about what you usually do at school and what is happening in your school this week.
Write five sentences about your family: what they usually do and what they are doing now.
Find a photo and write five sentences about what is happening in it.
lp.tip: The most common mistake is using the continuous for habits or the simple for actions happening now. Use time words as visual cues and do a quick correction round. State verbs are for stronger students: introduce them with two or three examples only.

occ.act: Halloween falls this weekend (31 Oct). Optional 10-minute task: the teacher shows a spooky party picture and students say what is happening ("A ghost is standing near the door. Two friends are laughing."), then write three present continuous sentences about it.

weeks.obj: talk about hobbies and interests with like/love/hate/enjoy + -ing and want/hope/plan + to + infinitive
weeks.lang: like/love/hate/enjoy/don't mind + -ing; be good at / be interested in + -ing; want/would like/hope/plan/decide + to + infinitive; What do you enjoy doing? Why do you like it?
weeks.res: Gerunds and infinitives worksheets; Free time and hobbies worksheets
weeks.act: Hobby survey and graph; verb pattern sort; one-minute hobby talk; hobby profile writing
weeks.hw: write eight sentences about a hobby using both verb patterns

skills.L: Listen to three teens talk about their hobbies and note the verb patterns
skills.S: Give a one-minute talk about a hobby
skills.R: Read short hobby profiles and find the verb patterns
skills.W: Write eight sentences about a hobby with two verb patterns

lp.wu: Hobby bingo: students receive a card with nine hobbies (draw, cook, gaming, football, photography, coding, dance, read, volunteering) and mingle asking "Do you enjoy cooking?" to find a person for each. The first to complete a line shouts "Bingo".
wuAlt: Top five: students write their five favourite free-time activities, then rank them with a partner and explain.
Mime a hobby while the class guesses with "You enjoy swimming!"
lp.pres: Write four sentences on the board: "I love playing the guitar. I don't mind washing up. I'm good at drawing. I want to learn the piano." Elicit what comes after each verb and group the verbs into two patterns: verb + -ing (like, love, hate, enjoy, don't mind, be good at, be interested in) and verb + to + infinitive (want, would like, hope, plan, decide). Show a scale of feeling from love to hate. Check with a gap-fill on the board: "She enjoys ___ (dance). He wants ___ (learn)."
presAlt: Show two hobby profiles with highlighted patterns and ask students to complete the rule themselves.
Sort verbs onto two posters on the wall in teams, then check with the teacher.
lp.prac: Verb pattern sort and speak: groups receive 16 verb cards and sort them into two patterns, then use them to ask each other questions ("What do you enjoy doing at the weekend? What do you want to do this summer?"). The teacher listens for wrong patterns ("I enjoy to swim") and writes them on the board for correction. Pairs then complete a short survey of five questions and report results.
pracAlt: Gerunds and infinitives card game in groups of four.
Find someone who is good at / interested in... with a mingle grid.
lp.ls: The teacher reads three short descriptions twice (Nour: "I love taking photos. I'm interested in learning to edit videos." Ilyas: "I enjoy playing football but I hate getting up early for training." Salma: "I want to be a vet. I'm good at looking after animals."). Students tick the hobbies and note one verb pattern for each person. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Four corners: the corners are love, like, don't like, hate. The teacher says an activity (getting up early, doing homework, playing video games, cooking) and students move to a corner and tell a neighbour a sentence with the right pattern.
lp.prod: One-minute hobby talk: students plan a talk about a hobby with a mind map (what it is, how often, why they like it, what they want to do next) and give it to a partner, who asks two follow-up questions. Then groups choose the most interesting hobby and share it with the class.
lp.rw: Read three short hobby profiles (about 50 words each) and find the verb patterns. Then write eight sentences about your own hobby using at least three verbs + -ing and two verbs + to + infinitive.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence with enjoy + -ing and one with want + to + infinitive and hand it in at the door.
g: Students mingle to find a classmate for each hobby square.
Students move to a corner of love, like, don't like or hate and justify.
Pairs rank their favourite activities and defend the order.
Groups sort verbs into -ing and to patterns and use them in sentences.
The class gives clues about a hobby for the student in the hot seat to guess.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short blog post about a hobby you would like to try, with three plans using hope/plan/want.
Support: give a two-column pattern table with six verbs and a model sentence for each.
hw: Write eight sentences about a hobby using both verb patterns.
Interview a family member about their hobbies and write three sentences with enjoy + -ing.
Make a list of five things you hope to do this year using hope to / plan to.
lp.tip: The two patterns are the main target. Do not worry about like + to at this level. Teens can talk for a long time about hobbies so keep the talk task short and use the follow-up questions to give everyone a role.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute reading: "Every year Moroccans celebrate the Green March on 6 November. Many families watch the speech and some schools organise events." Students underline the verbs and tell a partner what they enjoy doing on a national holiday.
occ.hw: Write three sentences about what you enjoy doing on a national holiday.

weeks.obj: talk about what they can and could do now and in the past and describe how well they do things with adverbs of manner
weeks.lang: can/can't and could/couldn't for ability; be good at / be bad at; adverbs of manner (well, badly, fast, hard, quickly, carefully, quietly); How well can you...? When I was seven I could...
weeks.res: Modal verbs of ability worksheets; Miming games
weeks.act: Skills challenge stations; past and present abilities mingle; How well can you...? interview; sports hero profile
weeks.hw: write eight sentences about a sports hero or someone you admire using can, could and adverbs

skills.L: Listen to a teen compare what she can do now and what she could do at seven
skills.S: Interview a partner with How well can you...? and When you were seven, could you...?
skills.R: Read a short profile of an athlete and complete a skills grid
skills.W: Write eight sentences about a person's abilities past and present

lp.wu: Challenge cards: students pick a one-minute challenge (balance on one leg, say a tongue twister, draw with the other hand, spell a word backwards) and try it while the class says what they can and can't do: "He can balance, but he can't spell backwards."
wuAlt: Superpowers: each student invents an unusual ability and the class guesses with "Can you...?"
Sport categories: teams write sports under headings (ball, water, winter, team, individual) in two minutes.
lp.pres: Show a photo of a famous athlete and write on the board: "She can run very fast. She could swim when she was five. She can't ski. She wasn't good at tennis." Elicit can/can't for present ability and could/couldn't for past ability. Teach adverbs of manner: regular adverbs with -ly (carefully, quietly) and the irregular ones (well, fast, hard). Show the position after the verb: "He plays well". Check with quick sentence transformations: "She is a fast runner" becomes "She runs fast".
presAlt: Show two short videos of the same skill done well and badly and elicit adverbs.
Use a table of past and present abilities of a class survey and read it aloud.
lp.prac: Skills circuit: groups of three rotate through five stations, each with a prompt card ("Can you whistle? How well? Could you do it when you were seven?"). At each station they interview a partner using can/could and an adverb and note the answer. The teacher listens for the form after can (no -s, no to). Then groups report the most surprising skill they found.
pracAlt: Find someone who can... and could... when they were seven.
Adverb charades: a student mimes an action in a manner (sleepily, quickly) and the class guesses the adverb.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a monologue twice. Rania: "I can swim well now but I couldn't swim when I was seven. I'm quite good at running but I'm bad at tennis because I can't hit the ball hard." Students complete a table of can now and could at seven for Rania and tick the adverbs they hear. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Superhero relay: teams build a sentence chain "Yesterday I couldn't fly, but today I can run fast because..." and race to complete five different sentences. The best sentence of the round wins a bonus point.
lp.prod: Sports hero profile: in pairs, students choose an athlete or a person they admire and prepare a short presentation (five sentences) about what the person can do now, what they could do as a child and how well they do it. Pairs present to another pair, who guess the person from the clues before the name is revealed.
lp.rw: Read a short profile of an athlete (about 80 words) and complete a skills grid (can, could, how well). Then write eight sentences about a person's abilities past and present using at least three adverbs.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you can do well and one thing you couldn't do two years ago, and hand it in at the door.
g: Groups rotate through stations interviewing each other about skills.
A student mimes an action in a manner and the class guesses the adverb.
Students invent abilities and the class asks Can you...? questions.
Students find classmates who could do something when they were seven.
Pairs give clues about an athlete using can, could and adverbs.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short speech "Why I admire ___" with six ability sentences.
Support: give a table with can/could in two columns and a list of adverbs with example sentences.
hw: Write eight sentences about a sports hero or someone you admire using can, could and adverbs.
Ask an older relative what they could do at your age and write three sentences.
List five things you want to be able to do next year and say how you will learn them.
lp.tip: Check that students do not add -s after can ("She can swims") and that adverbs come after the verb, not before it. Link to Week 5: ask students how their hobbies connect to their abilities.

weeks.obj: tell a partner what they did last weekend using regular and irregular past simple, and ask and answer Did you...? questions
weeks.lang: past simple regular and irregular verbs (statements, negatives, questions with did); was/were review; time expressions (yesterday, last night, last weekend, two days ago, in 2024); common irregular verbs (go, have, see, eat, buy, make, take, get, come, meet)
weeks.res: Irregular verbs flashcards; Past simple questions worksheets
weeks.act: Past simple question survey; two truths and a lie about the weekend; irregular verb relay; weekend story writing
weeks.hw: write a story of eight sentences about your best weekend or a day out

skills.L: Listen to two teens describe their weekend and note what they did and did not do
skills.S: Ask and answer past simple questions about last weekend
skills.R: Read a short weekend blog and find the irregular verbs
skills.W: Write eight sentences about a weekend with regular and irregular verbs

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie about the weekend: students write three sentences about what they did last weekend (two true, one false) and read them to a partner, who asks two questions ("Where did you go? Who did you go with?") before guessing the lie.
wuAlt: Verb tennis: partners say a base verb and the other answers with the past form, scoring a point for each correct form.
Photo memories: students show one photo from last weekend and the partner asks three questions.
lp.pres: Tell a short true story about your own weekend on the board with key verbs ("On Saturday I got up late. I had breakfast, then I went to the market with my mother. We bought some fruit and I met my cousin."). Underline the verbs and elicit which are regular (-ed) and which are irregular. Build the three forms on the board: positive (went), negative (didn't go) and question (Did you go? Yes, I did / No, I didn't). Show the -ed endings (/t/, /d/, /id/) and the spelling (study, studied; stop, stopped). Check by asking five Did you...? questions about the story.
presAlt: Give a jumbled weekend diary and ask students to order it, then underline the verbs.
Show a verb list with ten irregular verbs and ask students to sort by pattern (go-went, buy-bought, etc.).
lp.prac: Past simple question survey: students receive a grid with ten activities (watch a film, visit family, go shopping, play sport, eat out, play video games, study, meet friends, cook, help at home) and ask "Did you ... last weekend?" to find a classmate who did each one. They then report: "Hamza played football on Saturday and Salma visited her grandmother." The teacher monitors the question form (no -ed after did).
pracAlt: Irregular verb relay: teams race to write the past of verbs on cards and use each in a sentence.
Past simple dominoes in groups of four.
lp.ls: The teacher reads two short monologues twice (Imane: "On Saturday I got up late and had a big breakfast. We went to the beach but it was cold, so we didn't swim." Adam: "I stayed at home and played video games with my brother. We ordered pizza and watched a film."). Students tick what each person did and cross what they did not do. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Past simple chain story: students sit in a circle and add one sentence to a weekend story ("On Saturday Karim went to the market. He bought a jacket. Then he met..."). If a student repeats a verb or uses the wrong form, the story starts again from that point.
lp.prod: Weekend reporters: pairs interview each other about their last weekend for a "School radio" news item. They ask at least six questions (Where, Who with, What, When, How, Why), note the answers and then retell the partner's weekend to another pair in six sentences, including one thing that the partner did not do.
lp.rw: Read a short weekend blog (about 80 words) and underline the irregular verbs. Then write eight sentences about your own weekend or a day out using at least four irregular verbs and one negative sentence.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you did yesterday and one thing you didn't do, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students tell three weekend sentences and the class guesses the lie.
Teams race to write the past forms and sentences.
Groups match base forms and past forms.
Students ask Did you...? questions to complete a grid.
Pairs interview each other and report in a news item.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dialogue between a reporter and a teen about a great day out, using eight past simple questions.
Support: give the list of ten irregular verbs with pictures and a sentence frame "On Saturday I ___. I didn't ___."
hw: Write a story of eight sentences about your best weekend or a day out.
Write six Did you...? questions you would ask a friend about their holiday.
Ask a family member what they did on their last holiday and write three sentences.
lp.tip: The most frequent error is "Did you went?" Write it on the board and let students correct it. Keep a list of irregular verbs on the wall for the rest of the term and add two or three new ones each week.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute timeline: students put six cards about Morocco's road to independence (the exile of King Mohammed V in 1953, his return in November 1955, independence in 1956) in order and retell them with the past simple.

weeks.obj: talk about food and amounts using countable and uncountable nouns and quantifiers, and plan a menu within a budget
weeks.lang: countable and uncountable nouns; a lot of / lots of, much, many; a little, a few; some and any; How much...? How many...?; containers (a bottle of, a packet of, a kilo of)
weeks.res: Food lesson plans; Expressions of quantity worksheets
weeks.act: Kitchen survey; fridge inventory pair talk; party menu budget task; recipe writing
weeks.hw: write a healthy eating plan for one day or a recipe with quantities

skills.L: Listen to a teen planning a party shopping list and note the quantities
skills.S: Ask and answer How much / How many questions and plan a menu
skills.R: Read a short recipe and classify the nouns
skills.W: Write a recipe or eating plan with quantities

lp.wu: Food sort: teams receive 20 food cards (rice, tomatoes, milk, bread, eggs, olives, sugar, water, chicken, apples, flour, harira) and race to sort them into countable and uncountable. They then add one container to each card ("a packet of rice").
wuAlt: Fridge inventory: students draw what is in their fridge from memory and compare with a partner.
Category game: in two minutes write as many uncountable foods as possible.
lp.pres: Show two shopping baskets (one with items you can count, one with liquids and powders). Elicit "How many apples?" and "How much milk?" and build the rule on the board: many and a few with countable nouns, much and a little with uncountable nouns, a lot of and some with both. Teach the containers (a bottle of, a carton of, a packet of, a kilo of, a slice of). Add some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions. Check understanding with a quick quiz: "How many ___ or how much ___? tea, eggs, oil, sandwiches."
presAlt: Use a short video about much and many and pause to check.
Show a recipe and ask students to circle the quantifiers and the containers.
lp.prac: Party budget: groups of four plan a class party for 12 people with a budget of 200 dirhams. They receive a price list and ask each other "How many bottles of juice do we need? How much cheese is there?" and write a shopping list with quantities. The teacher listens for much/many errors and asks groups to justify their choices ("We need a lot of bread because...").
pracAlt: Quantifier race: teams write a sentence for each of 10 food items using a different quantifier.
Pair information gap: two fridges with different contents and questions with How much / How many.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a phone call twice. Salma: "We need some bread, a few tomatoes and a lot of juice. How much cheese do we have? A little. And how many eggs? Only two." Students complete a shopping list with quantities. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Food pyramid debate: pairs get a card with a food (chocolate, vegetables, fast food, water) and say "You should eat a lot of... because..." in 20 seconds. The class votes agree or disagree with a thumbs up.
lp.prod: Menu pitch: each group plans a balanced menu for a school sports day for 20 students, writes down quantities for each dish and presents it in one minute ("We are going to serve two kilos of rice and a few bottles of water.") The class asks one How much / How many question to each group.
lp.rw: Read a short recipe (about 70 words) and circle the countable and uncountable nouns. Then write a healthy eating plan for one day (breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks) with at least eight quantity expressions.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one How much and one How many question about the school canteen and ask a classmate at the door.
g: Teams sort food cards into countable and uncountable.
Groups plan a party menu within a budget using quantifiers.
Teams write sentences with different quantifiers for food items.
Pairs ask questions to find the differences between two fridges.
Pairs argue what we should eat a lot of or a little of.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dialogue in a cafe between a customer and a waiter using eight quantity expressions.
Support: give a table with countable and uncountable foods and the quantifiers that go with each.
hw: Write a healthy eating plan for one day or a recipe with quantities.
Write five sentences about what is in your kitchen using a lot of, a few and a little.
Ask a family member for a family recipe and write the ingredients with quantities.
lp.tip: Teens often say "How many water?" so show the pair much/many on two posters. Use real prices and real Moroccan dishes to make the budget task meaningful.

occ.act: Thanksgiving falls on Thursday 26 November. Optional 10-minute comparison: students list the foods of a Thanksgiving meal (turkey, potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie) and a Moroccan family meal, then count which are countable and uncountable and say how much or how many people usually eat.
occ.hw: Ask one person at home what they usually cook for a big family meal and write three sentences with quantities.

weeks.theme: At the cafe: polite requests and ordering
weeks.obj: order food and drink politely, make requests and offers, and deal with a small problem at a cafe
weeks.lang: Could I have...? Can I...? I'd like...; Would you like...? Anything else?; Excuse me, could you...?; polite problem phrases (I'm sorry, but... I didn't order this); reading a menu and the bill
weeks.res: Ordering food and drink worksheets; Requests and permission worksheets; Role-playing games
weeks.act: Menu reading task; cafe roleplay with problem cards; polite or rude sorting; dialogue writing
weeks.hw: write a cafe dialogue (8 to 10 lines) that includes a problem and a polite solution

skills.L: Listen to a teen ordering at a cafe and note the order and the price
skills.S: Order politely and solve a problem at a cafe in a roleplay
skills.R: Read a short menu and cafe review and answer questions
skills.W: Write a cafe dialogue with a problem

lp.wu: Polite or rude? The teacher reads ten requests in two tones ("Give me water." / "Could I have some water, please?") and students show a green card for polite and a red card for rude. They then rewrite the rude ones.
wuAlt: Menu memory: students look at a menu for 30 seconds and then write as many items as possible.
Guess the order: one student mimes ordering and the class guesses the food and drink.
lp.pres: Show a cafe menu on the board (tea, coffee, orange juice, sandwiches, pastries, a prices list in dirhams). Role-play a short order with a volunteer: "Hello, could I have a mint tea, please? And I'd like a chicken sandwich." "Anything else?" "No, thank you. How much is that?" Write the key phrases in three groups: ordering (I'd like, Could I have), offering (Would you like...? Anything else?), problems (I'm sorry, but this is cold. Could you bring another one?). Check with a polite/rude sorting activity.
presAlt: Play the AEF Practical English cafe scene or read a short script aloud and ask students to underline the polite phrases.
Show a bill and practise reading prices aloud.
lp.prac: Menu pairs: Student A is the waiter and Student B is the customer. They use a menu with prices and role-play the whole conversation (greeting, order, extra request, bill). Then they swap and add a problem card (cold food, wrong order, no change). The teacher monitors polite phrases and the intonation of requests.
pracAlt: Role-play cards: pairs draw a situation card and prepare a 6-line dialogue.
Mingle: students move round the room taking orders from three customers each.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short cafe dialogue twice. Customer: "Hello, could I have a tea with milk, please? And a cheese sandwich." Waiter: "Would you like something to drink with that? Anything else?" Customer: "No, thanks. How much is that?" Waiter: "That's 28 dirhams." Students write the order, the total and one polite phrase for each speaker. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Order relay: teams stand in lines and the first student whispers an order to the next; the last student writes it on the board and the team scores a point for each correct item and polite phrase.
lp.prod: Cafe roleplay with surprise: groups of three (waiter, two customers) perform a three-minute roleplay including an order, a problem and a solution. The audience writes down one polite phrase that they heard and gives feedback after each group.
lp.rw: Read a short menu and a cafe review (about 80 words) and answer five questions. Then write a cafe dialogue of eight to ten lines with a problem and a polite solution.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two polite sentences you would say in a cafe (one request and one problem) and hand them in at the door.
g: Students show green or red cards for polite and rude requests.
Teams pass orders along a line and the last student writes them.
Pairs role-play an order, then add a problem.
Students recall menu items after a 30-second look.
One student mimes an order and the class guesses.
diff: Fast finishers: write a polite email to a cafe manager about a problem with an order.
Support: give a phrase bank (ordering, offering, problems) with the polite versions highlighted.
hw: Write a cafe dialogue (8 to 10 lines) that includes a problem and a polite solution.
Design a menu for a teen cafe with six items and prices in dirhams.
Write five polite requests you could make at school or at home.
lp.tip: Intonation matters for politeness: model rising intonation for requests and let students copy. Keep the problem cards realistic and light-hearted so students feel comfortable complaining politely.

weeks.obj: describe a place and ask for and give directions using landmarks and prepositions
weeks.lang: there is/there are, is there...? Are there any...?; prepositions of place (next to, opposite, between, behind, in front of, on the corner); directions (go straight on, turn left/right, take the second left, cross the road, it's on your right); Excuse me, how do I get to...? Is there a ... near here?
weeks.res: Giving directions PowerPoints; There is / there are worksheets; Directions flashcards (map)
weeks.act: Map information gap; directions treasure hunt; describe my neighbourhood; directions writing
weeks.hw: write directions from the school to your home or to a place in the city (six to eight lines)

skills.L: Listen to directions and follow the route on a map
skills.S: Ask for and give directions using landmarks
skills.R: Read a short town guide and label a map
skills.W: Write directions using at least two landmarks

lp.wu: Map memory: the teacher shows a simple map for 30 seconds and students write down as many places as they remember. They compare with a partner and then say where each place is ("The pharmacy is opposite the bank").
wuAlt: Describe my street: students draw a quick map of their street and describe it to a partner, who draws it.
Place quiz: the teacher gives a definition ("You buy medicine here") and students say the place.
lp.pres: Draw a city map on the board with ten places (post office, bank, mosque, pharmacy, supermarket, park, cafe, library, cinema, bus station). Elicit "Is there a pharmacy near here? Yes, there is. It's next to the bank." and show the prepositions with arrows. Model a route from the school to the library with "Go straight on, take the second right, cross the road, it's on your left." Check with a quick "follow the route" game where students raise a hand when they reach the place.
presAlt: Play a short directions dialogue (the AEF Practical English episode on getting lost) and ask students to underline the phrases.
Use an online map of the local area and ask students to give a route.
lp.prac: Map information gap: Student A and Student B have the same map with different places missing. They ask "Where is the bakery? Is there a bank near here?" and give directions to complete the map. After that, pairs do a route challenge: one student chooses a starting point and gives directions to a secret place, and the partner guesses it.
pracAlt: Treasure hunt: groups follow written directions around the Space to find hidden cards.
Directions dominoes with prepositions of place.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short route twice: "Go straight on and take the second left. Walk past the bank and the mosque. The library is on your right, opposite the park." Students follow the route on a map and mark the destination. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Human GPS: one student closes their eyes and a partner guides them around the classroom with directions (left, right, straight on, stop) without touching them. They swap after one minute.
lp.prod: My neighbourhood guide: pairs design a simple map of an area that is real or imagined and write directions to three places. They swap maps with another pair and follow the directions, then give feedback on how clear they were.
lp.rw: Read a short town guide (about 80 words) and label a map using the descriptions. Then write directions from the school to your home or a place in the city (six to eight lines) with at least two landmarks and three prepositions.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences giving directions from the door of the classroom to the school gate and hand them in at the door.
g: Students recall places from a map and describe their positions.
Pairs complete a map by asking and giving directions.
Groups follow written directions to find hidden cards.
One student guides a partner with closed eyes using directions.
The teacher gives a definition and students name the place.
diff: Fast finishers: write directions between two places in your city that include three landmarks and two prepositions.
Support: give a vocabulary strip with the direction phrases and a labelled map.
hw: Write directions from the school to your home or to a place in the city (six to eight lines).
Draw a map of your neighbourhood and label eight places with prepositions.
Ask a family member for directions to a place you do not know and write them down.
lp.tip: Use real places in Oujda (the stadium, the university, the main street) as examples and let students draw their own maps. Make sure that left and right are checked physically with students in the first minutes.

weeks.obj: shop for clothes, compare prices and products with comparatives and too/enough, and bargain politely
weeks.lang: clothes and sizes; this/that/these/those; How much is/are...? Can I try it on?; comparatives (cheaper than, more expensive than, better than); too + adjective and (not) + adjective + enough (too small, not big enough); bargaining phrases (Could you make it cheaper?)
weeks.res: This / that / these / those PowerPoint; Clothes and fashion worksheets
weeks.act: Shop roleplay with price cards; compare two products; souk bargaining task; product review writing
weeks.hw: write a short review comparing two products or shops (eight sentences)

skills.L: Listen to a customer buying a jacket and note the size and price
skills.S: Shop and bargain politely, comparing two products
skills.R: Read two online adverts and compare them
skills.W: Write a comparison of two products or shops

lp.wu: Clothes auction: students receive play money and bid for clothing cards (a leather jacket, red trainers, a school bag) with phrases like "I'll give you 80 dirhams". The class decides which bid is best and why.
wuAlt: What am I wearing? One student describes a classmate's clothes without naming them and the others guess.
Brand quiz: teams list as many clothes words as possible in two minutes.
lp.pres: Show two jackets with price tags on the board (80 and 150 dirhams). Elicit comparisons: "The blue jacket is cheaper than the black one. The black one is more expensive but it's better." Teach too and enough: "This jacket is too small. It isn't big enough. These shoes are too expensive." Add shop phrases (Can I try it on? Do you have it in a larger size? How much is it? Could you make it cheaper?). Check understanding with pictures of a customer's problems ("too short", "not warm enough") and students complete the sentence.
presAlt: Play the AEF Practical English clothing store scene and ask students to note the questions.
Show an online shop page and compare two products in pairs.
lp.prac: Shop and compare: pairs receive catalogue cards with two products each (a phone, shoes, a bag) with prices and features. They compare them using comparatives and too/enough, then role-play a shop dialogue (customer asks about size and price, tries, decides). The teacher monitors comparative forms (more expensive, not expensiver) and the use of than.
pracAlt: Comparative card game: students compare two cards and use a different comparative each time.
Too or enough? Mini-whiteboard quiz with pictures.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short shop dialogue twice. Customer: "Can I try this jacket on? It's too big. Do you have it in a smaller size?" Assistant: "Yes, here you are. It's 180 dirhams." Customer: "That's too expensive. Could you make it cheaper?" Assistant: "I can do 150." Students note the size, the price before and after bargaining and the final decision. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Bargain battle: pairs have a buyer card and a seller card with a price range. They negotiate for 90 seconds with polite phrases and the pair that agrees the closest price to their target wins a point.
lp.prod: Souk role-play: groups of four run a small market (two sellers with different products, two buyers). Buyers visit both stalls, compare the products with comparatives and bargain; at the end they decide which stall was better and give reasons ("Stall A was cheaper but the quality wasn't good enough").
lp.rw: Read two short online adverts for similar products (about 40 words each) and answer comparison questions. Then write a short review comparing two products or shops (eight sentences) using at least four comparatives and two too/enough sentences.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one comparison between two things in your bag with than and one sentence with too, then hand it in at the door.
g: Students bid for clothing cards and justify their offers.
Pairs negotiate a price using polite phrases.
Students complete sentences about pictures with too or enough.
Students compare two cards with a different comparative each time.
Groups run a market with buyers and sellers.
diff: Fast finishers: write an online review of a product, comparing it with another one, in eight sentences.
Support: give a comparative table (cheap-cheaper, big-bigger, expensive-more expensive) and a dialogue frame.
hw: Write a short review comparing two products or shops (eight sentences).
Write five sentences with too and not enough about things at home or in your school.
Find the price of two similar products online and compare them in four sentences.
lp.tip: Bargaining is part of daily life in Morocco, so students bring real experience: ask them to share how they bargain in Arabic and then transfer the phrases to English. Check that they use than after the comparative.

weeks.obj: make plans and arrangements with going to and the present continuous, and invite, accept and decline politely
weeks.lang: be going to for plans and intentions; present continuous for fixed arrangements (I'm meeting Sara at five); Let's / Shall we / Why don't we...? / Would you like to...?; accepting and declining (Good idea! Sorry, I can't, I'm...); future time expressions (tonight, tomorrow, next weekend); weather forecast language
weeks.res: Making suggestions worksheets; Future forms worksheets
weeks.act: Diary swap and arrangement making; invitation role-play; weather forecast and plans; weekend plan writing
weeks.hw: write a text message group chat (8 lines) planning a weekend activity

skills.L: Listen to two friends arranging to meet and complete a diary
skills.S: Invite, accept and decline and make a plan with a partner
skills.R: Read a group chat and complete a weekend diary
skills.W: Write a weekend plan with going to and times

lp.wu: Weekend wish list: students write three things they want to do this weekend, then walk around saying "I'm going to..." until they find two others with the same plan and form a team.
wuAlt: Weather forecast: pairs present a weather forecast for Saturday and Sunday and say what they will do.
Plan chain: one student says a plan, the next repeats it and adds one of their own.
lp.pres: Show two diary pages: a plan ("Saturday: go to the beach, play football") and an arrangement ("Saturday at 4: meet Sara at the cafe"). Elicit: "I'm going to play football" for a plan and "I'm meeting Sara at four" for an arrangement with a time and a person. Write the form: be going to + verb and am/is/are + -ing. Teach suggestions and responses: Let's..., Shall we...?, Why don't we...?, Good idea! / Sorry, I can't, I'm busy / I'd love to but... Check understanding with sentences on the board: "Which is a plan and which is an arrangement?"
presAlt: Show a group chat on the board with five messages making plans and underline the future forms.
Use a calendar and ask students about their own next week.
lp.prac: Diary swap: each student has a half-filled diary for the week. They ask and answer ("What are you doing on Saturday at six? Are you free on Sunday afternoon?") to find a time to meet that works for both and write an arrangement. The teacher listens for the form: be going to + verb, and the auxiliary in present continuous questions.
pracAlt: Invitation mingle: students invite three people to different events and accept or decline with reasons.
Plan the perfect weekend in groups of four and rank the activities.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a phone call twice. Karim: "What are you doing on Saturday? I'm going to play football at three. Do you want to come?" Nora: "I'd love to, but I'm meeting my cousins at four. Shall we meet on Sunday?" Karim: "Good idea. Let's go to the cinema at five." Students complete Nora's diary and tick the invitation phrases. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Excuses game: one student invites a partner to an event and the partner must decline with a creative excuse beginning "I'm going to..." or "I'm ...ing". The class votes on the best excuse each round.
lp.prod: Plan a weekend trip: groups of four plan a day out (where, when, transport, food, activities) using going to and the present continuous and present it in two minutes. The class asks two questions and votes for the best plan.
lp.rw: Read a group chat of eight lines about a weekend plan and complete a diary with times and places. Then write your own group chat (eight lines) planning a weekend activity with at least two invitations and two responses.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one invitation and one polite excuse and hand them in at the door.
g: Students find classmates with the same weekend plan.
A student invites and the partner gives a creative excuse.
Pairs find a time that works for both.
Students repeat and add plans in a memory chain.
Pairs present a forecast and plan activities.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue between two friends making and changing plans (10 lines).
Support: give a table of plan sentences and arrangement sentences with time expressions and a response bank.
hw: Write a text message group chat (8 lines) planning a weekend activity.
Write five sentences about your plans for next week using going to.
Write an invitation to a friend for an event with time, place and what to bring.
lp.tip: Do not over-teach the difference between going to and the present continuous: both are acceptable for arrangements. Focus on the form and use the plan/arrangement contrast only as a first step. Keep the diary task realistic by using students' own timetable.

occ.act: Christmas week (25 December). Optional 10-minute winter party task: pairs plan a party with Shall we / Let's and a budget, and read two short facts about how people celebrate Christmas and New Year.
occ.hw: Write a short invitation (4 lines) to a winter party.
