weeks.obj: describe what was happening at a past moment with the past continuous and combine it with the past simple using when and while
weeks.lang: past continuous (was/were + -ing; negatives and questions); when and while; past simple vs past continuous (I was walking when I saw an accident); time phrases (at 8 o'clock last night, all evening)
weeks.res: When and while worksheet; Past continuous worksheets
weeks.act: Alibi interrogation game; picture story with was/were + -ing; when/while sentence building; what were you doing at...? writing
weeks.hw: write what you and five other people were doing at 8 p.m. yesterday (eight sentences)

skills.L: Listen to an alibi and note where each person was and what they were doing
skills.S: Ask and answer What were you doing at...? and tell a short story with when and while
skills.R: Read a short mystery and underline the past continuous
skills.W: Write eight sentences with was/were + -ing and when/while

lp.wu: Frozen picture: the teacher shows a crowded street photo for 20 seconds then hides it. Students write what people were doing ("A man was riding a bike. Two girls were laughing."). They compare with a partner and check against the photo.
wuAlt: Mime your evening: students mime what they were doing at 8 p.m. last night and the class guesses.
Pass the story: one student starts "Last night at eight I was..." and the next continues.
lp.pres: Draw a timeline with a cross at "8:00 last night". Say "At 8:00 I was doing my homework" and show that the action was in progress at that time. Teach the form: was/were + -ing, with negatives (wasn't studying) and questions (What were you doing? Were you sleeping? Yes, I was). Then show an interruption: "I was walking home when I saw an accident" with a longer line and a short cross. Teach when (short action) and while (long action): "While I was walking, it started to rain." Check with sentence halves to match: "I was watching TV when..., While we were playing football..."
presAlt: Use a short clip of a mystery scene and pause to describe what each person was doing.
Draw two timelines on the board and ask students to place sentences on the right line.
lp.prac: Alibi game: a crime has happened at 8:15 p.m. on Friday. Two students are suspects, the rest are detectives. The suspects leave the room and prepare an alibi with details ("I was having dinner with my cousin"), then they are questioned separately. The class compares their answers; if the details do not match, they are guilty. The teacher monitors the form of questions (What were you doing? Who was with you?).
pracAlt: Past continuous sentence race: teams write true sentences about the picture for two minutes.
Match sentence halves with when and while in pairs.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a statement twice. Sofia: "At eight I was in my room. I was doing my homework and my brother was playing video games. We weren't watching TV. At 8:15 the phone rang and I answered it." Students complete a grid with each person and what they were doing, and answer: "What happened at 8:15?" If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Interrupted! Students stand in a circle. One begins "I was cooking dinner when..." and the next completes with a short action ("...the phone rang") then starts a new sentence "While I was..." The chain continues without repeating.
lp.prod: Mystery story in pairs: students invent a small mystery (a missing phone or a school prank). They write a description of five people with what each was doing, with one hidden clue. They exchange stories with another pair and try to find the clue by asking questions.
lp.rw: Read a short mystery (about 90 words) and underline the past continuous in one colour and the past simple in another. Then write eight sentences about what you and five other people were doing at 8 p.m. yesterday using was/were + -ing and at least two when/while sentences.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence beginning "At nine o'clock last night I was..." and one with while, and hand them in at the door.
g: Suspects prepare an alibi and the class questions them.
Students describe a picture they saw for 20 seconds.
Students build when/while sentences in a chain.
Groups place sentences on a timeline of progress and interruption.
Teams write true sentences about a picture for points.
diff: Fast finishers: write a detective's report with eight sentences that use both tenses.
Support: give a sentence frame (At 8 I was ___ing when ___) and a verb list with -ing forms.
hw: Write what you and five other people were doing at 8 p.m. yesterday (eight sentences).
Write four sentences about an unusual event using when and while.
Find a picture and write what each person is doing as if it was taken yesterday.
lp.tip: The alibi game is popular with teens and gives a real need for questions, but it needs clear rules and time limits. Make sure that students use when for the short action and while for the long one.

occ.act: New Year week (1 January). Optional 10-minute memories: students write three sentences about where they were and what they were doing at midnight last New Year ("I was watching fireworks with my cousins") and share them with a partner.

weeks.obj: tell and write a short story in the past using sequencers, connectors and the past simple and continuous
weeks.lang: narrative tenses (past simple and past continuous); sequencers (first, then, after that, suddenly, in the end, finally); connectors (so, because, but, although); story vocabulary (suddenly, luckily, unfortunately)
weeks.res: Past simple worksheets; Reading tasks by topic
weeks.act: Story cubes; picture-story chain; mystery story writing; reading aloud
weeks.hw: write a story of 80 to 100 words about an unusual day

skills.L: Listen to a short story and number the pictures in order
skills.S: Tell a short story using sequencers and connectors
skills.R: Read a short story and order the paragraphs
skills.W: Write a story of 80 to 100 words with sequencers and both tenses

lp.wu: Story cubes: students roll dice with pictures (or draw word cards) and tell a one-sentence story using all three items. The class gives a thumbs up for the most creative one.
wuAlt: Sentence scramble: groups put eight jumbled sentences in order to make a mini story.
One word at a time: the class builds a story one word at a time in a circle.
lp.pres: Show a four-picture story (a boy loses his phone and finds it) and tell it with sequencers ("First he went to the park. Then he lost his phone. Suddenly he saw a girl with it. In the end he got it back.") Write the sequencers on the board in order and show how to use the past continuous for the background ("He was walking when he lost it"). Teach the connectors so, because, but, although with examples. Check understanding by asking students to reorder the sequencers and choose the right connector in four sentences.
presAlt: Read a short story aloud with missing sequencers and ask students to guess them.
Show a before and after pair of paragraphs (with and without connectors) and ask which is better and why.
lp.prac: Picture-story chain: groups of four receive eight pictures, tell the story in order (each student says two sentences) and then write it using at least five sequencers and two connectors. The teacher circulates and gives feedback on tense choice, particularly past simple for events and past continuous for background.
pracAlt: Story dice: each student rolls two dice (character and place) and writes the opening of a story.
Sequencer ladder: groups order sequencers on a ladder and compose sentences for each step.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short story twice ("Last Saturday Ali was walking in the market when he lost his wallet. First he looked on the ground. Then he asked a seller. Suddenly a girl called him: she found it near a shop. In the end Ali was very happy."). Students number five pictures in order and write the first sequencer they hear. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Telephone story: students sit in a row. The first whispers a two-sentence story to the second, who adds one sentence and passes it on. The last student tells the full story to the class and the group compares it with the original.
lp.prod: Mystery story: pairs choose a starter ("It was a dark night and I was walking home when...") and write the story in 80 to 100 words with at least five sequencers, two connectors and both tenses. They then read it aloud to another pair, who ask two questions about the characters.
lp.rw: Read a short story (about 100 words) in jumbled paragraphs and put them in order. Then rewrite it by adding three sequencers and two connectors, and write a one-sentence ending.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the first sentence of a story that begins with "Suddenly" and hand it in at the door.
g: Students tell a one-sentence story using three picture cubes.
Groups tell and write a story from eight pictures.
Groups order sequencers and make sentences for each step.
A story is whispered along a row and changes.
Groups put jumbled sentences into a story.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second story from a classmate's opening line (100 words).
Support: give a story map (who, where, problem, ending) and a list of sequencers.
hw: Write a story of 80 to 100 words about an unusual day.
Write three alternative endings to a story you know.
Retell the plot of a film or series you like in eight sentences.
lp.tip: Do not expect perfect narrative tenses: celebrate good stories and correct only the main pattern (past simple for events, past continuous for background). Use students' stories to build the class story book and read some aloud.

occ.act: New Year recap (first week of January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year with first, then and finally ("First we visited my cousins. Then I watched football. Finally...") and report one to the class.

weeks.obj: show what they can do after Semester 1 in a written paper (reading, grammar, writing), a short listening task and a paired speaking task
weeks.lang: all Semester 1 outcomes: question forms, present simple and continuous, past simple and continuous, going to, comparatives, quantifiers, polite requests and directions
weeks.res: Grammar tests bank; Speaking tests bank
weeks.act: Warm-up quiz; written paper (reading and grammar); listening task; paired speaking slots; writing task; self-assessment
weeks.hw: revise your notes and the irregular verb list before the next class

skills.L: Listening task (five questions) on a short conversation about plans
skills.S: Paired speaking task: personal questions and a picture comparison
skills.R: Reading and grammar paper across Semester 1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing: eight sentences about my weekend plans

lp.wu: Quiz Quiz Trade: each student has a card with a question from Semester 1 ("What were you doing at eight last night?", "How much cheese do we need?") and trades cards with partners, answering and asking.
wuAlt: Find someone who with a review grid (found someone who went somewhere last weekend, can swim well, is going to travel in the holidays).
Memory race: teams recall as many topics from Semester 1 as possible in two minutes.
lp.pres: Explain the assessment: the written paper has four tasks (a short reading text with five questions, a grammar gap fill with ten items, a matching task of mini dialogues and a short writing task). The listening task has five questions and the speaking test is in pairs with an examiner. Go through one example of each task type and show the success criteria (answer the question, use the right tense, write full sentences).
presAlt: Show a model answer for the writing task and ask students to say why it is a good answer.
Students list in pairs which task they feel most confident about and which they want to practise.
lp.prac: Written paper, reading and grammar: students work silently on the paper for 20 minutes. Task 1: read a short text about a teenager's week and answer five questions. Task 2: choose the correct form (past simple, past continuous, present simple) in ten gaps. Task 3: match five questions with answers in short dialogues. The teacher circulates only to clarify instructions. Build the paper from the Tests folder (A2 grammar and reading tests) and the Semester 1 Common Core tests.
pracAlt: Use the A2 Reading Test 01 and Grammar Test 01 from the Tests folder as the paper.
Split the class into two halves: half do the paper while the other half do the speaking test.
lp.ls: Listening task: the teacher reads a short conversation twice between two teens making weekend plans ("I'm going to play football at three. What are you doing tomorrow? I'm meeting my cousin at the cafe."). Students answer five questions (true or false and multiple choice) on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: While pairs wait for their speaking slot, the rest of the class complete a quiet review activity: a crossword with Semester 1 vocabulary, or a reading task with comprehension questions.
lp.prod: Paired speaking test: pairs take turns for about five minutes. Part 1: personal questions from the examiner (name, home, routine, hobbies). Part 2: the pair compares two pictures (two cities or two shops) and discusses which they prefer and why. The teacher scores communication, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation (1 to 3 each).
lp.rw: Writing task: write eight sentences about your plans for next weekend using going to, the present continuous and time expressions. Then complete the self-assessment: colour in each I can... statement on the checklist.
lp.st: Closing circle: students tell a partner one thing they did well in the assessment and one thing they want to practise next semester. Collect the papers and say goodbye.
g: Students swap question cards and answer a new partner each time.
Pairs complete a crossword with Semester 1 vocabulary.
Students find classmates who match review statements.
Teams recall as many topics from Semester 1 as possible.
Pairs correct mistakes in mixed tense sentences.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 10-sentence story from a picture using three tenses.
Support: allow use of a verb list and a sentence frame for the writing task.
hw: Revise your notes and the irregular verb list before the next class.
Write three questions you want the teacher to review next semester.
Write one goal for your English in the second semester.
lp.tip: Tell students that the assessment shows what they can do now and what to practise next. Use the checklist during the speaking test and give feedback on strengths first. Record the semester marks and issue the report cards this week. Note which structures were weakest to plan Semester 2 review.
checklist: I can answer personal information questions in the speaking task.
I can understand short conversations about daily routines.
I can read a short text and answer multiple-choice questions.
I can write 7-8 sentences about my weekend plans.
I can use present simple and past simple correctly.
I can use comparatives (e.g., 'bigger than').
I can follow a KET-style speaking task with a partner.

weeks.obj: set and talk about goals and promises using going to, would like to, hope to and will for decisions and promises
weeks.lang: goals and plans (I'm going to / I'd like to / I hope to / I want to); will for promises and spontaneous decisions (I'll help you; I'll study every day); going to vs will (planned vs decided now); goal vocabulary (improve, practise, save, learn)
weeks.res: Future forms worksheets; Creative writing prompts
weeks.act: Goal-setting poster; promise contract in pairs; spontaneous decisions game; goals writing
weeks.hw: write five goals for this semester and one promise for a classmate

skills.L: Listen to three teens talking about their goals and promises and tick the types
skills.S: Talk about my goals and respond to a classmate's problem with I'll...
skills.R: Read a short blog post about goals and find going to and will
skills.W: Write five goals and one promise

lp.wu: Goal graffiti: students write one goal on a sticky note and put it on the wall under a category (school, sport, family, language, money). The teacher reads out a few anonymously and the class guesses whose it is.
wuAlt: Guess my goal: a student mimes a goal (swimming, saving money, learning to cook) and the class asks yes/no questions.
Looking back: pairs say two things they are proud of from last semester.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "I'm going to improve my English this year. I'd like to travel. I hope to pass the exam." Elicit the form of each (going to + verb, would like to + verb, hope to + verb) and the difference between a plan and a wish. Then show spontaneous decisions: "Oh, I forgot my book! I'll share with you." "That's heavy. I'll carry it." Teach will for promises ("I'll call you tonight") and contrast with going to: "I'm going to study (I decided before) / I'll help you (I decide now)." Check understanding with four mini situations: students choose going to or will.
presAlt: Show a short video of New Year resolutions and ask students to note the forms.
Read two short messages (a plan and an offer) and underline the future forms.
lp.prac: Goal setting and promises: students write five SMART goals ("I'm going to read one English book a month") on a worksheet. In pairs, they swap goals and respond with a promise to help ("I'll test your vocabulary every Friday"). Then they play a spontaneous decision game: the teacher reads problems ("I'm hungry", "I've lost my pen", "It's raining") and the class responds quickly with "I'll...". The teacher notes any going to/will errors for correction.
pracAlt: Goal ladder: students order four steps to reach one goal with going to.
Pair role-play: one student has a problem and the other offers help with I'll.
lp.ls: The teacher reads three short messages twice. Amine: "I'm going to practise English every day. I'll watch a series with subtitles." Nora: "I'd like to be a doctor. I hope to get good marks this year." Hamza: "I forgot my homework! I'll copy it at lunch." Students tick whether each message is a plan, a wish or a decision. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Goal pitch: students stand in a circle and each says one goal and one promise in 20 seconds. After each pitch, the group says "Good luck!" and one student asks "How are you going to do it?".
lp.prod: Goals poster: groups design a poster called "Our Class Goals" with five shared goals (language, behaviour, a class trip) and a promise for each ("We'll speak English in group work."). They present it and the class votes on the best goal to put on the wall.
lp.rw: Read a short blog post about goals (about 80 words) and underline going to and will. Then write five goals for this semester using different forms and one promise for a classmate.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one goal and one promise for a classmate and stick them on the goals wall.
g: Students stick anonymous goals on a wall and the class guesses the owners.
The teacher reads a problem and the class replies with I'll.
Students give a 20-second pitch of a goal and a promise.
Groups order the steps to reach a goal.
A student mimes a goal and the class guesses.
diff: Fast finishers: write a letter to yourself to open at the end of the year with five predictions and goals.
Support: give two frames (I'm going to ___ because ___. I'll ___ to help.) and a list of goal verbs.
hw: Write five goals for this semester and one promise for a classmate.
Write a short message to a friend offering help with a problem using I'll.
Make a plan for one goal with three steps and a date for each.
lp.tip: Use students' own goals (learning, school, hobbies) and keep them on the wall to revisit at the end of the year. Be positive: celebrate effort, not only results.

weeks.obj: talk about jobs and what people have to do in them, and explain a dream job with reasons
weeks.lang: job vocabulary (nurse, engineer, mechanic, journalist, vet, programmer); What does she do? She works in/at...; have to / has to / don't have to for duties and rules; I want to be... because I'm good at...; adjectives for jobs (stressful, well-paid, creative)
weeks.res: Jobs flashcards; Jobs and careers lesson plans
weeks.act: What's my job? guessing game; job description cards; career fair interviews; job profile writing
weeks.hw: write a job profile (eight sentences) using have to and don't have to

skills.L: Listen to three people describing their job and match them to pictures
skills.S: Describe a job and ask and answer What do you have to do?
skills.R: Read a profile of a famous person and note their job duties
skills.W: Write a job profile with have to

lp.wu: What's my job? Students draw a job card and mime it for the class, who ask yes/no questions ("Do you work indoors? Do you wear a uniform?") until they guess.
wuAlt: Alphabet jobs: pairs write one job for each of ten letters in two minutes.
Job categories: teams sort 20 job cards into groups (health, technology, education, creative, trades).
lp.pres: Show job pictures with a short description of each ("A vet works with animals. She works at a clinic."). Teach have to / has to for duties: "A nurse has to wear a uniform. A pilot doesn't have to work in an office." Write the form on the board (have/has to + verb; don't/doesn't have to for no obligation) and the question "Do you have to...?" Add personality and job adjectives (stressful, well-paid, creative, dangerous). Check understanding: "Does a doctor have to study for many years? Does a chef have to wear a suit?"
presAlt: Show a short video of people describing their job and ask students to note their duties.
Use job description cards on the board and ask students to guess the job from the duties.
lp.prac: Job description cards: pairs receive six cards with duties ("work at night, wear a helmet, speak to customers") and decide which jobs they belong to. They then ask each other "What does a mechanic have to do? Does a teacher have to work on Saturdays?" and write four sentences with have to and don't have to. The teacher monitors the third person form (has to) and the negative.
pracAlt: Jobs matching: students match 10 jobs with 10 duties on cards.
Mingle: each student has a job card and answers questions from three partners until they are guessed.
lp.ls: The teacher reads three short descriptions twice (Rania: "I'm a nurse. I work at a hospital. I have to work at night and I have to wear a uniform." Ali: "I'm a mechanic. I don't have to wear a uniform but I have to be strong." Nora: "I'm a programmer. I work at home so I don't have to travel."). Students match each speaker with a picture and tick the duties they hear. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Job interview speed: students sit in two lines. One line are interviewers with a card of questions ("What do you have to do? Why do you want this job?"), the other line are candidates with a job card. They interview for one minute and then candidates move down the line.
lp.prod: Career fair: each student chooses a dream job and prepares a one-minute stall with five sentences (the job, what you have to do, what you don't have to do, why you want it, what you need to study). Students visit three stalls, ask one question at each stall and vote for the best stall.
lp.rw: Read a short profile of a famous person (about 80 words) and note their job and duties. Then write a job profile (eight sentences) for a job you would like with at least three have to / don't have to sentences and two reasons.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one job you want to do and one thing you have to do in it, and hand it in at the door.
g: A student mimes a job and the class guesses with yes/no questions.
Pairs match duties to jobs on cards.
Students interview each other in short rounds.
Students present their dream job at a stall.
Pairs find a job for each letter.
diff: Fast finishers: write an advert for a job with duties and requirements (eight lines).
Support: give a table of jobs with three duties each and a sentence frame "A ___ has to ___."
hw: Write a job profile (eight sentences) using have to and don't have to.
Interview an adult about their job and write four sentences about what they have to do.
Write six questions you would ask someone with your dream job.
lp.tip: Teens often confuse "don't have to" with "mustn't". Use two pictures (a no-entry sign and a day off) to show the difference. Link jobs to students' school subjects and talents to keep the topic personal.

weeks.obj: compare two or more things with comparative adjectives, as...as and modifiers (much, a lot, a bit) and justify a choice
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more + adjective, better, worse, further); as...as and not as...as; modifiers (much, a lot, a bit, slightly); than; comparing places (cities, schools), people and objects
weeks.res: Comparatives and superlatives PowerPoints; Comparatives and superlatives worksheets
weeks.act: Which is better? debate; city comparison survey; class survey with graph; comparison paragraph
weeks.hw: write a paragraph (eight sentences) comparing two cities or two schools

skills.L: Listen to two teens comparing two phones and note the differences
skills.S: Compare two places and justify a choice with reasons
skills.R: Read an article comparing two cities and find the modifiers
skills.W: Write a comparison paragraph with modifiers and as...as

lp.wu: Which is bigger? The teacher puts two objects or pictures on the board (a lion and a tiger, a bus and a taxi) and students compare them in pairs ("A lion is stronger than a tiger"). They score a point for each correct comparison in 60 seconds.
wuAlt: Compare and guess: one student describes two classmates without naming them ("She is taller than him") and the class guesses.
Opposite pairs: students write ten adjectives and their opposites.
lp.pres: Show two photos of cities (Oujda and Casablanca) with a fact box (population, distance from the sea, number of universities). Elicit comparisons: "Casablanca is bigger than Oujda. Oujda is quieter." Review the rules: one-syllable (bigger, taller), -y (noisier), longer (more expensive) and the irregular (better, worse, further). Add the modifiers: "much bigger, a bit cheaper, slightly hotter" and as...as: "Oujda isn't as big as Casablanca." Check with a quick whiteboard quiz: "Complete: Rabat is ___ (small) than Casablanca."
presAlt: Use a short video comparison of two cities and pause to note the language.
Give a table of facts about two phones and ask students to write five sentences.
lp.prac: City comparison: pairs receive a fact sheet for two cities (population, climate, price of a cinema ticket, number of beaches) and write six sentences using comparatives, one as...as sentence and two modifiers. Then they swap facts with another pair and check each other's sentences. The teacher monitors the use of than, more/-er and the irregular forms.
pracAlt: Comparative cards: students compare two cards using a different adjective each time.
Class survey: students ask four classmates which is better (phones, cities, sports, series) and report.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a dialogue twice. Karim: "My new phone is much faster than my old one and the camera is a lot better, but it isn't as cheap." Sara: "Mine is a bit smaller but the battery lasts longer. I think it's the best for the price." Students tick the features of each phone and note which one each speaker prefers and why. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Who is right? Students stand in two lines facing each other. The teacher reads a statement ("Football is more exciting than basketball") and students move to the side that agrees or disagrees and give one reason with a comparative.
lp.prod: Choose and justify: groups of four have to choose between two options (two holiday destinations, two school trips, two phones, two sports) and they prepare a one-minute argument with six comparisons. Each group presents and the class votes.
lp.rw: Read an article that compares two cities (about 90 words) and underline the modifiers and as...as. Then write a comparison paragraph (eight sentences) about two cities or two schools with at least four comparatives, one as...as and two modifiers.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one comparison with much or a bit and hand it in at the door.
g: Pairs compare objects in 60 seconds for points.
A student compares two classmates without names and the class guesses.
Students move to agree or disagree with a comparison.
Students compare two cards using different adjectives.
Groups argue which product is best with facts.
diff: Fast finishers: write a speech for a class debate "City life is better than village life" with six comparisons.
Support: give a table with 12 adjectives and their comparative forms with an example sentence.
hw: Write a paragraph (eight sentences) comparing two cities or two schools.
Compare yourself now and two years ago in five sentences.
Compare two TV series or two football players in six sentences.
lp.tip: Link comparatives to real opinions so that students argue: it makes the target language meaningful. Check that they never say "more bigger". Use the as...as structure only as a second step for strong students.

weeks.obj: use superlatives to talk about the best and worst things and give class awards, and introduce the pattern the best ... I've ever ...
weeks.lang: superlatives (the -est, the most + adjective, the best, the worst, the furthest); one of the + superlative + plural noun; the best/worst... I've ever ... (set phrase for present perfect); nominations and reasons
weeks.res: Comparatives and superlatives PowerPoints; Comparatives and superlatives worksheets
weeks.act: Class awards nominations; superlative survey; ranking debate; award speech writing
weeks.hw: write six sentences about the best and worst things you have ever eaten, seen or done

skills.L: Listen to an awards speech and note the winners and the reasons
skills.S: Nominate a classmate and justify with a superlative
skills.R: Read a short article about world records and find the superlatives
skills.W: Write six sentences with superlatives and the best... I've ever...

lp.wu: Class superlatives: the teacher asks "Who is the tallest? Who is the funniest? Who has the longest name?" and students point or vote. They then check facts with a partner (measure, count) to find the real winner.
wuAlt: Ranking line: five students line up from the tallest to the shortest and explain how they know.
Top three: pairs write their top three films and compare with another pair.
lp.pres: Show a table of facts about five students or famous places (height, age, distance, price) and elicit: "Karim is the tallest. Amina is the most creative." Recall the comparative and build the superlative: the + -est or the most + adjective, and the irregular (the best, the worst, the furthest). Show the phrase one of the + superlative + plural noun ("It is one of the biggest cities in Morocco"). Introduce the chunk "the best film I've ever seen" as a fixed phrase and explain that it describes experience until now. Check understanding by correcting four wrong sentences ("the most big").
presAlt: Show a short video of world records and write the superlatives that appear.
Present a poster of the Space activities and ask students to say what is the most popular.
lp.prac: Superlative survey: students receive a grid with six questions ("What is the best film you have ever seen? What is the worst food you have ever eaten? Who is the funniest person you know?"). They interview four classmates, note answers and report the most popular ones ("The best film was..."). The teacher monitors the + -est/most forms and the pattern with ever.
pracAlt: Superlative card game: students compare three cards and say the superlative.
Superlative olympics: groups compete to complete the most superlative sentences in a minute.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short awards speech twice. "The award for the funniest student goes to Yassine, who tells the best jokes. The award for the most helpful student goes to Salma, who is always ready to help. The best performance of the year was Nour's presentation." Students note the three winners and the reason for each award. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Awards ceremony: the teacher announces award categories (most creative, funniest, hardest working, best listener) and students vote on who gets each one by writing the name. Winners accept the award with "Thank you, it's the best award I've ever received."
lp.prod: Class awards: groups choose six award categories for the class (including one non-person such as the best lesson of the year) and write a short speech for each winner (two sentences with a superlative and a reason). They present to the class and the class applauds.
lp.rw: Read a short article about world records (about 80 words) and underline the superlatives. Then write six sentences about the best and worst things you have ever eaten, seen or done using the pattern the + superlative + I've ever + past participle.
lp.st: Exit ticket: nominate a classmate for an award with a superlative and a reason ("Karim is the funniest because...") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students vote or measure to find the winner of each category.
Students nominate and vote for the winners.
Students interview classmates about the best and worst.
Groups write the most superlative sentences in a minute.
Pairs rank items and defend their order.
diff: Fast finishers: write a speech for the best teacher or best friend of the year in eight sentences.
Support: give a table of regular and irregular superlatives with example sentences.
hw: Write six sentences about the best and worst things you have ever eaten, seen or done.
Write five sentences about the most interesting places in Morocco.
Write a nomination for a friend for an award with three reasons.
lp.tip: Use peer nominations to build rapport: teens respond well to positive recognition from classmates. Keep nominations kind and specific. Do not explain the present perfect: the pattern with ever is a chunk that prepares Week 20.

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students share "the best thing about Ramadan" with a superlative ("The best part is iftar with my family") and write one sentence about it.

weeks.obj: talk about life experiences with the present perfect (have you ever...? I have/haven't) and give details with the past simple
weeks.lang: present perfect form (have/has + past participle); ever and never; short answers (Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.); been to; regular and irregular past participles (been, seen, done, eaten, gone, had, made, taken); moving to the past simple for details (When did you go? I went in 2024)
weeks.res: Present perfect questions worksheets; Already, yet, before, just worksheets (extension)
weeks.act: Have you ever...? bingo; two truths and a lie about experiences; bucket list mingle; experiences blog
weeks.hw: write eight sentences about your experiences (four with have/has, four with details in the past simple)

skills.L: Listen to a teen talk about experiences and tick the ones she has had
skills.S: Ask and answer Have you ever...? and give details with the past simple
skills.R: Read a short text about a teen's bucket list and find the present perfect
skills.W: Write about experiences with have/has and details with the past simple

lp.wu: Have you ever...? bingo: students receive a card with nine experiences (eaten sushi, been on a plane, met a famous person, slept outside, broken a bone, ridden a horse, been to another country, won a prize, climbed a mountain) and mingle asking "Have you ever...?" to find one person for each. They write a name in the square if the answer is yes.
wuAlt: Two truths and a lie about experiences: students tell three sentences with I have... and the class guesses the lie.
Photo from the past: students show one photo of a place they visited and ask a partner to guess where it is.
lp.pres: Write "I have eaten snails" and "I ate snails in France last year". Elicit the difference: the first tells us an experience at any time until now, the second says when. Build the form: have/has + past participle, with a list of regular (visited, played) and irregular (been, seen, done, eaten, gone, had) participles. Teach ever in questions and never in answers, and the short answers. Show been vs gone: "She has been to Spain (she's back). She has gone to Spain (she's there now)." Check with a quick quiz: "Which sentence gives the time? Which tells the experience?"
presAlt: Show a short video on the present perfect and pause to repeat the examples.
Use a timeline on the board with "now" at the end and a wavy arrow to show life until now.
lp.prac: Find someone who has...: students mingle with a grid of ten experiences and must ask "Have you ever...?" and then a follow-up question in the past simple ("When did you go? Who did you go with?"). They report the most interesting answers to a partner. The teacher monitors the participle forms and the shift to the past simple after the first question.
pracAlt: Present perfect board game (ever/never) in groups of four.
Verb forms table: groups complete a three-column table (base, past, participle) for 15 verbs.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short interview twice. Interviewer: "Have you ever been to another country?" Leila: "Yes, I have. I've been to Spain and France. I went to Madrid last summer." "Have you ever eaten snails?" "No, I haven't, but I've eaten oysters." Students tick the experiences that Leila has had and note when she went to Madrid. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Never have I ever: students sit in a circle. One says "Never have I ever ridden a camel" and everyone who has done it stands up and says "I have!" Then one of them gives a detail in the past simple ("I rode one in Merzouga last year").
lp.prod: Bucket list interview: pairs interview each other about ten experiences (past and still to do) and prepare a short report: three things the partner has done, two things they haven't done and one thing they would like to do ("Hamza has been to Marrakech but he hasn't been to the sea."). They present to another pair and answer follow-up questions.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a teen's bucket list (about 90 words) and underline the present perfect forms. Then write eight sentences about your experiences: four with have/has + participle and four with details in the past simple.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you have done and one thing you have never done, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students find classmates for each experience on their card.
Students stand up if the experience is true for them and give a detail.
Students tell three experiences and the class guesses the lie.
Groups play a board game with ever/never questions.
Groups complete the three forms of 15 verbs.
diff: Fast finishers: write a blog post called "My top five experiences" with details in the past simple.
Support: give the participle list with pictures and a frame "I have ___. I went to ___ in ___."
hw: Write eight sentences about your experiences (four with have/has, four with details in the past simple).
Write six Have you ever...? questions for a friend and note the answers after asking them.
Make a bucket list of five things you want to do before you are 18.
lp.tip: Introduce the present perfect through experience only and keep the contrast with the past simple simple: first an experience, then the details. Delay yet, just and already to the optional extension for stronger students. Keep a participle list on the wall.

weeks.obj: make and justify predictions about the future with will, won't, might and probably, and distinguish them from going to plans
weeks.lang: will/won't for predictions; might/might not for possibility; probably, definitely, perhaps; I think / I don't think it will...; going to for evidence (Look at the clouds, it's going to rain); future time (in 2050, next year, in ten years)
weeks.res: Predictions worksheets; Future forms worksheets
weeks.act: Life in 2050 posters; fortune teller roleplay; prediction debate; predictions writing
weeks.hw: write eight predictions about your life or the world in 20 years with a reason for each

skills.L: Listen to teens predicting life in 2050 and note the certainty words
skills.S: Make predictions and justify them with a reason
skills.R: Read a short article about life in 2050 and rank the predictions
skills.W: Write predictions with will, might and probably

lp.wu: Fortune teller: students draw a card with a name and role and make a prediction for a partner ("You will meet a famous person. You will probably travel a lot."). The partner rates how likely it is on a scale.
wuAlt: Weather and exams: pairs make three predictions about tomorrow's weather and next week's test.
Crystal ball: one student predicts the next student's weekend and the class votes if it will come true.
lp.pres: Show a picture of a futuristic city and write on the board: "In 2050 people will drive flying cars. Robots will do the cleaning. We might not use money." Elicit the form: will + verb, won't + verb, might + verb. Add certainty words on a scale: definitely will, probably will, might, probably won't, definitely won't. Contrast with going to: "Look at those dark clouds. It's going to rain" (evidence) and "I think it will rain tomorrow" (opinion). Check with four sentences: students choose will or going to.
presAlt: Show a short video about future technology and ask students to note the predictions.
Use a picture of the school in 2050 and let students describe it.
lp.prac: Life in 2050: groups of four receive cards for six topics (transport, school, jobs, food, health, free time). They discuss each topic and write two predictions using will, might and probably, ranking them from the most to the least likely. They report to another group, who agree or disagree with "I don't think that will happen because...".
pracAlt: Prediction dominoes: students match sentence halves with will and might.
Horoscopes: students write short horoscopes for each other and read them aloud.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short discussion twice. Sara: "I think robots will do most of our homework in 2050." Hamza: "I don't think so. Teachers will probably still teach us, but we might use more screens." Sara: "We definitely won't use paper." Students note the three predictions and the word for each (think, probably, definitely). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Agree or disagree: the teacher reads a prediction ("People will live on Mars in 2050") and students move to one side of the room (agree) or the other (disagree) and justify in one sentence with will or might.
lp.prod: Future news: groups prepare a TV news report from the year 2050 with three headlines and two predictions for the next decade, using will, won't, might and probably. They present as news anchors and the class votes on the most likely report.
lp.rw: Read a short article about life in 2050 (about 90 words) and rank the predictions from the most to the least likely. Then write eight predictions about your own life or the world in 20 years with a reason for each (will, might, probably).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you are sure will happen in your life and one thing that might happen, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students predict a partner's future and the partner rates it.
Students move to one side of the room and justify their opinion.
Groups present a news report from 2050.
Pairs match sentence halves with will and might.
Students write and read short horoscopes for classmates.
diff: Fast finishers: write a letter from the year 2050 to the class today (eight sentences).
Support: give a table of certainty words with example sentences and a topic card with pictures.
hw: Write eight predictions about your life or the world in 20 years with a reason for each.
Write five sentences about a technology that will exist in 2050.
Ask a family member What will the world be like in 2050? and write their answer in three sentences.
lp.tip: Use will for opinions and predictions, going to for plans or clear evidence. Do not let students use will for plans ("I will go to the cinema tonight" for a fixed plan) without a correction round. Keep predictions light: teens love speculating about technology and jobs.

weeks.obj: describe common health problems and give advice with should/shouldn't and if clauses
weeks.lang: body and illness vocabulary (headache, cough, sore throat, fever, tired, stressed); What's the matter? I've got a... / My ... hurts; should/shouldn't + verb; Why don't you...? If I were you, I'd...; first conditional chunk (If you don't sleep, you'll feel tired)
weeks.res: Body flashcards; Giving advice worksheets
weeks.act: Agony aunt problem page; doctor and patient roleplay; advice chain; healthy habits survey
weeks.hw: reply to two problem letters with advice (six to eight sentences)

skills.L: Listen to a short consultation and note the problem and the advice
skills.S: Describe a problem and give advice in a doctor roleplay
skills.R: Read a problem page and match the advice to the problems
skills.W: Write replies to two problem letters

lp.wu: Body parts race: teams write as many body parts and health words as they can in 90 seconds and label a drawn figure. The team with the most correct words wins.
wuAlt: Problem charades: students mime a health problem (toothache, cough, stress) and the class guesses.
Healthy or not? Students sort 12 cards into healthy and unhealthy habits.
lp.pres: Show a picture of a teenager with a problem (a headache, a sore throat) and elicit "What's the matter?" "I've got a headache. My throat hurts." Teach the advice forms: "You should drink water. You shouldn't stay up late. Why don't you rest? If I were you, I'd see a doctor." Write the form: should + verb (no -s, no to). Add a simple first conditional: "If you don't sleep, you'll feel tired." Check understanding with three problem cards and students give advice orally.
presAlt: Read a short problem page with three letters and underline the advice phrases.
Play a short consultation video and ask students to note the advice.
lp.prac: Agony aunt: pairs choose a problem card (can't sleep, too much homework, not enough friends, stress before an exam, a sore back from a school bag) and write a short letter. They swap letters with another pair and write advice with should, shouldn't, Why don't you...? and If I were you. They read the answers aloud and the writers choose the best advice. The teacher monitors the form after should (no -s, no to).
pracAlt: Advice dominoes: students match problems and advice in groups of four.
Pair role-play: one student has a problem and the other gives three pieces of advice.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short doctor and patient dialogue twice. Doctor: "What's the matter?" Patient: "I've got a headache and a sore throat. I feel tired." Doctor: "You should rest and drink warm tea. You shouldn't go to school tomorrow. If you don't feel better in three days, come back." Students note the problems and the three pieces of advice. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Advice chain: one student states a problem ("I can't concentrate in class") and the next gives advice and then states a new problem, and so on around the circle. If the advice is not logical, the class says "Why?" and the speaker explains.
lp.prod: Doctor's surgery: pairs prepare a role-play of a consultation with a problem, three questions, three pieces of advice and a closing phrase. They perform for another pair and the audience notes the problem and the advice. Then they switch roles with a new problem card.
lp.rw: Read a problem page with three letters (about 90 words in total) and match each letter to the correct advice. Then write replies to two problem letters (six to eight sentences) using should, shouldn't and one if clause.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one health problem and one piece of advice and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams write body parts and health words in 90 seconds.
Students mime health problems and the class guesses.
Pairs write and answer problem letters.
Students give advice and state a new problem in a circle.
diff: Fast finishers: write a leaflet "Ten tips for a healthy school year" with should and shouldn't.
Support: give a table of problems and a list of advice phrases to match.
hw: Reply to two problem letters with advice (six to eight sentences).
Write six tips for a healthy teenager with should/shouldn't.
Ask a family member for their best health advice and write three sentences.
lp.tip: Avoid medical advice and keep the problems everyday (sleep, stress, a headache after a screen day). Check the form after should: no -s and no to. Use the first conditional only as a chunk this week because it comes back in Week 25.

weeks.obj: talk about travel experiences and plans with the present perfect and past simple, and ask for information and book a trip
weeks.lang: present perfect vs past simple (Have you ever been to...? When did you go?); been vs gone; travel vocabulary (book, ticket, luggage, passport, delay, platform, single/return); requesting information (Could you tell me...? I'd like to book...); how long, how much
weeks.res: Holiday and travel worksheets; Vacation lesson plans
weeks.act: Travel questionnaire; booking roleplay at a station; plan a trip budget; postcard or email writing
weeks.hw: write an email to a friend about a trip you have taken or want to take (eight to ten sentences)

skills.L: Listen to a booking phone call and complete a form
skills.S: Ask and answer travel questions and book a ticket in a roleplay
skills.R: Read a travel blog and a timetable and answer questions
skills.W: Write an email about a trip

lp.wu: Travel quiz: teams answer ten questions about famous places ("Where is the Eiffel Tower? Have you ever seen it?") and then ask each other which of the places they have visited.
wuAlt: Passport stamps: students draw a mini passport and mingle collecting stamps from classmates who have been to a country.
Travel word race: teams write 15 travel words in two minutes.
lp.pres: Write a short blog on the board: "I have been to Spain twice. Last summer I went to Madrid with my family. We travelled by plane and stayed in a small hotel." Elicit the two tenses: present perfect for experience and past simple for details with a time. Add been vs gone. Teach travel vocabulary with a timetable and ticket pictures (single, return, platform, delay, luggage) and the polite request forms: "Could you tell me what time the train to Fes leaves? I'd like to book two tickets." Check understanding with a table: students sort sentences into experience and detail.
presAlt: Play the AEF Practical English airport or hotel scene and note the requests.
Show a short video about travelling by train and pause for vocabulary.
lp.prac: Travel questionnaire: pairs ask "Have you ever...?" (been on a plane, travelled by train, stayed in a hotel, lost luggage) and for each yes answer ask two past simple follow-up questions (When? Where? Who with?). They then fill in a form for the partner (destinations, transport, favourite trip) and report to another pair. The teacher monitors the shift from present perfect to past simple.
pracAlt: Travel dominoes: students match words and pictures.
Holiday habits: pairs ask questions from a worksheet and compare answers.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a phone call twice. Customer: "Hello, could you tell me what time the train to Fes leaves tomorrow?" Clerk: "There's one at 8:15 and one at 11:30." Customer: "I'd like two return tickets for the 8:15, please. How much is that?" Clerk: "That's 240 dirhams." Students complete a booking form (destination, time, tickets, price). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Travel agent: students sit in pairs, one is the travel agent and one is the customer. The customer has a card with a budget and wishes ("I want a cheap trip to a beach for three days"). The agent suggests two options and the customer chooses.
lp.prod: Plan a trip: groups of four plan a three-day trip in Morocco or abroad with a budget of 2,000 dirhams. They decide destination, transport, accommodation and activities, and then present it in two minutes with one experience they have already had in a similar place ("I have been to Chefchaouen. It was..."). The class votes for the best trip.
lp.rw: Read a short travel blog (about 90 words) and a train timetable and answer five questions. Then write an email to a friend about a trip you have taken or want to take (eight to ten sentences) using at least two present perfect and three past simple sentences.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one place you have been and one place you went last year, and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams answer questions about famous places.
Students collect stamps from classmates who have been to a country.
Pairs role-play a customer and an agent.
Groups plan a trip with a budget and present it.
diff: Fast finishers: write a travel blog post about a trip with eight past simple and two present perfect sentences.
Support: give a booking phrase bank and a form to complete.
hw: Write an email to a friend about a trip you have taken or want to take (eight to ten sentences).
Write five Have you ever been to...? questions and ask a family member.
Plan a weekend trip with a small budget and write the itinerary.
lp.tip: Keep the contrast simple: present perfect for the experience, past simple for the details. If students overuse the present perfect with finished times ("I have gone yesterday"), write it on the board and ask them to fix it. Use real Moroccan destinations to make the topic relevant.

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: pairs ask "Where did you go on Eid? What did you eat? Who did you visit?" and write three sentences about their last Eid.
occ.hw: Write five sentences about your best Eid memory.

weeks.obj: give and support opinions about music and other topics, agree and disagree politely, and describe people and things with who, which and that
weeks.lang: opinion language (I think, In my opinion, I agree, I don't agree, Me too, Me neither); because / but / so / although; -ed and -ing adjectives (bored/boring, excited/exciting); defining relative clauses with who, which, that (a singer who writes her own songs, a song that makes me happy)
weeks.res: Relative clause games; Relative clauses worksheets; Giving opinions worksheets
weeks.act: Four corners opinion game; relative clause describing game; song review writing; agree and disagree discussion
weeks.hw: write a review of a song, album or artist (eight sentences) with three relative clauses

skills.L: Listen to teens discussing their favourite songs and note agree/disagree phrases
skills.S: Give an opinion with a reason and agree or disagree politely
skills.R: Read a short music review and find the relative clauses
skills.W: Write a song review with reasons and relative clauses

lp.wu: Music poll: students stand along a line from "I love it" to "I hate it" for different genres (rap, pop, classical, raï, rock) and explain in one sentence why with because. A partner agrees or disagrees ("Me too" / "Really? I think it's boring").
wuAlt: Playlist swap: students list their top three songs and a partner guesses why they like them.
Who is it? One student describes an artist without naming them and the class guesses.
lp.pres: Write four statements on the board: "I think hip-hop is exciting. In my opinion raï is better than pop. I agree with you. I don't agree because..." Teach the opinion phrases, agreeing and disagreeing, and softening ("I see what you mean, but..."). Contrast -ed and -ing adjectives with pictures (a boring concert, a bored student; an exciting song, an excited fan). Introduce relative clauses: "She is a singer who writes her own songs. This is a song that everyone knows." Show who for people and which/that for things. Check with a quick quiz: "Choose who or which: a band ___ plays loud music."
presAlt: Play a short interview with a musician and note the opinion phrases.
Show two reviews (one positive and one negative) and underline the language.
lp.prac: Relative clause definitions: pairs receive cards with people, places and things (a teacher, a cafe, a phone) and write one definition each with who/which/that ("A teacher is a person who helps students learn."). They swap with another pair, who guess the word. Then they use opinion language to discuss five statements ("Music is more important than sport") and agree or disagree with reasons. The teacher monitors who/which and the use of because.
pracAlt: Four corners: agree, strongly agree, disagree, strongly disagree, with opinion statements about music and school.
Relative clause bingo with definitions.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short discussion twice. Imane: "I think this song is exciting because the rhythm is fast." Adam: "I don't agree. I find it a bit boring, but I like the singer who plays the guitar." Imane: "Me too! I like musicians who write their own songs." Students tick the opinion phrases and note one thing each speaker likes. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Four corners: the corners are strongly agree, agree, disagree and strongly disagree. The teacher reads an opinion (Social media is bad for teenagers) and students move to a corner and give a reason using because. A student from each corner explains their choice.
lp.prod: Song review: students prepare a one-minute talk about their favourite song, album or artist: who the artist is (relative clause), why they like it (because), one thing they do not like (but) and an invitation to listen ("You should listen to it if you like..."). They present in groups and the group agrees or disagrees with one point.
lp.rw: Read a short music review (about 90 words) and underline the relative clauses and opinion phrases. Then write a review of a song, album or artist (eight sentences) with at least three relative clauses and two opinion phrases.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one definition with who or which and one opinion with because, then hand it in at the door.
g: Students line up from love to hate and explain their choice.
Students move to a corner of opinion and defend it.
One student describes an artist and the class guesses.
Students match definitions to words on a card.
Students give a one-minute review of a random topic.
diff: Fast finishers: write a review of a film or series with five relative clauses and two opinion phrases.
Support: give a table of opinion phrases and a frame "A ___ is a person who ___."
hw: Write a review of a song, album or artist (eight sentences) with three relative clauses.
Write five definitions with who, which or that for words of your choice.
Ask two friends for their opinion on a song and write one sentence each.
lp.tip: Opinions about music are personal and teens enjoy talking about them, but keep disagreements polite and model the soft phrases. Use clean, school-appropriate songs and artists, and let students choose. Relative clauses are the main new structure: spend time on who versus which.

weeks.obj: talk about technology and its effects with the first conditional, and discuss rules for phones and devices
weeks.lang: technology vocabulary (charger, battery, app, download, password, screen time); first conditional (if + present simple, will/won't + verb); when vs if; What will happen if...?; giving reasons and consequences
weeks.res: Conditionals worksheets; Technology lesson plans
weeks.act: What will happen if...? chain game; phone rules debate; tech problem role-play; consequence writing
weeks.hw: write six first conditional sentences about rules for phones at school or at home

skills.L: Listen to a teen discussing phone rules and note the conditions
skills.S: Discuss consequences with if + will and propose rules
skills.R: Read a short article about screen time and find the conditionals
skills.W: Write first conditional sentences about rules

lp.wu: Gadget guess: students describe a gadget without naming it ("You use it to listen to music. You charge it every night") and the class guesses. They then say which gadget they could not live without and why.
wuAlt: Tech word race: teams write as many technology words as possible in two minutes.
One minute offline: students say what they would do for one minute without a phone.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "If you don't charge your phone, it won't work. If you study with your phone off, you will concentrate better." Elicit the form (if + present simple, will/won't + verb) and the order (the if clause can come first or second, with a comma only when it comes first). Contrast if and when: "When I get home, I'll charge it" (sure) and "If I get a message, I'll answer" (possible). Teach the question: "What will happen if you lose your phone?" Check understanding with four cause and effect cards that students complete orally.
presAlt: Show a short video on screen time and ask students to note the consequences.
Give a short text on online safety and underline the conditionals.
lp.prac: What will happen if...? chain: groups sit in circles. One student starts with "If I lose my phone, I'll ..." and the next continues with "If I ..., I'll..." using the previous result as the condition. After five rounds, they write the chain and read it. Then they complete six cards in pairs ("If you don't back up your files..."). The teacher monitors the tense after if (no will after if).
pracAlt: Conditional cards: students match if clauses and results.
Conditional board game for groups of four.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short discussion twice. Dad: "If you don't turn off your phone, you won't sleep well." Yassine: "If I turn it off, I'll miss my friends' messages." Dad: "If you sleep well, you'll do better at school." Students note the three conditions and the results. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Phone rules vote: the teacher reads five possible rules ("No phones in class", "Phones are allowed at lunch", "Phones must be in a bag") and students move to one side to agree or disagree and justify with an if sentence.
lp.prod: School phone policy: groups of four write five rules for phone use at school, each with a consequence ("If you use your phone in class, you will lose it for the day"), then pitch their policy to the class. The class votes on the fairest rules and the group with the most votes presents to a "head teacher" (the teacher).
lp.rw: Read a short article about screen time (about 90 words) and underline the conditionals. Then write six first conditional sentences about rules for phones at school or at home.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one first conditional about your phone and hand it in at the door.
g: Students continue a chain of conditional sentences.
Students describe a gadget and the class guesses.
Students agree or disagree with possible rules and justify.
Pairs match if clauses with results.
Teams write as many technology words as possible.
diff: Fast finishers: write a story with six conditional sentences ("If he finds the key, he will open the door").
Support: give a table of cause and effect pairs and the frame "If ___, I'll ___."
hw: Write six first conditional sentences about rules for phones at school or at home.
Write five consequences of spending too much time online using if.
Ask a family member What will happen if...? about a rule at home and write two sentences.
lp.tip: The main error is will after if ("If I will see him..."). Write it on the board and let students correct it. Keep the topic balanced: teens have strong views on phones, so require every group to include a reason and a consequence.

weeks.obj: talk about rules and obligations using must, mustn't, have to, don't have to, can and can't, and understand common signs
weeks.lang: must / mustn't for rules and prohibition; have to / don't have to for obligation or no obligation; can / can't / be allowed to for permission; should for advice; signs and rules (No entry, Keep off the grass, Wear a helmet); rules at school, online and on the road
weeks.res: Safety flashcards (signs); Class rules flashcards
weeks.act: Sign matching; rules for the Space; class contract; poster design
weeks.hw: write eight sentences about the rules in a place you know (school, home, library or sports club)

skills.L: Listen to a teacher explaining the rules to new students and note the rules
skills.S: Talk about rules and give reasons
skills.R: Read a list of rules and match them to signs
skills.W: Write the rules for a place

lp.wu: Sign or rule? The teacher shows eight common signs (no phones, no entry, wear a helmet, keep quiet) and students say what each means ("You mustn't use your phone here"). They race to match signs with rules in pairs.
wuAlt: Rule or advice? Students sort 12 sentences into rules (must, mustn't) and advice (should, shouldn't).
Draw a sign: one student draws a sign and the class says the rule.
lp.pres: Show four signs and elicit: "You mustn't park here. You must wear a helmet. You don't have to pay. You can't take photos." Write the meaning of each on the board: must (a rule or strong obligation), mustn't (prohibited), have to (obligation from outside), don't have to (no obligation, it is your choice), can/can't (permission). Contrast mustn't with don't have to with two pictures (a stop sign and an open door). Add be allowed to: "Students aren't allowed to use phones." Check understanding with a quick quiz: "Is it a rule or a choice?"
presAlt: Read the rules of a school or library aloud and underline the modal verbs.
Show a short video about road safety and note the rules.
lp.prac: Rules of the Space: groups receive cards showing places (the library, the classroom, a swimming pool, a bus) and write five rules for each with must, mustn't, can, can't and have to. They then read a rule aloud and the class says which place it belongs to. The teacher monitors the difference between mustn't and don't have to.
pracAlt: Modal verbs board game for groups of four.
Rules mingle: students ask "What must you do at the cinema? What can't you do at school?" and write answers.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short welcome talk twice. "Welcome to the school. You must wear your uniform. You mustn't use your phone in class, but you can use it at lunch. You don't have to bring a pen on Friday because we have computer class. You have to be on time." Students tick the rules and note which ones are obligations and which are choices. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Rule detectives: the teacher shows a picture of a place with several people ignoring the rules. Students work in teams to find and say as many rules as possible ("The boy mustn't run near the pool").
lp.prod: Our class contract: groups of four write a contract with six rules for the class (three musts, two mustn'ts, one choice), with a reason for each. They design a poster with signs and present it. The class votes on the final rules, and each student signs the contract.
lp.rw: Read a list of rules for a swimming pool or school (about 80 words) and match each rule to a sign. Then write eight sentences about the rules in a place you know using must, mustn't, have to, don't have to and can't.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you must do and one thing you don't have to do at school, and hand it in at the door.
g: Pairs match signs with rule sentences.
Teams find people ignoring the rules in a picture and state the rule.
Groups write and guess rules for different places.
Groups write and vote on class rules.
A student draws a sign and the class says the rule.
diff: Fast finishers: write a code of conduct for a school trip with eight rules and reasons.
Support: give a table of modals with meanings and signs for each.
hw: Write eight sentences about the rules in a place you know (school, home, library or sports club).
Design a sign for the Space and write the rule.
Ask a family member about rules when they were your age and write three sentences.
lp.tip: The main contrast is mustn't (prohibition) and don't have to (no obligation). Use physical signs and gestures to make the difference visible. Revisit the class rules later in the term and use them in the review.

weeks.theme: A2 Key (KET) orientation: reading and writing
weeks.obj: understand the A2 Key reading and writing tasks, use reading strategies, and write a short message and a picture story
weeks.lang: A2 Key reading parts (signs and messages, matching, long text, multiple-choice gap fill, open gap fill) and writing parts (a short message of about 25 words and a picture story of about 35 words); skimming and scanning; mixed tenses from the year
weeks.res: Writing guides (all levels); Reading tasks by topic
weeks.act: Strategy stations (parts 1 to 5); timed reading practice; short message and picture story writing; self-check checklist
weeks.hw: write a short message (about 25 words) and a picture story (about 35 words)

skills.L: Listen to a text read aloud and answer gist questions (as practice for exam listening)
skills.S: Explain which strategy to use for each reading part
skills.R: Practise A2 Key reading parts 1 to 5 with strategies
skills.W: Write a short message (about 25 words) and a picture story (about 35 words)

lp.wu: Reading race: teams receive five signs and notices (Closed on Mondays, Wet paint, Bring your own lunch) and race to match each with its meaning in a short sentence. The first team to finish correctly wins.
wuAlt: Skim or scan? The teacher shows a short text and asks students to find the topic in 10 seconds (skim) and then one detail (scan).
Vocabulary pictionary: teams draw exam words (library, receipt, ticket, deadline) for others to guess.
lp.pres: Introduce the exam: A2 Key is a Cambridge exam at A2 level with three papers (reading and writing, listening, speaking). Show the reading and writing task types on a slide: signs and messages, matching people to texts, a long text with multiple-choice questions, a gap fill with multiple choice and a gap fill with open answers, then a short message and a picture story. Model skimming (read the title and first lines for the gist) and scanning (look for a name or number). Check understanding by asking students which strategy to use for each question type.
presAlt: Play a short video introducing the A2 Key reading part 1 with tips (KET folder in the library).
Use a one-page overview of the exam and ask students to complete a fact box (how many papers, how long).
lp.prac: Strategy stations: groups rotate through five stations (parts 1 to 5), each with a short task and a strategy card. At part 1 they match signs to meanings; at part 2 they match people to texts; at part 3 they answer multiple-choice questions about a short text; at parts 4 and 5 they complete gaps in a message. The teacher times each station (3 minutes) and checks the strategy at each one. Use the A2 Reading Test and the Objective KET student's book for the tasks.
pracAlt: Timed individual practice with A2 Reading Test 01, with a strategy checklist.
Peer teaching: stronger students explain strategies to weaker ones in pairs.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short message from a friend twice ("Hi Sara, I can't come on Saturday because I have a football match at five. Shall we meet on Sunday at ten at the cafe near the library? Bring your notes.") Students answer three gist questions (Who is writing? What is the problem? What is the new plan?) and underline the key information. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Exam word relay: the teacher writes exam words on the board (receipt, notice, deadline, ticket, timetable, instructions). Teams race to give a definition or an example sentence for each word.
lp.prod: Writing task: students write a short message (about 25 words) to a friend inviting them to an event (Part 6 style) and then a picture story of about 35 words from three pictures (Part 7 style). They swap with a partner, who checks the five points: task completed, correct tense, linking words, clear handwriting and word count.
lp.rw: Read a short text and answer five multiple-choice questions, noting which part of the text gave the answer (strategy review). Then check the writing of a partner and complete the checklist.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one strategy you will use in the reading test and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams match signs with meanings against the clock.
Students find the gist or a detail in a short text in 10 seconds.
Teams define exam words in sentences.
Groups rotate through five reading task stations.
Pairs find mistakes in a sample message.
diff: Fast finishers (bridge to B1 Preliminary): try a short B1 Preliminary reading or writing part 1 email from the PET folder and compare the length (about 100 words).
Support: give a task-by-task checklist and a highlighted text with key words circled.
hw: Write a short message (about 25 words) and a picture story (about 35 words).
Do one A2 reading practice test from the Tests folder and note the three hardest questions.
Write five new exam words with a sentence for each.
lp.tip: The aim is to show students the exam format and strategies, not to drill. Use short familiar texts (a message, a menu, a notice) so students learn the format without extra difficulty. This is an optional bridge: if the group is strong, use the B1 Preliminary tasks as extension. Check that students stay within the word limits.

weeks.theme: A2 Key (KET) orientation: listening and speaking
weeks.obj: understand the A2 Key listening and speaking tasks, use strategies, and complete a mock paired speaking test
weeks.lang: A2 Key listening (short conversations, matching, multiple choice, gap fill); listening strategies (read the question first, listen for numbers, names and times); A2 Key speaking (part 1: personal questions; part 2: asking and answering with prompt cards); fillers and clarification phrases (Sorry, could you repeat that?)
weeks.res: Listening library (graded talks, mp3); Speaking tests bank
weeks.act: Listening strategies practice; speaking prompt cards; mock speaking test with peer examiner; feedback and self-check
weeks.hw: prepare answers to eight personal questions and one speaking prompt card

skills.L: Practise A2 Key listening parts with strategies (numbers, names, times)
skills.S: Mock A2 Key speaking test in pairs with prompt cards
skills.R: Read the instructions and questions before listening
skills.W: Write notes for personal answers and prompt card questions

lp.wu: Number dictation: the teacher reads ten numbers, times and prices (a train at 7:45, a room number 312, 25 dirhams) and students write them. They compare answers with a partner and list the words that were hard to hear.
wuAlt: Spell it: students spell their names and street names aloud to a partner, who writes them down.
Fast questions: pairs ask each other eight personal questions in two minutes.
lp.pres: Explain the A2 Key listening paper: five parts with short conversations, matching and multiple-choice or gap-fill answers. Model the strategy of reading the questions first, predicting the answer type (a number, a name, a place) and writing short answers in the gaps. Show the speaking test format: part 1 is an interview with the examiner about yourself (name, home, family, hobbies, routine); part 2 is a question and answer task with a partner using prompt cards. Teach useful phrases: "Sorry, could you say that again? I'm not sure. Let me think." Check with a quick Q and A round.
presAlt: Play a short video example of an A2 speaking test and ask students to note good strategies.
Present a list of common mistakes in the test (one-word answers, silent pauses) and ask students to say how to avoid them.
lp.prac: Listening practice: the teacher reads or plays three short conversations twice (about shopping, plans and a phone call) and students complete a grid of names, times, prices and a short answer. After each conversation, they say how they found the answer. Use the Tests folder A2 listening material or the American English File audio if available.
pracAlt: Listening bingo: students tick the words they hear from a grid.
Dictogloss: the teacher reads a short text twice and students reconstruct it in pairs.
lp.ls: The teacher reads a short phone call between two friends twice ("Hi, it's Karim. Are you free on Saturday? The film starts at 6:30 at the Mega cinema. The tickets cost 45 dirhams. I'll wait for you outside at six."). Students complete the notes: day, film time, place, price, meeting time. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Question tennis: pairs stand and ask each other personal questions as fast as possible; if a student hesitates for more than three seconds or answers with one word, the partner gets a point.
lp.prod: Mock speaking test: groups of three (candidate A, candidate B, examiner). The examiner asks part 1 questions and then hands out prompt cards ("School library: open? when? books? computers?"). Candidates ask and answer questions about the cards. The examiner marks a simple score (grammar, vocabulary, communication) from 1 to 3 and gives one piece of feedback. Roles rotate. Use the Speaking tests folder for cards.
lp.rw: Read the part 2 prompt cards and write four questions for each card (Is it open on Sundays? How much is a ticket?). Then complete a self-check list of what went well in the mock test.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one phrase you will use in the speaking test when you do not understand and hand it in at the door.
g: Students write numbers and times they hear.
Pairs ask and answer quickly without hesitation.
Groups rotate roles of candidates and examiner.
Students tick words they hear from a grid.
Pairs reconstruct a short text they hear twice.
diff: Fast finishers (bridge to B1 Preliminary): practise a photo description of 45 seconds (what is in the photo, what the people are doing, what you think) using the Speaking tests folder.
Support: give a card with six question words and a model answer for each part 1 question.
hw: Prepare answers to eight personal questions and one speaking prompt card.
Listen to a short English audio (a podcast or a story) and note five numbers or names.
Record yourself answering three personal questions and listen to check your pronunciation.
lp.tip: The goal is confidence. Keep the mock test friendly and give feedback on strengths first. Use the examiner role to give students a different perspective: they learn the criteria by marking. The B1 Preliminary stretch is only for students who are ready.
