weeks.obj: review the year across stations with accuracy and speed and identify the structures they still need to practise
weeks.lang: all year outcomes: question forms, present simple and continuous, past simple and continuous, present perfect experience, comparatives and superlatives, going to and will, modals (can, have to, should, must), first conditional, relative clauses
weeks.res: Grammar tests bank; Earth Day worksheets (optional 10-minute overlay)
weeks.act: Five stations with a passport; team challenge quiz; error auction; self-assessment of structures
weeks.hw: make a revision card for each grammar point (one example sentence each)

skills.L: Listen to two short texts and answer questions at the listening station
skills.S: Ask and answer review questions at the speaking station
skills.R: Read short texts and correct mistakes at the grammar stations
skills.W: Write an 8-sentence paragraph about myself using four tenses

lp.wu: Station passports: hand each team of four a passport and explain that they stamp each station when they reach 80 percent. Warm-up: show five flashcards from across the year and students say a sentence for each using a different structure.
wuAlt: Quick quiz with one question for each term (past, present, future, modals).
Pair talk: tell your partner one thing you can do now that you could not do in October.
lp.pres: Explain the five stations (grammar 1, grammar 2, listening, vocabulary, speaking) and the rules. Run a quick class poll on the grammar the class found hardest (past continuous, present perfect, first conditional, relative clauses) and re-teach the winner for three minutes with a clear example on the board and a correction of a common error.
presAlt: Show a year-in-pictures poster and ask students to say what they did in each term.
Pairs write three questions they would like the class to answer.
lp.prac: Stations 1 and 2 (grammar): error correction cards (past tenses, present perfect, comparatives and superlatives, will vs going to) and a verb-form quiz (modals, first conditional, relative clauses). Teams correct the mistakes in 8 minutes at each station and stamp the passport. The teacher circulates and notes recurring errors.
pracAlt: Mini whiteboard grammar race with mixed prompts.
Error auction: teams bid on correct sentences from a mixed list.
lp.ls: Station 3 (listening): the teacher reads two short texts twice (a phone call making plans and a short travel story). Students tick or number answers on the grid. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Station 4 (vocabulary): Pictionary and Taboo with the year's topics (food, shopping, health, travel, technology, jobs). Teams score points for words guessed in 60 seconds.
lp.prod: Station 5 (speaking): interview cards with ten questions from the year ("What were you doing at eight last night? Have you ever been abroad? What will your life be like in ten years? What must you do at school?"). Pairs ask and answer and the teacher stamps the passports. Students swap roles for the second round.
lp.rw: Final round: each student writes an eight-sentence paragraph about themselves using four tenses and the frame "My name is ___. I usually ___. Yesterday I ___. I have never ___. Next year I'm going to ___. If I ___, I'll ___."
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one grammar point you feel sure about and one you want to practise again and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams collect stamps at each station.
Teams bid on correct sentences and fix the wrong ones.
Teams draw words from the year and guess them.
Students describe words without saying the taboo words.
Pairs ask and answer review questions.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short story that uses four tenses and a conditional.
Support: give a grammar summary card with one example sentence for each structure.
hw: Make a revision card for each grammar point (one example sentence each).
Practise the interview questions with a family member.
Choose the three words you found hardest this year and write a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Photograph the stations for your records. Tick the checklist during the speaking station and note which grammar points need more work before the final assessment. Use the poll results to plan the last review lesson.

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: groups design an eco poster for the Space with five rules using must, mustn't and should ("You mustn't leave the lights on. You should recycle paper."). These forms are already taught.
occ.hw: Write three sentences about what you can do to help the planet using should and if.

weeks.obj: show what they can do in the final written, listening and speaking assessments and celebrate the year
weeks.lang: all year outcomes and A2 Key style tasks: personal questions, narrative and experience tenses, comparing, giving advice, planning, rules and short written messages
weeks.res: General tests bank; Speaking tests bank
weeks.act: Final papers; speaking slots; listening task; awards and thank-you circle
weeks.hw: choose one thing you will do this summer to practise English and write it in a sentence

skills.L: Listen to a short text and answer six questions
skills.S: Take part in a paired speaking test (personal questions and prompt cards)
skills.R: Read short texts and answer questions in an A2 Key style paper
skills.W: Write a short email and a picture story

lp.wu: Find someone who: students mingle with year-review prompts ("has been to another country", "was studying at 8 last night", "is going to learn something new this summer") and ask the questions to find a name for each prompt.
wuAlt: Quick quiz from the year (teams, five questions).
Pair talk: tell your partner your favourite lesson of the year and why.
lp.pres: Explain the assessment: Part 1 is a written paper of about 35 minutes with four tasks (a reading text with five multiple-choice questions, a gap fill with ten items, a short message of about 25 words and a five-sentence picture story). Part 2 is a short paired speaking test. Go through one example of each task type and display the marking criteria.
presAlt: Show a model answer for the email task and discuss why it is a good answer.
Students list the tasks they feel confident about.
lp.prac: Part 1 written paper: students complete four tasks. Task 1: read a short text and answer five multiple-choice questions. Task 2: a gap fill with ten items (mixed tenses and modals). Task 3: a short message (about 25 words) inviting a friend. Task 4: a five-sentence picture story. The teacher circulates only to clarify instructions. Build the paper from the Tests folder (A2 reading and grammar tests) or from the task types above.
pracAlt: Use the Semester 1 paper as a model and write new items for the second half.
Split the class into two halves: half do the paper while the other half do the speaking test.
lp.ls: Listening task: the teacher reads a short text twice about a teen's trip ("Last July Sofia went to Chefchaouen with her cousins. They stayed in a small hostel and visited the market. It rained on the second day, so they didn't climb the mountain. Next year they are going to visit Fes.") and students answer six questions (true or false and short answers). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: While pairs wait for their speaking slot, students play a quiet year-review quiz (teams, five questions) or complete a puzzle sheet.
lp.prod: Paired speaking test: in pairs, students take turns for about five minutes. Part A: personal questions (name, family, routine, past weekend). Part B: prompt cards (ask your partner questions about a place or event). Part C: a short roleplay (order food or ask directions). The teacher scores communication, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation (1 to 3 each).
lp.rw: Self-assessment: students complete "I can..." statements (colour in each) and write one goal for the next level.
lp.st: Awards circle: each student receives one positive comment from the teacher and nominates a classmate for a class award (best helper, funniest, most improved). Students write thank-you notes on sticky notes.
g: Teams answer review questions from the whole year.
Teams order and tell a picture story.
Students nominate classmates for fun awards using superlatives.
Students write short thank-you notes to classmates and the teacher.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second picture story or a longer email (50 words).
Support: write the frames on the board and give a verb chart during the written paper.
hw: Choose one thing you will do this summer to practise English and write it in a sentence.
Write a thank-you message to a classmate or the teacher (three sentences).
Read one short English text and note five new words.
lp.tip: Keep the tone celebratory and use the checklist for the speaking test. Send the final reports home and hand out the certificates at the closing ceremony. Record which students are ready for the next level (Teens Advanced) and which need more support.
checklist: I can ask and answer questions about myself and others
I can talk about the past, present and future
I can compare people, places and things
I can give advice and talk about rules
I can understand short texts and conversations
I can write a short email and a simple story
I can take part in a paired speaking test

occ.act: Optional speaking finale: dream-job interviews (What do you want to be? Why?) in pairs, using the language from Week 17 and the future forms from Week 21.

weeks.obj: ask accurate and natural questions, talk about yourself and your strengths in longer turns, and agree a personal goal contract for the year
weeks.lang: question forms with more range (subject and object questions, indirect questions such as Could you tell me...?, question tags for checking); follow-up questions (Really? How come? What happened next?); strengths and learning vocabulary (be good at, improve, practise, revise, mistake)
weeks.res: Question correction worksheet (word order); Guess the question worksheet

skills.L: Listen to a learner describe how he studies and note two things that help him and one he would change
skills.S: Hold a two-minute conversation with a partner using at least five different questions and two follow-ups
skills.R: Read a short class contract and a model goal paragraph and underline the useful phrases
skills.W: Write 60-80 words about my goals and my study habit

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie, teen edition. Each student writes three sentences about their summer, a trip or an unusual experience (two true, one false). In groups of four they read them out and the others ask two follow-up questions each, one of which must start with "How come" or "What exactly". The group votes for the lie. While they talk, the teacher listens for missing auxiliaries and wrong word order and keeps a private list for the diagnostic.
wuAlt: Find someone who: students mingle with a grid (has been to another country, plays an instrument, can cook one dish well, has a pet with a funny name) and must write the whole question they asked for each name.

Name and talent: in a circle each student says their name and one thing they are good at, and the next student must repeat it before adding their own ("Imane is good at drawing. I'm Yassine and I'm good at...").
lp.pres: Write six faulty questions on the board from typical errors ("Where you live?" "What means this word?" "Who did come first?" "Do you know where is the cafe?"). Pairs correct them and explain the rule. Elicit the four patterns: object questions with an auxiliary (Where do you live?), subject questions with no auxiliary (Who called you?), indirect questions with statement order (Do you know where the cafe is?), and tags to check information (You're from Oujda, aren't you?). Then put three follow-up phrases on the board and ask for a real teacher example for each.
presAlt: Use the question forms unit of American English File 2 or Life Pre-Intermediate as the model, then ask students to write one subject, one object and one indirect question about the same topic.
Dictate six answers ("Since 2019." "My cousin." "Not really.") and students write the most natural question for each.
lp.prac: Interview and report: pairs choose a topic card (music, school, sport, phones, food, the future) and write eight questions, including two subject questions and two indirect questions. They interview each other for four minutes and take notes. Then each student joins a new partner and reports what they learned in three full sentences ("Salma told me that she plays football twice a week."). The teacher writes three typical errors on the board without names and the class corrects them together.
pracAlt: Question auction: teams bid on twelve questions, some correct and some faulty, and the team that buys the most correct ones wins.
Guess the question: the teacher reads an answer and pairs write the best question for it, scoring a point for every correct question and a bonus for an indirect one.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a monologue of about 100 words by a 17-year-old (Amine, who learns English from football videos and songs, writes ten new words in a notebook every Sunday, is afraid to speak in class, and wants to talk more this year). Students complete a three-column table: what he does, what helps, what he should change. Check in pairs, then ask "Which of his habits would you copy?" If audio is available, use the learning interview named in the kit.
lp.re: Four corners: the teacher reads five statements about learning English ("Making mistakes is useful." "Watching films with subtitles is a bad habit." "You need to live abroad to speak well.") and students go to a corner (agree a lot, agree a bit, disagree a bit, disagree a lot). In each corner they prepare one full sentence with "I think... because..." and a spokesperson defends it. After each statement one student from another corner asks a question.
lp.prod: Speaking diagnostic. Pairs talk for three minutes about "Something you learned outside school and how you learned it" while the teacher circulates with a grid (range, accuracy, fluency, pronunciation, interaction) and listens to each student for about a minute. Then students swap partners, summarise what they heard in 30 seconds and the listener asks one follow-up question. Keep the mood relaxed: tell students the grid is for planning, not for marks.
lp.rw: Goal contract. Show the PET-style tip sheet from the kit briefly so students know what the course is aiming at. Then students write 60 to 80 words headed "My English contract" with two goals, one habit for each ("I will learn five words a day and use them in a message") and one problem with a plan to solve it. In the last five minutes they swap, underline one thing they like and circle one question form to check. The teacher keeps a copy to revisit in week 15.
lp.st: Exit ticket: on a slip write one sentence beginning "This year I want to be able to..." and one question you still have about the course, and hand it in at the door. The teacher uses the slips to make mixed-level pairs for the next weeks.
g: Students ask yes/no questions to find the identity on a card taped to their back or forehead.
Teams bid on correct and faulty questions and fix the faulty ones.
Groups ask follow-up questions to find the false statement.
Students move to the corner that matches their view and defend it.
The class has two minutes to prepare indirect questions for the teacher and the best question wins a point.
diff: Fast finishers: write five indirect questions you would ask a teenager from another country and predict the answers.
Support: give a question table (question word + auxiliary + subject + verb) with six examples, three follow-up starters and a model goal sentence.
hw: Write 60 to 80 words about your goals for English this year and one habit you will use.
Start a vocabulary notebook: write five new words with an example sentence each.
Watch or listen to five minutes of English on a topic you like and write three questions you would ask the speaker.
lp.tip: Day one routines: agree an attention signal (a raised hand, a clap pattern or a countdown from five), a phone rule (phones in bags unless the teacher says they are needed for a task, with a box on the desk at the start) and pair rules (English first, listen without interrupting, change partners every activity). Be warm and fair, learn names in the first ten minutes with name cards, and pair stronger and weaker students on purpose. Use the diagnostic only to plan, and pick two or three class errors to recycle all term.

weeks.obj: describe character and appearance with more range, say how people usually behave and what they are doing now, and give reasons for opinions about friends
weeks.lang: personality adjectives (loyal, moody, confident, sensitive, easygoing, talkative); intensifiers and softeners (quite, really, extremely, a bit, not very); present simple vs present continuous (usual behaviour vs now, and always with annoying habits); reasons with because, so and that is why
weeks.res: Character traits (vocabulary); Where does the adverb go? (quite, really, extremely)
weeks.act: Guess who adjective game; adjective scale with intensifiers; present simple vs continuous picture task; qualities of a good friend ranking; paragraph about a friend
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words about a good friend or relative, describing their character and giving two reasons

skills.L: Listen to two teens talk about the qualities they admire in a friend and note the quality and the reason each gives
skills.S: Describe a person you know for one minute using intensifiers and two reasons
skills.R: Read a short text about two very different friends and match the sentences to the people
skills.W: Write 70-90 words describing a friend with reasons

lp.wu: Guess who: each student writes three clues about a famous person (a footballer, singer or character) such as "He's extremely confident and he's usually wearing red". Other students guess who it is after each clue. Groups of five play for five minutes. The teacher listens for have/has and the -s endings and notes what the class can already say about personality.
wuAlt: Hot seat: one student sits with their back to the board, the group describes a word with adjectives and the student guesses.
Two minute friend: students speak for 60 seconds about a friend without using the word "nice" or "good" (teacher counts).
lp.pres: Draw a line from "not very" to "extremely" and place quite, a bit, really, very, extremely on it. Elicit sentences with personality adjectives ("My cousin is really loyal. My brother is a bit moody.") and teach the pattern: intensifier + gradable adjective, with absolutely for strong adjectives (absolutely hilarious). Add a second board for tense: present simple for what someone is like, present continuous for now or for an annoying habit ("She is always borrowing my charger!"). Finish with three because/so sentences ("He is easygoing, so everybody likes him.").
presAlt: Use the character traits sheet and the adverb word-order sheet from the kit to give a short reading and gap-fill.
Show eight photos of famous people on the phone and elicit one sentence each about what they are like and what they are doing.
lp.prac: Adjective scale: pairs get a card with 12 personality adjectives and place them on a scale from positive to negative, then write one sentence with an intensifier for four of them. Next, "Describe your classmate": each student writes three sentences about the partner (no names) using one adjective, one present simple and one present continuous for what the person is doing now. The class guesses who is described. Keep descriptions kind and positive.
pracAlt: Present simple vs continuous worksheet from the kit: pairs complete the sentences and invent two more about their own friends.
Quiz time: pairs do the personality quiz from the kit and explain their result in three sentences using intensifiers.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short dialogue of about 120 words between two teens (Hind and Omar) about their best friends. Hind admires a friend who is loyal and always listens, Omar prefers a friend who is funny and easygoing but is annoyed because he is always checking his phone. Students complete a table with the friend, the quality, the reason and the annoying habit. Check in pairs, then discuss: "Which quality matters most to you in a friend, and why?" If audio is available, use the qualities listening named in the kit.
lp.re: Intensifier challenge: the teacher calls out a situation or a person type ("a teacher who gives too much homework", "a friend who never replies") and teams have 20 seconds to write the best sentence with an intensifier and a reason. Two points for a correct sentence, a bonus for a strong adjective with absolutely.
lp.prod: What makes a good friend? In groups of four, students rank six qualities (loyal, funny, honest, generous, easygoing, interesting) from most to least important, using "I think... is the most important because..." and "I agree/I see it differently". After six minutes each group presents its top two to the class with reasons, and the class votes for the most surprising ranking.
lp.rw: Read a short text about two very different friends and answer true/false questions, underlining the personality adjectives and the intensifiers. Then students write a paragraph of 70 to 90 words about a friend or a relative: who they are, two adjectives with intensifiers, what they usually do together and one reason they get on well. Partners check for have/has and the -s endings.
lp.st: Exit ticket: finish "A good friend is someone who..." with a relative clause or a verb phrase, add one reason with because, and read it to the class at the door.
g: Students give three clues about a famous person using adjectives and the group guesses.
One student guesses a person or word from the group's descriptions.
Teams write sentences with different intensifiers in 20 seconds.
Students read profile cards and choose the best friend match with reasons.
A student mimes an action and the class says what he is doing now and what he usually does.
diff: Fast finishers: write a character profile of an imaginary friend with eight adjectives and four intensifiers, then read it to another pair.
Support: give a word bank with 12 adjectives in three groups (positive, negative, neutral), a scale poster of intensifiers and a model sentence for each tense.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about a good friend or a relative, describing their character and giving two reasons.
Interview an older person at home about what a good friend is and write three sentences.
Write six sentences with an intensifier about people in a series or film you like.
lp.tip: Teens love talking about people, so set one clear rule early: describe, do not insult, and keep names of classmates out of negative sentences. Correct the -s on has/likes and the word order of intensifiers gently by writing the sentence on the board for the whole class. Use mixed pairs so that quieter students can use the word bank while confident students extend with absolutely and reasons.

weeks.obj: talk about experiences and recent news with the present perfect, contrast it with the past simple, and tell a first-time experience in a short paragraph
weeks.lang: present perfect for experience (have you ever, never, once, twice, several times); just, already, yet; present perfect vs past simple (unfinished vs finished time, details in the past simple); first-time vocabulary (for the first time, the first thing I did was)
weeks.res: Ever and never worksheet; Lesson plan: Present perfect simple
weeks.act: Find someone who survey; ever and never practice; present perfect vs past simple sorting; bucket list interviews; first-time story paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words about something you did for the first time, using the present perfect to introduce it and the past simple for the details

skills.L: Listen to two people describe a first experience and note what happened, when, and how they felt
skills.S: Interview a partner about five experiences and report the most surprising one with details
skills.R: Read a short article about a young person with an unusual life and decide which verbs are present perfect and which are past simple
skills.W: Write 70-90 words about a first-time experience

lp.wu: Find someone who has: students receive a grid (has eaten something unusual, has travelled by plane, has met a famous person, has broken a bone, has never used a mobile phone for a whole day). They mingle and ask "Have you ever...?" and then one follow-up question in the past simple ("When was that?"). The first student with six names and six details wins. The teacher notes how students form the participle of common irregular verbs.
wuAlt: Have you ever survey: pairs ask each other ten questions from a short list and tick or cross. They report the most surprising answer to another pair.
Three things: each student writes three things they have never done and the class guesses why.
lp.pres: Elicit two sentences from a student: "I went to Marrakech last year" (finished time) and "I've been to Marrakech twice" (no time, experience). Show the timeline: the present perfect links the past with now, so we cannot use it with yesterday, last week or in 2019. Teach the structure have/has + past participle and the rule: present perfect to introduce, past simple for details ("I've been to Spain. I went there in 2022 and I loved Seville."). Add ever, never, just, already and yet with one example each, and a quick irregular participle table to complete in pairs.
presAlt: Use the matching present perfect unit of American English File 3 as the model text and the ever/never worksheet from the kit.
Show a short timeline of a famous person's life and ask students to say what they have done and when they did it.
lp.prac: Experience cards: pairs get 12 cards with experiences (ride a camel, learn to swim, win a prize, lose a phone, cook for the family, speak English to a tourist). Student A asks "Have you ever...?" and if the answer is yes, A must ask two questions in the past simple (when, where, what, who with). They then write three sentences for A's partner. Next, sort ten sentences into present perfect and past simple groups and fix the five faulty ones with time words.
pracAlt: Present perfect with yet, just and already: pairs complete a worksheet and make a to-do list for a school trip with ticks and crosses ("We have already bought the tickets, but we haven't booked the bus yet.").
Simple past or present perfect grammar sheet: pairs complete the gaps and explain their choices.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short account of about 120 words by a teenager, Nadia, who has recently flown for the first time. She has been on a plane once, last August, to visit her uncle in Spain. She felt nervous at the start but the take-off was exciting and she has already asked her parents for another trip. Students note what she has done, what she did in Spain, and how she felt. Check in pairs, then ask "What have you done for the first time this year?" If audio is available, use the best-and-worst experience listening named in the kit.
lp.re: Just say yes: student A asks a partner a question with "Have you ever...?" and the partner can only answer "Yes, I have" and must invent a detail in the past simple. The class votes whether the story is true or a lie. Rotate partners every three minutes and keep a score per team for convincing stories.
lp.prod: My bucket list interview: students write four things they would like to try (and two things they have already done) and interview two partners, who ask follow-up questions in the past simple. Then each student tells the class the most unusual thing they heard from a partner using reported sentences ("Rania has been to a desert camp. She went there with her cousins and she slept under the stars."). The class votes for the most interesting experience.
lp.rw: Read a short article about a teen with an unusual life and underline all the present perfect forms in one colour and the past simple forms in another, explaining why each tense is used. Then students write 70 to 90 words about something they did for the first time: begin with a present perfect sentence, then give four details in the past simple (when, where, who with, how it felt). Partners circle every time word and check which tense follows it.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences, one beginning "I've never..." and one beginning "I'd like to...", and read them to a partner as you leave. The best "never" sentence is read to the class next lesson.
g: Students mingle with a grid and ask "Have you ever...?" plus a follow-up question.
Students answer yes and invent a past simple detail for the class to check.
Teams sort sentences into present perfect and past simple and fix errors.
Students tick squares of experiences as they interview classmates.
A student tells a short experience story and the class decides whether it is true or false.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue of ten lines in which one person has done many things and the other has done nothing, using ever, never, already and yet.
Support: give a participle table of 15 irregular verbs, a card with the time words that go with each tense and a model question and answer pair.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about something you did for the first time, using the present perfect to introduce it and the past simple for the details.
Ask two people at home "Have you ever...?" about one experience and write what they said in six sentences.
Learn the past participles of ten irregular verbs and write a sentence with each.
lp.tip: Teens often mix tenses when they give a time word: write "yesterday" and "ever" on opposite sides of the board and make students point to the correct side before they speak. Keep irregular participles on a wall chart or in a shared photo. Give extra time to quieter students to prepare a story before they speak and avoid forcing anyone to share a personal story if they would rather invent one.

weeks.theme: Social media, phones and screen time
weeks.obj: talk about how you use your phone and social media, give opinions with reasons, and write a short balanced paragraph on screen time
weeks.lang: present perfect with for and since (How long have you...?); quantifiers (too much, too many, enough, not enough, a few, a little, a lot of); opinion and balance phrases (In my opinion, On the one hand, On the other hand, However, I agree up to a point); technology vocabulary (notification, post, follower, scroll, log in, screen time, addicted)
weeks.res: For vs since worksheet; Much, many, some and any
weeks.act: Phone survey with for and since; quantifier sorting and race; opinion statements on a line; pros and cons group discussion; balanced paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words saying whether you spend too much time on your phone and what you could change

skills.L: Listen to two teens discuss how long they have used social media and how much time they spend online, and note numbers and opinions
skills.S: Take part in a two-minute discussion about phones in school with three opinions and two reasons
skills.R: Read a short article about teens and screen time and find the writer's main argument and two examples
skills.W: Write 70-90 words with one advantage, one disadvantage and a personal opinion

lp.wu: Phone survey (phones used for a purpose). Each student takes out their phone and checks their screen time or app time for yesterday (or estimates it). Students who prefer not to share can use a made-up number. In groups of four they ask "How long have you had your phone?" and "How many hours do you spend on it a day?", then report the highest and lowest total to the class. The teacher writes the numbers and notices how students use for and since.
wuAlt: Statement line: the teacher reads five opinions ("Teens spend too much time online.") and students stand on a line from agree to disagree and say one reason.
Emoji talk: students write three emojis that describe their week and explain them to a partner in two sentences.
lp.pres: Write "I've had this phone for two years. I've had it since 2023." and elicit the difference: for + a period of time, since + a starting point. Ask the class "How long have you...?" questions and build a table of time expressions. Then teach quantifiers with a phone context: too much/too many (more than we want), enough/not enough, a few/a little (a small amount) and a lot of, with countable and uncountable nouns (too many notifications, too much homework, a little time, a few friends). Check with six sentences where students choose the correct quantifier in pairs.
presAlt: Use the present perfect unit of American English File 3 for for and since, and the video on much, many, a few and a little from the kit.
Give a worksheet on for and since where students complete 10 gaps and write two true sentences about themselves.
lp.prac: Quantifier race: teams of four stand in lines. The teacher reads a gap sentence ("There are too ___ ads on this site.") and the first student in each line runs to the board to write the quantifier; correct answers score a point, but an uncountable noun with "many" loses a point. Next, pairs write six sentences about their phone habits (two with for/since, two with quantifiers, two with a mix) and read them to another pair, who say "You should..." if the habit sounds unhealthy.
pracAlt: Exercises for or since from the kit: pairs complete them, then ask each other five "How long have you...?" questions about things they own or do.
Betting game: pairs bet points on whether each of ten quantifier sentences is correct, and win or lose the bet.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short dialogue of about 130 words between two teens, Yasmine and Adam. Yasmine has been on social media since she was 12 and posts a lot, but says she has too many notifications and not enough sleep. Adam has had his account for six months, scrolls for about two hours a day and thinks it helps him follow football. Students note for how long, how much time and each opinion. Check in pairs, then discuss "Who is more careful?" If audio is available, use the media or phone listening named in the kit or the screen-time mini lesson video.
lp.re: Pros and cons line: the teacher calls a statement about phones or social media and students must say one advantage and one disadvantage in 20 seconds, using On the one hand and On the other hand. Teams get a point for each different idea not said before. End with a vote on the best argument.
lp.prod: Group discussion: "Should phones be allowed in school?" In groups of four, each student takes a role (teacher, parent, student, school director) and prepares two reasons for 3 minutes. Then they discuss for 6 minutes while an observer ticks a checklist (uses In my opinion, gives a reason, disagrees politely, uses a quantifier). The observer gives two points of praise and one suggestion, and each group announces its decision.
lp.rw: Read a short article about teens and screen time (the Facebook text from the kit or a similar text) and answer multiple-choice questions on the main idea and details, underlining three opinion phrases. Then students write 70 to 90 words in two paragraphs or four sentences: a balanced opinion on screen time with one advantage, one disadvantage, a personal opinion and a quantifier. Partners check that each sentence has a reason.
lp.st: Exit ticket: complete "I have used my phone for ... hours today and I think that is too much/not too much because..." and read it aloud on the way out, or hand it to the teacher.
g: Groups collect screen-time numbers and report the highest and the lowest.
Teams race to write the correct quantifier in each gap.
Pairs bet on whether sentences are correct.
Students stand on a line and defend their position.
Students pass a ball and say a pro or a con in turn.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue (8 lines) between a teenager and a parent about screen time with at least three quantifiers and two present perfect sentences.
Support: give a quantifier table (countable and uncountable columns) and a card with three frames: In my opinion..., On the one hand..., However....
hw: Write 70 to 90 words saying whether you spend too much time on your phone and what you could change.
For one day, note your screen time every three hours and write four sentences with for, since or quantifiers.
Ask two people at home "How long have you had a phone?" and write what they said.
lp.tip: This is a topic where teens have strong opinions, so set a rule that students criticise ideas and never people. Use phones only for the first activity and then put them away; this models the discussion. If someone is uncomfortable sharing screen time, allow an estimate or an invented number.

occ.act: Halloween falls this weekend (31 Oct). Optional 10-minute task: in groups students plan a short spooky story post (not a real post) of four sentences about a Halloween night, using the present perfect ("I have never seen such a dark house") and for or since, then read it aloud. They compare it with how Moroccan families prepare for a different occasion, such as Eid, and say what they have done to prepare.

weeks.obj: talk about your passions in detail, compare hobbies, and use verb patterns accurately
weeks.lang: like/love/hate/enjoy/prefer + -ing; want/would like/decide/hope/plan + to; stop and remember with both forms; comparing hobbies (more... than, as... as, the best thing about...); fandom and hobby vocabulary (fan, collect, take part in, practise, level up, subscribe)
weeks.res: Gerund and infinitive master sheet; What do you like doing?
weeks.act: Find someone who likes; verb pattern sorting; hobby presentation prep; interview chain; hobby paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words about a hobby or a fandom, saying why you love it and what you would like to do next

skills.L: Listen to two teens talk about their hobbies and note what they enjoy, what they want to do and why
skills.S: Talk for one minute about a hobby with three reasons and one future plan
skills.R: Read a short article about an unusual sport or hobby and answer questions
skills.W: Write 70-90 words about a hobby or a fandom

lp.wu: Find someone who likes... : students mingle with a grid (likes playing video games, hates getting up early, enjoys drawing, would like to learn an instrument, wants to be a streamer). They ask "Do you like...?" or "Would you like to...?" and write the name and one extra detail. After five minutes the teacher reads four names and the class guesses the match. The teacher notes which patterns students avoid.
wuAlt: Hobby charades: students mime a hobby and the class asks "Do you enjoy...?" until they guess.
Rank it: pairs rank six hobbies from most to least popular in the class and compare.
lp.pres: Put three verbs on the board in two columns: enjoy, love, hate, prefer + -ing; want, would like, decide, hope, plan + to. Elicit examples about the class ("Karim enjoys playing chess. Nora wants to learn to skate.") and show that some verbs take both forms (like, love, start) with almost no change, but stop and remember change the meaning (I stopped to buy a drink / I stopped buying drinks). Add comparison frames: "I prefer gaming to reading", "Football is more exciting than chess", "The best thing about..." and ask students to complete them.
presAlt: Use the gerund and infinitive master sheet and the unit on verb patterns in American English File 3 from the kit.
Show a short text about a famous YouTuber, gamer or athlete with verbs blanked and students choose the right form.
lp.prac: Sort and speak: pairs get 20 cards with verbs and sort them into -ing, to + verb and both. Then they play dominoes or the verb pattern board game from the kit in groups of four, making true sentences about their lives. Finally, each student writes five true sentences ("I hate waking up early. I want to learn guitar.") and reads them to a new partner, who asks one follow-up question for each.
pracAlt: Gerund or infinitive card game from the kit: students draw a card, say a sentence about themselves and score a point when they use the right form.
Find the mistake: the teacher shows eight wrong sentences ("I enjoy to swim.") and pairs correct them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a monologue of about 120 words by Walid, 16, who loves playing football in the street with friends, enjoys editing short videos of matches, hates losing but wants to be a coach, and has decided to start a small YouTube channel in the summer. Students fill a grid with what he loves, hates, wants and has decided. Check in pairs, then ask "What would you like to try?" If audio is available, use the sports or rap listening named in the kit, or the History of Film video.
lp.re: Passion pitch: each student has 45 seconds to convince the group to try their hobby, using at least three patterns (enjoy -ing, would like to, want to) and one comparison. After each pitch the group asks one question. Groups choose the best pitch and that student repeats it for the class.
lp.prod: Hobby presentation: students prepare for 4 minutes with a planning card (What is it? Why do I like it? What do I do? What would I like to do next?) and talk for one minute to a group of three. Listeners complete a feedback card (one thing I learned, one question, one phrase I liked) and change groups for a second try with a new audience, aiming to add detail and fewer pauses.
lp.rw: Read a short article about an unusual hobby or sport (the obscure sports text from the kit) and complete a task with matching sentences and true/false/not stated questions, underlining verb patterns. Then students write 70 to 90 words about their hobby or fandom: what it is, how often they do it, three reasons they love it and something they would like to do next. Partners check the verb patterns with a coloured pen.
lp.st: Exit ticket: finish "One day I would like to... because I enjoy..." with the right verb forms and read to a partner on the way out.
g: Students mingle to find classmates who match hobby statements.
A student mimes and the class guesses with Do you enjoy...?
Groups match verbs with correct forms and make true sentences.
Students convince the group to try their hobby in 45 seconds.
A student describes a hobby and the group guesses if it is real.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short fan letter (60 words) to a person you admire using at least six verb patterns.
Support: give a two-column verb chart (-ing and to + verb) with eight examples each and a model paragraph with gaps.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about a hobby or a fandom, saying why you love it and what you would like to do next.
Interview a family member about a hobby they had when they were young and write five sentences.
Make a poster of your hobby with five sentences using verb patterns.
lp.tip: Teens will talk happily about gaming and music, so let them use their own vocabulary, but ask for English explanations of local words. Watch out for "I enjoy to play" and "I want playing" and correct by writing the pair of forms on the board. Pair a gamer with a non-gamer so that each has to explain the hobby to a beginner.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: in groups students talk about what they enjoy doing on national days ("I enjoy watching the parade with my family. We like going to the beach if the weather is nice.") and what they would like to do next year. Each group reports one pattern sentence and one wish to the class.

weeks.obj: talk about childhood and how life in Morocco and in teens' lives has changed, using used to and past simple with confidence
weeks.lang: used to / didn't use to / did you use to...? for past habits and states; contrast with present simple (now) and would for habits; time markers (when I was little, in those days, back then, nowadays, these days); change vocabulary (replace, disappear, improve, become, get used to)
weeks.res: Then and now (used to); People used to...
weeks.act: Used to memory mingle; then and now picture comparison; interview about childhood; Morocco then and now mini-talk; memory paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words about how your life has changed since you were seven, using used to and the present simple

skills.L: Listen to a teenager talk about a grandparent's childhood and note what was different then and what is different now
skills.S: Talk for 90 seconds about childhood habits and how they have changed
skills.R: Read a short text about life 50 years ago and compare with life today
skills.W: Write 70-90 words about how your life has changed

lp.wu: Memory mingle: each student writes three things they used to do at seven (play outside until dark, watch cartoons, be afraid of dogs) and one thing they never used to do. They mingle and read the sentences, and partners must guess which is the false one. The teacher listens for "used to" with the wrong auxiliary ("I didn't used to") and notes what to teach.
wuAlt: Photo then and now: students show a photo from their phone of themselves as a child, if they have one (or draw a sketch), and describe it in four sentences.
Childhood bingo: a grid of activities and students tick the squares of things their partner used to do.
lp.pres: Write four sentences on the board about the teacher: "I used to play outside until dark. I didn't use to have a phone. Did you use to...?" Elicit the three forms (used to + verb, didn't use to + verb, did + subject + use to + verb) and the meaning: past habits or states that are not true now. Contrast with present simple using "now" and "nowadays". Show that "would" can replace used to for repeated actions but not states (I used to have a bike, not I would have a bike). Check with eight gaps on the board.
presAlt: Use the matching used to unit of American English File 3 and the then and now sheet from the kit.
Dictate six sentences (four true about Morocco, two false) and students write "used to" or "didn't use to" for each.
lp.prac: Then and now pairs: students get two pictures or word lists (a school in 1980 and today, a street in Oujda 30 years ago and now, a phone in 2005 and now) and write six sentences about the differences. Next, a board game or the "Did you use to...?" cards from the kit in groups of four: players move, read a prompt and answer in a full sentence. Wrong sentences are corrected by the group.
pracAlt: Recent changes worksheet from the kit: pairs complete the gaps and add two sentences about their own town.
Used to or past simple? Pairs sort ten sentences and decide which one cannot use used to (a single event) and explain why.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a monologue of about 130 words by Sara, 16, about her grandmother Fatima. Her grandmother used to walk three kilometres to school, didn't use to have electricity at night, would help her mother bake bread every morning and never used to watch TV. Now she lives in the city, uses a tablet and calls her grandchildren on video. Students note what she used to do and what she does now in a two-column table. Check in pairs and ask "What do you think was the hardest thing for her?" If audio is available, use the high school listening named in the kit.
lp.re: Growing up game: groups of four play the growing up board game from the kit, or the teacher reads prompts (first phone, favourite cartoon, a place you used to visit) and each student answers with "I used to...". A student who cannot answer in a full sentence must pass the question to a teammate.
lp.prod: Interview a grandparent (in class). Pairs prepare six questions to ask an older relative about life in Morocco when they were young (What did you use to do after school? Did you use to have a TV?). They role-play the interview, one as the teenager and one as the grandparent, using ideas they know from home. Then they swap partners and tell the new partner two surprising differences, using nowadays and used to.
lp.rw: Read a short text about life 50 years ago (the "this week in history" text from the kit or a similar text) and answer true/false questions, underlining used to forms. Then students write 70 to 90 words about how their life has changed since they were seven: two used to sentences, two present simple sentences with nowadays and one reason for a change. Partners check the form after didn't (use to, not used to).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write "When I was little I used to..., but now I..." and read it aloud, then add one sentence about what you will never do again.
g: Students listen to sentences and mark their grid if it matches their childhood.
Groups play a board game and answer with used to.
Students find who used to do the same things.
Teams write as many sentences about two pictures as they can in 3 minutes.
A student reads clues about a childhood and the group guesses the person.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short text (60 words) imagining life in Oujda in 2060 compared with now, using used to and nowadays.
Support: give a sentence builder with columns (I / My grandparents + used to / didn't use to + verb), a list of 10 childhood verbs and a model paragraph.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about how your life has changed since you were seven, using used to and the present simple.
Ask a grandparent or older neighbour three questions about their childhood and write their answers in six sentences.
Find a photo of your town from the past, describe it in five sentences and compare it with now.
lp.tip: Students often write "I didn't used to" or forget that used to is only for the past. Put "used to = past only" on the board and a thumbs-up or thumbs-down check at the end of each sentence. Be sensitive about family stories: some students may have difficult memories, so offer an alternative topic such as a favourite toy or a game.

Life Pre-Intermediate B1 Student Book (use the matching unit)
Murphy English Grammar in Use Intermediate (matching grammar unit)

weeks.obj: tell a clear story with a beginning, middle and end using past simple and past continuous, and use linkers to organise events
weeks.lang: past continuous and past simple (when, while, as); sequencing and linking (first, then, after that, suddenly, in the end, meanwhile, as soon as); story structure (setting, problem, climax, ending); mystery vocabulary (footprint, clue, suspect, disappear, notice, strange)
weeks.res: When or while? worksheet; Past continuous + past simple worksheet
weeks.act: Story starter circle; when/while sentence building; story map; mystery story in groups; story paragraph
weeks.hw: write a mystery story of 80-100 words that begins "It was a dark night and I was walking home when..."

skills.L: Listen to a short true story and put the events in order, noting what was happening in the background
skills.S: Tell a story in one minute with a setting, a problem and an ending
skills.R: Read a short mystery and find the clues and the linkers
skills.W: Write a story of 80-100 words with linkers

lp.wu: Story circle: the teacher gives an opening ("It was raining when the phone rang.") and each student adds one sentence in turn, using a different tense each time (past continuous for background, past simple for the main event). Groups of six pass the story round twice. Sentences that sound wrong go on a slip for the error stage later. Keep it fast and funny.
wuAlt: Excuses excuses: the teacher asks "Why were you late?" and students invent an excuse using the past continuous ("I was helping an old man when his bag broke.").
Five photos: students look at five pictures and say what was happening in each one a minute ago.
lp.pres: Draw two lines on the board. Line one is a long action (I was walking home) and a short action crosses it (my phone rang). Teach: past continuous (was/were + -ing) for the background or the long action, past simple for the main event. Show when for the short action (When the bus arrived, I was waiting), while for the long action (While I was waiting, I saw a cat). Add as for two actions together. Then show five linkers on strips (first, then, after that, suddenly, in the end) and ask for a one-minute story from the teacher using them.
presAlt: Use the when/while sheet and the past continuous with past simple sheet from the kit, then ask pairs to write four sentences of their own.
Use the narrative tenses unit in American English File 3 as the model text and ask students to underline the past continuous in one colour.
lp.prac: Story map: groups get four cards (a character, a place, a problem, a surprise) and build a story in six sentences with two when/while sentences and three linkers. They draw four quick pictures to match. They tell the story to another group, who ask two questions and note one tense error. The teacher writes three typical errors on the board and the class fixes them together. Quick practice: pairs complete the "What were you doing?" worksheet from the kit.
pracAlt: Past continuous correct the sentence PowerPoint from the kit: teams win a point for each corrected sentence.
Dream world worksheet from the kit: pairs write what they were doing in a dream and compare.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a true story of about 140 words told by a teenager, Imad. Last winter he was walking home from football practice when it started to snow heavily. While he was crossing the park, he heard a small noise and found a puppy under a bench. He took it home, his mum phoned the vet and, after that, the family kept the dog. Students number six events in order and underline the background actions. Check in pairs, then ask "What would you have done?" If audio is available, use the moments or incident listening named in the kit.
lp.re: Excuses excuses board game from the kit: players move, land on a question ("Why were you late for class?" "Where were you last night at 9?") and answer with a past continuous sentence and a past simple sentence. Other players decide if the excuse sounds believable, and the owner gets a point if two players believe it.
lp.prod: Mystery story in groups of four. Each group gets a mystery opening (a missing bike, a strange noise at night, a stranger at the school gate, a lost phone). They plan a story on a map (who, where, what was happening when, what did they find, how does it end) and then tell it to another group, who guess the explanation. The listening group gives one thing they liked and one question. Use the Skit Kit idea from the kit for groups that want to act it out.
lp.rw: Read a short mystery (the Skeleton Lake text or a Marfa Lights passage from the kit) and underline clues in one colour and linkers in another. Answer true/false/not stated questions. Then students write the opening paragraph of 80 to 100 words of a mystery story: setting in the past continuous, the first strange event in the past simple, three linkers and a question at the end ("Who was it?"). Partners check the tenses with a coloured pen.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the first sentence of a story that begins "While I was...,", read it aloud and let a classmate say what happened next in a single sentence.
g: Students add one sentence in turn to create a class story.
Players invent believable excuses with the past continuous.
Teams race to choose the correct word in sentences.
Groups write three clues for a mystery and others guess.
Students roll for a character, place and problem and tell a story in one minute.
diff: Fast finishers: write the ending of the story in two different ways, one funny and one serious, using at least two linkers.
Support: give a story frame (It was... when... suddenly... in the end...) and a card with five linkers and an example for when and while.
hw: Write a mystery story of 80 to 100 words that begins "It was a dark night and I was walking home when...".
Retell a film, series or video game scene in 70 words using the past continuous for background.
Record a one-minute voice message telling a real story and listen for tense mistakes.
lp.tip: Students often use only past simple, so require at least one past continuous in every story and put "background" and "event" labels on the board. Stories are a good place for humour and drama, but remind teens to keep stories school-friendly. Let students tell the story first and correct grammar afterwards, and write good sentences on the board as you hear them.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs students tell a short story about how a family member celebrated Independence Day or heard the news, using the past continuous and past simple ("My grandfather was working in the fields when he heard the news."). They add one linker and share the best sentence with the class.

weeks.obj: talk about food and healthy living, give and ask for advice, and recommend things in a restaurant or a shop
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't/had better/ought to for advice; countable and uncountable quantifiers (some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little, enough); food and health vocabulary (nutrition, vitamins, junk food, balanced, fast food, fresh, recipe); ordering and recommending (I'd recommend, You should try, What's it like?)
weeks.res: Should and shouldn't (joke worksheet); Asking for and giving advice: what should I do?
weeks.act: Food habits survey; advice cards; menu role play; healthy day plan; advice paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words giving advice to a friend who wants to eat better and sleep more

skills.L: Listen to two people talk about health habits and note their problems and the advice they receive
skills.S: Give advice to a partner for five common problems and recommend a dish
skills.R: Read a short text about the food pyramid and decide what is true, false or not stated
skills.W: Write 70-90 words with advice for a friend

lp.wu: Food habits survey: pairs ask each other eight questions (How many meals do you eat a day? How much water do you drink? Do you ever skip breakfast? How often do you eat fast food?) using the Food and drink habits sheet. They tick answers and decide together whether their partner has a healthy week. The teacher listens for much/many and a few/a little and writes common errors on the board.
wuAlt: Snack survey: the class stands up and groups themselves by their favourite snack, then explains why in a sentence.
Healthy or not: the teacher names ten foods and students show thumbs up or down and justify.
lp.pres: Put six problems on the board (I'm always tired. I never have time for breakfast. I get headaches. I can't sleep.). Elicit advice from the class and write the three structures: should/shouldn't + verb, ought to + verb, had better + verb (stronger, a warning: You'd better go to the doctor). Then a quick review of quantifiers with food: some/any, much/many, a lot of, a few/a little, enough, with a mini table of countable and uncountable foods (apples, rice, bread, tea, olives, couscous).
presAlt: Use the should and shouldn't sheet and the what should I do sheet from the kit, and the food and advice unit of American English File 3.
Show a picture of a messy plate and ask students to give three pieces of advice to the person who ate it.
lp.prac: Problem and advice cards: pairs receive eight cards with problems (a teen who sleeps only five hours, a friend who eats only sweets, a cousin who does no sport). Student A reads the problem, student B gives advice with should or had better, and A says if the advice is good or not. Then groups play the countable and uncountable bingo from the kit, or race to write the correct quantifier for each food picture. End with each pair writing a healthy day plan for a teen with 8 sentences.
pracAlt: Advice game or problems and advice from the kit: students move round the class giving advice to cards.
Quantity pairs: pairs sort 20 foods into countable and uncountable and write six sentences with the correct quantifier.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short conversation of about 130 words between a pharmacist and a teen who feels tired all the time. She says he should drink more water, shouldn't skip breakfast, ought to sleep eight hours and had better visit the doctor if the problem continues. The teen explains he eats fast food a lot, drinks two energy drinks a day and uses his phone until 1 a.m. Students tick the problems and write the advice. Check in pairs, then discuss "What advice would you give?" If audio is available, use the health listening named in the kit or the Science of Stress video.
lp.re: Advice relay: teams stand in a line. The teacher reads a problem and the first student gives advice using a different structure each time (should, ought to, had better), then passes it down the line. A team loses a point if a student repeats the same advice or structure.
lp.prod: Restaurant role play: pairs write a short menu for a Moroccan cafe (using the Make a menu sheet) and take turns as waiter and customer. The waiter recommends dishes ("I'd recommend the tajine. It's really tasty and there isn't too much oil."), the customer asks about quantities ("How much sugar is there in the tea?") and orders politely. Pairs swap roles, then perform for another pair, who give feedback on the recommendation language.
lp.rw: Read a short text on the food pyramid and answer true/false/not stated questions on the main ideas. Then students write 70 to 90 words advising a friend who wants to eat better and sleep more: two should sentences, one had better warning, two quantifiers and one reason. Partners check the verb form after should (base form, no -ing).
lp.st: Exit ticket: complete "My best piece of advice is you should... because..." and give it to a classmate, who rates it from 1 to 5.
g: Pairs give advice for problem cards and the class votes on the best one.
Students mark food items and say a quantifier.
Groups design a menu and sell it to the class.
Teams race to give different pieces of advice.
Teams build a healthy plate from cards using quantifiers.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short advice column answer (60 words) to a teen who writes "I'm always tired and I eat junk food".
Support: give a sentence frame for advice (You should/shouldn't + verb), a list of 10 problems and 10 quantifier phrases.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words giving advice to a friend who wants to eat better and sleep more.
Keep a food diary for two days and write six sentences with quantifiers about what you ate.
Ask someone at home for their best health advice and write it in three sentences.
lp.tip: Teens enjoy giving advice but may be shy about talking about their own health or weight. Keep the focus on friends and imaginary teens, and avoid questions about body shape. Correct "should to" and "should + -ing" with a gesture and let students self-correct. If you have a mixed class, mix those with more vocabulary with those who need support.

occ.act: Thanksgiving falls on Thursday 26 November. Optional 10-minute task: students predict what an American family will cook and eat on Thanksgiving, then compare with a Moroccan family feast, using quantifiers ("There is a lot of turkey and a little salad. We have too many sweets at Eid."). Pairs say what they should eat less of and what they should eat more of.

weeks.obj: talk about plans, arrangements and spontaneous decisions, and make, accept and refuse invitations and requests politely
weeks.lang: be going to for plans and intentions; present continuous for fixed arrangements; will for decisions and offers; polite requests and indirect questions (Could you...? Would you mind...-ing? Do you think you could...?); invitations (Would you like to...? How about...? I'm afraid I can't because...)
weeks.res: Going to or will? worksheet; Be going to (intentions and predictions)
weeks.act: Plans mingle; going to vs present continuous vs will sorting; invitation role-plays; weekend plan and message; polite email or message
weeks.hw: write a 70-90 word message inviting a friend to an event and giving details about time, place and plans

skills.L: Listen to two people make plans and note the plans, the arrangements and the decisions
skills.S: Make and respond to three invitations and two polite requests in a role play
skills.R: Read a short email invitation and an answer and underline the polite phrases
skills.W: Write a message of 70-90 words inviting a friend

lp.wu: Plans mingle: students get a card with a situation (this weekend, next summer, after the exam) and walk around asking "What are you going to do...?" and "Are you doing anything on...?". They write the plan and one arrangement they hear ("I'm meeting my cousins at 4"). After five minutes they report the busiest person to the group. The teacher listens for the form after going to and notes errors.
wuAlt: Holiday plans: pairs plan a dream weekend in four sentences with going to and share the plan with another pair.
Diary swap: each student writes five plans in their diary and a partner asks questions.
lp.pres: Show a diary page on the board with five entries and elicit sentences: "I'm going to study (a plan or intention). I'm meeting Sara at 5 (an arrangement with a time and place). I'll call you later (a decision made now)." Compare the three forms with a rule of thumb: going to for what you have decided before, present continuous for fixed arrangements with a time, will for sudden decisions, offers and promises. Then teach the polite requests: Can you / Could you / Would you mind + -ing / Do you think you could, with the polite answers (Sure, of course / I'm afraid I can't).
presAlt: Use the going to or will sheet and the be going to intentions sheet from the kit, plus the future forms unit of American English File 3.
Use the ask politely sheet from the kit: pairs change direct questions into polite indirect ones.
lp.prac: Three forms sort: pairs get 16 sentences about plans, arrangements and decisions and sort them into three groups, correcting the six wrong ones. Next, "The long weekend" worksheet from the kit: pairs plan a weekend in Oujda or on a trip with at least three going to plans and two arrangements. Finally students practise requests with the Could you cards: a student draws a card ("You need to borrow a pen", "You can't hear the teacher") and makes a polite request.
pracAlt: Would you mind: students practise the form -ing with 10 situations and write polite replies.
Put in will or going to: pairs complete 10 gaps and write two more sentences for each.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a phone call of about 130 words between two friends, Leila and Hamza. Hamza asks if she is doing anything on Saturday, Leila says she is meeting her cousin at 3 but invites him to a small birthday party at her house in the evening. He says "Thank you, I'd love to" then realises he is going to a football match with his father until 6, so he says "I'll come late". Students complete a table with plans, arrangements and decisions. Check in pairs, then ask "Which invitation would you accept?" If audio is available, use the plans or birthday listening named in the kit.
lp.re: Party time: groups of four are planning a party. Each student has a role card with a request (you need a lift, you want music, you need an extra chair, you can't come until later). They must make polite requests using Could you/Would you mind, and the others respond with I'll... or I'm afraid I can't. Groups get a point for each polite request.
lp.prod: Invitation role-play. In pairs, students role-play three situations on cards (inviting a friend to a match, asking a neighbour for help with a heavy bag, refusing an invitation because of an exam). They must use going to for a plan, present continuous for an arrangement, will for a decision and one polite request. Then they swap partners and perform one scene for the class, who note one polite phrase they hear. Use the mingle or the day tripper task from the kit for groups who finish.
lp.rw: Read a short email invitation and a reply (such as a birthday party or school trip) and underline the polite phrases and the three future forms. Answer five questions. Then students write 70 to 90 words inviting a friend to an event: where and when, what you are going to do, what you are doing before, one polite request ("Could you bring...?") and a closing line. Partners check that the form after will and going to is a base verb.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write a one-line invitation to a classmate and reply to the one you receive with a polite accept or refuse; hand both slips to the teacher.
g: Students find who has the same plans for the weekend.
Teams sort sentences into plan, arrangement and decision.
The teacher reads requests and students say if they are polite or not, then improve them.
Groups plan a party and make polite requests.
Students invite the next person and the next person must refuse politely with a reason.
diff: Fast finishers: write a polite dialogue of ten lines in which someone declines an invitation but offers an alternative, using at least three polite request structures.
Support: give a three-column table (plan: going to, arrangement: present continuous, decision: will) with two examples each and a list of polite phrases with their answers.
hw: Write a 70 to 90 word message inviting a friend to an event and giving details about time, place and plans.
Write five sentences about your plans for the next holiday using going to and present continuous.
Ask three people at home what they are doing this weekend and report in five sentences.
lp.tip: Teens find "will" and "going to" confusing when both seem correct, so teach the rule of thumb (decided before = going to, decided now = will) and accept both when a reason is given. Polite language is often hard for teens who say "Give me", so model tone and ask for a smile and please in the role-plays. Keep real invitations safe (school events, class parties) and do not ask students to invite each other to private places.

weeks.obj: make predictions and talk about possibilities, use the first conditional to describe cause and consequence, and give a short opinion on the future
weeks.lang: will / won't / may / might / could for predictions and possibilities; probably, definitely, perhaps; first conditional (if + present simple, will + verb); zero conditional for facts (If you heat ice, it melts); unless and when as alternatives to if; cause and consequence phrases (so, as a result, that is why)
weeks.res: Learn English 2026: Conditionals Type 1 (video lessons and textbook); Will: predicting the future
weeks.act: Prediction poll; if chain game; cause and consequence cards; future life interview; prediction paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70-90 words about what you think life will be like in 2040, using will, might and at least two first conditional sentences

skills.L: Listen to a short talk about technology in the future and note the predictions, the probability words and the conditions
skills.S: Talk for one minute about your future using will, might and if sentences
skills.R: Read a short article of predictions that came true and decide which prediction is certain, possible or unlikely
skills.W: Write 70-90 words about the future with predictions and conditions

lp.wu: Prediction poll: the teacher reads eight statements about the next 20 years ("Everyone will have a flying car." "Most people will work from home." "Robots will teach in schools.") and students move to one side of the room for "definitely", "probably" or "no way". They give a reason with "I think... because...". Count how many predictions the class agrees on and write them on the board. The teacher notes how students form will and might.
wuAlt: Crystal ball: pairs take turns to predict the next five years for their partner ("You'll probably study abroad. You might become a doctor.") and the partner reacts.
If chain: the teacher starts "If it rains tomorrow, I will..." and students continue the chain with their own result.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "I will probably pass the exam. I might go to university in Rabat. Scientists may find a cure." Elicit the scale of certainty: will definitely, will probably, might/may/could, probably won't. Then show the first conditional: "If it rains, we will stay at home." Explain the pattern (if + present simple, will + verb) and that the if clause can come first or second with a comma only when first. Add unless (= if not) and when (sure) and the zero conditional for facts (If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils). Check with a mini quiz on cause and result.
presAlt: Use the Learn English first conditional video lessons and the matching conditionals unit in American English File 3 from the kit.
Use the "What will happen..." sheet from the kit and ask pairs to finish the sentences with their own ideas.
lp.prac: If chain game: students sit in groups of five. The first student says a first conditional sentence ("If I pass my exam, I will celebrate with my friends."), the next must use the result in a new if clause ("If I celebrate with my friends, I will..."). Groups keep the chain going for 3 minutes, with a point for the longest chain without error. Then pairs complete the "In the next 30 years..." sheet with will, may and might and compare with another pair. Quick practice: the day trip might sheet from the kit.
pracAlt: Zero conditional guessing game from the kit: students guess the fact from a clue ("If you mix red and blue, ...") and then write their own.
Prediction cards: pairs match 12 cards (a cause and a consequence) and write sentences with will, might or if.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short talk of about 140 words by a science teacher, Ms Nour, about life in 2040. She says that most cars will probably be electric, that many people may work from home and that robots might help in hospitals. She warns that if people continue to use plastic, the oceans will get dirtier, and that unless we plant more trees, cities will become hotter. Students complete a table with predictions, probability words and conditions. Check in pairs, then ask "Which prediction worries or excites you?" If audio is available, use the future family listening named in the kit or the solar power video.
lp.re: Predictor game from the kit: teams write predictions on cards (a sport team, the weather, a class result, a new phone) and the teacher keeps them in a box. Cards are read aloud and the class votes definitely/probably/might/no way, with a reason using if. Teams score when other teams agree with them.
lp.prod: Island adventure decision task (critical thinking). Groups of four are stranded on an island with eight items. They decide which three to take and what will happen if they make each choice, using first conditional and will/might ("If we take the radio, we will be able to call for help, but we might not have enough food"). Each group presents its decision in one minute and the class asks questions. This links cause and consequence with real teamwork.
lp.rw: Read a short article on ten predictions made 100 years ago that came true (the predictions text from the kit) and decide whether each prediction is true, false or not stated, underlining will and might. Then students write 70 to 90 words about life in 2040: two predictions with will/might, two first conditional sentences about what will happen if people do or do not change, and an opinion sentence. Partners check the verb after if (present simple, not will).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write "If I... next year, I will..." and share with a partner, then write one prediction for the class in 10 words and put it in a box. The teacher will read the predictions at the end of the year.
g: Teams write predictions and the class votes on probability.
Students create a chain of first conditional sentences.
Pairs predict each other's future with will and might.
Teams match cards for causes and results.
Groups decide what to take and explain consequences.
diff: Fast finishers: write a mini dialogue (8 lines) between two friends arguing about what the future will be like, using at least four conditional sentences.
Support: give a first conditional table (if + present simple, will + verb) with six examples, a probability scale poster and a model paragraph with gaps.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about what you think life will be like in 2040, using will, might and at least two first conditional sentences.
Make a poster with five predictions for your town, each with a result in a first conditional sentence.
Interview a grandparent about a prediction they once made and whether it came true; write five sentences.
lp.tip: Teens often write "if it will rain" so put a big sign on the wall: "If + present, will + verb". Make predictions funny and personal so students are willing to take risks, and avoid discussing frightening topics such as war. This unit closes the first block of ten weeks, so spend five minutes asking students to look at their week 1 contract and tick what they have already done.
