weeks.obj: talk about rules and obligations at school, at home and around the world, give and defend an opinion about a school rule, and write a short paragraph on a rule you would change
weeks.lang: obligation and permission (must / mustn't, have to / don't have to, can / can't, be allowed to / not be allowed to); the difference between mustn't and don't have to; giving opinions and reasons (I think students should..., In my opinion..., It would be better if...); school vocabulary (uniform, timetable, detention, break, term, exam)
weeks.res: School uniforms around the world (PowerPoint); Must and mustn't worksheet
weeks.act: Rules or not? sorting game; mustn't vs don't have to practice; school rules debate in teams; paragraph about a rule you would change
weeks.hw: write 70 to 90 words about a school rule you would change and why, using have to, don't have to and allowed to

skills.L: Listen to a student describing the rules in her school and tick which rules are strict and which are free
skills.S: Explain the rules of your school or home to a partner, then defend an opinion about one rule for 45 seconds
skills.R: Read a short text about school systems in three countries and find three differences
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about a school rule you would change, with a reason and an example

lp.wu: Rules or not? The teacher says a sentence about school ("You wear a uniform." "You use your phone in class." "You eat in the classroom.") and students stand on one side of the room for "always true here", the other for "never true here", or in the middle for "sometimes". Two students from different sides must explain in one sentence ("In my school we have to..., but we aren't allowed to..."). Keep it to 6 or 7 statements and finish with a quick vote on the most unfair rule.
wuAlt: Two truths and a lie about school: each student writes three sentences about their school or a school they imagine (two true, one false) using have to and can. Partners guess the lie.
Guess the rule: one student mimes a rule (no running, silence, hand up) and the group guesses with "You mustn't..." or "You have to...".
lp.pres: Draw two columns on the board, "It is necessary" and "It is forbidden", and elicit examples from the students' own school: "We have to arrive before 8.30. We mustn't leave the building at break." Then add a third column, "It is not necessary", with "We don't have to wear a uniform on Fridays." Show the key contrast: mustn't means forbidden, don't have to means free choice, and show that "be allowed to" is the same as "can" but sounds more formal ("Students aren't allowed to use their phones"). Practise the forms: have to / has to / had to for the past, and questions with "Do we have to...?" and "Are we allowed to...?". Check meaning with a fast true/false drill: "In Morocco you mustn't drive at 14. Is that forbidden or not necessary?"
presAlt: Use the matching unit in the American English File 3 Student Book on rules and obligation from the kit.
Use the Must and mustn't worksheet from the kit, then the School uniforms around the world PowerPoint to compare rules in different countries.
lp.prac: Mustn't or don't have to? Pairs get ten short situations on cards (a museum, an exam room, a Sunday morning at home, a football pitch, a library) and write a sentence with the correct form for each, then swap with another pair for checking. Next, a controlled error hunt with eight sentences such as "You don't have to run in the corridor" and "We must to wear a uniform", corrected in pairs. Finally, Class contract: pairs write six rules for this English class with must, have to, can and allowed to, then read them to the group and the class votes on the best five.
pracAlt: Use the Who has to do what worksheet from the kit for short question and answer practice.
Use the Obligation Game from the kit as a board game in groups of four.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short monologue (about 120 words) in which a girl called Salma describes the rules in her school: uniform every day, phones locked in a box, lessons from 8 to 5, no homework on Fridays, students may choose the last subject of the week. First listening: tick which rules she thinks are fair. Second listening: complete a table with "have to", "mustn't", "allowed to". If audio is available, use the Wendi (rules) or Jeyong (school) recordings from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Rule detective: the teacher gives each group a secret place (a swimming pool, a mosque, a cinema, an airport, a hospital). One student describes the rules with "You have to..." and "You mustn't..." without naming the place, and the group guesses it. Rotate the speaker after each round and keep score on the board.
lp.prod: School rules debate: groups of six split into two teams. The motion is "Schools should let students use phones in class" (other motions: "School uniform should be compulsory", "Students should choose some of their lessons"). Each team has 8 minutes to prepare three reasons with an example, using "I think students should..." and "It would be better if...". Each side speaks for two minutes, then they answer one question from the other team ("Do students really have to...?"). Another group acts as judges and scores reasons, examples and politeness on a tick sheet. Repeat with a new motion and new roles if there is time.
lp.rw: Read a short text from the kit (about 150 words) comparing school days in three countries and answer four true/false/not stated questions and two matching questions, underlining every obligation phrase. Then write 70 to 90 words: "A school rule I would change". Include one rule, why it does not work, what you suggest, and at least one have to, one don't have to and one allowed to. Partners swap and underline one good sentence and one that needs correcting.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one rule you would keep and one you would change in your school, each with a reason ("I would keep the uniform because it stops arguments, but students should be allowed to bring their phones to class.").
g: Move to a side of the room to show true, false or sometimes.
Mime a rule so the group says it with must or mustn't.
Describe a place by its rules only.
Correct sentences with must to, don't must and other errors.
Teams write and vote on class rules.
diff: Fast finishers: write 100 words comparing school in Morocco with a school in another country, using have to, don't have to and allowed to. Support: give a sentence frame card ("In my school we have to... We aren't allowed to... We don't have to...") and a table of must, mustn't and don't have to with example sentences.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words about a school rule you would change and why, using have to, don't have to and allowed to.
Ask two family members which rules they had at school and write four sentences comparing then and now.
Watch or listen to a short video about school life in another country and note three differences from your school.
lp.tip: Teens enjoy arguing about rules, so give each speaker a time limit and let the judges decide who wins. The most common mistake is "don't must" and "must to"; collect these on the board during the debate and correct them as a group afterwards. Keep school gossip about named teachers out of the lesson and talk about rules in general.

weeks.obj: plan a trip, book and solve problems at a hotel, compare places and write a short guide to Morocco for visitors
weeks.lang: comparatives and superlatives with as...as, not as...as, much / a bit / far more (comparing places and transport); travel vocabulary (book, check in, departure, delay, journey, sightseeing, souvenir); asking for information and making requests (Could you tell me..., Is it possible to..., I'd like to book...); describing a place (it's famous for, you can, there's plenty to see)
weeks.res: Comparatives + not as + as; Making and Confirming a Booking
weeks.act: Comparing places; hotel booking role play; plan a three-day trip; Morocco guide for visitors
weeks.hw: write 80 to 100 words recommending a place in Morocco to a foreign friend, comparing it with another place

skills.L: Listen to a conversation at a hotel reception and note the booking details and the problem
skills.S: Take part in a booking role play and then present a three-day trip plan for 60 seconds
skills.R: Read a short travel text and answer detail questions
skills.W: Write an 80-100 word recommendation of a place in Morocco

lp.wu: Where am I? The teacher describes a place with short clues ("It's far more crowded than my village. It's famous for its blue walls. You can buy souvenirs...") and teams write down their guess. Then teams of three write their own three clues for a Moroccan city or place (Chefchaouen, Marrakech, Oujda, Essaouira) and read them out for the others to guess. Award points for the earliest correct guess.
wuAlt: Would you rather: students stand on one side or the other for choices such as the beach or the mountains, train or plane, a hotel or a camp, and give one comparison with a reason.
Holiday bingo: students fill a card with travel words and tick them as the teacher describes situations.
lp.pres: Show two pictures, for example a train and a plane, and elicit comparisons from the students ("The plane is faster than the train, but it is much more expensive."). Add the structures "as...as" and "not as...as" ("A hotel isn't as cheap as a hostel.") and intensifiers a bit, much, far ("Marrakech is far busier than Oujda."). Put a mini-dialogue at a hotel on the board: "Good evening, I'd like to book a double room for two nights. Is breakfast included? Could you tell me what time check-out is?" Underline the polite request forms and give students two minutes to practise it in pairs, swapping roles. Add six words for problems: broken, noisy, dirty, no hot water, wrong room, lost key.
presAlt: Use the matching travel and comparison unit in the American English File 3 Student Book from the kit.
Use the Comparatives + not as + as worksheet from the kit and then the Vacation lesson plan for vocabulary.
lp.prac: Comparison pairs: pairs get a set of picture cards (cities, transport, hotels) and make three sentences for each pair of cards using -er, more, as...as and a modifier. Then Hotel problems: pairs get a card with a problem ("There is no hot water in room 12") and write a polite complaint and a request using "Could you...?" and "Would it be possible to...?". Finish with an information gap: Student A has the timetable of a Moroccan bus, Student B has the prices, and they ask each other questions to fill in the missing information.
pracAlt: Use the Hotel Problems worksheet from the kit for the complaint practice.
Use Making and Confirming a Booking from the kit as a reading and role play.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short hotel reception dialogue (about 130 words) between a guest and a receptionist: the guest has booked a double room for three nights, the room has a broken air conditioner, and the receptionist offers another room on a higher floor at the same price. First listening: tick the problem and the solution. Second listening: note the dates, the room type, the price and the time of check-out. If audio is available, use the Greg (travel tips) or Kate (travel) recordings from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Beat the clock: teams get a destination card (Fes, Agadir, Paris, Istanbul) and have two minutes to write as many comparisons as they can with Oujda or another city. One point for each correct sentence and a bonus point for as...as. Read the best sentences aloud.
lp.prod: Plan a three-day trip: groups of four get a budget of 2,000 dirhams per person and a map card. They choose a destination in Morocco, decide transport, accommodation and three activities, and prepare a 60-second presentation. During the presentation one student must use a comparison, one a superlative and one a polite request ("We'd like to ask you to join us."). The class asks one question to each group and then votes on the plan they would join.
lp.rw: Read a 150-word text from the kit on tourism or ecotourism and answer five questions (detail and true/false/not stated). Then write 80 to 100 words recommending a place in Morocco to a foreign friend: where it is, why it is special, how to get there, and one comparison with another place. Partners underline one good phrase and one thing to improve.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence comparing two places you know and one polite request you could make at a hotel.
g: Guess a place from short clues.
Stand on a side and explain with a comparison.
Teams write comparisons from picture cards.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 100-word tourist leaflet for your city with at least three comparisons and one superlative. Support: give a comparative table (adjective, comparative, superlative) and a booking dialogue with gaps.
hw: Write 80 to 100 words recommending a place in Morocco to a foreign friend, comparing it with another place.
Find a short travel video or webpage in English about a place in Morocco and note five useful words.
Interview a family member about the best trip they have taken and write five sentences.
lp.tip: Students often have good local knowledge and enjoy telling visitors what to see, so let them lead the Morocco guide and correct their language afterwards. Watch for "more cheaper" and "the most biggest"; do a quick error correction on the board each lesson. Keep budgets realistic so the planning is a genuine decision task.

occ.act: Christmas (25 December) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: pairs write and perform a short conversation in which a friend invites them to a winter party and they accept or politely decline ("Thanks for inviting me, but I have to study for an exam. Maybe next time!") using have to, could and a reason, then compare how different families celebrate the end of the year.

weeks.obj: define and describe people, objects and places with relative clauses, play a definitions game and write a short description
weeks.lang: defining relative clauses (who, which, that, where, whose); relative pronouns as object (the film that I saw, the girl whom I met); describing function and material (a thing that is used for..., made of); opening a definition (It's a person who..., It's a place where...); circumlocution when a word is missing (it's a kind of..., it's like...)
weeks.res: Relative clauses (PowerPoint); Who, Which, When, Where
weeks.act: Guess the object; relative clause building; definitions game with teams; describe-and-draw task; description paragraph
weeks.hw: write 70 to 90 words describing an object, place or person from your life using at least four relative clauses

skills.L: Listen to a student describing three souvenirs and match each to a picture
skills.S: Describe a word to a partner without saying it for 45 seconds
skills.R: Read a short text about a famous landmark and find the relative clauses
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word description of a place or object with four relative clauses

lp.wu: Guess my object: the teacher holds an object in a bag and gives three clues ("It's something that you use to... It's made of... You find it in a place where..."). Students guess. Then each pair picks an everyday object from the room, thinks of three clues and reads them to the class. Keep it fast and award a point for each correct guess after the first clue.
wuAlt: Taboo cards with school words: one student describes a word without using the forbidden words and the team guesses.
Odd one out: the teacher says four words and students explain which one does not belong with a relative clause ("A doctor is a person who...").
lp.pres: Write four short definitions on the board and ask what is the same: "A teacher is a person who helps students learn. A library is a place where you can borrow books. A phone is a thing that you use to call people. Samira is the girl whose brother plays football." Elicit that who is for people, which and that for things, where for places and whose for possession. Explain that in defining clauses there is no comma and that we can leave out the pronoun when it is the object ("The film (that) I saw was great"). Do a fast transformation drill: join "I met a girl. She plays the guitar." into "I met a girl who plays the guitar." Check meaning with the question "Can we say the book who I read?"
presAlt: Use the relative clause PowerPoint and the Who, Which, When, Where worksheet from the kit.
Use the AEF 3 Student Book unit on relative clauses from the kit, then the Grammar Sense relative clause exercises.
lp.prac: Sentence puzzle: pairs get cut-up cards (the beginning, the pronoun, the end) and build ten sentences such as "A refrigerator is a machine which keeps food cold." Then error hunt: eight sentences with typical errors ("The boy which lives next door", "The place where I went there", "She is the teacher who she teaches us"). Finally, Make your own: students write five definitions of school or Moroccan life words (tajine, souk, medina, riad, bus pass) with relative clauses and test them on a partner.
pracAlt: Use Fold Your Arms from the kit as a relative clauses fluency task.
Use the Word Bluff worksheet from the kit for a speaking game.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short monologue (about 120 words) in which a traveller describes three souvenirs from her trips: a lamp that she bought in Fes, a ring which her grandmother gave her, and a postcard from a town where her parents met. First listening: match each description to a picture. Second listening: write the relative pronoun used and one more detail. If audio is available, use the AJ (souvenirs) recordings from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Relative clause bingo: students write nine words from a list on the board (tourist, kitchen, nurse, laptop, bakery, referee, hero, passport, neighbour) in a 3 by 3 grid. The teacher gives definitions with relative clauses ("It's a person who works in a hospital") and students cross out the matching word. First to complete a line shouts "Bingo!" and reads their definitions back.
lp.prod: Definitions challenge: teams of four get a pack of 20 word cards. One student describes the word on the card without using it, using a relative clause ("It's a place where you go when you are ill"), and the team has 60 seconds to get as many as possible. Rotate the describer. Then Describe and draw: Student A describes a picture of a room or a Moroccan street with relative clauses and Student B draws it without seeing it; they compare the drawing with the original and talk about the differences.
lp.rw: Read a 150-word text from the kit about a famous landmark or invention and underline the relative clauses. Answer four comprehension questions and say what each underlined clause adds. Then write 70 to 90 words describing your favourite place or object, with four relative clauses (a place where I relax, a thing that I use every day, a person who inspires me). Partners circle the relative pronouns and check commas.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two definitions with who and where about places or people in Oujda ("A baker is a person who makes bread.") and one word you could not say today and how you explained it. Hand in at the door.
g: Clues with relative clauses for a hidden object.
Describe a word without saying it.
Cross out words that match definitions.
Draw a picture from spoken description only.
diff: Fast finishers: write a riddle with four clues using who, which, that and where and read it to the class. Support: give a table of pronouns (people, things, places, possession) with one example each and a gapped definitions card.
hw: Write 70 to 90 words describing an object, place or person from your life using at least four relative clauses.
Write five definitions of school words with who, which and where for a younger student.
Find a description of a famous place in English online and copy three relative clauses from it.
lp.tip: Teens love a competitive definitions game, so keep teams small and switch roles often. The usual errors are "the man who he" and "the place where I went there", so display two models on the wall. Do not worry about whom and whose in speaking; make sure who, which, that and where are secure.

occ.act: New Year week. Optional 10-minute task: students describe the things they want to do this year using relative clauses ("I want a friend who makes me laugh. I want to visit a place where there is snow.") and share them in groups of three.
occ.hw: Write three New Year wishes using who, which or where.

weeks.obj: write a clear informal email and a short article, organise ideas in paragraphs and use linkers and an appropriate register
weeks.lang: informal email phrases (Hi Sara, Thanks for your message, I hope you're well, Write soon, Best wishes); linkers (and, but, so, because, although, however, then, after that); giving news and invitations (I'm writing to tell you..., Would you like to..., Why don't you...); register (contractions, short sentences vs formal phrases)
weeks.res: Writing guide: E-mail writing; Writing paragraphs, essays, emails and letters
weeks.act: Message register game; email structure; PET Writing Part 1 task; short article; peer editing with a checklist
weeks.hw: write a 100-word email to a friend inviting them to an event, describing the plan and asking two questions

skills.L: Listen to a voicemail and note the invitation, the plan and the reply
skills.S: Role play a phone conversation about a plan and then retell the message
skills.R: Read an email and answer questions about who, what and when
skills.W: Write a 100-word informal email responding to a message and answering four points

lp.wu: Pass the message: in groups of five, the first student whispers a short message ("Hi Ali, can you meet me at 5 outside the library? Bring your notebook") and the last student writes it down. Compare the final version with the original and talk about what changed. Then, in pairs, rewrite one text message from "u r 4 5?" style into a full sentence, so students see the difference between texting and writing an email.
wuAlt: Spot the register: the teacher shows six sentences and students sort them into "to a friend" and "to a head teacher".
Send me a message: students write a 15-word message to a partner and the partner replies, then they read both aloud.
lp.pres: Show a model email on the board with 4 paragraphs: greeting, reason for writing, main content, and ending ("Hi Nora, Thanks for your email! I'm writing to answer your questions. Yes, I'd love to come on Saturday, but I have to help my mother in the morning. Can I arrive at about 2 o'clock? By the way, shall I bring anything to eat? Write back soon, Yassine"). Underline the greeting, the opening line, the linkers and the closing. Compare it with a formal version and list the differences (contractions, exclamation marks, short phrases). Introduce the PET Writing Part 1 rule: the email has three or four content points, and you must answer them all in 100 words. Show the useful phrases: Thanks for..., I'm sorry to hear..., Why don't we..., I can't wait to....
presAlt: Use the B1 Preliminary Writing Part 1 lesson plan and the video with tips from the kit.
Use the E-mail writing guide and the Writing paragraphs, essays, emails and letters guide from the kit.
lp.prac: Sentence upgrade: pairs get a list of short sentences ("I went to the cinema. It was good. I met my cousin.") and join them with linkers into one flowing paragraph. Then, Email puzzle: pairs get a jumbled email cut into 8 parts and put it in order, marking the greeting, the reason, the content and the closing. Finally, a quick answer-all-points task: they read a short message from a friend with four questions and underline which points they must cover in their answer.
pracAlt: Use the Auction on linking words game from the kit in teams.
Use the Agony aunt writing prompts from the kit for short advice emails.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short voicemail (about 100 words) from a friend: she invites you to her cousin's birthday, tells you it is at a cafe near the station on Sunday at four, asks you to bring a small gift, and asks you to call her back if you cannot come. First listening: note the day, the time and the place. Second listening: write what you would answer in two sentences. If audio is available, use the Ruth (invitation) or Ruth (gift) recordings from the Listening folder.
lp.re: Linker auction: the teacher reads 10 sentences with linkers, some correct and some not ("I was tired so I went to bed early", "Although it was raining, but we played"). Teams bid with imaginary money on the sentences they think are correct. After each round correct the wrong sentences on the board.
lp.prod: PET email task: pairs get a task card (for example, "Your English friend Sam is coming to Morocco for a week. Write to him: say which city he should visit and why, tell him what to bring and ask him two questions"). Pairs plan four content points in two minutes, then write alone for 12 minutes (100 words) using the structure from the board. In the last 5 minutes, partners swap and tick a checklist: greeting, all four points answered, linkers, correct tenses, closing.
lp.rw: Read two short emails from the kit (one to a friend and one to a school director) and answer questions about the difference in register and about the details. Then write a 100-word article for a school magazine about "The best way to spend a free weekend", with a title, an introduction, two paragraphs and a short ending, and at least three linkers (because, although, however). Partners circle the linkers and mark one good idea.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write a two-line message to a friend that you would send today, and then rewrite it as a short note to a teacher.
g: Whisper a message along a line and compare it with the original.
Sort sentences into friendly and formal.
Bid on correct sentences with linkers.
Put a jumbled email in order.
Teams answer a message with four points in 3 minutes.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second email, this time to a head teacher, on the same topic, and underline the differences. Support: give an email frame with the greeting, four sentence starters and a closing, and a list of ten linkers with examples.
hw: Write a 100-word email to a friend inviting them to an event, describing the plan and asking two questions.
Read an English email or message from a friend or an example online and underline five informal expressions.
Write a short article of 80 words about a favourite place in your town, using three linkers.
lp.tip: Many students write long single paragraphs; teach them to start a new paragraph for each content point. Give a clear word count (100 words for PET Writing Part 1) and have students count and mark their own words. Give feedback as two strengths and one target so that students stay motivated.

occ.act: New Year recap (first week of January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year using the past simple, then write two lines of an email telling a friend about it ("Hi Rayan, I had a great break. I visited my cousins in Nador and...").

weeks.obj: show what you can do in speaking, listening, reading, writing and use of language, using PET-style tasks, and set targets for Semester 2
weeks.lang: review of Semester 1: question forms, personality and appearance, present perfect, for and since, quantifiers, verb patterns, used to, past continuous, advice, plans, first conditional, modals of obligation, comparisons, relative clauses, informal writing
weeks.res: PET Advice: Do's and Don'ts; PET Grammar Test 01
weeks.act: Short speaking pair task with rubric; listening; reading; writing; language use; self-assessment and targets
weeks.hw: write three sentences about what went well in the assessment and two targets for Semester 2

skills.L: Listen to a short recording and answer multiple choice and note completion questions
skills.S: Speak in pairs: personal questions, describe a photo and agree a decision
skills.R: Read a 250-word text and answer eight questions
skills.W: Write a 100-word email answering a message with four content points

lp.wu: Error carousel (10 minutes): pairs receive an anonymous text with 10 common errors from the semester (tenses, word order, articles, prepositions) and correct it. They compare with another pair and then check with the key. Keep it light and tell students that today is a progress check, not a test to pass or fail.
wuAlt: Four-question warm-up: each student asks their partner four questions from the semester (about plans, experience, habits and opinions) and answers in two sentences each.
Quick quiz: the teacher reads 10 sentences and students decide if each is correct and fix the mistakes.
lp.pres: Explain the assessment plan: 8 minutes for the paired speaking, 15 minutes listening, 25 minutes reading and language use, 20 minutes writing. Show the speaking rubric on the board with four lines: grammar and vocabulary, pronunciation, interaction (do you listen and answer), and task completion, each from 1 to 5. Give one example of a 4 and a 2 for each line, using a sample answer ("I like football because it is fun" vs "I like football because I can play with my friends, and it also keeps me fit, so I try to play at least twice a week"). Remind students of the strategies from the semester: read the question first, underline key words, never leave a gap empty, and write the number of words.
presAlt: Use the PET Advice document from the kit for a short strategy discussion.
Use the PET Teacher's Book from the kit for the format and marking notes.
lp.prac: Language use section (20 minutes): students complete a test with 15 items made from the kit (a grammar test and a fill-in-the-blank test) covering the semester's grammar (present perfect, quantifiers, verb patterns, used to, past continuous, relative clauses, modals) and 5 sentence transformations ("I haven't seen him for two years" becomes "I last saw him two years ago"). Students work alone, then swap papers for marking with the key and note their score on a record card.
pracAlt: Use a second set of grammar items from the PET exercises in the kit.
Use the Grammar Sense test from the kit as a shorter alternative.
lp.ls: Listening (15 minutes): the teacher reads twice a 150-word conversation between two friends planning a school trip (three speakers or two voices; the teacher reads at normal speed). Part 1: five multiple choice questions on place, time, cost, activity and decision. Part 2: complete five notes with a word or number from the second listening. If audio is available, use the high school recordings (Tres or Mark) from the Listening folder in the kit and write five questions yourself.
lp.re: Error check and consolidation (10 minutes): students work in pairs to compare answers from the language use section. For every wrong answer they must explain the rule to their partner in one sentence. The teacher goes round and notes the three most common errors for the next lesson.
lp.prod: Paired speaking (about 8 minutes per pair, the teacher is examiner while the others read). Part 1: three personal questions each (home, school, free time). Part 2: each student looks at a photo and describes it for 30 seconds (what they see, where it is, what the people are doing). Part 3: together they decide how to spend a small budget for a class party and agree on a final choice. The teacher scores with the rubric on the board (grammar and vocabulary, pronunciation, interaction, task completion, 1 to 5). The next pair starts as the first pair finishes, and waiting students read in silence.
lp.rw: While pairs are examined, students read a 250-word article from the kit and answer eight questions (four multiple choice and four true/false/not stated). Then everyone writes a 100-word email responding to a message with four content points (for example, a friend invites you to a weekend in a new city and asks four questions). Students count their words, check the greeting and the closing and hand the email in.
lp.st: Closing: students complete a self-assessment sheet with the seven "I can" statements below (tick: easily, with help, not yet), choose two targets for Semester 2 and hand it in at the door.
g: Correct a text with 10 mistakes in pairs.
Match each task type to the best strategy.
Describe a photo for 30 seconds without stopping.
Teams answer grammar questions from Semester 1.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second email of 100 words on a different topic using at least three linkers and a relative clause. Support: give a word bank of linkers and verb patterns and a sentence frame for the email.
hw: Write three sentences about what went well in the assessment and two targets for Semester 2.
Choose three grammar areas from Semester 1 and write two sentences for each.
Read a short article in English and note ten words you want to learn, with a short example.
lp.tip: Present this as a progress check and keep a calm atmosphere. Give clear timings and use the same rubric lines in the speaking and writing feedback so students understand their marks. Record two strengths for each student when you return their results, and avoid correcting everything in red.
checklist: I can answer personal questions and give reasons in a paired speaking task.
I can describe a photograph for 30 seconds and say what the people are doing.
I can agree a decision with a partner and give my opinion politely.
I can follow a short conversation and answer multiple choice and note completion questions.
I can read a 250-word text and answer detail and true/false questions.
I can write a 100-word informal email that answers four points.
I can use the main grammar of Semester 1 (present perfect, used to, past continuous, modals, comparatives, relative clauses) in sentences and short texts.

occ.act: Yennayer (Amazigh New Year, 14 January) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task after the assessment: students tell their group how their family celebrates it, what food is prepared, and why traditions like this matter, using at least one relative clause ("It's a day when we eat a big meal with the family").
occ.hw: Write 6 sentences about a festival in your family and why it is important.

weeks.theme: New year, mid-year review and PET orientation
weeks.obj: reflect on Semester 1 results, understand the PET (B1 Preliminary) exam format, practise one task from each paper and start a personal error log
weeks.lang: describing goals and plans (I'd like to..., My main aim is to..., I'm going to focus on...); exam strategy language (skim, scan, underline key words, guess the word, check the tense); review of tenses and grammar from Semester 1; reflecting on progress (I've improved at..., I still find... difficult, I need to practise...)
weeks.res: PET Objective Student's Book (exam overview pages); Target PET Student's Book (exam strategies)
weeks.act: Goal-setting circle; PET exam format quiz; one task from each paper; error log; speaking in pairs
weeks.hw: complete your error log with eight mistakes from the semester and write one correct sentence for each

skills.L: Listen to a short announcement and answer multiple choice questions
skills.S: Describe your goals for the semester to a partner and answer questions about the PET speaking test
skills.R: Read a short notice and a text and choose the correct answer
skills.W: Write the first three sentences of a PET email and mark the points to cover

lp.wu: Look back, look forward: students write on a sticky note one thing they did well in Semester 1 and one thing they want to improve. In groups of four they read their notes aloud and the group suggests how to improve ("You could watch a series with subtitles. Why don't you read short stories?"). Each group chooses the best tip and shares it with the class.
wuAlt: New Year interview: pairs ask each other five questions (What are you going to do this semester? What are you proud of? What do you find hardest in English?) and then introduce their partner to the group.
Two truths and a lie about your New Year.
lp.pres: Show the four parts of the PET exam on the board: Reading (45 minutes, six parts), Writing (a short email and a story or article), Listening (about 30 minutes, four parts) and Speaking (10 minutes in pairs, four parts). Match each part with its task type using a simple card game (for example, "gapped text", "multiple choice", "note completion", "describe a photo"). Explain three strategies: read the questions before the text, underline key words, and always write an answer. Show where marks are won: content, organisation, language. Ask students to say which part they think is hardest and why, to prepare the error log.
presAlt: Use the PET Objective Student's Book or the Target PET Student's Book from the kit for the format overview.
Use the PET Advice document and the writing rubric guide from the kit.
lp.prac: Mini-exam stations (4 stations, 5 minutes each): Station 1, a gapped sentence task with 6 items; Station 2, multiple choice reading of three signs and notices; Station 3, a sentence transformation task with 5 items; Station 4, matching people to short texts. Students go in pairs and write their score on a card. Afterwards they discuss which station was easier and which strategy helped most.
pracAlt: Use the PET grammar and fill-in-the-blank tests from the kit as extra practice.
Use the Test It Fix It book from the kit for error correction practice.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short announcement (about 100 words) on a school trip: the bus leaves at 8.15, students must bring lunch and a jacket, the museum visit lasts two hours, and the group returns at 5.30. Students answer five multiple choice questions. Then the teacher reads a second short text and students note the answers in a table. If audio is available, use the New Year recording from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Error hunt: the teacher gives each pair a text of 10 sentences with common mistakes from the semester (articles, word order, past forms, prepositions). They find and correct them in 5 minutes and then add two sentences of their own with mistakes for another pair to find.
lp.prod: PET speaking practice (pairs): Part 1, personal questions about family, school and free time (2 minutes). Part 2, each student describes a photo for one minute while the partner listens. Part 3, together they choose the best present for a friend from five options. Part 4, they talk about what they usually do in their free time. The observers (a third pair) tick a simple checklist: did they listen and react, give reasons, and speak without long pauses. Swap roles twice.
lp.rw: Read a short text from the kit and answer four multiple choice questions. Then start an error log: students open a page headed with four columns (my mistake, correct form, rule, example) and add six mistakes from the Semester 1 assessment. Write the first three sentences of an email answering a PET writing task and underline the points the email must cover.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two goals for this semester (one for speaking, one for writing) using "I'm going to..." and one strategy you will try.
g: Share a success and a goal in groups.
Match each paper with its task type.
Find and fix mistakes in a text.
Describe a photo in one minute.
diff: Fast finishers: write 80 words about what you would like to be able to do in English by June and how you will do it. Support: give a goal sheet with four sentence starters and a picture of the exam parts.
hw: Complete your error log with eight mistakes from the semester and write one correct sentence for each.
Choose one PET listening or reading practice from the kit and do it with a timer.
Write 80 words about your goals for the semester and what you will do each week.
lp.tip: After the assessment week some students feel discouraged, so open with success and show progress. Keep the PET explanation short and visual and avoid dumping the whole exam on students in one hour. Make the error log a tool they can use every week.

weeks.obj: talk about jobs and skills, answer interview questions and write a short CV profile, using the present perfect for experience and the past simple for details
weeks.lang: jobs and skills vocabulary (apply for, qualification, experience, skills, volunteer, part-time, internship, reliable, hard-working); present perfect for experience (I've worked as..., I've never..., Have you ever...?) vs past simple for details (I worked there last summer); interview phrases (I'd like to apply for..., My main strength is..., I'm good at..., I'm available...); CV profile sentences
weeks.res: Lesson plan: Jobs (lesson 2); Business English video: The Job Interview
weeks.act: Jobs guessing game; interview questions in pairs; present perfect vs past simple practice; mock interview; CV profile writing
weeks.hw: write a CV profile of 70 to 90 words for a part-time job you would like to have

skills.L: Listen to two short interview extracts (one good, one poor) and decide who gets the job
skills.S: Answer three interview questions in 30 seconds each
skills.R: Read a short job advertisement and a CV and match skills to the job
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word CV profile or letter of application

lp.wu: What do I do? A student picks a job card in secret and the group asks yes/no questions to guess it ("Do you work outdoors? Do you wear a uniform? Have you studied for many years?"). The student answers only yes or no. Use jobs from the teens' world (YouTuber, football coach, nurse, mechanic, graphic designer, tour guide, barista) and aim for 6 or 7 rounds.
wuAlt: Skills bingo: students tick skills they have on a card (speak three languages, cook, draw, play an instrument, fix a phone) and find a classmate for each.
Dream job: students write a job on a paper, fold it and pass it around; the next student guesses by asking three questions.
lp.pres: Write "I've worked as a waiter" and "I worked as a waiter last summer" on the board and ask which one gives the time. Elicit the rule: use the present perfect for experience when the time is not important, and the past simple when we give the time or details. Practise with a chain: "Have you ever worked? Yes, I have. I worked in my uncle's shop last August. What did you do?" Add interview language in three boxes: introduction (I'd like to apply for the job of...), strengths (I'm good at..., I'm reliable and hard-working), questions (What are the working hours? Is there any training?). Show a short example CV profile of 60 words: "I'm a 17-year-old student who is looking for a part-time job in a shop. I've worked as a volunteer at a library and I'm good at helping people. I speak Arabic, French and English." Students underline the skills and the experience.
presAlt: Use the Business English interview video from the kit with the sound on and ask students to list questions they hear.
Use the AEF 3 Student Book unit on experience and the present perfect from the kit.
lp.prac: Experience quiz: pairs get cards with a job and ask each other "Have you ever...?" questions to complete a profile (have you ever worked in a shop, looked after children, used a computer program?). Then, true or false: students write six sentences about their own experience, three present perfect and three past simple, and the partner guesses which one is false. Finally, interview question practice: groups write ten interview questions (for a tourist guide, a shop assistant, a swimming instructor) and practise answering them in 30 seconds each.
pracAlt: Use the Unemployable worksheet from the kit for present perfect experience practice.
Use The Job Interview question worksheet from the kit.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice two short interview extracts (about 60 seconds each). The first candidate gives examples, speaks clearly and asks one question; the second gives one-word answers and complains about a past employer. Students tick a checklist (gives an example, speaks clearly, asks a question, answers too briefly, criticises a past employer) and decide which candidate they would hire and why. If audio or video is available, use the Business English good and poor interview videos in the kit.
lp.re: Likes and dislikes at work: students sort ten work-related actions (work in a team, work alone, work outside, deal with customers, use a computer, be creative) into "I would love", "I wouldn't mind" and "I'd hate" and compare in pairs. Then they say which job from the warm-up suits them best, using "I'd be good at... because I've...".
lp.prod: Mock interviews: groups of three, with an interviewer, a candidate and an observer. Each candidate gets a job card (cafe assistant, football coach for children, shop helper, sports camp helper) and a short advertisement. The interviewer asks five questions (Tell me about yourself. Have you ever worked before? What are you good at? Why do you want this job? Do you have any questions?). The observer ticks a rubric (gives examples, speaks clearly, polite, asks a question). Rotate roles twice, then the class shares what made a good answer.
lp.rw: Read a short job advertisement and a CV from the kit and match four skills to the job. Then write a 70 to 90 word CV profile or a short application message for a part-time job you would like, with three skills, one experience with the present perfect and one detail with the past simple. Partners circle the verb forms and tick whether the profile gives a reason to hire the writer.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you have done that would impress an employer and one thing you would like to try, each in a full sentence.
g: Guess a job with yes/no questions.
Find classmates who have particular skills.
Ask three questions to guess a job.
Spot the false present perfect sentence.
diff: Fast finishers: write a one-paragraph reference letter for a friend (80 words) explaining their skills and experience. Support: give a CV profile frame with gaps (I'm a... I've worked as... I'm good at... I'd like to...) and a list of ten skills words with a picture.
hw: Write a CV profile of 70 to 90 words for a part-time job you would like to have.
Ask an adult about their first job and write five sentences about it.
Find a job advertisement in English and note five skills the employer wants.
lp.tip: Teens have little job experience, so include volunteering, helping family and school clubs as real experience. Role plays are more useful if students prepare answers for three questions in advance. Keep the tone realistic, and avoid pushing students into career decisions.

weeks.obj: talk about imaginary situations and give advice with the second conditional, and write a short story or paragraph about a dream scenario
weeks.lang: second conditional (If I won the lottery, I would..., If I were you, I'd...); giving advice (If I were you, I'd..., Why don't you..., You'd better...); wishes and dreams (I'd love to..., I'd rather..., What would you do if...?); dilemma vocabulary (decide, choose, risk, regret, afford, option); contrast with the first conditional
weeks.res: Second conditional (worksheet and explanation); Advice + If I were you
weeks.act: What would you do? game; second conditional structure; dilemma cards in groups; advice role play; dream paragraph
weeks.hw: write 80 to 100 words about what you would do if you could change one thing in your life, using at least four second conditional sentences

skills.L: Listen to two short dilemmas and choose the best advice
skills.S: Discuss a dilemma in a group for two minutes and give advice using If I were you
skills.R: Read a short text about a difficult choice and find the second conditional sentences
skills.W: Write an 80-100 word dream scenario with the second conditional

lp.wu: What would you do? The teacher asks funny and serious questions and students answer in pairs: "What would you do if you found 1,000 dirhams in the street? What would you do if you could be invisible for one day? What would you do if you missed the last bus?" Then each pair writes one new question and asks another pair. Collect the best answers on the board.
wuAlt: Chain game: Student A says "If I had a million dirhams, I would buy a house." Student B repeats and adds ("If I bought a house, I would invite my friends...") and the chain continues.
Dream quiz: students rank five dreams (travel the world, be famous, be rich, be happy, be clever) and explain their top choice.
lp.pres: Write on the board "If I win the match, I will celebrate" and "If I won the lottery, I would travel the world." Ask which one is real and which one is imaginary and elicit the forms: if + past simple, would + infinitive. Explain that we use were for all persons in advice ("If I were you, I'd talk to him"). Contrast with the first conditional by asking "What will you do if it rains tomorrow?" and "What would you do if you were the king of Morocco?". Drill the contraction: I'd, you'd, he'd, and the question "What would you do if...?". Check with three quick sentence completions: "If I had more time, I...; If I could speak Chinese, I...; If I were the head teacher, I...".
presAlt: Use the Second conditional worksheet and the Advice + If I were you worksheet from the kit.
Use the AEF 3 Student Book unit on the second conditional from the kit.
lp.prac: Sentence pairs: pairs get ten prompts ("lived in Canada / learn French", "have a car / drive to the sea") and make second conditional sentences, saying them aloud and writing them. Then, an error check: eight sentences with typical mistakes ("If I would have money", "If I will go", "If he would come") corrected in pairs. Finally, Dilemma cards: groups get a card (your best friend copied your homework; you found a wallet with money; you are invited to two parties on the same night) and discuss "What would you do?" for 3 minutes, then report one idea with "We think that if we were..., we would...".
pracAlt: Use the Going Away or The Panel worksheets from the kit for second conditional speaking.
Use the Characterizations worksheet from the kit for a more imaginative task.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice two short dilemmas (about 80 words each). In the first, a girl called Imane is invited to a friend's birthday on the same night as her cousin's engagement party, and she does not know which to choose. In the second, a boy finds a phone on the bus and cannot decide whether to return it. For each, students listen for the problem and write advice using "If I were him, I'd...". If audio is available, use the Eucharia (choices) or Tim (dream job) recordings from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Conditional chain: seated in a circle, the teacher gives a starter ("If I had a time machine, I would..."), and each student must continue the chain with their own second conditional sentence that begins with the previous student's ending. Anyone who hesitates for more than 5 seconds or makes an error moves out. The last three win.
lp.prod: Dilemma panel: groups of four are given a dilemma card (for example, "A friend asks you to lie to his parents", "You have an exam tomorrow and a football final tonight", "You are offered a job that pays well but you will have to leave your family"). Each group discusses for 6 minutes, writing three pieces of advice with "If I were you, I'd... because...". Then each group presents its dilemma to another group, who give their advice and vote on the best one. Rotate twice.
lp.rw: Read a 150-word text from the kit on a difficult choice or an imaginary scenario and underline the second conditional sentences. Answer four comprehension questions. Then write 80 to 100 words: "If I could change one thing in my life..." with at least four second conditional sentences, one wish with I wish, and one sentence of advice for a friend. Partners swap and tick whether each sentence uses past simple in the if clause and would in the main clause.
lp.st: Exit ticket: complete two sentences: "If I had a free day tomorrow, I would..." and "If I were my best friend, I would...".
g: Answer funny dilemma questions in pairs.
Continue a chain of second conditional sentences.
Discuss and give advice in groups.
Bid on the best advice in a role play.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dilemma of 60 words and give two different pieces of advice. Support: give a sentence frame (If I..., I would...) and a mini table that shows the if clause and the main clause.
hw: Write 80 to 100 words about what you would do if you could change one thing in your life, using at least four second conditional sentences.
Ask three people the question "What would you do if you won a million dirhams?" and write their answers in full sentences.
Find a short story or video in English about a difficult choice and note the decision.
lp.tip: Dilemmas about family and friendship are rich for teens but keep them light and imaginary, and avoid questions that could be too personal. Students often say "If I would have"; model the correct form often and put a visible reminder on the board. Let students choose the dilemma they like so that they have real opinions to share.

weeks.obj: report what people said, asked and told you, change tenses and time expressions accurately and write a short news report or a message summary
weeks.lang: reported statements (She said (that) she was tired; He told me he had finished); said vs told; reported questions (She asked me where I lived; He asked if I could come); reported requests and orders (She told me to sit down; He asked me not to be late); tense and time changes (now / then, today / that day, tomorrow / the next day, here / there)
weeks.res: Reported speech (PowerPoint); Reported yes/no questions (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Gossip chain; tense backshift practice; reporting questions; news interview and report; short news paragraph
weeks.hw: write a 70 to 90 word report of a conversation you had this week using said, told and asked

skills.L: Listen to a conversation and write what each person said in reported speech
skills.S: Interview a partner and report their answers to a different student
skills.R: Read a short news report that uses reported speech and underline the reporting verbs
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word news report from three interview quotes

lp.wu: Gossip chain: in groups of five, the first student whispers a short sentence to the second ("My brother is going to move to Casablanca"), who must report it to the third ("She said that her brother was going to move to Casablanca"), and so on to the last student, who writes the final sentence. Compare it with the original, notice what changed and which words were changed by speakers.
wuAlt: Telephone game: the teacher whispers a message to the first student in each team and the last student writes it down and reads it out.
He said, she said: the teacher shows three short direct quotes on the board and students say what the person said in indirect speech.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "I'm tired," said Karim. Karim said that he was tired. Show how the tense goes one step back (am becomes was, will becomes would, have done becomes had done) and how time words change (today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there). Contrast said and told: "He said that he was late. He told me that he was late." Then do reported questions: "Where do you live?" becomes "She asked where I lived" (no auxiliary, no question mark) and yes/no questions with if ("Are you coming?" becomes "She asked if I was coming"). Finish with requests: "Please be quiet" becomes "She asked us to be quiet", and "Don't touch it" becomes "He told me not to touch it". Give a mini quiz of 6 sentences for students to report in their notebooks.
presAlt: Use the reported speech PowerPoints on statements, yes/no questions and imperatives from the kit.
Use the video on reported speech and direct speech in the kit, then do the first practice worksheet together.
lp.prac: Backshift ladder: pairs get 12 direct sentences on cards (present simple, present continuous, past simple, will, can) and write the reported version of each in a table, noting the tense change. Next, Reporting questions: each student writes five questions to ask a partner (Where were you born? Do you like football? What are you doing this weekend?), asks them, writes the answers and reports to the group using "asked", "wanted to know" and "said". Finally, an error hunt: eight sentences such as "She said me that she was ill" and "He asked where did I live" are corrected in pairs.
pracAlt: Use the You said, Somebody told me that, and But he told me worksheets from the kit.
Use the Oxford Practice Grammar section on reported speech from the kit.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short phone conversation (about 100 words) between Hamza and his cousin Salma about a weekend plan: Hamza says he is going to visit his grandmother, asks if Salma can come, says the bus leaves at 9 and asks her not to forget her jacket. First listening: tick what each person said. Second listening: write four sentences in reported speech (Hamza said that..., He asked if..., He told Salma not to...). If audio is available, use the Ruth (media) or Ruth (banter) recordings from the Listening folder.
lp.re: Rumour mill: each student gets a card with a direct sentence (a rumour about a school event or a celebrity, invented by the teacher). They mingle, tell one classmate the rumour in direct speech, and that classmate must report it to a third student: "Ahmed told me that the school was going to close on Friday." Finish by asking who heard the rumour and who passed it on.
lp.prod: News interview and report: pairs interview each other for 3 minutes about a topic (my best day, my favourite app, what I want to do after school). Each student takes notes with the exact words. Then each student joins a new partner and reports what the first partner said ("Amina told me that her best day was when she won a prize. She said that she had been very nervous..."). Finally, groups of four prepare a 60-second news report with three quotes and present it as a TV news bulletin (one presenter, one reporter, two interviewees).
lp.rw: Read a 150-word news report from the kit and underline all reporting verbs (said, told, asked, explained, added, suggested). Answer four detail questions and say which tense change each reporting verb caused. Then write a 70 to 90 word news report using three interview quotes, at least one reported question and one request, and a headline. Partners underline the reporting verbs and check each tense change.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence beginning "My friend told me that..." and one beginning "The teacher asked me if...".
g: Whisper a rumour and report it down the line.
Pass a message and compare it to the original.
Change direct quotes into reported speech on mini whiteboards.
Mingle and report what you heard.
diff: Fast finishers: rewrite a short dialogue of 8 lines as a paragraph of reported speech using four different reporting verbs. Support: give a table with the tense changes and time changes and a gapped reporting practice.
hw: Write a 70 to 90 word report of a conversation you had this week using said, told and asked.
Interview a family member about their day and write five reported sentences.
Read or watch a short news item in English and report two things people said.
lp.tip: Backshift is a hard topic, so use lots of short oral practice before writing and display the tense change table on the wall. Keep the drills quick and personal, since teenagers enjoy gossip and messages. Be strict about "asked where I lived" and "told me", the two most common errors.

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students report what a family member said about their Ramadan plans ("My mother said she was going to cook harira. My brother told me he would fast for the first time.") and what they asked ("My cousin asked me if I wanted to go to the mosque with him.") in groups of three.
occ.hw: Write 5 sentences reporting what a family member said about their plans for Ramadan.

weeks.obj: describe how things are made and where they come from using present and past passive, write a short process description and talk about local products
weeks.lang: present simple passive (Tea is served to guests); past simple passive (The tower was built in 1195); by + agent when it matters; passive questions (How is argan oil made? When was it invented?); process vocabulary (first, then, after that, finally, is added, is heated, is poured, is sold); local crafts (argan oil, zellige, tea, leather)
weeks.res: The Passive Voice (explanation); Passive voice: verb 3 (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Fact finder; present and past passive practice; process description; local crafts presentation
weeks.hw: write a 80 to 100 word description of how a Moroccan product is made, using at least five passive sentences

skills.L: Listen to a description of how tea or bread is made and put the steps in order
skills.S: Describe how a product is made in 45 seconds using the passive and linkers
skills.R: Read a short text about the history of a famous product and find the passive forms
skills.W: Write an 80-100 word process description using the passive

lp.wu: Fact finder: the teacher puts 8 fact cards around the room (for example, "Mint tea is served in small glasses", "The Hassan II Mosque was built in 1993", "Argan oil is made from nuts"). In pairs, students walk around, find the fact that answers each question on a sheet (When was the mosque built? What is argan oil made from?) and write the answer. Ask the class which verbs they noticed and what they have in common.
wuAlt: Who invented it? Teams guess the inventor or the country of a famous product (jeans, football, coffee) and then see the answer on cards in the passive.
Guess the product: the teacher describes a product with passive clues ("It is made from sugar. It is drunk hot. It is often served with mint").
lp.pres: Show a process picture series for making mint tea in Morocco and elicit the steps in the active ("People put tea in the pot..."). Rewrite them in the passive on the board: "Tea is put in the pot. Boiling water is added. Sugar is added. The tea is poured from a height." Teach the form: be + past participle (present: is, are; past: was, were), and the rule that the object of the active sentence becomes the subject. Explain when to use the passive: when the action matters more than the person, or when we do not know who did it. Add by + agent for important information ("The Karaouine library was founded by Fatima al-Fihri"). Check with 4 quick transformations and one question: "Is it right to say 'The window broke by the boy'?"
presAlt: Use the Passive Voice explanation and the Processes worksheet from the kit.
Use the passive voice PowerPoint and the AEF 3 Student Book unit on the passive from the kit.
lp.prac: Active to passive: pairs get 10 sentences ("They make zellige in Fes", "Someone stole my bike") and rewrite them in the passive, then check with another pair. Next, a past passive quiz: students complete 8 facts ("Penicillin ... (discover) in 1928", "The first football World Cup ... (hold) in 1930") and guess the answers. Finally, Process cards: in groups of four, they get a set of pictures showing how paper, bread, leather or olive oil is made, put them in order and write 5 passive sentences with first, then and finally.
pracAlt: Use the Present Passive Quiz and Past Passive Quiz from the kit.
Use the Passive Descriptions worksheet from the kit.
lp.ls: Teacher reads twice a short description of how Moroccan bread or mint tea is made (about 100 words) with the steps in scrambled order on a worksheet. First listening: students number the pictures in order. Second listening: they write the missing verb in each passive sentence (the dough is mixed, the bread is baked...). If audio is available, use the Lisa (tea) or Alan (bread) recordings from the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Passive snap: pairs get a set of cards, half with active sentences and half with passive sentences that mean the same. They play snap: when two cards match they say "Snap!" and read both sentences aloud. The pair that finds the most matches in 6 minutes wins.
lp.prod: Local crafts talk: groups of four choose a Moroccan product or craft (argan oil, zellige, Moroccan tea, leather, couscous, a local sweet) and prepare a 90-second talk on how it is made and where it is sold. The talk must include at least four passive sentences with first, then, after that and finally, one past passive for the history, and one question for the audience ("Do you know where argan trees are grown?"). Each group presents in turn, and the class gives one thing they learned and one passive question.
lp.rw: Read a 150-word text from the kit on the history of a famous product, for example Coca Cola, and underline the passive forms. Answer four detail questions and say who did the action in two of the sentences. Then write 80 to 100 words describing how a Moroccan product is made, with at least five passive sentences, linkers (first, then, after that, finally) and one date in the past passive. Partners tick that each passive has the correct form of be and a past participle.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two passive sentences, one present and one past, about something in Morocco ("Mint tea is served to guests. The Karaouine library was founded in 859.") and hand them in.
g: Find passive facts around the room.
Describe a product with passive clues.
Put a process in order and describe it.
diff: Fast finishers: write the passive description of a second process (for example how a football is made) in 80 words. Support: give a process picture sheet with verbs and a table of is/are/was/were + past participle, and a gapped model text.
hw: Write a 80 to 100 word description of how a Moroccan product is made, using at least five passive sentences.
Ask a family member how they make a traditional food and write the steps in the passive.
Find a short video in English about how an everyday object is made and note five passive sentences.
lp.tip: The passive is easy to explain but students overuse it in speaking, so say clearly when to choose it. Local crafts make the topic meaningful, and students are proud of them; invite them to bring a photo or a small object. The main errors are missing be ("The tea served") and wrong participles; correct these on the board after the talks.

weeks.obj: describe what things are used for and how they work, make predictions about technology with will and might, and give and defend an opinion in a short class debate
weeks.lang: describing function (It is used for + -ing, It is used to + verb, You can use it to...); the difference between used to (past habit) and be used to / used for; predictions with will, won't, might, probably, definitely; technology vocabulary (device, app, charger, battery, update, download, software, robot, artificial intelligence, privacy); debate phrases (In my opinion, I strongly believe, On the other hand, I see your point but)
weeks.res: Lesson plan: Technology, lesson 1; Game sheet: made of / used for (definition cards)
weeks.act: Gadget guessing game; function sentences; predictions about 2040; four corners opinion game; a two-team debate on "Technology does more good than harm for teenagers"
weeks.hw: write a paragraph of 70-90 words about one invention you could not live without, what it is used for and how life would change without it

skills.L: Listen to two speakers talk about gadgets and decide who has a positive and who has a negative view
skills.S: Describe a device without naming it, make predictions and take part in a short debate
skills.R: Read a text about a modern invention and answer true, false and not stated questions
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about an invention that matters to you

lp.wu: Mystery object: the teacher puts five photos or drawings of objects on the board (a USB stick, a smartwatch, a power bank, a drone, headphones) and describes one without naming it: "You use it to listen to music without bothering other people. It is used for..." Teams guess in thirty seconds. Then each team writes a description of one object from their bags (phone, charger, calculator) and the others guess. Quick review of present simple passive through "It is made of plastic."
wuAlt: Phone-free minute: students put their phones face down and list in pairs ten things a phone does that is not calling. Compare and see which pair has the strangest one.
Evolution of technology cartoon: show the picture and pairs say what has changed and what has stayed the same.
lp.pres: Write three sentences on the board: "A drone is used for taking photos from the air." "People use a smartwatch to check the time and their heartbeat." "I used to use a keypad phone, but now I use a smartphone." Elicit the three patterns: be used for + -ing (function), use something to + verb (purpose) and used to + verb (past habit). Add a short contrast with be used to + -ing ("I am used to getting messages all day"). Then write predictions on a line from 0 to 100 percent (definitely will, will probably, might, probably won't, definitely won't) and give examples about technology in 2040: "Robots will probably clean our houses. Cars might drive themselves." Students copy a mini table of function and prediction phrases.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in Life Intermediate (B1+) Student Book on technology and read the example sentences aloud together.
Use the Technology lesson plan from the kit and the made of / used for definition cards for a quick drill.
lp.prac: Definition cards: in pairs, student A reads a card ("It is used for cutting paper. It has two blades.") and student B guesses the object, then they swap. Next, each pair writes five of their own definition cards about school or phone objects, using used for, used to and at least one relative clause (which / that). They give the cards to another pair. Finish with Prediction Dominoes or a slip task: each pair writes six predictions about school life in 2040 with will, might and probably, and puts a percentage next to each.
pracAlt: Inventions auction: teams bid dirhams on correct sentences about inventions and fix the wrong ones.
Oxford Practice Grammar exercises on will and might for pairs who need extra controlled practice.
lp.ls: Teacher-read or recording-based listening. Option 1: play the Jeff, technology or Phil, gadgets recording from the kit. Option 2 (works without audio): the teacher reads two short monologues aloud twice. Speaker A (positive): "My phone helps me learn English and talk to my cousins in France. I could not live without it." Speaker B (negative): "I check my phone about a hundred times a day. I think I'm addicted and I sleep badly." First listening: students decide who is positive and who is negative. Second listening: they note two reasons each speaker gives and one phrase of opinion. Pairs compare and say which speaker they agree with.
lp.re: Quick predictions race: teams of four stand in lines. The teacher calls a topic (school, football, food, transport, money) and the first student runs to the board to write a prediction with will, might or probably. The next student corrects or adds a reason ("because..."). One point for a correct sentence and one for a logical reason. Play five rounds, then read the funniest predictions aloud.
lp.prod: Class debate "Technology does more good than harm for teenagers." First play Four Corners: students stand in the corner that shows how much they agree (strongly agree, agree, disagree, strongly disagree) and give one reason with because. Then divide into two teams, each with ten minutes to prepare three arguments with an example from daily life (for example, learning from videos, losing sleep, online bullying, finding jobs). Each speaker has one minute using phrases from the board. Each team asks one question to the other. The class votes, and the teacher gives feedback on language, not on who won.
lp.rw: Read "Robotic bees" or "How has technology improved healthcare?" from the kit and answer eight true, false and not stated questions, underlining the sentence that proves each answer. Then write a 70-90 word paragraph answering: What is one invention you could not live without, what is it used for, and how would your life change without it? Use at least two function phrases and one prediction with will or might. Swap with a partner and check each other for the three criteria on the board.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: students complete "One invention I could not live without is..., because it is used for... In the future it might..." on a slip. The teacher then tells a two-minute true story of an invention that was an accident (for example, how the microwave oven was discovered) and students predict what happened next before the teacher finishes.
g: Describe an object so the team can name it.
Match prediction halves with will, might and probably.
Bid on correct sentences about inventions.
Move to the corner that shows your opinion and defend it.
Read a definition and name the object.
List everything a phone does apart from calling.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short advert (40 words) for an imaginary gadget, saying what it is used for and what it will do for you.
Support: give a sentence frame card ("It is used for..., You can use it to..., I think it will...") and a picture list of six gadgets for the definition cards.
hw: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about one invention you could not live without, what it is used for and how life would change without it.
Interview an older family member about technology when they were young (used to) and note five sentences to share next week.
Watch one short video about a new technology in English and write three predictions with will and might.
lp.tip: Teens are experts in technology, so let them be the experts while you work on accuracy of the target structures. Keep the debate fair by giving each student one speaking turn and a language target (for example, one used for sentence and one might sentence). Phones stay face down except when you ask them to look up a word, and a short phone-free minute at the start makes this easy to enforce.
