weeks.obj: use skimming, scanning and careful reading to answer the main PET reading task types: signs and notices, matching, true or false, multiple choice and gapped texts
weeks.lang: reading strategies (skim for gist, scan for names, numbers and times, read for detail, check the distractors); language of signs and notices (No entry, Keep off the grass, Closed for lunch, Please do not...); linking and reference words (however, although, this, they, so, because); inferring unknown words from context
weeks.res: PET advice: Do's and Don'ts for exam day; Objective PET Student's Book (reading unit tips)
weeks.act: Skimming race; signs and notices matching; a PET-style reading part done in pairs and checked together; strategy cards; a real multi-paragraph text with a gapped sentence task
weeks.hw: complete one reading part from the PET pack and write one sentence of evidence for each answer

skills.L: Listen to the teacher think aloud while solving a PET reading question and note the strategy words
skills.S: Explain to a partner why one answer is right and one distractor is wrong
skills.R: Practise PET reading parts: signs, matching, multiple choice and gapped text
skills.W: Write a 40-word summary of a text and one-sentence evidence notes for answers

lp.wu: Sign it: the teacher shows or draws ten signs and notices (No mobile phones, Wet floor, Staff only, Sale ends Saturday, Back in 10 minutes, Please queue here) and pairs say where you would see each one and what it means. Then pairs choose a sign and act out a short dialogue in which someone breaks the rule. Students see how much meaning is in very few words.
wuAlt: Sixty-second skim: the teacher shows an article for sixty seconds and hides it. Students write the topic, the text type and who wrote it, then check.
Guess the word: show a text with five words covered and pairs predict the word from context.
lp.pres: Explain the PET Reading paper in simple terms: five parts of increasing length (short signs and messages, matching people to texts, a longer true or false text, a longer multiple-choice text and a gapped text). Give a three-step routine on strategy cards: read the question first and underline key words; find the part of the text that matches and look for a paraphrase, not the same words; check the other options and say why each is wrong. Model one multiple-choice question with a think-aloud on the board, showing a distractor that is true but does not answer the question. Teach three reference tricks: this and they point back, however and although show contrast, so and because show cause.
presAlt: Use the Objective PET Student's Book or Target PET Student's Book and pick the reading units; read the exam tip boxes together.
Use the PET Advice document (Do's and Don'ts) as a checklist and ask students to tick the points they already follow.
lp.prac: Timed pair practice: give each pair one PET Reading Test part (for example the signs and notices and the matching parts). They have ten minutes, then compare answers with another pair and for every difference they find the sentence in the text that decides it. The teacher circulates and asks "Which words in the text are the same idea as the words in the question?" Pairs write the paraphrase pairs on strips (for example "not allowed" and "forbidden") and stick them on the wall.
pracAlt: Use the A2 to B1 reading exam for pairs who find the full PET text too long.
Faster pairs continue with a second PET Reading Test part and mark the answers themselves with the key.
lp.ls: Think-aloud listening: the teacher reads one multiple-choice question and a paragraph aloud twice, then talks through the decision ("The question asks why she changed her plan. I listen for because and so. Option B is true in the text but it is about a different day."). Students write down five strategy phrases they hear. Then the teacher reads a short notice (a bus company changing its timetable) and students answer two questions. If you have audio, use the Deane, signs recording as a second text on signs and notices.
lp.re: Distractor hunt: show a multiple-choice question and its paragraph. In pairs, students label each wrong option with the reason: too extreme, true but not the answer, from another part of the text, or the opposite meaning. Repeat with three questions from the Comprehension quiz and compare labels as a class. The class creates a poster of "four ways a wrong answer looks right".
lp.prod: Strategy circles: in groups of four, each student takes one answer they gave earlier and explains in forty seconds, using "The text says... so the answer is... I did not choose B because...". The group gives a score out of three for evidence, clearness and use of paraphrase words. Rotate until everyone has explained twice. Finish with one volunteer who explains an answer they changed after hearing a partner.
lp.rw: Read a longer text from the kit ("The mystery of Skeleton Lake" or "Otzi the Iceman") in three paragraphs. Answer four multiple-choice questions, then add a gapped task: the teacher removes one sentence from each paragraph and the students put the sentences back using clues (this, however, a date). Then write a 40-word summary of the text in your own words, and underline two unknown words with a guess of the meaning before checking.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: write on a slip the strategy that helped you most today and the part you want to practise this week ("I will look for paraphrases. I will do the signs part twice."). The teacher reads the first paragraph of a mystery story aloud and stops at the most exciting moment, then tells students to read the end in class next week.
g: Say where you see a sign and what it means.
Decide text type and topic quickly.
Name why each wrong answer looks right.
Match a question phrase to the text phrase.
Put cut-out sentences back into a text using clues.
Teams find the sentence that proves an answer first.
diff: Fast finishers: write three PET-style multiple-choice questions on a short text and swap with another pair.
Support: give a strategy card and a shorter text with only three questions and the paragraph already marked.
hw: Complete one PET Reading Test part and write one sentence of evidence for each answer.
Read one English article of about 300 words and write a 40-word summary and three vocabulary guesses.
Find five real signs or notices in your town or online, copy them in English and write what each means.
lp.tip: Teenagers often guess from the first line they recognise. Make them point to the evidence in the text for every answer, even when they are correct, and time each part so that they feel what the exam is like. Keep the mood relaxed: this is practice, and a wrong answer with a good explanation earns more than a correct guess.

weeks.obj: use prediction, keywords and note-taking to answer PET-style multiple choice, note completion and speaker attitude listening tasks and understand fast, natural speech
weeks.lang: listening strategies (read the questions first and predict; listen for the idea, not every word; do not change an answer too quickly); connected speech (gonna, wanna, I'll, could've, linking such as "a lot of" and "turn it off"); numbers, times, dates, prices and spelling of names; attitude words (annoyed, excited, worried, bored, pleased)
weeks.res: PET advice: Do's and Don'ts for exam day; Objective PET Student's Book (listening unit tips)
weeks.act: Connected speech dictation; prediction and keyword underlining; three listening tasks in the PET style; attitude matching; transcript check and a short discussion
weeks.hw: complete one listening task and bring five words or phrases you misheard

skills.L: Understand short extracts, a dialogue and a monologue and answer multiple choice and note completion questions
skills.S: Compare answers and explain why a wrong option is wrong
skills.R: Read a transcript and underline the words that gave the answer
skills.W: Complete notes with numbers and names and write a four-sentence summary of a recording

lp.wu: Say it fast: the teacher says eight sentences at natural speed with linking and weak forms ("What are you gonna do?" "I'd have called her." "Can you turn it off?" "She's got a lot of homework.") and students write what they hear. Pairs compare and the teacher writes the full forms. Then students practise saying the same sentences fast with a partner and notice which words are stressed.
wuAlt: Number and name check: dictate phone numbers, prices (14.50 and 15.40), times and spell names at normal speed.
Gist before detail: read a short announcement once and students write who, where and why only.
lp.pres: Present the four PET Listening parts in simple terms: Part 1 (short extracts with a picture or multiple choice), Part 2 (a longer talk or dialogue with three-option questions), Part 3 (a monologue with note completion, one to three words) and Part 4 (a conversation with true or false or yes or no). Show the routine: before the recording read the questions and underline the key words, predict what kind of word is missing (a number, a place, a day), listen once for the answer and again to check. Practise with a quick prediction: the teacher writes "The museum opens at ___ on Sundays." and students say what kinds of answers are possible. Explain that the recording usually mentions two similar answers and only one fits ("It opens at ten, no, sorry, at nine thirty on Sundays").
presAlt: Use the Q Skills for Success Listening and Speaking book or Listening and Notetaking Skills 1 for a first note-taking practice.
Use the Objective PET Student's Book listening unit and read the exam tips together.
lp.prac: Three-round listening cycle. Round 1: a short extract (for example Keren, plans) with multiple choice questions. Round 2: a note completion task (for example Martin, the bus) with a form to complete with times and numbers. Round 3: a dialogue (for example Ruth, an invitation) where students decide how the speaker feels. After each round, pairs check answers, and for every difference one student argues with "I think the answer is B because I heard...". Play each recording twice. If no audio is available, the teacher reads the same type of text aloud, twice, at normal speed.
pracAlt: Use the Learn English British Council podcast episode for a longer listening with a note-taking sheet.
Use the Listening and Notetaking Skills 1 book for pairs who need a gentler start.
lp.ls: Extended listening for the second half of the unit: the teacher reads a 200-word talk by a teenager about a class trip (with a date, a price, two places and a problem). Students listen twice and complete notes (Where, When, Cost, Problem, What happened in the end). A third time, they listen only for the speaker's feelings and underline three words that show it (excited, disappointed, relieved). Pairs retell the story in four sentences, checking their notes. Option with audio: Tini, studying for attitude.
lp.re: Misheard lyrics and phrases: the teacher writes five sentences with possible mishearings ("I'll go to the beach" and "I'd go to the beach", "can" and "can't", "fifteen" and "fifty"). Read one at random and teams show a card to say which one they heard. Teams win a point for each correct card, then for each pair they write a sentence where the difference matters.
lp.prod: Interview a classmate and take notes: pairs interview each other for two minutes on "your last weekend or your best day out" and write notes only (names, places, times, numbers, feelings). Then they join another pair and report in four to five sentences what they learned ("Sara went to Saidia on Saturday. She left at eight and paid 40 dirhams for the bus."). The listeners check the details against their own notes. Praise good questions and clear speech.
lp.rw: Read the transcript of one recording from today (or the teacher's talk) and underline the words that gave each answer. Then write a four-sentence summary and a 60-80 word message to a friend telling them about the plan you heard, using the notes. Mark with a colour any word that you misheard and add it to your listening log.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: write on a slip the word or phrase you misheard today and how it really sounds. The teacher reads a very short mystery message (a voicemail with a wrong number) and students decide what the speaker really wants.
g: Write what you hear at normal speed.
Shout the right number when you hear it.
Show A or B for the word you hear.
Race to underline keywords in five questions.
One student whispers a sentence down the line.
diff: Fast finishers: write three PET-style questions for a short recording and swap with another pair.
Support: give a transcript with the answers gapped and let students read as they listen the second time.
hw: Complete one listening task from the PET pack or a British Council podcast and bring five misheard words.
Listen to a one-minute English clip, write what you hear and compare with the transcript.
Record yourself saying five sentences with gonna, wanna and linking, and listen back.
lp.tip: Teens often feel that native speakers talk too fast. Start with the transcript, then take it away: first they listen and read, then they listen only. Always play twice, give a quiet minute to check answers, and praise students who say "I do not know this word, but I understood the idea". If audio fails, read from a script at natural speed rather than slowing down too much.

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students tell each other about their best Eid memory using the past simple and used to ("We used to visit my grandmother first. She always made...") and the listener takes notes and asks two follow-up questions ("Who was there? What did you eat?"). Then each student reports one detail to the class.

Warmer for teens: activities and warmers

Listening and Notetaking Skills 1 (note completion practice)

weeks.obj: write a clear informal email and a short story or article of 100 words in the PET style, using a plan, linking words and a self-checking list
weeks.lang: informal email phrases (Thanks for your message, I'm writing to tell you, Guess what, Write back soon); linking words (first, then, after that, finally, however, although, so, because, as soon as, while); narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect for one earlier event); article features (a title, an introduction, opinions with reasons, a conclusion); common errors (word order, prepositions, spelling of high frequency words)
weeks.res: PET writing Part 1 tips (2020 tips document); PET writing lesson plan: understanding the rubric
weeks.act: Rubric reading; planning with a mind map; email writing and peer feedback; story writing with picture prompts; checklist and self-correction
weeks.hw: write the second piece (a story or an article) of about 100 words and use the checklist to correct it

skills.L: Listen to a model email read aloud and note the sections
skills.S: Explain a plan to a partner and give feedback on a text
skills.R: Read model answers and mark the features that earn marks
skills.W: Write an informal email and a short story or article of 100 words

lp.wu: Sentence builders: the teacher writes six jumbled sentences on the board ("tell / I'm / you / writing / to / about / my trip") and teams race to put them in order, then add a linking word to join two sentences. Review quickly: the teacher reads a mistake from last week's writing (anonymous) and the class corrects it.
wuAlt: Linking word auction: show ten sentences with linking words, some correct and some wrong, and teams bid on the correct ones.
Fast writing: two minutes to write as many sentences as possible about last weekend using five different linkers.
lp.pres: Show the PET Writing paper: Part 1 is a short message or email (about 100 words, three points to include) and Part 2 is a story or an article (about 100 words, choose one). Read a real rubric with students and mark what earns marks: content (all three points), communicative achievement (the right register), organisation (paragraphs, linkers) and language (range, accuracy). Show a model email: "Hi Sam, Thanks for your message! I'm writing to tell you about my school trip to Fes. First, we..." and label greeting, reason for writing, the three points and a closing sentence. Teach a three-step plan: read the task, underline the three points, write a note for each before starting.
presAlt: Use the PET Writing Part 1 lesson plans and the 2020 tips document with the video from the PET folder.
Use the Writing guide on writing an article for the second task.
lp.prac: Plan and write an email: the teacher gives a task ("Your English friend Tom is coming to visit you in Oujda. Write him an email. Tell him what you will do on his first day, what clothes to bring, and ask him one question."). In pairs, students underline the three points, make a mind map and write the email in ten minutes. They swap and use a peer checklist: Did they cover all three points? Did they use at least three linkers? Did they start and finish like an email? Then the writer improves one sentence using the feedback.
pracAlt: Use the Agony aunt writing prompts for a reply to a problem as an alternative Part 1.
For students needing more support, give a gapped model email with the structure written in the margin.
lp.ls: Teacher-read model email and story: the teacher reads an email aloud (about 100 words) twice. First time, students write down the greeting, the reason for writing and the closing. Second time, they note three linkers they hear. The teacher then reads a short story aloud with a wrong ending and the students decide which of two possible endings is right and why. If recordings are available, use the Martin, life recording as a model of past experience.
lp.re: Transformation relay: write six sentences on cards and paste them on the walls (for example "She last visited me in May." / "She hasn't ___ since May."). Teams of three run to a card, rewrite it with a different structure, return and send the next runner. The teacher checks accuracy at the end. Use the PET writing transformations or the Rewrite Sentences Test for the cards.
lp.prod: Story in pictures: show two or three pictures (or use the story starter What is going to happen) and tell pairs to write a 100-word story in 15 minutes starting with "It was a rainy Saturday when...". They must use one past continuous, one past perfect, two linkers (while, as soon as, after that) and a surprising ending. Then each pair reads their story to another pair, who guess the feelings of the characters and mark the best sentence. Volunteers read to the class.
lp.rw: Self-checking: students take the story or email they wrote today and correct it using a code on the board (T tense, WO word order, SP spelling, P punctuation, ? unclear, WW wrong word). They rewrite the second version of at least three sentences and add a title. Homework preview: they plan an article for next time. Finally, a mini quiz of five common errors from the class is read aloud, and students fix them in pairs.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: on a slip, write "My biggest writing mistake is... Next time I will..." and hand it in. The teacher reads aloud the best final sentence from the day and invites students to guess who wrote it.
g: Race to put jumbled words in order.
Run and rewrite a sentence with a different structure.
Judge if a sentence is correct or wrong and fix it.
Roll a dice and continue the story with a given linker.
Find which feature earns marks in a model answer.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second version of the email in a more formal style (to a school head) and list the differences.
Support: give a gapped email model and a word bank of linkers and let them write the missing parts.
hw: Write the second piece (a story or an article) of about 100 words and use the checklist to correct it.
Write an email to an English friend about your plans for the summer (80-100 words).
Choose five of your own mistakes and write the correct sentence and a rule for each.
lp.tip: Teens at this level write quickly but plan little. Insist on a two-minute plan before every piece, and give a clear word limit (80 to 100 words). Mark with a code rather than rewriting, so students correct themselves. Give each text one positive comment before any correction.

weeks.obj: take part in the four PET speaking tasks: personal interview, describing a photo, a collaborative decision and a short discussion, with clear turns, fewer pauses and polite interaction
weeks.lang: personal questions (Tell me about..., How often do you...?, What did you do last weekend?); describing a photo (In the picture I can see..., It looks as if..., She is probably..., In the background); suggesting and deciding (Why don't we...?, I think we should..., What about...?, I agree, but..., Let's choose...); buying thinking time (Well, let me think, That's an interesting question); keeping going when you do not know a word (It's a kind of..., something that you use to...)
weeks.res: Speaking test: interview questions; Speaking test: mock exam
weeks.act: Warm-up interview; photo description with a timer; collaborative decision role-play; a discussion with a rubric; peer scoring and feedback
weeks.hw: record a one-minute photo description on your phone and listen to it

skills.L: Listen to a model speaker and tick the phrases used
skills.S: Practise interview, photo description, collaborative decision and discussion in pairs
skills.R: Read the PET speaking rubric and a mock exam script
skills.W: Write a 60-80 word description of a photo

lp.wu: Quick interview: students stand in two lines facing each other. The teacher asks a PET-style question ("Where do you live? What do you like doing at weekends? Tell me about your best friend."). Students answer in two sentences with a reason, then the outside line moves one place. After four rounds, pairs say which question was easiest and which was hardest.
wuAlt: Two truths and a lie: each student tells three facts about last weekend and the partner guesses the lie.
Conversation questions by category: pairs pick a card and talk for one minute.
lp.pres: Explain the four parts of the PET speaking test with a visual on the board: Part 1, the examiner asks each candidate personal questions (about two minutes); Part 2, you describe a photo for about one minute; Part 3, you and your partner talk together to make a decision (about two to three minutes); Part 4, you talk about your own experience on the same topic (about three minutes). Write a four-step photo description pattern on the board: where is it (location), who and what (people and objects), what are they doing (action) and what do you think (guess). Teach useful rescue phrases for missing words and polite phrases for decisions: "What do you think? I agree with you, but... Shall we choose the second one?"
presAlt: Use the mock exam script from the Tests folder and read the examiner's lines aloud with a student.
Use the PET Advice document (Do's and Don'ts) to build a class list of three tips for speaking.
lp.prac: Round robin of three stations. Station 1 photo description: student A describes a photo for one minute (use Talk about the pictures slides or photos from the kit) while student B times, then B asks one question. Station 2 collaborative task: pairs get a prompt (Holiday decisions or A Day Out, e.g., "Your class has 500 dirhams for a trip. Choose the best place.") and have three minutes to discuss five options and decide, using the phrases on the board. Station 3 interview: pairs ask five personal questions. Rotate every six minutes and use a scoring card.
pracAlt: Timesaver Speaking Activities for pre-intermediate pairs who need controlled prompts.
Use the Speaking about photographs worksheet for guided phrases.
lp.ls: Teacher-read or recorded model: the teacher (or a stronger student) does a one-minute photo description with deliberate mistakes in structure, and the class listens twice. First, they tick the pattern parts they hear (place, people, action, opinion). Second, they note two phrases that make the speaker sound fluent ("It looks as if", "I think she might be"). Then they listen to a recording of a speaker (Greg, travel tips) and decide which phrases he uses to fill pauses.
lp.re: Photo taboo: the teacher shows a photo. A student describes it without using five forbidden words (man, woman, thing, nice, good) while the group guesses which photo among six it is. Keep the pace fast. After, students say which synonyms they used ("person", "kind of", "lovely").
lp.prod: Mini mock speaking test in groups of three: one examiner, two candidates. The examiner uses a card and a rubric (grammar and vocabulary, discourse management, pronunciation, interaction, each 1 to 5). Round 1 interview (two minutes), round 2 photo (one minute each), round 3 decision (three minutes), round 4 discussion (three minutes). The examiner scores both candidates and gives one star (a strength) and one wish (a target). Then roles rotate until every student has been a candidate twice. The teacher listens to two groups and gives short feedback.
lp.rw: Read the rubric and a mock script for the photo task. Students highlight what the candidate did well and underline one phrase they can borrow. Then write a 60-80 word description of a photo from the kit (or one on their phone) using the four-step pattern, and swap with a partner who checks for place, people, action and opinion.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: write "My star today was... My wish for next time is..." and hand it in. The teacher shows a funny photo with no caption and tells a one-minute story about it, then asks students to tell a different version in pairs.
g: Answer a question with a reason in two sentences.
Describe a photo without banned words.
Agree on one option in three minutes.
Mime the words in your photo description and guess.
Use rescue phrases to keep talking for thirty seconds.
diff: Fast finishers: prepare a two-minute talk on "a place I would love to visit" and record a version on their phone.
Support: give a phrase card with the four-step pattern and sentence starters, and let them prepare notes for a photo for two minutes.
hw: Record a one-minute photo description on your phone and listen to it, then write two things to improve.
Practise the interview questions with a family member and note one new fact.
Write a 60-80 word description of a photo of your family or town.
lp.tip: Speaking exams worry teens more than any other part. Practise in pairs and trios first, then with the whole class watching only when volunteers want to. Keep feedback to one star and one wish for each student, and pair a confident speaker with a quieter one so the quieter one gets longer turns.

weeks.obj: talk about environmental problems and possible solutions with zero and first conditionals, give opinions and write a short proposal or letter and a poster text
weeks.lang: zero conditional for general truths (If you leave rubbish on the beach, it harms animals); first conditional for real future possibilities (If we recycle more, there will be less waste); unless and as long as; environment vocabulary (pollution, recycle, reuse, waste, plastic, climate change, energy, solar power); suggestion and persuasion (We should..., Why don't we...?, It would be great if we...); formal letter phrases (I am writing to..., I would like to suggest...)
weeks.res: Zero conditional worksheet; First conditional worksheet
weeks.act: Earth Day ice-breaker; conditional chains; a debate with Earth Day cards; community action planning; a short letter and poster text
weeks.hw: write a 70-90 word letter to the school or town council with one problem and two suggestions

skills.L: Listen to a talk about global warming and complete notes
skills.S: Give opinions and plan a community action with a partner
skills.R: Read a text about an environmental project and answer questions
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word letter or a 60-word poster text

lp.wu: Ice-breaker cards: the teacher gives pairs ice-breaker cards about plastic pollution ("What is the most common rubbish in your street? Do you use a reusable bottle? What happens to plastic after you throw it away?"). Pairs discuss each question for one minute and report the most surprising answer. The teacher adds a first conditional line on the board: "If we ban plastic bags, ..." and students finish it in two ways.
wuAlt: Video: The story of plastic (short): watch two minutes and pairs write three facts they remember.
Brainstorm race: teams write as many environment words as possible in two minutes.
lp.pres: Write two pairs of sentences on the board: "If you heat ice, it melts." (zero, always true) and "If we plant more trees, the air will be cleaner." (first, a real possibility in the future). Elicit the rule: if + present simple, then present simple (general truth) or will + verb (future result). Add "unless" ("Unless we act, the beach will be dirty") and "as long as". Show that the if-clause can come second, and then there is no comma. Students make a conditional chain: "If we recycle, there will be less waste. If there is less waste, the sea will be cleaner. If..." Finally, teach three suggestion phrases: "We should... It would be great if... Why don't we...?"
presAlt: Use the Oxford Practice Grammar exercises on zero and first conditional for printed practice.
Use the Zero conditional worksheet and 1st conditional worksheet from the Conditionals folder.
lp.prac: Three quick activities. First, "What will happen...?" cards: pairs read a situation (If you drop litter in the street..., If the factory closes...) and give a result with will. Second, a Zero conditional guessing game: one student gives the second half and the partner guesses the first ("... it turns into water" and "If you heat ice"). Third, a conditional chain race: groups of four stand in a circle and add the next link for sixty seconds, trying not to repeat or hesitate. The teacher corrects tense errors at the end.
pracAlt: Board game on conditionals for groups who finish early.
If and When worksheet to help weaker students see the difference between zero and first conditional.
lp.ls: Teacher-read or recording-based listening. Option with audio: Tim, global warming, or Marion, trash. Option without audio (the teacher reads): "Last month our town started a recycling project. If people sort their rubbish, the town collects it for free. If they do not sort it, they pay a fine of 50 dirhams. Already the beach is cleaner, and shops will use paper bags from January." Students listen twice and complete notes (what the project is, what happens if you sort, if you do not, one result, a date). Pairs discuss whether the project would work in Oujda.
lp.re: Conditional dominoes or tennis: the teacher reads the first half of a conditional ("If it rains tomorrow,...") and students stand and complete it in turn, without repeating and within five seconds. A student who hesitates sits down. The winner picks the next first halves. Keep the topic on the environment and daily life ("If I forget my bottle,...").
lp.prod: Community action plan. In groups of four, students choose a problem in their neighbourhood (rubbish in the street, no recycling bins, plastic bottles at the beach, waste of water, traffic fumes) and plan an action. Each group completes a plan sheet: Problem, Action, Who helps, Result ("If we organise a clean-up, volunteers will collect 20 bags of rubbish"), Slogan. After ten minutes, each group pitches the plan to the class in sixty seconds with at least two conditionals and two suggestions. The class votes on the best plan and asks one question.
lp.rw: Read "Young inventor makes bricks from plastic trash" (or a Time Zones DVD reading like Coastal Cleanup) and answer five questions. Then write a 70-90 word letter to the school or town council: "Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to suggest... At the moment... If you provide..., students will... Thank you for your time. Yours faithfully," or a 60-word poster text with a slogan, two facts and a call to action. Check with a partner for two conditionals and one suggestion.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: finish "If I could change one thing in my town, I would..." in a single sentence, and write one thing you will do this week. The teacher tells a true two-minute story about a teenager who started a beach clean-up and students predict what happened next with will and might.
g: Discuss a question for one minute and report back.
Add the next link to a chain of if sentences.
Predict the result of a situation with will.
Guess the first half from the second.
Sell your plan in sixty seconds.
Tick habits classmates have and add if sentences.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second paragraph for the letter with a polite complaint and a threat that is not rude ("If nothing changes, we will contact the newspaper.").
Support: give a sentence frame card for the letter (I am writing to..., I think..., If you..., we will...) and a picture word list of environment words.
hw: Write a 70-90 word letter to the school or town council with one problem and two suggestions.
Interview two people at home about what they recycle and write five sentences with if.
Design a poster with a slogan and three facts about water, plastic or energy.
lp.tip: Topics like climate change can feel big for teens, so keep the focus on local, realistic actions that they can do. Keep the conditionals visible on the board as a chain, and let students correct each other. Do not accept answers with will in the if-clause, and remind them gently that the if-clause stays in the present.

weeks.obj: describe traditions and how things are made using used to and the present and past passive, compare customs in different cultures, and prepare a short Moroccan culture project
weeks.lang: used to for past habits and changed traditions (We used to make bread at home; now we buy it); present and past passive for processes and facts (Tea is served in small glasses. Zellige tiles are cut by hand. The mosque was built in...); comparing cultures (In Morocco... whereas in Japan..., Unlike..., Similar to...); festival and tradition vocabulary (celebrate, custom, ceremony, handmade, recipe, heritage, symbol, ingredient)
weeks.res: Passive voice: The Passive Voice (explanation); Present passive quiz
weeks.act: Then-and-now chat; passive process cards; culture listening; Moroccan culture project in groups; short descriptive paragraph
weeks.hw: write a 70-90 word paragraph about a Moroccan tradition or craft and how it is made or celebrated

skills.L: Listen to speakers comparing cultures and note two differences
skills.S: Describe a tradition, how something is made and compare it with another culture
skills.R: Read a text about a world tradition or heritage site
skills.W: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about a Moroccan tradition

lp.wu: Then and now: pairs complete "Fifty years ago people in Morocco used to ... but now they ..." with five ideas (shop at souks, write letters, walk to school, cook on a wood fire). Each pair shares the most interesting one. The teacher asks "What tradition in your family has not changed? What has changed?" for a one-minute pair chat.
wuAlt: People used to...: groups of three write ten sentences about how life was different for their grandparents and read them for the others to guess the time.
Heritage quiz: show five photos of places or objects and teams name them and say where they are.
lp.pres: Review used to (past habits that have stopped) and teach it together with the passive: "Mint tea is made with green tea, mint and sugar. It is served in small glasses. Many years ago, copper pots were used for cooking, but now they are used for decoration." Show the form (is/are + past participle; was/were + past participle) and the question form ("How is argan oil made? When was this mosque built?"). Explain that the passive is used when the action matters more than the person. Give a process model with first, then, after that, finally: "First the argan nuts are collected. Then they are cracked..." Students underline the passive forms and number the steps.
presAlt: Use the Passive voice worksheets and the Present passive quiz and Past passive quiz in the kit.
Use the Close-Up DVD video The Art of Making Silk for a visual process to describe.
lp.prac: Process cards: pairs get a card with a process (how zellige is made, how bread is baked, how tea is served, how an olive is made into oil) in jumbled steps. They put the steps in order, then say them aloud with the passive and sequence words. Next, each pair writes the process of a tradition they know (couscous on Friday, preparing for Eid) in six sentences with at least four passives. Pairs swap and check with a mini rubric: tense, order, sequence words. Finish with Passive Snap or Fact Finder.
pracAlt: Use the Longman English Grammar Practice (Intermediate) passive exercises for pairs who need a controlled practice.
Passive Descriptions for students who need picture support.
lp.ls: Teacher-read or recording-based listening. Option with audio: Rina, cultures, or Keiko, culture shock. Option without audio: the teacher reads a short monologue of a student from Japan living in Morocco: "In Japan, we take off our shoes, and in Morocco we do that too in the house. But here tea is served with a lot of sugar, and it is always poured from high above the glass. In my country, we used to eat quietly, but here meals are loud and friendly." Students listen twice and complete a table: Japan / Morocco / What surprised her. Then pairs add one more similarity.
lp.re: Tradition auction or true and false: the teacher reads ten sentences about customs and the passive (some correct, some with errors: "Couscous is eating on Fridays." "Mint tea is served in small glasses.") and teams bid dirhams on the correct ones. After the auction, teams correct the wrong ones and name the mistake.
lp.prod: Moroccan culture project in groups of four. Choose one topic (a festival such as Eid or Yennayer, a craft such as zellige, argan or leather, a food such as couscous or tea, a place such as Chefchaouen or the Atlas). Make a one-page plan: three facts, a process or a history paragraph with at least three passives, one then-and-now point with used to, and one comparison with another country. Prepare a two-minute talk where each member speaks for thirty seconds. Groups present to another group, who ask one question and give one compliment. Final presentations are next week.
lp.rw: Read "Seven wonders of the ancient world" or "The Terracotta army" and answer five questions, circling all passive forms. Then write a 70-90 word paragraph about a Moroccan tradition or craft: what it is, how it is made or celebrated, how it used to be different, and why it matters to you. Use at least three passives and one used to. Peer check with the mini rubric.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: write one question about another culture that you would like to ask a visitor to Morocco. The teacher tells a short story from a tradition (for example, why mint tea is poured from a height) and students guess the true reason from three choices.
g: Say how life was different with used to.
Put steps in order and describe them in the passive.
Bid on correct sentences about customs.
Name the place or object in the photo.
Compare two countries with whereas and unlike.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short quiz of six questions about their project topic (using the passive: "When was...? How is... made?") for another group.
Support: give a process template with the first sentence and sequence words and a bank of passive verbs (is made, is cut, is baked, is served).
hw: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about a Moroccan tradition or craft and how it is made or celebrated.
Interview a grandparent about how a tradition used to be and write five sentences with used to.
Find one Moroccan craft or food video with English subtitles and note five passive sentences.
lp.tip: This is a topic where your students are the experts, so ask genuine questions and let them teach you. Check that every project uses the passive for a process, with more than a list of facts. Welcome different home languages (Arabic, Tamazight, French) when students explain a word, then ask them to say it in English.

weeks.obj: complete an adapted PET mock covering reading, listening, writing, speaking and language use, mark it with a key and set three personal targets
weeks.lang: exam skills and time management; all the grammar taught in the course (tenses, conditionals, reported speech, passive, used to); vocabulary for common PET topics; polite interaction in the speaking test
weeks.res: PET (B1) Reading Test 03 (mock reading); Objective PET Student's Book (mock test material)
weeks.act: Reading part; short listening; language use (cloze and transformations); a writing task; speaking pairs with a rubric; self-marking and target setting
weeks.hw: write three targets for the final assessment and one action for each

skills.L: Complete a short PET-style listening paper with multiple choice and note completion
skills.S: Complete a pair speaking test with an interview, photo description and decision task
skills.R: Complete a PET reading part with matching and multiple choice
skills.W: Write an email of about 100 words

lp.wu: Calm start: the teacher explains the plan of the session on the board (reading 20 minutes, language use 15, listening 10, writing 20, speaking 10 per pair, marking at the end) and reads the PET Advice Do's and Don'ts list. Each student chooses one strategy card (read the question first, check the time, do not leave any gap blank) and keeps it on the desk. One-minute pair chat: "What part of the exam makes you most nervous?"
wuAlt: Silent review: two minutes of looking at the error log and the strategy cards.
Pairs test each other on five irregular verbs and five linkers.
lp.pres: Reading section (20 minutes). Hand out an adapted PET reading part: a short text of 250 to 300 words with five multiple-choice questions and a matching task of five short texts (or a part from the PET Reading Test 03 in the kit). Explain the rules: no talking, no dictionary, answer in pencil and underline the proof in the text. At the end, students swap papers and mark with the key, writing a tick or a cross and the line number that proves the answer. The teacher gathers the score for each part on a chart.
presAlt: Use a shorter reading task of three questions if time is short.
Use the A2 to B1 reading exam for a gentler level in a mixed group.
lp.prac: Language use (15 minutes). Students complete a grammar cloze with 10 gaps (PET Grammar Test 01 or a Fill in the Blank test) and five transformations (for example "I haven't seen her since 2020. I last saw her in 2020."). Pairs then check each other's papers with the key and note the three grammar points that caused the most mistakes. These go into the error log with a corrected example.
pracAlt: A shorter cloze of 6 gaps and three transformations for students who need more time.
The Test It Fix It Verbs and Tenses book for students who want a harder challenge.
lp.ls: Listening section (10 minutes). Play two short extracts from the Jeff, trip or Tim, dream job recordings, or if there is no audio, the teacher reads two short texts aloud twice at natural speed. Students answer five multiple-choice questions and complete notes (a place, a time, a price, a name). After the second play, students have a minute to check. The teacher reads out the answers and students mark. Ask students to circle any question where they changed their answer: was the change correct?
lp.re: Quick language-use game: teams of three play a revision race with the questions that caused most mistakes. The teacher chooses 10 sentences from the class error log (anonymous), teams decide if each is correct or incorrect and fix it. The teacher awards points for each right decision and each right fix. Alternatively, play the Rewrite Sentences Test 02 as a team challenge with a timer.
lp.prod: Speaking test (10 minutes per pair, while the others do the writing task silently). The teacher sits with a pair and uses the mock exam script: Part 1 interview (two questions each), Part 2 photo (one minute each), Part 3 decision (two minutes, e.g., "Choose a present for a friend's birthday"), Part 4 discussion (two minutes). The teacher marks on a rubric card of 1 to 5 for grammar and vocabulary, discourse, pronunciation and interaction. Students who are not speaking write the email below. Write short comments: one strength and one target for each student.
lp.rw: Writing section (20 minutes, done during the speaking test rotation). Task: "You received an email from your English friend Alex: 'I am coming to Morocco next month! What can we do together? Where can we go? What should I bring?' Write an email to Alex (about 100 words). Answer the three questions and add one extra idea." Students plan for two minutes, write, count words and check with the code list. At the end, a classmate checks that all three questions are answered.
lp.st: Self-marking and target setting. Students total their scores on a result card by skill (reading, listening, language use, writing, speaking) and mark a cross on a chart of strengths. They write three targets and one action for each ("I will practise numbers in listening twice a week."), and the teacher collects the cards. The teacher gives out a very short compliment per student and tells a short funny story about a famous student who failed a test and then succeeded, to close on a positive note.
g: Choose the strategy for each task.
Bid on correct sentences from the class error log.
Rewrite a sentence in a new structure.
Give a classmate a sincere compliment about their progress.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second short message (40 words) of an invitation to a party for a different Part 1 task.
Support: give a plan template for the email and extra five minutes in the reading section; the teacher may read a question aloud on request.
hw: Write three targets for the final assessment and one action for each.
Redo the three questions you got wrong with the key and write why the right answer is right.
Practise a one-minute photo description with a family member and record it.
lp.tip: Keep this a friendly mock and not a trial. Tell students the marks are for planning the last weeks and are not shared in public, and mark with ticks rather than harsh words. Keep strict timing and quiet during silent sections, and record the scores by skill so you can plan the review in week 29 and the final in week 30.
checklist: I can read a text and choose the right answer using evidence.
I can follow a short recording and choose or write the key information.
I can write an informal email of about 100 words that covers all the points.
I can talk about myself and describe a photo for about a minute.
I can make a decision with a partner and give reasons politely.
I can use tenses, conditionals and the passive correctly in a gap fill and rewrite task.
I can name three targets for the final weeks.

weeks.obj: review the year's key grammar and skills through stations, then present a two to three minute group project with a clear structure and answer questions from the audience
weeks.lang: grammar review (present perfect, past simple and continuous, used to, comparatives, conditionals, reported speech, passive); presentation language (Today we are going to talk about, First of all, Another point is, Finally, Thank you for listening, Do you have any questions?); handling questions (That's a good question, I think the answer is, I'm afraid I don't know, but I think); feedback language (I liked..., It would be even better if...)
weeks.res: Preparing EFL learners for oral presentations; Writing guide: Writing an article (poster and talk text)
weeks.act: Review carousel in four stations; project preparation; group presentations with Q and A; peer feedback; class vote
weeks.hw: write a 70-90 word reflection on your project and one thing you would change

skills.L: Listen to presentations and note one fact and one question for each
skills.S: Give a group presentation and answer questions
skills.R: Read a model presentation outline and a peer feedback sheet
skills.W: Write a short reflection and feedback comments

lp.wu: Mingle review: each student gets a card with a question from the year (Have you ever...? What did you use to do when you were seven? If you won a lot of money, what would you do? What was the best film you have seen?). They mingle for six minutes, asking and answering five different questions and noting one new fact. Then they report one fact to the class using reported speech: "Sara said she had been to Tangier twice."
wuAlt: Intermediate revision board game: groups throw a dice and answer questions on the squares.
Warmers booklet game: choose a two-minute quick game, such as Chain Story, as a calm start.
lp.pres: Explain the presentation structure on the board with a model: Introduction (greeting, topic, plan), Main part (three points with a fact and an example), Conclusion (summary and thanks), Questions. Show how to share speaking time: each member says an introduction line and one point. Give useful phrases in a box and show a short model presentation read by the teacher about "My town Oujda" that uses one used to, one passive and one comparison. Hand out the feedback sheet (Content, Language, Delivery, Teamwork, each one star and one wish).
presAlt: Use the Preparing EFL learners for oral presentations document for tips on posture, voice and eye contact.
Use the article writing guide for groups that choose a poster text.
lp.prac: Review carousel (four stations, eight minutes each). Station 1 Tenses: a board game on present perfect and past simple. Station 2 Conditionals and passive: grammar auction with 12 sentences to bid on and fix. Station 3 Reported speech: pairs report the lines on a card ("I'm going to learn to swim" and "She said she was going to learn to swim"). Station 4 Language challenge cards. Each station has a key at the side, and pairs record in a table the mistakes they made and the correct form. At the end, groups report which station was hardest.
pracAlt: Grammar auction as a whole-class game.
Hadfield Intermediate Grammar Games for groups who finish early.
lp.ls: Audience listening task. While groups prepare, the teacher reads a two-minute model presentation aloud (about a school club) twice. On the first listening students note the structure phrases (First of all, Another point is, To sum up). On the second, they write one question to ask the speaker. Later, during real presentations, each student has a note sheet to write one fact and one question for every group. If recordings are available, use the Martin, life recording as a model of speaking over time.
lp.re: Correct Sentence Auction: the teacher prepares 12 sentences from the class's real mistakes of the year (anonymous). Groups of four bid dirhams on sentences they think are correct. After the auction, the groups fix the wrong sentences and name the error type (tense, word order, preposition, spelling). Points are given for each correct bid and each correct repair. The last bid winner explains the rule to the class.
lp.prod: Group presentations and Q and A. Each group presents the project prepared in week 27 or a new topic of their choice (Culture project, Earth Day action plan, an invention or a career) for two to three minutes, using a poster, a few slides or notes only. Each member speaks. After each presentation, the audience asks two questions and the group answers. Audience members write one star and one wish on the feedback sheet. Phones can be used for a timer, photos of posters and slides only. At the end the class votes for the Most Interesting, Best Teamwork and Clearest Speaker.
lp.rw: Reflection and feedback. Students read the feedback sheets they received and highlight one star and one wish. They write a 70-90 word reflection: "Our project was about... The best part was... If I did it again, I would... I learned that..." and swap with a partner who writes a comment. Early finishers prepare a thank-you message to their group.
lp.st: Exit ticket and story: write one thing you are proud of this year in English on a slip. The teacher reads a few out anonymously. Then the teacher tells a short story about learning something difficult (a language, a sport) and students guess what helped the character most.
g: Ask and answer year questions with five classmates.
Bid on correct sentences and fix the rest.
Report a line from a card.
Answer questions on the squares of a board.
Give two compliments and one suggestion.
diff: Fast finishers: prepare three difficult questions to ask other groups.
Support: give a presentation script frame with sentence starters and allow notes cards.
hw: Write a 70-90 word reflection on your project and one thing you would change.
Practise your final speaking test: record a one-minute photo description and a one-minute talk about your year.
Revise the error log and choose five rules to check before the final assessment.
lp.tip: Presentations can scare teens, so form groups of three or four with mixed levels and let every student speak a little. Practise the first sentence of each speaker aloud. Give the audience a job (a note sheet) so they listen politely. Keep the feedback kind and specific.

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: groups plan a short action for the American Space or their neighbourhood (a clean-up, a recycling corner, a plant swap) and pitch it in sixty seconds using conditionals from Week 26 ("If we organise a clean-up, the beach will be safe for families.") and suggestions ("We should...").

weeks.obj: show progress at A2+ to B1 in a four-skills assessment (reading, listening, writing, speaking and language use), receive feedback, celebrate and set goals for next year
weeks.lang: all year outcomes at A2+ to B1: tenses, conditionals, reported speech, passive, used to, modal verbs, comparatives, linking; functional language for talking about experiences, plans and opinions; PET-style task types
weeks.res: PET (B1) Reading Test 02 (final reading); PET Reading and Writing Paper 1 (final reading and writing)
weeks.act: Reading paper; listening paper; language use; writing task; speaking pairs with a rubric; feedback conferences; certificates and celebration
weeks.hw: write three goals for your English for next year and one action for each

skills.L: Complete a PET-style listening paper with short extracts and note completion
skills.S: Complete a speaking test in pairs and take part in a feedback conversation
skills.R: Complete a PET-style reading part with multiple choice and gapped text
skills.W: Write a story or an email of about 100 words

lp.wu: Calm start: the teacher reviews the plan of the session on the board (reading 20 minutes, listening 10, language use 15, writing 20, speaking 10 per pair, celebration at the end). Each student takes a strategy card and a pencil. Pair chat for one minute: "What is the biggest change in your English since September?" with a follow-up question from the partner. Remind students that the assessment is a chance to show progress.
wuAlt: Quiet review: two minutes of silent reading of personal notes and the error log.
Pairs test each other on five irregular verbs and five phrases for opinions.
lp.pres: Reading section (20 minutes). Hand out an adapted PET reading part from the PET Reading Test 02 or the Reading and Writing Paper 1: one text of 300 words with six multiple-choice questions and a gapped text or matching task of five items. Remind students to underline key words in the questions, use the strategy cards, and not to leave any answer blank. When time is up, students check their own answers with the key, and mark each question with a tick or a cross.
presAlt: Use a shorter set (one text with four questions and one matching task of three items) if time is short.
Use the A2 to B1 reading exam as a reading option for weaker groups.
lp.prac: Language use (15 minutes). Give students a cloze with 10 gaps (PET Grammar Test 02 or Fill in the Blank 02) and five sentence transformations. They complete the paper alone in silence. The teacher reads the answers aloud and students mark. Pairs then circle the three items that were still difficult and add them to the target list for next year. Compare with the mini mock results of Week 28: Have the scores improved?
pracAlt: A shorter set with six gaps and three transformations for students who need more time.
A Grammar Sense test as an extra language-use set for students who finish early.
lp.ls: Listening section (10 minutes). Play two or three extracts from the audio in the kit (for example Keren, plans and Lucinda, the visa) twice each, or, if there is no audio, the teacher reads three short texts aloud twice at natural speed (a voicemail with a time and a price, a dialogue between two friends making a plan, and a short talk with five items to note). Students answer five multiple-choice questions and complete five gaps. Mark with the key.
lp.re: Pair reflection: students tell a partner the three biggest improvements since September and give an example for each ("In September I could not describe a photo. Now I can talk for a minute."). Each partner then reports one improvement back to the class using reported speech: "Yassine said that he had improved his listening."
lp.prod: Speaking pairs (10 minutes per pair, while the other students write). The teacher uses the PET speaking format: interview (two questions each), photo (one minute each), decision task (two minutes), and discussion (two minutes). Score each candidate 1 to 5 on grammar and vocabulary, discourse management, pronunciation and interaction. Give each student one strength and one target for next year in a short, friendly conversation of one minute.
lp.rw: Writing section (20 minutes, during the speaking rotation). Choose one task: (1) an informal email of about 100 words to an English friend, answering three questions about school and free time; or (2) a short story of about 100 words beginning "It was the best day of my life when...". Students plan for two minutes, write, count words and check with the code list. Then complete the course feedback form (What helped me, What I want next year) and write three goals for next year with one action each.
lp.st: Closing ceremony: the teacher hands out certificates, thanks the class and gives a short message about next steps (the next level, B1 Preliminary preparation, free online resources and an English club or conversation partners). Students share one wish for the future and take a group photo. Finish with the 'Two Stars and a Wish' game, where each student receives two compliments from classmates on a paper strip.
g: Choose the best strategy for each task.
Complete a short cloze against the clock.
Write three goals with an action for each.
Give a classmate a short spoken compliment.
Write two compliments and a wish for a classmate.
diff: Fast finishers: write a thank-you message to a teacher or classmate (50 words) or an extra sentence transformation.
Support: allow a word bank of linkers and a checklist for the writing paper, and give a bit more time.
hw: Write three goals for your English for next year and one action for each.
Choose one English resource to use every week over the summer (a podcast, a series, a book) and write why.
Write a thank-you message to someone who helped you learn English this year.
lp.tip: Treat this session as a celebration of progress and not a judgement. Prepare the certificates, the result cards and the feedback forms before the lesson, and keep the room calm and quiet during the papers. Give each student one real compliment, and show students who are ready how to continue towards the PET exam.
checklist: I can talk about myself, my interests and my plans for a minute or more with few pauses.
I can understand a recording and note key information such as times, places and feelings.
I can read a text of about 350 words and answer questions on detail and opinion.
I can write an email or story of 100 words with a clear plan and linking words.
I can use the past simple, present perfect, conditionals, reported speech and the passive correctly.
I can give and receive feedback politely and discuss an opinion with a partner.
I can name my goals in English for next year and one action for each.

occ.act: Labour Day (1 May) is close. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students discuss "What makes a job worth doing?" and "What job would you like in ten years?", giving two reasons and an example for each, with the present perfect for experience and conditionals ("If I became a doctor, I would help people in my town.").

levels.desc: For teens aged 14-18 who have a solid A2 and are moving towards B1. Semester 1 adds the present perfect, used to, narrative tenses, verb patterns, the first conditional, modals of obligation and relative clauses through topics teens care about: friends, social media, gaming, school, travel. Semester 2 brings the second conditional, reported speech and the passive, then trains B1 Preliminary (PET) reading, listening, writing and speaking, with a mock exam, a culture project and a final showcase. Longer speaking turns, 60 to 100 word writing and multi-paragraph reading throughout.

weeks.obj: introduce themselves, state learning goals, and use key classroom language

weeks.res: Games/Downloadable games (icebreakers)

skills.L: Listen to introductions and catch names and goals
skills.S: Introduce myself and state my learning goals
skills.R: Read classroom-language phrases and match them to moments
skills.W: Complete a personal-details form (Worksheets)

lp.wu: Human Bingo: Students mingle with bingo cards listing traits like 'likes tea' or 'has a car', asking 'Do you like tea?' and marking names. First to get BINGO wins.
wuAlt: Name Chain: Students stand in a circle, each saying 'I'm [Name] and I like [hobby]', repeating all previous names and hobbies.
Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three statements about themselves, two true and one false; others guess the lie.
lp.pres: Teacher introduces a self-introduction model: 'I'm [Name]. I'm [Age]. I'm from [City]. I want to learn English for [Job/Travel].' Uses flashcards with flags and job icons. Checks understanding with 'What's my name? Where am I from?'
presAlt: Guest Speaker: A volunteer student (prepped) introduces themselves first, then the teacher breaks down their sentences.
Video Model: Show a short clip of two people introducing themselves, then pause to elicit key phrases.
lp.prac: Speed Introductions: Students form two lines, facing each other. They introduce themselves with the model, then one line moves. Teacher monitors and corrects 'be' errors. After 5 rounds, students report their partner's name and goal.
pracAlt: Introduction Circle: Students sit in a circle, passing a ball. The holder introduces themselves and asks 'What's your name?' to the next person.
Fill-in-the-Blank: Students complete a worksheet with 'I ___ [Name]. I ___ from [City]. I ___ to learn English for ___.'
lp.ls: Listen and Match: Teacher reads 5 short introductions (e.g., 'I'm Ali. I'm 25. I'm from Casablanca. I want to learn English for work.'). Students match each to a photo on their worksheet.
lp.re: Stand Up If...: Teacher calls out 'Stand up if you want to learn English for travel!', 'Stand up if you're from Oujda!', etc. Students stand and say 'I want to learn English for [reason]!'
lp.prod: Pair Goal Discussion: Students interview their partner using 'Why do you want to learn English?' and note their answers. Then, each student introduces their partner to the class: 'This is [Name]. He/She wants to learn English for [reason].'
lp.rw: Classroom Language Matching: Students read 10 phrases ('Can I borrow a pen?', 'Open your book, please.') and match them to classroom situations (e.g., 'Someone needs a pen'). Then, they complete a personal-details form with name, age, phone, email.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write your name, one sentence introducing yourself ("I am Ali. I am from Oujda.") and one goal for the course, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students ask 'Do you like...?' to fill their bingo cards.
Students repeat names and hobbies in a circle.
Students guess false statements about peers.
Students stand and state goals for prompts.
Partners ask 'Why learn English?' and report back.
Students pass a ball and introduce themselves.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 5-sentence introduction including a hobby.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'My name is ___. I am ___. I want to learn English for ___.'
hw: Write a 4-sentence self-introduction on paper.
Record a 30-second video introducing yourself to a friend.
Find 3 classroom language phrases online and practice them.
lp.tip: Use local examples (e.g., 'I want to learn English for a job at the American Space') to make goals relevant. Avoid correcting every error·focus on communication.

weeks.obj: give and spell personal details; complete a simple form
weeks.lang: the alphabet; numbers 0-100; name/age/address fields
weeks.res: Worksheets/Print outs (forms); Listening (spelling dialogues)
weeks.act: Form-filling pairs; spelling bee (names and cities); number dictation race
weeks.hw: complete the sample registration form

skills.L: Listening folder: spelling dialogues - catch the letters
skills.S: Spell my name and details aloud
skills.R: Read form fields and match them to answers
skills.W: Complete a simple registration form

lp.wu: Name spelling circle: each student says their name and spells it letter by letter; the next student repeats the previous name and spells it, and the circle grows.
wuAlt: Alphabet Chain: Students stand in a circle and say 'A is for apple, B is for banana...' taking turns.
Number Race: Teacher calls out numbers 0-20, students write them on mini-boards.
lp.pres: Show a sample registration form on the board; model filling it with your details ('My name is... I am... years old. I live at...'); drill pronunciation of 'name', 'age', 'address'.
presAlt: Realia props: Hold up an ID card, ask 'What's this? It's my ID. My name is...'; students repeat.
Dialogue: Roleplay a registration scene with a student ('Hello, what's your name? My name is...').
lp.prac: Form-filling pairs: Students get blank forms, take turns asking and writing partner's details; teacher circulates to correct spelling and pronunciation.
pracAlt: Spelling Bee: Teacher says a name/city (e.g., 'Oujda'), students spell it aloud; fastest wins a point.
Number Dictation Race: Dictate ages (e.g., 'twenty-five'), students write numbers on paper; first pair correct wins.
lp.ls: Listen and fill: Play a dialogue where two people exchange personal details; students listen and complete a half-filled form with missing letters/numbers. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Alphabet and number quick-fire: the teacher calls a letter ("G") or a number ("15"). Students call out a word that starts with the letter, or write the number in words on a mini-whiteboard.
lp.prod: Registration Roleplay: Students pretend to register at the American Space Oujda; one asks 'What's your name? How old are you? Where do you live?', the other answers and fills a form.
lp.rw: Read and Match: Students read short form fields ('Name: __', 'Age: __') and match them to answers ('Fatima', '25') from a list; then copy the completed form.
lp.st: Exit ticket: spell your full name aloud to the teacher at the door and write your phone number in words.
g: Teams race to write the alphabet on the board, one letter per student.
Teacher calls numbers, students cross them off cards; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students spell names in a line; one mistake and they sit down.
Students guess teacher's age by asking 'Are you 20? 25? 30?' until correct.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph introducing themselves (e.g., 'My name is... I am... I live at...').
Support: Use a word bank with alphabet letters and numbers 0-20 for spelling practice.
hw: Complete the sample registration form from class (write name, age, address).
Interview a family member: Ask their name, age, address and write it down.
Write 5 names and 5 ages in English (e.g., 'Layla: 22', 'Omar: 30').
lp.tip: Use Moroccan names and addresses (e.g., 'Oujda, Morocco') to make the task relevant; praise effort over accuracy to build confidence.

weeks.obj: say where people are from and ask follow-up questions
weeks.lang: countries/nationalities; from / live in; he/she + is
weeks.res: Flashcards/Countries... (topics set); world map task
weeks.act: World map mingle; guess the country quiz; where-are-you-from chain
weeks.hw: Complete the 'Where Are You From?' survey with 5 family members.

skills.L: Listen to where-people-are-from dialogues
skills.S: Say where people are from and ask follow-ups
skills.R: Read short profiles and complete the country table
skills.W: Write 3 sentences about countries (he/she is from)

lp.wu: Teacher greets students and shows a world map. Students point to their home country and say: 'I am from Morocco.' Teacher models and drills pronunciation.
wuAlt: Teacher holds up flag flashcards; students say the country name and nationality in chorus.
Teacher says a country; students jump and say the nationality.
lp.pres: Teacher presents 5 country flashcards (Morocco, USA, UK, France, Spain) with flags and nationalities. Models 'He is from Morocco. She is from Spain.' Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Teacher draws simple country outlines on the board; students guess and repeat the country name.
Teacher uses a short video clip of people saying 'I am from...' with subtitles.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs with a country table worksheet. They take turns asking 'Where are you from?' and answering 'I am from [country].' Teacher monitors and corrects errors.
pracAlt: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of countries; they ask classmates and write names.
Teacher gives each student a country card; they mingle and ask 'Where are you from?' to the group.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three people introducing themselves twice ("I am Ali. I am from Morocco. I am Maria. I am from Spain.") and students complete a table with names and countries. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Teacher calls out a country; students race to point to it on the world map. Fastest student gets to call the next country.
lp.prod: Students stand in a circle. The first student says 'I am from Morocco.' The next student says 'He is from Morocco. I am from France.' The chain continues around the circle.
lp.rw: Students read 3 short profiles (e.g., 'My name is Amina. I am from Morocco.') and fill in a table with countries. Then they write 3 sentences: 'He is from Spain. She is from France. I am from Morocco.'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences about people in the class ("Amina is from Morocco. Pierre is from France.") and hand them in at the door.
g: Students mingle, ask 'Where are you from?', and mark countries on their map.
Teacher describes a country (language, flag); students guess the name.
Students write nationalities on a grid; teacher calls them out.
Students sit in a circle; each adds a country to the growing list.
Students match country flags to their names on flashcards.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 5 sentences about famous people's countries.
Support: Use word bank with countries/nationalities for writing task.
hw: Complete the 'Where Are You From?' survey with 5 family members.
Draw 3 flags and write the country names.
Write 3 sentences about your classmates from today's class.
lp.tip: Use countries and people learners know (Morocco, France, Spain, the USA) so they feel connected. Keep the focus on "I am from..." and "He/She is from...".

weeks.obj: describe jobs with a/an and say where people work using present simple he/she
weeks.lang: jobs vocabulary; a/an; he/she works in/at/on; What does he/she do?; Does he/she work in...? Yes, he does
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Jobs-Careers
weeks.act: Job charades; workplace matching; What does she do? guessing game
weeks.hw: describe 3 family members' jobs

skills.L: Listen to short job descriptions and write the job and the workplace
skills.S: Ask and answer What does he/she do? and Where does he/she work?
skills.R: Read short job ads and correct a/an and in/at/on mistakes
skills.W: Write 3 sentences about people's jobs and where they work

lp.wu: Job charades: the teacher mimes a job (doctor, teacher, driver, cook, nurse) and students say "You are a doctor!" Then each student draws a slip, mimes the job and the class guesses.
wuAlt: Picture pairs: match job pictures to words in two minutes.
Quick round: say your own job, or the job of someone in your family.
lp.pres: Show job flashcards (doctor, teacher, chef, driver, nurse, engineer, farmer, pilot, waiter, shopkeeper) and teach "He is a doctor. She is a teacher." Elicit the a/an rule (a doctor, an engineer). Show workplace flashcards (hospital, school, restaurant, taxi, office, farm, shop) and model "He works in a hospital. She works at a school. He works on a farm." Point out the -s on works and helps and mark it in colour. Ask "What does a doctor do? Where does she work?" and "Does a nurse work in a school? No, she doesn't."
presAlt: Use real objects (a stethoscope, chalk, a spoon) to elicit the job.
Put a short text about a taxi driver on the board with the he/she verbs underlined; students find the -s forms.
lp.prac: Workplace matching: pairs match 10 job cards to 10 workplace cards and say "A nurse works in a hospital." Then they ask each other "Where does a pilot work?" and answer with the full sentence. The teacher monitors the -s ending and in/at/on.
pracAlt: Odd one out: three jobs and one workplace; students find the odd one and say why.
Sentence building: reorder the words to make "She works in a school."
lp.ls: Teacher reads three descriptions twice: "He is a pilot. He works on a plane. She is a teacher. She works at a school. He is a farmer. He works on a farm." Students write the job and the workplace for each person. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Guess the job: the teacher says "He works in a kitchen. He cooks food." and students call out the job. Then pairs take turns giving clues.
lp.prod: Guess the job in pairs: Student A thinks of a job and says "He works in a hospital. He helps people." Student B asks "Is he a doctor?" Then each student tells a new partner about a family member's job: "My brother is a driver. He works for a company."
lp.rw: Read five short job ads ("We need a nurse. Work in a hospital.") and circle the mistakes with a/an or in/at/on. Then write three correct sentences about a family member's job using he/she + -s.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about someone's job and where he or she works ("My sister is a teacher. She works at a school.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Mime a job; the class guesses You are a...
Match job cards to workplace cards and say the sentence.
Give clues with He works in... and the class guesses.
Find the job or workplace that does not belong.
Bingo with job pictures called out by the teacher.
diff: Fast finishers: write about three jobs and the tools each person uses.
Support: sentence frame "He/She is a ___. He/She works in/at ___." and a word bank of jobs and workplaces.
hw: Describe 3 family members' jobs (He/She is a... He/She works in/at...).
Find 5 job words around town (signs, shops) and bring them.
Ask a family member about their job and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: The -s on he/she verbs is the first big grammar hurdle: mark it in colour and correct it gently every time. Respect adults' work experience and let learners talk about their real jobs.

occ.act: Halloween falls this weekend (31 Oct). Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students say one thing people do at Halloween ("People wear costumes.") and one thing people do at a Moroccan celebration ("People visit family."). Use the frame "People ___."
