weeks.obj: describe their day with present simple and times, and say what other people do
weeks.lang: present simple I/you/we and he/she; at + time (o'clock, half past, quarter past); always, usually, sometimes, never
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Time; Flashcards/Daily Routine
weeks.act: Routine survey mingle; my-day timeline; adverb line-up (always to never)
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about your day

skills.L: Listen to a daily routine and fill in the times
skills.S: Ask and answer What time do you...? and describe my day
skills.R: Read a short text about a person's day and underline the times
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about my day with at + time and one adverb

lp.wu: Routine relay: students stand in two lines. The teacher shows a routine flashcard (get up, have breakfast, go to work). The first student mimes it, the team says "You get up!", then the next student mimes the next card.
wuAlt: Picture sequence: students put six routine pictures in order and say the first three.
Pair talk: tell your partner one thing you do every morning.
lp.pres: Draw a timeline on the board from 6:00 to 22:00. Place routine flashcards on it (get up, have breakfast, go to work, have lunch, go home, go to bed) and teach the times with a clock face: 7 o'clock, half past two, quarter past eight. Model "I get up at 7 o'clock." "You get up at 7." and "She gets up at half past six." Show always, usually, sometimes, never on a line. Check understanding: "What time do I have breakfast? What time does she go to work?"
presAlt: Use a real clock to practise o'clock, half past and quarter past in pairs.
Show a short video clip about a day in the life and pause after each routine.
lp.prac: Routine survey mingle: students get a worksheet with routines and ask "What time do you get up?" or "Do you always have breakfast?" and write the answers. Then they tell a partner about one classmate: "Karim gets up at 6 o'clock."
pracAlt: Time dominoes: match times in words to times on a clock.
Sentence cards: put the words in order ("I / at / get up / seven").
lp.ls: Teacher reads a daily routine twice: "Fatima gets up at half past six. She has breakfast at seven. She goes to work at eight. She has lunch at one. She goes home at five." Students fill in the missing times on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Adverb line-up: four cards on the wall (always, usually, sometimes, never). The teacher says a routine ("I drink tea in the morning.") and students stand under the card that is true for them and tell the person next to them.
lp.prod: My day: students draw a timeline of their own day and tell a small group three sentences: "I get up at 7. I go to work at 8. I have lunch at 1." The group asks one question each ("What time do you have lunch?").
lp.rw: Read a short text about a Moroccan taxi driver's day (six sentences) and underline the times. Then write five sentences about your own day with at + time and one adverb.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about your day with a time and one with always, usually, sometimes or never, and hand it in at the door.
g: Mime a routine; the team says the sentence.
Ask What time do you...? and note the answers.
Stand under always, usually, sometimes or never.
Match times in words and on clocks.
Draw a timeline of your day and tell a group about it.
diff: Fast finishers: write about a family member's day (6 sentences with he/she).
Support: sentence frame "I ___ at ___ o'clock." and a clock face with the time phrases.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your day (use times).
Ask a family member "What time do you get up?" and write 3 sentences.
Make a timeline of your weekend and be ready to tell it.
lp.tip: Teach times with a real clock and keep it on the wall. Practise he/she with real people the learners know. Use prayer times, work and school as natural examples.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute reading in the present simple: "Every year Moroccans celebrate the Green March on 6 November. People hang flags and families watch the speech." Students underline the verbs and tell a partner what their family does that day.
occ.hw: Write 3 sentences about what your family does on a national day.

weeks.obj: talk about free-time activities and preferences
weeks.lang: like/love/enjoy + -ing; free-time activities
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Likes and Dislikes
weeks.act: Find someone who...; preference corners; weekend plan discussion pairs
weeks.hw: 5 sentences about your free time

skills.L: Listen to like / enjoy + -ing mini-talks
skills.S: Talk about my free-time preferences
skills.R: Read free-time profiles and underline the -ing forms
skills.W: Write my free-time paragraph (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Students stand up. Teacher shows flashcards of free-time activities (playing football, reading books, cooking). Students walk around and ask each other: 'Do you like...?' and respond with 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Teacher writes 'free time' on the board. Students brainstorm activities in pairs, writing 3 each on sticky notes and sticking them up.
Teacher mimes an activity (e.g., swimming). Students guess: 'Do you like swimming?' Teacher responds with 'Yes, I love it' or 'No, I enjoy reading'.
lp.pres: Teacher presents 3 model sentences: 'I like playing football', 'I love reading books', 'I enjoy cooking'. Uses flashcards to show each activity. Checks understanding by asking: 'What do I love?' and 'Do I like cooking?'
presAlt: Teacher tells a short story: 'On weekends, I like walking in the park. I love drinking mint tea. I enjoy listening to music.' Underlines the -ing forms.
Teacher uses realia: a football, a book, a cooking pot. Holds each up and says the sentence, then gestures for students to repeat chorally.
lp.prac: Students do 'Find Someone Who...' with a grid of activities. They walk around and ask: 'Do you like...?' and write names. Teacher monitors and models questions.
pracAlt: Students work in pairs. Teacher gives each pair a set of activity cards. They take turns saying: 'I like/love/enjoy...' and the partner responds with 'Me too' or 'I don't, I prefer...'.
Teacher plays 'Guess the Activity'. Mimes an activity; students guess using: 'Do you like...?' Teacher responds with 'Yes, I love it' or 'No, I enjoy...'
lp.ls: Students listen to 3 short audio clips of people talking about their free time. They tick the activities mentioned on their worksheet. Teacher plays each clip twice. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Preference line: a line on the floor from "love it" to "hate it". The teacher says an activity ("swimming") and students stand at their place on the line and tell the person next to them: "I like swimming."
lp.prod: Students work in pairs. They plan their ideal weekend using 'I like/love/enjoy...'. They then present their plan to the class: 'On Saturday, I like... On Sunday, I love...'
lp.rw: Students read 3 short profiles of people's free-time activities. They underline all the -ing forms. Then they write 4 sentences about their own free time using 'like/love/enjoy + -ing'.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you like doing and one thing you don't like doing in your free time, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students match flashcards to sentences like 'I love swimming'.
Teacher labels corners of the room: 'love', 'like', 'enjoy'. Students go to the corner for an activity when called out.
Student mimes an activity; others guess using 'Do you like...?'
Students have bingo cards with activities. They ask classmates: 'Do you like...?' to mark off squares.
Student 1 says: 'I like playing football'. Student 2 repeats and adds: 'I love reading books'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 6 sentences about their friends' free time.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I like ___. I love ___. I enjoy ___.'
hw: Write 5 sentences about your free time using like/love/enjoy + -ing.
Interview a family member about their free time and write 3 sentences.
Draw a picture of your ideal weekend and label 3 activities with -ing words.
lp.tip: Connect activities to learners' real lives: ask about weekends and holidays. Real examples like "I like drinking mint tea with friends" build rapport.

weeks.obj: say and write the date, use days and months, and talk about appointments, birthdays and festivals
weeks.lang: days of the week; months; ordinal numbers (1st to 31st); What is the date? / When is...? It's on the...; in/on with months and dates
weeks.res: Worksheets (dates and months); Games (calendar and ordinal games); festival pictures
weeks.act: Birthday line-up; calendar poster; When is...? pair quiz; appointment cards
weeks.hw: write the dates of 5 birthdays, appointments or festivals in your life

skills.L: Listen to dates in a short dialogue and write them in numbers
skills.S: Ask and answer When is your birthday? and When is...?
skills.R: Read a short text about festivals and underline the dates
skills.W: Write the date and 4 sentences about important dates

lp.wu: Birthday line-up: without speaking, students line up in order of their birthdays (January to December). They then check by asking "When is your birthday?" and answering "It's on the 5th of March." This recycles numbers and be.
wuAlt: Number bingo 1 to 31: the teacher calls numbers and students mark them.
Alphabet race: teams spell a month or a name on the board, letter by letter.
lp.pres: Teach the days and months with a calendar poster and repeat chorally, marking the stress (Jan-u-ary, Feb-ru-ary). Teach ordinal numbers: 1st, 2nd and 3rd are irregular, then 4th to 31st with -th. Model the date: "Today is Monday, the 16th of November. My birthday is on the 3rd of May." Show festival and appointment cards: "Independence Day is on the 18th of November. The doctor's appointment is on Tuesday, the 4th of March." Check understanding: "When is Independence Day? Is the appointment on Monday?"
presAlt: Class calendar on the wall: students stick a birthday star on the right date and read it aloud.
Photo quiz: show festival pictures and students say the month.
lp.prac: Date dictation in pairs: A reads six dates ("the 5th of March") and B writes them in numbers (5/3); then they swap. Then a When is...? chain with fact cards: Throne Day 30 July, New Year 1 January, Labour Day 1 May, Green March 6 November, Independence Day 18 November, Earth Day 22 April.
pracAlt: Ordinal number steps: students step on numbered floor cards and say the ordinal.
Appointment cards: pairs match a day and a date to a short appointment note.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short dialogue twice: "When is your appointment?" "It's on Tuesday, the 4th of March." "And your daughter's birthday?" "On the 30th of September." Students write the dates they hear on a form with four names. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Month relay: teams race to write the months in order on the board; then the teacher calls a month and one student from each team writes a festival or birthday that happens in it.
lp.prod: Class calendar: groups get a blank 12-month calendar and a set of fact cards. They place each festival or birthday on the correct date and write one sentence for each ("Independence Day is on the 18th of November."). Groups present the calendar and quiz another group: "When is...?"
lp.rw: Read a short text "Festivals in Morocco" (six sentences with dates: Throne Day 30 July, Green March 6 November, Independence Day 18 November, New Year 1 January). Underline the dates, then write four sentences about important dates in your own family.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the date of your birthday and one festival in words (for example "the 3rd of May") and hand it in at the door.
g: Line up in birthday order without speaking, then check with When is your birthday?
Bingo with dates written in numbers and words.
Pairs dictate dates to each other and race to write them correctly.
Teams answer date questions from fact cards.
Match each appointment to its day and date.
diff: Fast finishers: add the weekday of each date for this year.
Support: months word wall with first letters and an ordinal number chart from 1st to 31st.
hw: Write the dates of 5 birthdays, appointments or festivals in your life.
Ask a family member "When is your birthday?" and write the date in words.
Make a mini calendar of this month with 3 important dates.
lp.tip: Ordinals and month spelling need repeated recycling. Keep the class calendar on the wall for the rest of the year and ask learners to write the date at the top of every page. Dates are essential for appointments and invitations later in the course.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute timeline: students put national days (6 Nov, 18 Nov) on a class calendar and say "Independence Day is on the 18th of November."
occ.hw: Write one sentence: "My favourite festival is ___. It is in/on ___."

weeks.obj: describe family members, their relationships and what they do
weeks.lang: possessive 's; family vocabulary; have got; he/she present simple (works, lives, likes)
weeks.res: Flashcards/Family; Lesson Plans/Family lesson plan
weeks.act: Family photo description circle; possessive relay; family riddles
weeks.hw: describe 3 people in your family

skills.L: Listen to a person describing a family and tick the members mentioned
skills.S: Describe my family with possessive 's, have got and he/she verbs
skills.R: Read a short text about a family and find the possessive 's
skills.W: Write 4 sentences about my family

lp.wu: Family chain: students stand in a circle. The first student says "This is my mother." The next says "This is my mother. This is my brother." and the chain grows.
wuAlt: Photo pairs: students show a family photo (or draw one) and name two people.
Quick round: say one family word and a name.
lp.pres: Show a large family tree flashcard. Point to each member and model sentences: "This is my uncle. He's my mother's brother. He works in a bank. He's got two children." Drill the sentences chorally, then ask students to point to their own family members on the card. Mark the possessive 's and the -s on works and lives in colour. Check with thumbs up/down: "Is Karim Amina's brother?"
presAlt: Use the teacher's own family photo and tell a short story about two people.
Put a short text on the board about a family with the 's forms underlined.
lp.prac: Possessive relay: divide the class into two teams. Give each team a set of family cards (mother, father, sister, brother, uncle, aunt...). The teacher says "Amina's brother" and one student from each team finds the right card and says the sentence "He is Amina's brother."
pracAlt: Family riddles: "She is my father's sister. Who is she?"
Sentence building: reorder the words to make "My sister has got two children."
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short description twice: "This is my family. My father is a driver. My mother works at a school. I have got one sister. Her name is Nadia. She lives in Rabat." Students tick the family members they hear and write one fact about each. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Family charades: one student mimes what a family member does (cooking for "mother", reading for "grandfather") and the class says "She cooks. She is his mother."
lp.prod: Family photo description in pairs: each student describes a real or imaginary family photo to a partner ("This is my brother. He is a teacher. He has got two sons.") and the partner draws a family tree. Then they tell the class one fact about their partner's family.
lp.rw: Read a short text about a family (six sentences) and circle all the possessive 's ("My father's name is..."). Then write four sentences about your own family using "This is my..." and "He/She has got..." or "He/She works in...".
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about a family member with a possessive 's or has got ("My sister's name is Nadia.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Add one family member to the chain each turn.
Find the family card for the possessive phrase the teacher says.
Give clues about a family member; the class guesses.
Listen to a description and draw the family tree.
Mime what a family member does; the class guesses.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph about your family (6 sentences with he/she verbs).
Support: sentence frame "This is my ___. He/She is ___. He/She works in ___." and a family word bank.
hw: Describe 3 people in your family (name, job, one thing they like).
Draw your family tree and label each person.
Ask a family member about their day and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Adults have rich family lives: let them talk about their own roles as parents, children or siblings. Accept every family shape and keep the model sentences flexible.

occ.hw: Write one sentence: "I am thankful for ___."

weeks.obj: ask and answer about prices; handle a simple purchase
weeks.lang: How much...?; numbers/prices; this/that
weeks.res: Listening (shopping mp3); Worksheets
weeks.act: Market roleplay with real price lists; bargaining dialogues; listening gap-fill
weeks.hw: Write a 6-line shopping dialogue for buying fruit

skills.L: Listening folder: shopping mp3 - prices and totals
skills.S: Ask and answer about prices; buy an item
skills.R: Read price tags and a receipt
skills.W: Write a shopping dialogue (6 lines)

lp.wu: Students play 'Price Guess' with realia: teacher holds up items (apple, pen, notebook), students guess 'How much is it?' in Moroccan Dirhams, then reveal the price tag.
wuAlt: Students match picture cards to price tags (e.g., 'book' to '20 DH')
Students count out play money for simple amounts (e.g., 'Show me 50 DH')
lp.pres: Teacher introduces 'How much is this/that?' using fruit flashcards, models asking and answering, then mimes shopping gestures; students repeat chorally and individually.
presAlt: Teacher uses a simple dialogue script on the board: 'How much is this?' 'It's 10 DH'
Teacher draws a market scene on the board, labeling items with prices
lp.prac: Students do 'Find the Price' in pairs: each has a flyer with items, they ask 'How much is this?' and mark the prices; teacher monitors for pronunciation.
pracAlt: Students play 'Bargaining Bingo': listen to teacher say prices, cross off matching numbers on their grid
Students do 'Price Dictation': teacher says items/prices, students write them down
lp.ls: Students listen to a market dialogue (MP3) and fill in gaps in a receipt worksheet (e.g., '1 apple = ___ DH, total = ___ DH') If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Students play 'Quick Shop': teacher calls out an item, students race to grab the correct price tag from the board.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a market stall in pairs: one is the seller (with price list), one is the buyer; they bargain using 'How much is this?' and 'Can I have this, please?'
lp.rw: Students read a simple receipt (e.g., 'Milk: 5 DH, Bread: 3 DH, Total: 8 DH') and write 3 sentences about what they bought.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one question and one answer about a price ("How much is this? It is 10 dirhams.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students race to match picture cards to price tags on the board
Students repeat a dialogue chain: 'How much is this?' 'It's 10 DH.' 'How much is that?'
Students mime bargaining and others guess the price
Students race to circle matching items and prices on a worksheet
Students roleplay a quick bargain with a discount (e.g., 'It's 20 DH.' 'Okay, 15 DH.')
diff: Fast finishers: write a 6-line shopping dialogue with bargaining
Support learners: use sentence starters like 'How much is ___?' and 'It's ___ DH.'
hw: Write a 6-line shopping dialogue for buying fruit
Draw a market scene with 5 items and prices
Ask a family member about the price of 3 items in the souk
lp.tip: Use Moroccan Dirhams in all activities to build real-world relevance; praise bargaining attempts as culturally authentic. Check the roleplay performance this week.

weeks.obj: order a meal and ask about dishes politely
weeks.lang: would like; menu vocabulary; Can we have...?
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Food; Listening (restaurant mp3)
weeks.act: Restaurant roleplay with menus; dish-of-the-day presentations; ordering dialogues
weeks.hw: write a 6-line restaurant dialogue

skills.L: Listening folder: restaurant mp3 - orders
skills.S: Order a meal and ask about the dishes
skills.R: Read a menu and match dishes to courses
skills.W: Write my order in full sentences

lp.wu: Students play 'Menu Pictionary' in pairs. Teacher shows a food flashcard, student draws it, partner guesses 'Is it...?' and names the dish.
wuAlt: Students play 'Food Bingo' with 9 images on a grid; teacher calls out dishes and students mark them.
Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their favorite foods using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'.
lp.pres: Teacher presents a laminated menu with images and prices. Models 'I would like...' and 'Can we have...?' for ordering. Asks comprehension questions 'What would you like?' to check understanding.
presAlt: Teacher uses a story about a person ordering food, highlighting key phrases.
Teacher acts out a dialogue with a student waiter using real plates and cutlery as props.
lp.prac: Students complete a 'Fill the Gap' worksheet with sentences like 'I ___ like the soup.' They then practice in pairs using a dialogue prompt card with 'Would you like...?' and 'Can we have...?'
pracAlt: Students play 'Restaurant Role Cards' where one is a waiter and the other a customer using a provided menu.
Students play 'Memory Match' matching food images to their names while saying 'I would like...'.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a restaurant order twice ("I would like the soup, please. And can we have two teas?") and students tick the correct dishes on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Menu race: teams race to write the dishes for a starter, a main course and a dessert; then each team reads its menu aloud with "I would like...".
lp.prod: Students work in pairs to roleplay a restaurant scenario using laminated menus. One is the waiter, the other is a customer. They must use 'Can we have...?' and 'What is the dish of the day?'
lp.rw: Students read a short menu text and match dishes to courses (starter, main, dessert). They then write 3 simple sentences about what they would order, e.g., 'I would like the soup.'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write what you would like to eat and drink today ("I would like a tea, please.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students match food flashcards to menu words in a race.
Students race to write correct sentences from spoken prompts.
Students act out a food word for others to guess using 'Is it...?'
Students present a dish using flashcards and say 'The dish of the day is...'
Teams take turns running to a menu to find and write a dish name.
diff: Fast finishers write a 4-line dialogue with a waiter asking about allergies.
Support / weaker learners use a sentence frame: 'I would like the ______, please.'
hw: Write a 6-line restaurant dialogue between a customer and waiter.
Draw your ideal meal and write 3 sentences about it.
Find 5 food words in English and write a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Model polite intonation for 'Would you like...?' as Moroccan learners may use direct translations. Connect to local dining customs like offering tea to guests.

weeks.obj: ask for and give simple directions around town
weeks.lang: imperatives; prepositions of place/movement; transport words
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Directions; Flashcards/Directions
weeks.act: Map of Oujda task; listen-and-trace routes; transport survey mingle
weeks.hw: Write 5 directions from your home to the souk.

skills.L: Listen to directions audio and trace the route
skills.S: Ask for and give simple directions
skills.R: Read direction phrases and order them on a map
skills.W: Write directions to a nearby place

lp.wu: Direction dictation: the teacher gives directions aloud ("Go straight, turn left, turn right") and students draw the route on a mini map; then they check with a partner.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Draw the Route' - teacher draws a simple path on the board, students call out directions to describe it.
Alternative 2: 'Quick Survey' - students ask each other 'How do you get to class? Bus or walk?' and tally answers.
lp.pres: Presentation: Show a large map of Oujda with key landmarks (Poste, Med V, City Center). Model giving directions: 'Go straight, turn left at the mosque.' Use finger to trace route on map. Check by asking 'Where do I turn?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use realia - toy car and street signs to demonstrate movements.
Alternative 2: Draw a simple town map on the board with students naming the places.
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Map Pairs'. Students get a blank map of Oujda with streets. Student A traces a route with a pencil, Student B writes directions. Teacher circulates to correct prepositions (next to, opposite).
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Flashcard Directions' - students arrange transport flashcards (bus, taxi) to match a spoken route.
Alternative 2: 'Error Correction' - students fix preposition mistakes in a worksheet (e.g., 'turn in the bank' -> 'turn at the bank').
lp.ls: Listening slot: 'Trace the Route'. Students listen to an audio of someone giving directions from the American Space to the train station. They trace the route on their map with a different color crayon. Play twice. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Four Corners'. Label corners 'North', 'South', 'East', 'West'. Teacher calls out directions like 'Go to the corner opposite North!', students race there.
lp.prod: Production task: 'Mingle Survey'. Students ask 5 classmates 'How do you get to the souk?' and note answers (walk, taxi, bus). Then, in pairs, they give directions to one of the places mentioned using 'Go straight...'.
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: 'Order the Directions'. Students read 5 jumbled sentences (e.g., 'Turn right at the pharmacy.', 'Go straight.') and glue them in order on a mini-map worksheet. Then they write 3 directions from their home to the American Space.
lp.st: Exit ticket: draw a mini map with three places and write one direction sentence ("Go straight, turn left at the mosque.").
g: Teacher says a landmark, students point to it on the map.
Student mimes a direction (turn left), others guess.
Two teams race to trace a correct route on the board.
Students hop to 'next to' the chair, 'opposite' the door.
Students mark transport words called out.
diff: Fast finishers: Draw a map of their neighborhood and write directions to a friend's house.
Support: Use a pre-highlighted map with key words to trace routes.
hw: Write 5 directions from your home to the souk.
Record yourself giving directions to the train station.
Ask a family member for directions to a local place and write them down.
lp.tip: Use landmarks familiar to students (Poste, Med V) to make directions meaningful. Pair strong/weak learners to build confidence. Keep a participation checklist this week.

weeks.obj: describe their home with there is/there are
weeks.lang: there is/there are; rooms and furniture
weeks.res: Flashcards/Rooms; Flashcards/Furniture
weeks.act: Dream house presentations; furniture battle (describe-and-draw); listing races
weeks.hw: 6 sentences describing your home

skills.L: Listen to home descriptions (there is / there are)
skills.S: Describe my home room by room
skills.R: Read home ads and count the rooms
skills.W: Write about my home (4 sentences)

lp.wu: Quick Review: 'Find Someone Who'. Hand out a sheet with prompts like 'Find someone who has a big living room'. Students mingle and ask 'Do you have a big living room?', responding 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Room Pictionary'. Teacher draws a room on the board, students guess 'Is it a kitchen?'
Alternative 2: 'Memory Game'. Show 6 flashcards of rooms/furniture for 10 seconds, students list what they saw.
lp.pres: Show a large picture of a house. Point to different rooms and model: 'There is a living room. There are two chairs.' Use flashcards for 'bedroom', 'kitchen', 'sofa', 'table'. Check by asking 'What room is this?' and 'What is there?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a simple floor plan drawing on the board, adding furniture as you teach.
Alternative 2: Bring a small model house and point to the rooms inside.
lp.prac: Controlled Practice: 'Furniture Battle'. Pairs get a paper with a blank room outline. Student A says 'There is a bed', draws it. Student B says 'There are two windows', draws them. They take turns describing and drawing items in the room.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Race'. Write scrambled sentences like 'a / there / is / table' on the board, teams race to write the correct order.
Alternative 2: 'Matching Game'. Match picture cards of furniture to sentence cards with 'There is/are'.
lp.ls: Listening Slot: Play a short audio of someone describing their home. Students listen and tick the rooms/furniture they hear on a worksheet. Check answers by asking 'What did you hear?'. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Room tour: in pairs, one student describes a room from a picture ("There is a bed. There are two chairs.") while the partner points to each item; then they swap.
lp.prod: Production Task: 'Dream House Presentation'. In pairs, students design their dream house on a large paper. They present it to the class using 'There is/are', e.g., 'There is a big garden. There are five bedrooms.'
lp.rw: Reading and Writing Slot: Read a simple classified ad for a flat. Students count the rooms and write 4 sentences about it using 'There is/are', e.g., 'There is one kitchen. There are two bedrooms.'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences about your home ("There is a kitchen. There are two bedrooms.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams race to name as many rooms as possible in 60 seconds.
Teacher calls out items like 'There is a sofa', students cover the picture on their bingo card.
Student A draws a room, Student B guesses what is in it using 'Is there a...?'
Students compare two similar pictures of a home and spot differences using 'There is/are'.
Teacher describes a decorated Christmas home, students draw it.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 6 sentences about their dream home.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with 'living room', 'bedroom', 'sofa', 'table' to write sentences.
hw: Write 6 sentences describing your real home using There is/are.
Write 4 sentences about your dream home (There is/are).
Draw a picture of your home and label 5 rooms or furniture items.
lp.tip: Connect the lesson to local context by comparing Moroccan home layouts (e.g., 'dar') with Western homes, highlighting shared values like family spaces.

occ.act: Christmas week (25 December). Optional 10-minute task: students read a short text ("On 25 December many people in the USA and Europe celebrate Christmas. There is a tree in the living room. There are lights and gifts.") and compare it with how their home looks at Eid, using There is/are.

weeks.obj: talk about the past with was/were and last-time expressions
weeks.lang: was/were; last night/week/year
weeks.res: Worksheets/'Was' vs 'Were'
weeks.act: Last weekend board; where-were-you quiz; pair interviews about the past
weeks.hw: write 5 sentences about your last weekend

skills.L: Listen to last-weekend stories with was / were
skills.S: Talk about the past with was / were
skills.R: Read a diary text and underline was / were
skills.W: Write about last weekend (5 sentences)

lp.wu: Last Weekend Board: Teacher draws a 3x3 grid on the board with squares for 'Saturday morning', 'Saturday afternoon', 'Saturday night', 'Sunday morning', etc. Students ask 'Where were you last Saturday morning?' and teacher answers 'I was at home' or 'I was at the market', drawing a simple icon in the square. Students then ask each other in pairs.
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Hand out a sheet with prompts like 'Find someone who was at the cinema last weekend'. Students walk around asking 'Were you at the cinema last weekend?' and writing names.
Memory Chain: Teacher says 'Last weekend I was at home'. Student 1 says 'Last weekend [teacher] was at home and I was at the market'. Student 2 repeats the chain and adds their own.
lp.pres: Teacher shows two flashcards: one of a person sleeping at home, one of a person at a cafe. Teacher says 'Last night, I was at home' and 'Last night, Ali was at the cafe'. Elicits 'was' and 'were' from students. Teacher then presents last-time expressions: 'last night', 'last weekend', 'last year', pointing to a calendar. Checks understanding by asking 'Where were you last night?' to a few students.
presAlt: Timeline Drawing: Teacher draws a simple timeline from 'Friday' to 'Sunday' on the board. Asks students to draw a picture of where they were on Saturday and say the sentence 'I was at [place]'.

Photo Story: Teacher shows 3-4 photos of themselves from last weekend (e.g., at a restaurant, at home, at a park). Tells a short story using 'was' and 'were' and asks students to guess the location for each photo.
lp.prac: Where Were You? Quiz: Teacher writes 5 sentences on the board, some true, some false, about herself last weekend (e.g., 'I was at the cinema', 'I was at work'). Students in teams get points for guessing correctly. Then, in pairs, students write 3 true and 1 false sentence about their own last weekend. They read their sentences to their partner, who guesses the false one.
pracAlt: Grammar Auction: Teacher writes 10 sentences with was/were errors (e.g., 'I was happy'). Students in teams have 100 points. They 'bid' on sentences they think are correct. Correct sentences earn them points, incorrect ones lose points.

Sentence Race: In pairs, students race to write 5 correct sentences using 'was/were' and a last-time expression from a list of prompts (e.g., 'last year', 'last night'). The first pair to write all 5 correctly wins.
lp.ls: Listening for Details: Teacher plays a short audio recording (30-45 seconds) of two people talking about their New Year's Eve. The script is: 'A: Hi Leila! How was your New Year's Eve? B: It was great! I was at my cousin's house. We were very happy. A: Nice! And you, Sarah? A: I was at home. I was tired, so I was in bed at 11 pm.' Students listen and answer two questions: 'Where was Leila?' and 'Where was Sarah?' on a handout.
lp.re: Past Tense Charades: Teacher writes 'was/were' actions on small slips of paper (e.g., 'was happy', 'was at the market', 'was sleeping'). A student picks a slip, acts it out without speaking, and the class guesses, asking 'Were you...?' The student answers 'Yes, I was' or 'No, I wasn't'.
lp.prod: Pair Interviews: Students work in pairs. Student A asks Student B three questions: 'Where were you last night?', 'Where were you last weekend?', 'Were you happy last year?'. Student B answers. Then they swap roles. After, each student stands up and introduces their partner to the class: 'Last weekend, [partner's name] was at [place]'.
lp.rw: Diary Entry Reading: Students receive a short, simple diary entry about a person's last weekend. Example: 'Friday: I was tired. I was at home. Saturday: I was happy. I was at my friend's house. Sunday: I was busy. I was at the market.' Students read the text and underline all examples of 'was' and 'were'. Then, they write 5 simple sentences about their own last weekend using the same structure.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about last weekend with was or were and one question with Where were you...? and hand it in at the door.
g: Students write 9 places in a bingo grid (e.g., 'park', 'home', 'cinema'). Teacher calls out sentences like 'I was at the park last weekend'. Students mark the square if they have it.
Students work in pairs with two similar pictures of a 'last weekend' scene. They take turns asking 'Was he at the market?' to find the differences.
Teacher starts a story: 'Last weekend, I was at home...'. Each student adds one sentence using 'was/were' to continue the story.
Students play in teams. To place an X or O, a team member must correctly make a sentence with 'was/were' from a prompt.
Teacher shows a picture of a scene for 20 seconds. Hides it. Students write 5 sentences using 'was/were' to describe what was in the picture.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a short paragraph (6-7 sentences) about their last weekend using 'was/were'.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame: 'Last weekend, I was at ___. I was ___. I was ___.' to write their sentences.
hw: Interview 3 family members or friends about their last weekend. Ask "Where were you last night?" and write each answer in a simple sentence.
Write 5 sentences about your last weekend. Use was/were and a last-time expression in each sentence.
Write 3 sentences about last year: "Last year I was...".
lp.tip: Connect the language to learners' own experiences: ask about last weekend and last year. Keep the time words (last night, last week, last year) on the board all lesson.

occ.act: New Year week. Optional "last year" memories: students write three sentences about last year with was/were ("Last year I was at home in Ramadan." is fine, or "Last year my son was ten.") and share them with a partner.

weeks.obj: tell a simple story about the past with regular verbs, in statements, negatives and questions
weeks.lang: past simple regular (-ed and spelling); didn't + verb; Did you...? Yes, I did / No, I didn't; yesterday, last weekend
weeks.res: Worksheets; Seasonal/Christmas pack (culture text)
weeks.act: Yesterday story chain; -ed pronunciation sorting; Did-you bingo
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about a good day

skills.L: Listen to a short text about a weekend and tick what the person did
skills.S: Ask and answer Did you...? about yesterday and last weekend
skills.R: Read a short text about a good day and underline the -ed verbs
skills.W: Write 5 sentences about a good day with regular verbs

lp.wu: Yesterday timeline: students draw a simple timeline on paper. The teacher asks "What did you do yesterday?" and students write three words (for example work, market, cook). They tell a partner using the words.
wuAlt: Did-you bingo: a grid of activities; students ask "Did you cook yesterday?" and write the name.
Pair talk: tell your partner one thing you did last weekend.
lp.pres: Write a short story on the board: "Last Saturday I visited my sister. We cooked lunch and watched TV. I didn't work." Underline the -ed verbs. Teach the three endings by sorting (walked /t/, played /d/, visited /id/) and the spelling rules (visit, visited; live, lived; study, studied; stop, stopped). Teach "didn't + verb" and "Did you...? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't." Check: "Did I work? No, you didn't."
presAlt: Teacher mimes five actions ("I cooked.") and the class says what the teacher did.
Write ten verbs on the board and ask students to add the -ed in pairs.
lp.prac: -ed pronunciation sort: students receive 15 verb cards (walked, played, watched, visited, cooked...) and sort them into the three sounds /t/, /d/ and /id/, then say a sentence with each. Pairs check by listening to the teacher.
pracAlt: Spelling sort: students sort verbs by the -ed rule.
Sentence building: reorder words to make a past simple sentence.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short text twice: "Last weekend I visited my cousin in Nador. We played football and watched a film. I didn't do my homework! My cousin cooked dinner." Students tick the activities and answer "Did he play football? Yes or no?" If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Past tense relay: two lines of students. The teacher shows a verb card (clean, walk, call). The first student runs to the board and writes the -ed form; the next student continues. The first team with all correct wins.
lp.prod: Yesterday story chain: groups of four build a story about a day, each adding one sentence in the past (the first sentence comes from a card: "Yesterday morning I..."). Then pairs interview each other "Did you...? last weekend" and write three sentences about their partner.
lp.rw: Read a short text "A Good Day in Oujda" (six sentences) and underline all the -ed verbs. Then write five sentences about a good day of your own using regular verbs and one negative ("I walked in the park. I talked to my friend. I didn't work.").
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you did yesterday and one thing you didn't do ("I cooked dinner. I didn't watch TV.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Ask Did you...? to find a classmate for each box.
Race to write the -ed form on the board.
Add one past sentence each to build a story.
A student sits with a verb card behind them; the class gives past sentences until they guess it.
diff: Fast finishers: add two irregular verbs you already know (went, had) to the story.
Support: -ed spelling table and a sentence frame "Yesterday I ___ed. I didn't ___."
hw: Write 6 sentences about a good day (one negative).
Interview a family member: "What did you do last weekend?" and write 3 sentences.
Find 5 regular verbs in a text and write their -ed forms.
lp.tip: Teach the -ed sounds by listening and sorting, not only by rules. Keep irregular verbs for Week 25: mixing them in now overloads beginners. Let adults talk about real days from their lives.

occ.act: New Year recap (4 January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year ("I visited my family. I cooked a big meal. I watched football.") and report one thing to the class.

weeks.obj: complete the written paper and a short speaking interview
weeks.lang: all S1 outcomes
weeks.res: Tests (teacher-selected); assessment kit
weeks.act: Written paper (35 min); individual speaking slots while others review
weeks.hw: Review S1 vocabulary list and write 3 sentences using 3 new words.

skills.L: Listening paper (teacher-selected items)
skills.S: Short speaking interview
skills.R: Reading paper across S1 topics
skills.W: Guided writing task

lp.wu: Greetings and Name Chain: Students stand in a circle, one student says 'Hello, my name is [name]', the next repeats the name and adds their own, continuing around the circle to review personal introductions.
wuAlt: Interview Bingo: Students mingle asking 'What's your name?' and 'Where are you from?' to fill a bingo grid with classmates' names.
Flashcard Quick Review: Teacher holds up flashcards of S1 topics (food, shopping, directions) and students shout the English word.
lp.pres: Teacher distributes the S1 written paper (35 min) with clear instructions, modeling the first question on the board to ensure understanding before students begin individually.
presAlt: Oral Exam Demo: Teacher conducts a short mock speaking interview with a volunteer student, showing the format and questions to the class.
S1 Topic Review: Teacher uses a mind map on the board to recap all S1 vocabulary and functions (greetings, shopping, etc.).
lp.prac: While waiting for their speaking slot, students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' worksheet with S1 topics (e.g., 'Find someone who likes coffee'), practicing question forms in pairs.
pracAlt: Vocabulary Matching: Students match S1 words (e.g., 'apple', 'bread') to pictures on a worksheet, working in pairs to check answers.
Error Correction: Teacher writes 5 S1 sentences with errors on the board; students work in pairs to find and correct them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short text twice about a person's daily routine, then students answer four questions on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Stand Up Sit Down: Teacher calls out S1 verbs (e.g., 'eat', 'drink', 'walk') and students stand up if they do the action daily, sitting down if not, reactivating vocabulary physically.
lp.prod: Individual speaking interviews: Students take turns with the teacher for 2-3 minutes, answering KET-style questions (e.g., 'What's your job?', 'Where do you live?') while others quietly review S1 flashcards.
lp.rw: Writing Task: Students write 3-5 sentences about their weekend using past simple (e.g., 'I went to the market. I bought bread. I ate with my family.'), with a model sentence on the board for support. Put the irregular forms (went, bought, ate) on the board as a word bank.
lp.st: Closing circle: students tell a partner one thing they did well in the assessment and one thing they want to practise. Collect the papers and say goodbye.
g: Teacher calls out S1 words; students mark them on their bingo cards and shout 'Bingo!' when they have a line.
Students act out S1 verbs (e.g., 'shop', 'eat') for others to guess, saying the word when correct.
Two teams race to match S1 word cards to picture cards on the board.
Students use word cards to make correct sentences about S1 topics.
Students quiz each other with S1 questions, then trade cards and find a new partner.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write 5 extra sentences about their favorite S1 topic (e.g., food, shopping).
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with S1 verbs to complete the writing task.
hw: Review S1 vocabulary list and write 3 sentences using 3 new words.
Listen to a short English song (e.g., 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes') and write down 5 words they know.
Practice introducing themselves and asking 2 questions (e.g., 'What's your name?', 'Where are you from?') with a family member.
lp.tip: For adults, frame the assessment as a 'progress check' to reduce anxiety; emphasize their growth since S1 began to build confidence. Record the semester marks and hand out the feedback sheets this week.
checklist: Can introduce themselves and ask for personal information
Can ask and answer about daily routines
Can understand simple shopping dialogues
Can write 3-5 sentences about past events
Can give simple directions
Can order food in a restaurant
Can make a simple phone call

weeks.theme: New year: what I can do and how I will study
weeks.obj: say what they can and can't do, review Semester 1 and make a simple study plan
weeks.lang: can/can't (ability); Can you...? Yes, I can / No, I can't; I want to...; self-study strategies (listen every day, use a dictionary)
weeks.res: Listening (graded mp3 library tour)
weeks.act: Find someone who can...; my skills and study plan; Semester 1 team quiz
weeks.hw: choose 3 English listening files to practise this month

skills.L: Listen to people saying what they can and can't do
skills.S: Ask and answer Can you...? and talk about my skills
skills.R: Read a short text about a study plan and circle the strategies
skills.W: Write 3 sentences about my skills and my study plan

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie: students write three sentences about themselves using Semester 1 language (my job, my family, my day), two true and one false. Partners guess the false one.
wuAlt: Semester 1 quick quiz in teams (names, jobs, times, prices).
Pair talk: tell your partner one thing you learned in Semester 1.
lp.pres: Show pictures of skills (drive, cook, swim, use a computer, speak French, play football). Model: "I can cook. I can't swim. Can you drive? Yes, I can. / No, I can't." Teach the sounds: can is short and weak, can't is long and strong; students listen and sort sentences. Then link to study: "I can listen every day. I want to use a dictionary." Check: "Can I drive? Yes, you can."
presAlt: Teacher mimes skills and the class asks "Can you swim?"
Put short sentences on the board and ask students to mark can and can't.
lp.prac: Find someone who can...: students mingle with a grid (can cook, can drive, can speak French, can use a computer, can swim). They ask "Can you cook?" and write the name when the answer is yes. The teacher monitors short answers and pronunciation.
pracAlt: Skills bingo with pictures.
Pair questions: ask three Can you...? questions and report one answer.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short descriptions twice (for example: "My name is Karim. I can drive and I can cook. I can't swim."). Students tick a grid of skills for each person. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Can or can't? Two signs on the wall. The teacher says a skill ("fly a plane") and students stand under CAN or CAN'T for themselves and tell the person next to them.
lp.prod: My skills and my study plan: pairs interview each other ("What can you do? What do you want to learn?"), then write a plan card with three sentences ("I can cook. I want to learn English. Every day I listen for ten minutes."). Each student presents the partner's plan to a small group.
lp.rw: Read a short text about Ahmed's study plan (five sentences) and circle the strategies he uses. Then write three sentences about your own plan using "I can..." and "I want to...".
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you can do in English now and one thing you want to learn, and hand it in at the door.
g: Mingle and ask Can you...? to complete the grid.
Bingo with skill pictures called out by the teacher.
Stand under CAN or CAN'T for each skill.
Teams answer review questions from Semester 1.
Match each strategy to its benefit.
diff: Fast finishers: write a skills paragraph about a family member (can and can't).
Support: sentence frame "I can ___. I can't ___. I want to ___." and a skills word bank with pictures.
hw: Choose 3 English listening files (a song, a podcast, a video) to practise this month.
Write 5 sentences about what you can and can't do.
Ask a family member "Can you...?" three times and write their answers.
lp.tip: Can/can't is useful for work, CVs and daily life: use adult skills (drive, cook, use a computer). The first week back is also a routines week, so spend a few minutes on hello and goodbye routines.

weeks.obj: make an appointment and describe simple symptoms
weeks.lang: should/shouldn't; illness vocabulary; appointment language
weeks.res: Lesson Plans/Emergency; Listening
weeks.act: Doctor roleplay; pharmacy dialogues; advice-giving pairs
weeks.hw: Write 3 sentences about what you should/shouldn't do for the flu.

skills.L: Listen to a doctor-appointment dialogue
skills.S: Make an appointment and describe symptoms
skills.R: Read an appointment card and complete it
skills.W: Write 3 symptom sentences with should

lp.wu: Symptom Charades: Teacher writes 5 illness words (headache, fever, cough, stomach ache, cold) on slips. Students take turns acting them out while others guess, saying 'You have a ___.'
wuAlt: Illness Pictionary: Teacher draws illness flashcards; students say the word and a full sentence like 'I have a headache.'
Quick Survey: Students ask 3 classmates 'Do you have a headache?' and tally answers on the board.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of symptoms and model sentences like 'I have a headache.' Introduce 'should/shouldn't' with advice cards: 'You should rest' / 'You shouldn't go out.' Elicit examples from students using their own experiences.
presAlt: Dialogue Modeling: Read a short doctor-patient dialogue; highlight should/shouldn't phrases; students repeat in pairs.
Realia Demo: Teacher pretends to be sick; students give advice using should/shouldn't from cue cards.
lp.prac: Matching Game: Students match symptom cards (e.g., 'sore throat') to advice cards (e.g., 'You should drink tea') in pairs. Teacher monitors for correct sentences.
pracAlt: Sentence Building: Students arrange word cards into correct 'should/shouldn't' sentences (e.g., 'You / should / see / a doctor').
Advice Relay: Teams race to write advice on the board for symptoms like 'sunburn' using should/shouldn't.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short doctor-patient dialogue twice and students complete an appointment form (name, day, time, problem). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Advice pass: Student A says a problem ("I have a headache."), Student B gives advice with should ("You should rest."), then they swap.
lp.prod: Roleplay: In pairs, one is a patient, one is a doctor. Patient describes symptoms (e.g., 'I have a stomach ache'); doctor gives advice using should/shouldn't. Swap roles.
lp.rw: Read a short pharmacy dialogue. Students write 3 sentences about what they should/shouldn't do for a cold using the dialogue as a model.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one health problem and one piece of advice with should ("I have a headache. You should rest.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students mark off illness words called out by the teacher; first to shout 'Bingo!' wins.
Students roleplay booking an appointment over the phone using phrases like 'I want to see a doctor.'
Teams list as many 'should' sentences as possible for a symptom in 2 minutes.
Students match symptom pictures to advice sentences in a timed game.
Each student adds one sentence to a story about a visit to the doctor using should/shouldn't.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue for a pharmacy visit asking for medicine.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'I have ___' and 'You should ___' during roleplays.
hw: Write 3 sentences about what you should/shouldn't do for the flu.
Record yourself roleplaying a doctor-patient conversation on your phone.
Draw 4 symptom pictures and write advice for each using should/shouldn't.
lp.tip: Connect advice to local customs, e.g., 'You should drink mint tea for a headache' to build rapport with Moroccan learners. Check the roleplay performance this week.

weeks.obj: handle service calls: asking for information politely
weeks.lang: Could I...? / I would like to...; polite requests
weeks.res: Listening (phone dialogues mp3)
weeks.act: Phone roleplay with backs to each other; service request cards; politeness ranking
weeks.hw: Write 3 polite requests for different services

skills.L: Listening folder: phone dialogues - polite requests
skills.S: Handle service calls: Could I...? politely
skills.R: Read phone scripts and match the responses
skills.W: Write a short phone-request script

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Service Match' · students stand in two lines; teacher holds flashcards of city services (e.g., police, hospital, taxi); each student says a service and the partner responds with the number; teacher models first: 'Police?' '190!'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Service Charades' · students mime a service (e.g., fixing a pipe) and partners guess the word
Alternative 2: 'Service Bingo' · teacher calls out services, students cross them off their bingo cards
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of a phone and a service (e.g., hospital); model 'Could I speak to a doctor, please?'; drill the phrase with rising intonation; check understanding by asking 'What do we say to be polite?' and 'What number do we call for the hospital?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a real phone prop; dial a fake number and model the request
Alternative 2: Show a short video clip of someone making a polite service call
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Service Request Cards' · students pick cards with service scenarios (e.g., 'My taxi is late'); in pairs, they practice 'Could I...?' requests; teacher circulates and corrects pronunciation
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Polite Request Drill' · students repeat after teacher with different services
Alternative 2: 'Matching Game' · match requests to responses (e.g., 'Could I get a taxi?' to 'Yes, of course')
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short phone dialogue between a caller and a service twice; students tick the request and write the phone number they hear. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Number Relay' · students line up; teacher calls out a service (e.g., 'fire'); first student shouts the number (e.g., '150') and runs to the back of the line
lp.prod: Production task: 'Back-to-Back Roleplay' · students sit back-to-back with a partner; one is a caller, the other a service worker; they use 'Could I...?' to make requests and respond; swap roles after 3 minutes
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read short phone scripts and match requests to responses; then write their own polite request for a service (e.g., 'Could I book a table for two, please?')
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one polite request for a service ("Could I speak to a doctor, please?") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students mime a service (e.g., plumber) and partners guess
Teacher calls out service numbers, students cross them off
Students repeat 'Could I...?' with rising intonation
Teams race to match services to numbers
Students roleplay phone calls with backs to each other
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue for a tricky call (e.g., 'My electricity is out')
Support: Use sentence starters like 'Could I...?' on a worksheet
hw: Write 3 polite requests for different services
Record a phone call with a family member
Draw a picture of a service and write the number
lp.tip: Emphasize rising intonation in 'Could I...?' to sound polite; connect to local services in Oujda (e.g., police number) for relevance. Keep a participation checklist this week.

weeks.obj: describe a problem with a purchase and ask for help
weeks.lang: complaint language; item + problem frames
weeks.res: Lesson Plans (topics set); Listening
weeks.act: Customer service roleplay; problem-solution matching; dialogue repair task
weeks.hw: write a short complaint message

skills.L: Listen to a shop-problem dialogue
skills.S: Describe a problem with a purchase
skills.R: Read complaint phrases and order the dialogue
skills.W: Write a 6-line problem-and-return dialogue

lp.wu: Students play 'Find the Pair' with shopping flashcards. Teacher places 10 item cards on the board. Students take turns finding two matching cards and saying 'I have a [shirt].'
wuAlt: Students play 'Shopping Bingo' with 3x3 grids of food items. Teacher calls out items, students mark them and shout 'Bingo!' when full.
Students do a quick 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their favorite shops using 'I like...' and 'I don't like...'.
lp.pres: Teacher shows a broken toy and says 'This toy is broken. I need help.' Elicits complaint frames using flashcards: 'This [item] is [problem].' Models 'This T-shirt is too small.' Checks understanding with 'Show me a problem with a bag.'
presAlt: Teacher uses a dialogue video of a customer returning a phone. Pauses to elicit problem phrases.
Teacher writes a complaint on the board with gaps, students guess the missing words like 'This laptop is not working.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Problem-Solution Matching' in pairs. They match 6 problem cards ('This phone doesn't charge') to solution cards ('Can I have a refund?'). Teacher monitors and models pronunciation.
pracAlt: Students play 'Dialogue Repair' in groups. They get a jumbled dialogue and reorder it to make a logical complaint conversation.
Students do 'Chain Complaints' in a circle. Each student adds one problem to the previous one: 'This phone is broken. This charger is lost.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a shop dialogue and tick the problems they hear (e.g., 'too expensive', 'wrong color'). Teacher plays the audio twice, then checks answers as a class. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Students play 'Charades' with action words from the lesson (e.g., 'return', 'complain', 'refund'). One student mimes the word, others guess 'Are you returning?'
lp.prod: Students roleplay a customer service scenario in pairs. One is a customer with a problem (e.g., 'This dress is torn'), the other is a shop assistant. They must use at least 2 complaint phrases and 1 solution phrase.
lp.rw: Students read a short complaint message and circle the problem words. Then, they write their own 6-line complaint dialogue using frames like 'I bought this [item] yesterday. It is [problem]. Can I...?'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one complaint with this + item + problem ("This shirt is too small.") and one polite request for help, and hand it in at the door.
g: Teams race to write 3 problems on the board using 'This [item] is [problem].'
Students flip cards to find matching item and problem pairs.
Each student adds a problem to the previous one: 'This bag is old. This shirt is red.'
Pairs swap roles after each complaint practice.
Students find the mistake in a written complaint dialogue.
diff: Fast finishers write a second complaint with a different problem.
Support learners use a sentence frame handout with 'This [item] is [problem].' pre-filled.
hw: Write a short complaint message to a shop about a broken item.
Write a short phone message to a shop about a problem (4 lines).
Draw 3 shopping problems and write the complaint for each.
lp.tip: Practise complaint language politely ("Excuse me, this shirt is too small. Can I change it?"). Use a real broken item to make the language concrete. Keep a participation checklist this week.

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students describe their Ramadan day with present simple and times ("I wake up at 4:30 for suhoor.") in five sentences.
occ.hw: Write your Ramadan daily routine in 6 sentences.

weeks.obj: explain plans with going to and give reasons
weeks.lang: going to; because / so
weeks.res: Worksheets/'will'/'going to'
weeks.act: Plan a trip group task; intentions board; listening: what are their plans?
weeks.hw: Interview a family member about their weekend plans and write 2 sentences using 'going to' and 'because'.

skills.L: Listen to plans with because / so
skills.S: Explain plans with going to + reasons
skills.R: Read a plan text and find because / so
skills.W: Write my plans with reasons

lp.wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who' with future intentions prompts like 'Find someone who is going to travel next month'. They mingle, ask 'Are you going to...?', and write names. They report back: 'Ali is going to travel because he wants to see his family.'
wuAlt: Students draw a simple future plan on a sticky note and guess classmates' plans: 'Is she going to study?' 'Yes, she is because she wants to pass the exam.'
Students play 'Memory Race' with picture cards showing future actions (e.g., plane, book, diploma). They flip cards and make sentences: 'He is going to fly because he has a job.'
lp.pres: Show flashcards of a man packing a bag and a woman buying a book. Model: 'He is going to travel because he has a holiday. She is going to study because she has an exam.' Check understanding by asking 'Why is he going to travel?' and eliciting 'because he has a holiday.'
presAlt: Use a simple story about a boy who wants to be a doctor. Draw a picture of him with a stethoscope: 'He is going to study medicine because he wants to help people.'
Bring realia: a map, a textbook, a calendar. Point and say: 'I am going to use the map because I want to go to Casablanca. I am going to read the book because I want to learn English.'
lp.prac: Students do 'Going to Dominoes' matching cards with pictures and reasons (e.g., picture of cooking + 'because I want to eat'). In pairs, they place cards and say the full sentence. Monitor and correct errors like 'He go to' instead of 'He is going to'.
pracAlt: Play 'Sentence Auction' with correct/incorrect sentences about future plans. Students bid on true sentences like 'She is going to swim because it's hot.'
Do 'Chain Drill': Student A says 'I am going to cook tonight.' Student B repeats and adds 'because I am hungry.' Student C repeats and adds, 'so I am going to buy food.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio of three people talking about their weekend plans. They tick the correct reason from a list (e.g., 'Why is Fatima going to the market? a) She needs food b) She wants to meet friends'). Check answers by replaying and pausing at 'because'. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Plans chain: Student A says a plan ("I am going to visit my cousin."), B asks "Why?" and A answers with because. Swap after two minutes.
lp.prod: In groups of 3, students plan a one-day trip to Oujda using a worksheet with prompts: 'Where are you going? What are you going to do? Why?' They present their plan: 'We are going to the old medina because we want to buy spices. We are going to eat tagine because we are hungry.'
lp.rw: Students read a short paragraph about 'Amina's Plans' and underline all 'because' and 'so' sentences. Then, they write 3 simple sentences about their own plans using 'going to' and 'because', e.g., 'I am going to call my mother because I miss her.'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one plan for this weekend with going to and one reason with because, and hand it in at the door.
g: Students write 6 future plans on a grid (e.g., 'go to the cinema'). Teacher reads sentences like 'He is going to watch a movie', and students cross off matching plans.
Teams race to match picture cards (e.g., umbrella) with reason cards (e.g., 'because it might rain') and make a full sentence.
One student draws a future plan (e.g., a plane), others guess 'Are you going to travel?' and ask 'Why?'
Students act out future actions (e.g., studying) while others say 'He is going to study because he has a test.'
Groups unscramble word cards to make correct 'going to' sentences with 'because', e.g., 'She / going to / buy / because / she needs / food / is'.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph about their ideal future using 3 'going to' sentences with 'because' and 'so'.
Support / weaker learners: Use sentence frames: 'I am going to ______ because ______.' with picture prompts.
hw: Interview a family member about their weekend plans and write 2 sentences using 'going to' and 'because'.
Draw 3 pictures of your future plans and label them with 'going to' and 'because' sentences.
Complete a worksheet with 5 gaps to fill in 'going to' or 'because' in sentences about plans.
lp.tip: For adults, connect language to real-life goals like work or family. Use Moroccan examples (e.g., 'I am going to learn English because I want a better job') to increase relevance and motivation. Keep a participation checklist this week.

weeks.obj: invite, accept, and decline politely; fix a time and place
weeks.lang: Shall we...? / Would you like to...?; arrangements
weeks.res: Listening; Worksheets
weeks.act: Invitation roleplay cards; diary schedule negotiation; accept-decline race
weeks.hw: write an invitation message

skills.L: Listen to invitation dialogues (accept / decline)
skills.S: Invite, accept and decline politely; fix a time
skills.R: Read invitation messages and match the replies
skills.W: Write an invitation message with a reply

lp.wu: Find someone who...: students mingle with invitation prompts ("Find someone who likes cinema", "Find someone who is free on Friday") and ask "Would you like to...?" to find a name for each prompt.
wuAlt: Alternative warm-up 1: Students write 3 sentences about their last weekend using 'I went to...' or 'I ate...'. Volunteers share.
Alternative warm-up 2: Teacher shows flashcards of leisure activities (cinema, park, restaurant) and elicits 'What is this?' in chorus.
lp.pres: Introduce the theme with a model dialogue: Teacher asks 'Shall we go to the cinema on Friday?' and student replies 'Yes, that sounds good. What time?' Use flashcards of cinema, café, park to elicit places. Drill the model sentences chorally and individually. Check understanding by asking 'What do I say to invite?' and 'How do you accept?'
presAlt: Alternative presentation 1: Show a short video clip of two friends making plans. Pause after each line to ask 'What did he say?' and write on the board.
Alternative presentation 2: Use a roleplay with a realia prop like a diary. Teacher says 'I'm free on Saturday. Would you like to have lunch?' and student responds with 'Yes, let's meet at 1 PM.'
lp.prac: Distribute 'Invitation Roleplay Cards' with prompts like 'Invite a friend to the café'. Students practice in pairs, using the target phrases. Teacher monitors and provides sentence starters on the board: 'Shall we...?' / 'Would you like to...?' / 'How about...?'
pracAlt: Alternative practice 1: 'Accept-Decline Race'. Teacher calls out 'Would you like to...?' and students race to respond 'Yes, please' or 'No, thank you' with a reason.
Alternative practice 2: 'Fix the Time' drill. One student says 'Let's meet tomorrow' and the other suggests a specific time and place, e.g., 'OK, at 3 PM at the library.'
lp.ls: Students listen to a dialogue between two friends arranging to meet. They fill in a simple schedule with the day, time, and place (e.g., 'Saturday, 2 PM, café'). Play the audio twice; check answers as a class. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Reply practice: the teacher reads invitations ("Would you like to see a film on Saturday?") and pairs give a polite reply (accept or refuse with a reason).
lp.prod: Students work in pairs to negotiate a diary schedule. Each has a weekly planner with some free/busy slots. They must invite their partner to an activity, agree on a time, and write it in both planners, using phrases like 'Are you free on...?' / 'Let's meet at...'
lp.rw: Students read 3 short invitation messages (e.g., 'Would you like to come to my house for tea?'). They match each to a correct reply (e.g., 'Yes, that would be lovely. What time?'). Then, they write one simple invitation message to a friend, including a day and time.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one invitation and one polite reply ("Would you like to have tea on Friday?" "Yes, I would. What time?") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students match invitation phrases to replies on cards.
Students negotiate time slots on a shared planner to find a free meeting time.
Teams race to respond correctly to teacher's invitation prompts.
Pairs plan a real outing (e.g., coffee) and present it to the class.
Students draw cards with roles (e.g., 'You are busy') and practice declining politely.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a longer invitation message with two activity options, e.g., 'Would you like to go to the park or the cinema on Sunday?'
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame to write: 'Would you like to...? Let's meet at... on...'
hw: Write a text message inviting a classmate to an activity of your choice, including a day and time.
Create a dialogue between two friends making plans, using the phrases from class.
Draw a picture of you and a friend doing an activity together, and write a caption like 'We meet at the park on Saturday.'
lp.tip: Connect invitations to local life: tea invitations, family visits and school events. Real examples like "Would you like to come for mint tea?" make the language useful.

weeks.lang: travel vocabulary; I have a reservation...
weeks.res: Listening (travel mp3); Reading tasks (travel)
weeks.act: Hotel check-in roleplay; travel buddy interviews; reading jigsaw
weeks.hw: Practice the hotel roleplay with a family member.

skills.L: Listening folder: travel mp3 - reservations
skills.S: Handle booking and travel conversations
skills.R: Read a hotel confirmation and check the details
skills.W: Write a short booking email

lp.wu: Travel Bingo: Students draw 4 travel words on a grid. Teacher calls out words (e.g., 'hotel', 'reservation', 'passport'). Students cross off matches and shout 'Bingo!' when complete.
wuAlt: Travel Pictionary: Teacher writes words on slips (e.g., 'suitcase', 'check-in'). Students draw while others guess.
Travel Charades: Students act out travel actions (e.g., 'boarding a plane') for others to name.
lp.pres: Show flashcards of hotel items (key, room number, reception). Model: 'I have a reservation.' 'My name is...' 'I need a room.' Check understanding by asking: 'What do you say at a hotel?'
presAlt: Roleplay demo: Teacher acts as receptionist, student as guest. Use a toy phone and a fake registration form.
Realia: Display a hotel key and brochure. Point to items while modeling sentences.
lp.prac: Pair drill: Student A is receptionist, Student B is guest. They practice 'I have a reservation' and 'My name is...' with cue cards (e.g., 'Smith', 'double room'). Teacher monitors and corrects pronunciation.
pracAlt: Chain game: Students pass a toy phone, saying 'I have a reservation for...' and adding a new word each time.
Gap-fill worksheet: Complete sentences like 'I have a ______ for two nights.' with options (reservation, ticket, passport).
lp.ls: Listen to a hotel check-in dialogue. Students tick details heard (name, room type, nights). Play twice. Check answers as a class. If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Stand up, Sit down: Teacher calls out travel words. Students stand if they match 'hotel' or 'reservation', sit for others.
lp.prod: Travel buddy interviews: Students ask partners about their dream holiday. Use prompts: 'Where do you want to go?' 'What kind of room do you need?' Share 2 findings with the class.
lp.rw: Read a short hotel confirmation email. Circle the correct details (name: Ali/Amal, nights: 1/2). Then write 1 sentence: 'My name is...' using the email info.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences you would say at a hotel reception ("I have a reservation. My name is...") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students mark off hotel words called by the teacher.
Teams race to write 'I have a reservation' on the board.
Match cards with room numbers to guest names.
Act out travel words for others to guess.
Pass a box while music plays; say a travel word when it stops.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about their ideal hotel.
Support: Use sentence starters like 'My name is...' for the roleplay.
hw: Practice the hotel roleplay with a family member.
Write 3 questions you would ask at a hotel check-in.
Draw a picture of your dream hotel and label 2 items (bed, pool).
lp.tip: Use Moroccan travel examples (e.g., booking a hotel for Agadir or Marrakech) to make it relevant. Pair adults with similar life experiences for roleplays. Check the roleplay performance this week.
