weeks.obj: write a short clear email for work or daily life
weeks.lang: email openings/closings; formal vs informal
weeks.res: Worksheets; program email frames
weeks.act: Email transformation (text to email); pair editing; subject-line game
weeks.hw: write a real-life email draft

skills.L: Listen to model emails read aloud
skills.S: Say openings and closings formally and informally
skills.R: Read model emails and compare the registers
skills.W: Write a short clear email (greeting, body, sign-off)

lp.wu: Email word race: teams write as many email words as they can in two minutes (Dear, Hi, Best regards, Subject, send...) and then sort them into formal and informal.
wuAlt: Eid Pictionary: Teacher draws 'family gathering' or 'new clothes' for students to guess the English word.
Eid Word Association: Teacher says 'Eid', students shout related words like 'family', 'gifts', 'prayer'.
lp.pres: Show two emails on the board: a formal one to a boss (Subject: Holiday Request) and an informal one to a friend (Subject: Eid Plans!). Highlight openings (Dear Mr. Smith / Hi Fatima) and closings (Best regards / See you soon!). Ask students to spot the differences.
presAlt: Email Sorting Game: Print/email examples. Students sort them into Formal/Informal piles.
Realia Display: Show a physical Eid card vs. a printed email. Discuss which is for whom.
lp.prac: Email Transformation: Students receive a text message like 'Can we meet for coffee after class?' and transform it into a formal email to a teacher. They write the greeting, body, and sign-off. Circulate to help with 'Dear' vs. 'Hi'.
pracAlt: Pair Editing: Student A writes a short informal email, Student B adds a formal closing. Swap roles.
Subject Line Game: Give students a topic (e.g., 'Eid Party Invite'). They write 3 subject lines: formal, informal, and neutral.
lp.ls: Listen to two model emails being read aloud. Students raise a red card for formal and a blue card for informal. Check answers by asking, 'Why was the first one formal?' If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher says a phrase. Students stand if it's for a friend (e.g., 'See you later!'), sit if it's for a boss (e.g., 'Thank you for your consideration.').
lp.prod: Pair Work: Roleplay two scenarios. 1) Student A is a boss, Student B requests holiday leave. 2) Student A is a friend, Student B invites them to an Eid dinner. Use email language from the lesson.
lp.rw: Write a short email draft: Students choose one real-life purpose (e.g., request a day off, invite a cousin). Write 3 sentences: opening, one body sentence, closing. Teacher checks individually.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the opening and closing lines for a formal email and for an informal email, and hand them in at the door.
g: In teams, write the best subject line for a given topic (e.g., 'Eid Gift').
Match greetings (Dear Sir) with closings (Yours faithfully).
One student writes a greeting, the next adds a body sentence, the last a closing.
Ask 3 classmates 'What is your favorite Eid food?' and write the answers.
Write a formal email to a shop about a broken gift.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a second email with two body sentences.
Support: Use a template with sentence starters like 'I would like to request...'.
hw: Write a real email draft to a teacher or a colleague (opening, two sentences, closing).
Write a short Eid message to a friend or colleague (3 sentences).
Find an example of a formal email online and bring it to class.
lp.tip: Always connect functional language to students' real goals; in Oujda, emailing for work or study is highly relevant, so use authentic examples like leave requests.

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students write a short Eid greeting email to a friend or colleague (opening, Eid wishes, closing).
occ.hw: Write a short Eid message to a friend or colleague.

weeks.theme: Weather, small talk and what is happening now
weeks.obj: talk about the weather, say what people are doing now, and hold a short small-talk conversation
weeks.lang: weather words; present continuous (I am / she is + -ing); small-talk openers and closers (How are you? Nice weather today. See you soon!)
weeks.res: Flashcards/Seasons-Weather
weeks.act: Weather reports; what is she doing? picture game; small talk speed rounds
weeks.hw: write 3 small-talk exchanges

skills.L: Listen to a short weather conversation and circle the weather and the activities
skills.S: Ask and answer What are you doing? and make small talk about the weather
skills.R: Read three short messages and underline the -ing verbs
skills.W: Write 3 short small-talk exchanges

lp.wu: Weather charades: the teacher mimes weather (shivering for cold, fanning for hot) and students say "It's cold!" Then students draw a weather card and mime it for the class.
wuAlt: Weather picture bingo.
Quick poll: stand up if it is sunny today / if you like rain.
lp.pres: Show weather flashcards (sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, cold, hot) and teach "It's sunny. It's raining." Then present the present continuous with a picture: "It's raining. People are walking. A woman is carrying an umbrella." Write am/is/are + verb + -ing on the board. Ask "What are you doing?" and answer "I'm studying English." Show a model small-talk dialogue: "Hello! How are you?" "Fine, thanks. And you?" "Fine. It's hot today." "Yes, very hot." "See you soon!" "Bye!"
presAlt: Show two short video clips with the sound off and ask what people are doing.
Mime a verb and ask the class "What am I doing?"
lp.prac: What is he doing? In pairs, students have two street pictures with six differences. They ask "What is she doing?" and "Is he carrying a bag?" to find them ("In picture A she is walking. In picture B she is running."). The teacher monitors the -ing form.
pracAlt: Weather reporter: each student gives a two-sentence weather report for a city card.
Sentence cards: put the words in order (is / the woman / carrying / an umbrella).
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short dialogue twice: "Hello, Samira! How are you?" "Fine, thanks. It's very hot today." "Yes. What are you doing?" "I'm going to the market." Students circle the weather and tick what each person is doing. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Mime and guess: one student mimes an action and the class asks "Are you eating? Are you walking?" until they guess. The guesser mimes next.
lp.prod: Small-talk speed rounds: students pair up. Each pair has two minutes to have a small-talk conversation: greet, ask how you are, talk about the weather and say what you are doing. After two minutes, students change partners.
lp.rw: Read three short text messages from friends about the weather and what they are doing. Underline the -ing verbs. Then write three short small-talk exchanges using the model ("A: Hello! B: Hi! A: It's hot today. B: Yes, very hot!").
lp.st: Exit ticket: look out of the window and write two sentences: the weather and what one person is doing now. Hand it in at the door.
g: Mime the weather; the class guesses.
Pairs find differences between two street pictures with What is she doing?
Mime an action; the class asks Are you...?
Two-minute conversations with a new partner each round.
Give a two-sentence weather report for a city card.
diff: Fast finishers: write a weather report for three Moroccan cities with what people are doing.
Support: sentence frame "It's ___. I'm ___ing." and a small-talk phrase card.
hw: Write 3 small-talk exchanges (greeting, weather, what you are doing).
Look out of the window and write what 4 people are doing right now.
Have a two-minute small talk in English with a friend or family member.
lp.tip: Small talk is a social skill, so keep it light and friendly: weather first, then a simple question. Keep openers and closers on the board and praise attempts. Question tags such as "isn't it?" belong to the next level.

weeks.obj: talk about life stages and say what happened with past and present contrast
weeks.lang: past simple: regular and common irregular verbs (was born, went, had, got, made, bought, saw, ate); did/didn't + verb; now + present simple
weeks.res: Worksheets (mixed)
weeks.act: Timeline creation and narrating; guess whose life; pair interviews
weeks.hw: write 6 sentences about your life: 3 past and 3 present

skills.L: Listen to short life stories and match them to pictures
skills.S: Tell my life story with past and present sentences
skills.R: Read a short text about a person's life and match sentences to pictures
skills.W: Write 6 sentences about my life: 3 past and 3 present

lp.wu: Timeline race: two teams. The teacher writes "birth", "school", "now" on the board. Teams race to add words that belong at each point (born, student, work).
wuAlt: Quick round: say one thing you did when you were a child.
Picture sequence: put life-stage pictures in order and say a sentence.
lp.pres: Draw a personal timeline on the board: "I was born in 1990. I went to school in Oujda. I got a job in 2015. Now I work at a school and I live in Oujda." Teach eight irregular verbs on a wall chart with pictures: go-went, have-had, get-got, make-made, buy-bought, see-saw, eat-ate, come-came. Teach the questions "Where did you go to school? When did you get a job?" and "Did you go to Rabat? Yes, I did." Check: "Did I get a job in 2015? Yes, you did."
presAlt: Use the teacher's photos from childhood and tell a short story.
Put a short text about Fatima on the board and underline the irregular verbs.
lp.prac: Life stage dominoes: students match past and present sentence halves in pairs ("I was born in 1995." + "Now I live in Oujda."). Then pairs practise the question and answer with the eight irregular verbs ("When did you get a job?").
pracAlt: Irregular verb match: base form and past form cards.
Sentence building: reorder the words to make "I got a job in 2015."
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short life stories twice (for example: "Fatima was a student. She went to university in Rabat. Now she is a teacher and she lives in Oujda."). Students match each story to a picture and tick the true sentences. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Past or present? The teacher says a sentence ("I live in Oujda." / "I lived in Rabat.") and students stand for present and sit for past, then say a new sentence about themselves.
lp.prod: Guess whose life: students write three past and three present sentences about their own life on a paper timeline. In groups they take turns reading the sentences while the others guess who the timeline belongs to. The teacher models first.
lp.rw: Read a short text about Fatima's timeline (eight sentences with was, went, got and now). Students match each sentence to a picture of her past or present life, then write six sentences about their own life (three past, three present).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one past sentence and one present sentence about your life ("I went to school in Nador. Now I work in Oujda.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Add words to the timeline points on the board.
Match past and present sentence halves.
Match base forms and past forms.
Read timeline sentences; the group guesses the owner.
Stand for present and sit for past.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph about a family member's life (6 sentences).
Support: sentence frame "I was born in ___. I went to ___. Now I ___." and the irregular verb chart.
hw: Write 6 sentences about your life: 3 past and 3 present.
Learn the 8 irregular past forms with flashcards.
Ask a family member "Where did you go to school?" and write 3 sentences.
lp.tip: Respect learners' life experience: some have moved from rural to urban areas or changed careers. Frame comparisons as growth, not better or worse. Teach only the eight core irregular verbs and recycle them in every lesson from now on.

weeks.obj: describe how celebrations happen; write an invitation
weeks.lang: customs vocabulary; invitation writing
weeks.res: Reading tasks; Seasonal (culture)
weeks.act: Plan a celebration in teams; invitation texts; culture exchange presentations
weeks.hw: invitation text (5 sentences)

skills.L: Listen to celebration descriptions
skills.S: Describe how a celebration happens
skills.R: Read a customs text (Reading tasks)
skills.W: Write an invitation to my celebration

lp.wu: Warm-up: 'Celebration Charades'. Teacher writes 'wedding', 'birthday', 'Eid', 'Green March' on slips. Students take turns acting out a celebration while others guess, saying 'Is it a birthday?'
wuAlt: Alternative 1: 'Celebration Bingo' - Students have cards with words like 'cake', 'gifts', 'music', 'family'. Teacher calls out words, students mark and shout 'Bingo!' when complete
Alternative 2: 'Quick Share' - Students turn to a partner and say 'My favorite celebration is... because...'
lp.pres: Presentation: Show flashcards of celebration customs (cutting cake, dancing, gifts, praying). Model sentences: 'At a wedding, people dance.' 'On Eid, families visit each other.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down: 'Do people eat cake at Eid?'
presAlt: Alternative 1: Use a short story about a Moroccan wedding, highlighting customs like 'henna' and 'music'
Alternative 2: Bring in realia (a gift box, a small cake model) and describe each item's role in celebrations
lp.prac: Guided practice: 'Match the Custom' worksheet. Students match pictures of celebrations to sentences (e.g., 'At a birthday party, people sing Happy Birthday'). In pairs, they practice saying the sentences with correct stress.
pracAlt: Alternative 1: 'Sentence Auction' - Write correct and incorrect sentences on the board. Students 'buy' the correct ones with play money
Alternative 2: 'Chain Drill' - Teacher starts 'At a wedding...', next student adds 'and people dance', next adds 'and eat cake'
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short description twice ("On Independence Day people hang flags. Families visit each other. They eat together.") and students tick the customs they hear on a worksheet. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Reactivation game: 'Stand Up, Sit Down'. Teacher says celebration words (e.g., 'gifts' - stand, 'prayer' - sit). Students move quickly to check recall of vocabulary.
lp.prod: Plan a celebration: in teams of three, students plan a community celebration at the American Space. They decide: 1) What food? 2) What music? 3) What activity? Each team presents the plan using "We are going to..." and "People...".
lp.rw: Reading and writing slot: Students read a short text about a typical Moroccan wedding custom (e.g., 'henna night'). Then, they write 5 sentences for an invitation: 'You are invited to my wedding. It is on... We will... Please bring... Wear...'
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about how people celebrate a festival ("On Eid, families visit each other.") and hand it in at the door.
g: Students draw a celebration custom (e.g., 'gifts') while others guess
Walk around asking 'Find someone who has been to a wedding. When?'
Teacher asks 'What do people eat at Eid?' Students race to answer 'couscous'
Match invitation phrases ('You are invited...') to celebration pictures
Students race to write 5 celebration words from memory on the board
diff: Fast finishers: Design a poster for their celebration with 3 customs and a date
Support learners: Use a sentence frame for writing: 'My celebration is on... We will... Please come...'
hw: Write 5 sentences about your favorite Moroccan celebration
Create an invitation to a family event using the phrases from class
Draw a picture of a celebration and label 3 customs
lp.tip: Include Moroccan celebrations (Eid, weddings, national days) alongside other cultures. This builds relevance and respect for learners' backgrounds.

weeks.obj: understand A2 Key formats and complete sample tasks
weeks.lang: KET reading/writing part formats
weeks.res: KET folder (samples)
weeks.act: Guided KET practice; strategy notes; team answer hunt
weeks.hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet (5 tasks).

skills.L: KET listening part 1 tour
skills.S: KET-style personal questions
skills.R: KET reading part 1 samples (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style form filling

lp.wu: KET Bingo: Students write 5 words from last week's KET practice (e.g., 'form', 'tick', 'name', 'address', 'date') on a grid. Teacher calls out clues like 'You write this with a pen', and students cross off matches. First to 3 in a row wins.
wuAlt: KET Flashcard Race: Two teams race to match KET reading/writing part 1 flashcards (e.g., 'form' card with 'fill in a form' card).
KET Word Association: Teacher says 'KET', students shout related words like 'exam', 'reading', 'writing', 'parts'.
lp.pres: Teacher projects a KET reading part 1 sample (3 short texts with A, B, C options). Models reading aloud and thinking aloud: 'Text A says 'Open 9am-5pm', but question asks 'When does it close?', so answer is C.' Checks understanding by asking students to explain why B is wrong.
presAlt: Teacher uses a KET form filling sample on the board, filling it in step by step with student input (e.g., 'What's my surname?').
Teacher shows a KET writing part 1 email sample, highlighting key phrases like 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Yours faithfully'.
lp.prac: Students work in pairs on a KET reading part 1 worksheet (3 tasks). Teacher circulates, prompting with 'Read the question first' or 'Check the text again'. Fast finishers write their own KET-style question for a classmate.
pracAlt: Team Answer Hunt: Teams race to find correct answers to KET reading part 1 questions hidden around the room, then match them to the questions on the board.
KET Jigsaw: Each team gets one KET reading part 1 task, teaches it to another team, then swaps.
lp.ls: The teacher reads three short conversations twice and students tick the correct picture (A, B or C) for each, as in an exam listening part. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: KET Relay: Two lines of students race to the board to write a KET word (e.g., 'form', 'address', 'date') from memory. First team to write all 5 correctly wins.
lp.prod: Students roleplay a KET-style form filling scenario: one is a receptionist at a clinic, the other is a patient filling in a form. They use phrases like 'What's your first name?' and 'Can I have your address, please?'
lp.rw: Students complete a KET-style writing part 1 task: writing a short email to a friend about a weekend plan (5-6 sentences). They use 'I'm going to...' and 'I want to...'. Teacher checks for correct punctuation and basic spelling.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one reading strategy you will use in an exam (read the question first, find the key word, check the options) and hand it in at the door.
g: Students match KET reading part 1 questions with correct answers from a list.
Teams take turns answering KET questions to place X or O.
Students race to read 3 short texts and find the answer to a question.
Teams race to fill in a KET-style form correctly on the board.
Teams answer KET reading/writing questions for points.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a KET-style question for a reading part 1 text.
Support / weaker learners: Use a word bank with KET keywords to complete the reading tasks.
hw: Complete a KET reading part 1 worksheet (5 tasks).
Write a short email to a friend using KET writing part 1 format (5-6 sentences).
Review KET vocabulary words (e.g., 'form', 'address', 'date') and make flashcards.
lp.tip: Connect the exam to real goals such as applying for a visa or a job: it increases motivation. Use short, familiar texts (notices, messages, forms) so learners focus on the task, not on difficult language.

kit.l: Reading tasks by topic and level

weeks.obj: complete a mini practice test under time
weeks.lang: all A1-A2 core language
weeks.res: KET folder; Tests
weeks.act: Mini-test administration; self-marking with key; error discussion
weeks.hw: Complete a KET reading Part 2 worksheet (multiple choice).

skills.L: KET listening mini-set
skills.S: KET-style interview practice
skills.R: KET reading mini-paper (KET folder)
skills.W: KET-style short message

lp.wu: Quick Quiz: Teacher shows flashcards of daily routines (brush teeth, eat breakfast, go to work). Students stand up and say the action when they see it, then sit down. Teacher asks, 'What do you do in the morning?'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students walk around asking, 'Do you like tea?' and writing names. Share results.
Word Race: Write 'daily routines' on the board. Students race to write 5 verbs in 1 minute.
lp.pres: Show a KET-style reading paper (Part 1: matching questions). Model answering Q1 with a think-aloud: 'I see a picture of a man buying bread. The text says 'He is at the bakery.' So, I match them.' Check with thumbs up/down: 'Is the man at the bakery?'
presAlt: Realia Demo: Bring a shopping list and coins. Say, 'I need milk and bread.' Ask, 'What do I need?'
Storyboard: Draw 3 pictures (buying fruit, paying, leaving). Narrate: 'First, she buys apples. Then, she pays. Finally, she leaves.'
lp.prac: Pair work: Students get a KET reading Part 1 worksheet with 5 pictures and 5 short texts. They take turns matching and saying, 'Picture 1 matches text C because it shows a market.' Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Flashcard Match: Students match picture cards to sentence cards (e.g., 'He is buying a newspaper' + picture of a newsstand).
Board Game: Roll dice, land on a square, match a picture to a sentence to move.
lp.ls: The teacher reads five short descriptions of what people bought and students tick the correct picture for each, as in an exam listening part. If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: Quick review: teams answer questions about shopping and places ("Where do you buy bread? How much is milk?"). One point per full-sentence answer.
lp.prod: Roleplay: In pairs, one student is a customer (with a shopping list), the other is a shopkeeper. They use target language: 'Can I have some bread, please?' 'Yes, that's 5 dirhams.' 'Thank you.' Switch roles.
lp.rw: Writing task: Students write a short message (3-4 sentences) to a friend about their shopping. Example: 'Hi Fatima. I went to the market. I bought apples and milk. See you soon.' Use the board for sentence starters.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two questions you would like an examiner to ask you, and hand them in at the door.
g: Teacher calls out shopping words (e.g., 'bread'), students cross them off if on their card.
Students flip over picture/sentence cards and find matching pairs.
Start with 'I went to the market,' each student adds one item.
Students race to circle 5 food items in a supermarket flyer.
Teacher writes wrong sentences on board (e.g., 'I buyed bread'), students fix them.
diff: Fast finishers: Write 3 more sentences about their favorite shop.
Support: Use sentence frames like 'I need ______.' and 'I bought ______.'
hw: Complete a KET reading Part 2 worksheet (multiple choice).
Write 5 sentences about what you bought yesterday.
Record yourself saying a short shopping dialogue and send to teacher.
lp.tip: For KET practice, focus on task strategy (e.g., 'Read the question first') over perfection. Moroccan learners may need extra time with British English terms like 'chemist' (pharmacy). Record the practice test scores this week.

weeks.obj: review the year through stations and games
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.res: Games; Tests/Grammar tests
weeks.act: Station carousel; error auction; team challenge
weeks.hw: make a revision card for each grammar point

skills.L: Listening station - mixed audio
skills.S: Speaking stations with games
skills.R: Reading station - mixed texts
skills.W: Writing station - forms and messages

lp.wu: Students play 'Memory Chain' with Earth Day vocabulary: I say 'recycle', student 1 says 'recycle, reuse', student 2 says 'recycle, reuse, reduce', and so on. Use flashcards for prompts.
wuAlt: Students brainstorm Earth Day words on the board in pairs, then share with the class.
Students match picture flashcards (e.g., bottle, tree, bin) to word cards on the table.
lp.pres: Show a short video clip about Earth Day actions. Elicit sentences like 'I can recycle bottles' and 'We should save water'. Use a poster with key phrases: 'I can...', 'We should...', 'I will...'. Check understanding by asking 'What can you do?'
presAlt: Use a story about a Moroccan family planting trees on Green March Day to elicit past simple and future forms.
Model a roleplay between a shopkeeper and customer using 'paper or plastic?' to introduce environmental choices.
lp.prac: Students play 'Error Auction': listen to sentences like 'I can to recycle' and bid on correct/incorrect ones. In pairs, they then correct the sentences on a worksheet.
pracAlt: Students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' grid with questions like 'Find someone who turns off lights'.
Play 'Green Bingo' with prompts like 'has a reusable bag'.
lp.ls: Students listen to a short audio clip of a radio interview about Earth Day and tick the actions mentioned (e.g., 'plant trees', 'use less water'). If no recording is available, the teacher reads the script aloud twice at normal speed.
lp.re: Action mime: students act out eco actions (recycling, saving water) and the group guesses with "You are...ing".
lp.prod: In teams, students complete a 'Team Challenge' poster: draw a local problem (e.g., plastic in streets) and write three solutions using 'We can...'. Present to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short email from a friend asking about green habits and reply with three sentences using "I can..." and "We should...". Focus on correct punctuation.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one grammar point you feel sure about and one you want to practise again, and hand it in at the door.
g: Listen to sentences, bid if correct/incorrect, then fix errors.
Add an Earth word each turn: recycle, reuse, reduce...
Ask classmates about green habits using 'Do you...?'
Act out eco-actions for teams to guess.
Draw a local problem and write three solutions on a poster.
diff: Fast finishers write a short paragraph: 'My family and Earth Day'.
Support learners use sentence starters: 'I can...', 'We should...' on a worksheet.
hw: Make a revision card for each grammar point (one example sentence each).
Write 3 sentences about what you can do to help the planet ("I can recycle bottles. We should save water.").
Watch a 2-minute video about Earth Day and list three new words.
lp.tip: Connect local context by discussing Morocco's Green Generation Initiative and how small actions align with Islamic values of stewardship (khalifa).

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls this week. Optional eco poster: groups design a poster for the American Space with five rules using imperatives and should ("Don't litter." "We should save water."). Both forms are already taught.
occ.hw: Write 3 sentences about what you can do to help the planet.

weeks.obj: complete the final assessments and a feedback interview
weeks.lang: all year outcomes
weeks.res: Tests; certificates pack
weeks.act: Final paper; speaking interviews; course feedback forms; celebration
weeks.hw: write one thing you want to do to practise English over the summer

skills.L: Listen to a short text and answer six questions
skills.S: Take part in a short speaking interview
skills.R: Read short texts and answer questions
skills.W: Write a short email and fill in a form

lp.wu: Find someone who...: students mingle with year-review prompts ("has a brother", "gets up at 6", "went to a new place last year") and ask classmates the questions to find a name for each prompt.
wuAlt: Quick quiz from the year (teams, five questions).
Pair talk: tell your partner your favourite lesson of the year.
lp.pres: Explain the assessment: Part 1 is a written paper of about 35 minutes with four tasks (gap fill, matching questions and answers, a short email of about 30 words, filling in a form). Part 2 is a short speaking interview. Go through one example of each task type before starting.
presAlt: Show a model answer for the email task and discuss why it is a good answer.
Students list the tasks they feel confident about.
lp.prac: Part 1 written paper: students complete four tasks. Task 1: gap fill with ten items. Task 2: match questions to answers. Task 3: write a short email (about 30 words) to a friend about a trip or an invitation. Task 4: fill in a registration form. The teacher circulates only to clarify instructions. Build the paper from the Tests folder or use the task types above.
pracAlt: Use the Semester 1 paper as a model and write new items for the second half.
Split the class: half do the paper while half do the speaking interview.
lp.ls: Listening task: the teacher reads a short text twice about a woman's weekend ("Last Saturday Amina got up at eight. She went to the market with her sister...") and students answer six questions (true/false and short answers). If a recording is available, play it instead.
lp.re: While learners wait for their speaking slot, they play a quiet year-review quiz (teams, five questions) or complete a puzzle sheet.
lp.prod: Speaking interview: each student talks to the teacher for about five minutes. Part A: personal questions (name, job, family, day). Part B: a picture description. Part C: a short roleplay (order food, ask directions or buy something). The teacher scores communication, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation (1 to 3 each).
lp.rw: Self-assessment and feedback: students complete "I can..." statements (colour in each) and fill in a short course feedback form with three questions (What did you like? What was difficult? What do you want next?). Offer the form in English with Arabic or French support so learners can answer fully.
lp.st: Closing circle: each student says one thing they can do now in English ("I can order food.") and receives a round of applause. Hand out certificates and take a group photo.
g: Teams answer review questions from the whole year.
Describe a picture in a minute with as many sentences as possible.
Practise the speaking roleplay with a partner.
Write short thank-you notes to classmates and the teacher.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second email or a longer paragraph about your year.
Support: frame sentences on the board and a verb chart during the written paper.
hw: Write one thing you want to do to practise English over the summer (I want to...).
Write a thank-you message to a classmate or the teacher (3 sentences).
Read one short English text and note 5 new words.
lp.tip: Keep the tone celebratory and use the checklist for the speaking interview. Send the final reports home and hand out the certificates at the ceremony. Treat the feedback form as useful for next year: read every answer.
checklist: I can introduce myself and give basic personal information.
I can ask and answer simple questions about daily routines.
I can understand short, simple texts on familiar topics.
I can write short, simple sentences about my life.
I can make simple transactions (e.g., buying something).
I can give reasons for my opinions (e.g., 'I like... because...').
I can participate in a short conversation about work and jobs.

occ.act: Labour Day (1 May) is close. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students ask "What is your job? Do you like it?" and report one answer to the class using present simple.

levels.desc: Survival English for adults aged 18+ with little or no previous English. Thirty weeks cover the language of daily life · greetings, personal information, shopping, food, directions, health, appointments, phone calls · through functional, needs-based learning and roleplays, with KET-style tasks appearing from mid-S2.

levels.label: Adults · Intermediate

weeks.obj: ask and answer accurate questions about themselves and others, give an opinion with a reason, and set a personal English goal for the year
weeks.lang: question word order with do/does/did, be, have and can; wh- questions; opinion phrases (I think, In my opinion, I'd say); goals (I want to, I need to, I'd like to)
weeks.res: Question correction worksheet (word order); Guess the question worksheet
weeks.act: Two truths and a lie with follow-up questions; question chain interviews; speaking diagnostic in pairs; goal-setting paragraph
weeks.hw: write 80-100 words about your English goals and how you will practise each week

skills.L: Listen to short self-introductions and note each person's job and reason for learning English
skills.S: Interview a partner with correct question order and give an opinion with one reason
skills.R: Read the course outline and match each unit type to a personal goal
skills.W: Write 80-100 words about my goals for the year

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie, summer edition: students write three sentences about their summer (two true, one false). In groups of four they read them aloud and the others ask two questions each ("Where did you go?" "Did you enjoy it?") before guessing the lie. The teacher listens for question word order and notes common errors for the diagnostic.
wuAlt: Find someone who: students mingle to find a classmate who works in health or education, has travelled abroad or speaks a third language, and must ask a full question to get each name.
Name and goal circle: each student says their name, job or studies and one reason for learning English; the next student repeats the previous person's reason before adding their own.
lp.pres: Write four sentences with word-order mistakes on the board ("Where you live?" "What you do at weekends?" "Did you went there?" "How long you are learning English?"). Students correct them in pairs. Elicit the pattern: question word + auxiliary + subject + main verb, and show it for be, can, have and the past. Then teach opinion and goal phrases on cards (I think..., In my opinion..., I'd say..., I want to..., I need English to..., I'd like to...) with one real example from the teacher for each.
presAlt: Use the Student Book Unit 1A word-order page from the kit as the model; students then write one question for each wh- word.
Dictate six short answers ("In Oujda." "Since 2019." "By bus.") and students write the question that fits each answer.
lp.prac: Question chain interviews: pairs take a topic card (work and study, free time, travel, family, technology, food) and write eight questions with correct order, using at least four different auxiliaries. They interview each other, then swap with another pair and ask the best two questions again. The teacher notes errors on the board without naming students.
pracAlt: Question auction: teams bid on twelve questions, some correct and some wrong, and fix the wrong ones.
Speed interviews: two rows face each other and every minute one row moves down to answer the same new question card.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short self-introductions twice (a nurse who needs English for an exchange course, an online seller who wants to talk to foreign customers, a student who wants to pass PET). Students complete a table: name, job or study, reason for English, goal for the year. Check in pairs, then as a class. For a recording instead, use one of the short interviews from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Opinion statements: the teacher writes a statement ("Learning English online is better than learning in class." "Everyone in Morocco should speak three languages.") and students write I agree or I disagree plus one reason on a slip, then discuss in threes using I think, In my opinion and because.
lp.prod: Speaking diagnostic in pairs: each pair talks for three minutes about "Why do you need English and how will you use it?" while the teacher circulates with a simple grid (fluency, accuracy, pronunciation, range) and listens to each student for about one minute. Then students interview a new partner and report back: "Samira wants English for her job at the bank. She has studied for two years."
lp.rw: Short diagnostic writing: students write 80 to 100 words about their English goals and one time they used English outside class. In the last five minutes they swap texts and underline one thing they like and write one question for the writer.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write your goal for the year in one sentence beginning "By April I want to..." and hand it in at the door. The teacher uses these slips to plan groupings.
g: Students ask questions to match bingo squares and write a name for each.
Teams bid on correct questions and fix the wrong ones.
Groups ask follow-up questions to find the false statement.
Students write agree or disagree plus a reason and compare.
Students match goals to the best class activity for reaching them.
diff: Fast finishers: write five questions you would ask a famous person and predict the answers.
Support: give a question table (wh- + do/does/did + subject + verb) and sentence starters for goals and opinions.
hw: Write 80 to 100 words about your English goals and how you will practise each week.
Find one English video or article on a topic you like and write two questions about it.
Interview someone who uses English at work and write three of their answers.
lp.tip: Respect what adults already know and tie everything to real needs such as work, visas, study and travel. Use the diagnostic to build mixed-level pairs and note two or three class-wide errors (word order, tenses, articles) to recycle all term. Do not correct every error in this first lesson; build confidence first.

weeks.obj: describe routines and what is happening now, and compare healthy and busy lifestyles
weeks.lang: present simple vs present continuous (usually/now, these days); action and state verbs (I know, I want, I like); adverbs of frequency; a lot of, too much/many, enough
weeks.res: Simple present and continuous explanation sheet; Video: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
weeks.act: Lifestyle survey and report; usually/right now contrast pairs; mistake spotting in short texts
weeks.hw: write 8-10 sentences comparing a normal day and a different day this week

skills.L: Listen to people describe their routines and note what they usually do and what they are doing this week
skills.S: Compare my lifestyle with a partner's using adverbs of frequency
skills.R: Read a short article on work-life balance and underline present simple and continuous verbs
skills.W: Write about a normal day and a different day this week

lp.wu: Lifestyle line-up: the teacher says a habit (go to bed after midnight, cook at home, walk to work, drink coffee, check my phone first thing). Students arrange themselves in a line from "never" to "always" without speaking, then explain to a neighbour: "I usually...", "I hardly ever...".
wuAlt: Quick survey: students ask three people "How often do you exercise?" and report the results to the class.
Word race: teams list as many free-time and health words as they can in two minutes.
lp.pres: Put two pictures on the board: a woman at her desk and the same woman at a gym on an unusual day. Elicit "She usually works late but this week she is training for a race." Contrast the two forms on a timeline (habit and now). Teach the state verbs that avoid -ing (know, want, like, need, believe) with a quick true/false check, and the quantifier set for lifestyle talk (a lot of, too much/too many, enough, not enough).
presAlt: Read a two-line blog post aloud ("I usually walk to work, but this week I am taking the bus because my knee hurts.") and students mark the habit and the temporary situation.
Concept check with questions: "Is it a habit? Is it happening now?" for ten teacher sentences.
lp.prac: Usually/this week pairs: each student gets a card with a habit ("study at night") and a different situation ("this week: working on a project"). Pairs write two sentences for each card and say them to a partner, who asks a follow-up ("Why?" "Do you like it?"). Then a gap-fill on action and state verbs where students choose the correct form (I know/I am knowing).
pracAlt: Present simple or continuous worksheet from the kit, done in pairs and checked by swapping.
Error hunt: eight sentences from a short text with tense mistakes; students find and fix them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short descriptions of a person's routine and a different thing the person is doing this week twice (a baker working nights during the festival season, a student preparing for exams, a taxi driver changing shift). Students fill a two-column table: usually / this week. If available, play a routine or lifestyle recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Mime and guess for adults: one student quietly shows an everyday action (typing, cooking, driving, reading, stirring tea) and the class asks "Are you cooking?" until they guess, then makes a sentence about the habit: "Do you usually cook at night?"
lp.prod: Lifestyle survey: students move around with a six-question survey (How often do you...? How much sleep do you get? What are you doing differently this month?). They interview three classmates, then in groups write four findings ("Most of us rarely eat breakfast.") and present them. The teacher listens for tense choice and frequency adverbs.
lp.rw: Read a short text about an unusual job (Reading: The world's strangest jobs, in the kit) and underline all present simple and present continuous verbs, deciding for each whether it describes a habit or a temporary situation. Then write 6-8 sentences: a normal day and a different day this week.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you usually do and one thing you are doing differently this month ("I usually walk to work, but this month I am cycling.") and hand it in.
g: Arrange yourselves from never to always and explain your place.
Write sentences for habit cards and temporary situation cards.
Ask Are you...? questions to guess an action.
Find and fix tense mistakes in short texts.
Interview classmates and report the results.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph comparing a healthy lifestyle and a busy lifestyle using at least six adverbs of frequency.
Support: give a table of time expressions (usually, every day, now, this week, at the moment) and a model sentence for each tense.
hw: Write 8 to 10 sentences comparing a normal day and a different day this week.
Keep a one-day diary in English and circle every habit and every temporary situation.
Listen to one short recording from the Listening folder and note five things the speaker usually does.
lp.tip: Adults often over-use the present continuous for habits because of Arabic and French patterns, so keep the timeline visible and do concept checks every time. Link topics to real routines: shift work, family duties, studying. Keep state verbs on a poster all term.

weeks.obj: tell a short story about the past using past simple and past continuous, with time linkers
weeks.lang: past simple (regular and irregular); past continuous (was/were + -ing); when/while; first, then, after that, in the end; time expressions (ago, in 2015, last year)
weeks.res: Past simple and continuous explanation sheet; What were you doing? (past continuous)
weeks.act: Photo memories in pairs; the alibi interview; story chain with when and while
weeks.hw: write a 100-word story about a memorable day

skills.L: Listen to a short story and note what was happening when the main event happened
skills.S: Tell a memory with past simple and past continuous
skills.R: Read a short anecdote and order the events
skills.W: Write 100 words about a memorable day

lp.wu: Memory photo talk: each student chooses a photo on their phone (or draws a quick sketch) from a memorable day and has two minutes to tell a partner what happened. The partner asks two questions in the past simple ("Who did you go with?" "What did you eat?").
wuAlt: Past simple chain: seated in a circle, students take turns; the teacher calls an infinitive and the student gives the past form and a sentence.
Pair quiz: ten irregular past forms on slips; students test each other.
lp.pres: Tell a short true story ("Last year I was driving to Nador when it started to snow. While I was waiting for help, a man stopped...") and write six key sentences on the board. Show the contrast: past simple for the events, past continuous for the background and the interrupted action. Teach when/while with a two-line timeline, and the sequence words first, then, after that, in the end. Concept-check with "Which action was longer?".
presAlt: Show a four-picture story (a lost wallet at a station) and elicit the story line by line, building the tenses on the board.
Read a short anecdote with the verbs missing and students choose past simple or past continuous.
lp.prac: Controlled practice: students complete 10 sentences ("I ___ (cook) when the power ___ (go) out.") then compare. Next, in pairs they write three of their own with while and when about real events. The teacher monitors the form of was/were + -ing and regular and irregular endings.
pracAlt: Sentence halves: match the interrupted action to the background action ("I was shopping" + "when I saw my old teacher.").
Past continuous worksheet from the kit completed in pairs and checked in class.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a 90-second story twice (a bus journey interrupted by a flat tyre, a lost phone found at a cafe). Students note: where the person was going, what was happening in the background, and what interrupted it. If available, use one story-type recording named in the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: The alibi game: two students are "suspects" who left the room and prepare an alibi for "Where were you at 8 pm last night? What were you doing?" The class (detectives) interviews them separately and spots differences in their stories. Swap suspects.
lp.prod: Story chain and retell: in groups of four, each student has a story prompt card (an unexpected visitor, a lost key, a missed train, a surprise at work). They tell the story in four turns, adding what was happening and what happened next. Then each group retells the best story to another group in three minutes.
lp.rw: Read the anecdote "My Worst Job" (Reading task in the kit) and number the events in order, underlining past continuous and past simple verbs. Then write the first five sentences of your own story using when, while and one sequencing word in each sentence.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences about a memory, one with when and one with while ("I was walking home when it started to rain.") and hand them in.
g: Tell a partner about a photo and answer two past questions.
Detectives interview suspects and look for differences.
Add what was happening and what happened next.
Test each other on irregular past forms.
diff: Fast finishers: add a second event to the story and use past perfect for something that happened before (had already left).
Support: give a story skeleton with verbs in brackets and the linkers first, then, after that, in the end.
hw: Write a 100-word story about a memorable day, using at least three examples of past continuous.
Ask an older family member about a memory and write three sentences about it.
Find a short English news story about the past and underline the past simple and continuous verbs.
lp.tip: Adults love telling real stories, so build on their own anecdotes rather than invented characters. Keep the irregular verb list on the wall. Correct the was/were form and the -ing form, and avoid asking students to tell personal stories they may find sensitive.

weeks.obj: talk about future plans and fixed arrangements, make offers and decisions, and arrange to meet
weeks.lang: be going to for plans; present continuous for fixed arrangements; will for instant decisions and offers; time expressions (tomorrow, next week, this weekend); Let's / How about / Shall we
weeks.res: Going to or Will? worksheet; Put in will or be going to
weeks.act: Diary swap to arrange a meeting; plan or decide role-plays; weekend plans mingle
weeks.hw: write a message to a friend arranging to meet this weekend

skills.L: Listen to a phone call arranging to meet and complete a diary page
skills.S: Arrange a meeting using going to, present continuous and will
skills.R: Read three short messages and decide who has a plan, an arrangement or a decision
skills.W: Write a short message arranging to meet

lp.wu: Weekend plans mingle: students ask three people "What are you doing this weekend?" and note the answers. They report the most interesting plan to the group with "Karim is going to...".
wuAlt: Chain: "This weekend I am going to... and I am going to..." each student adds one plan.
Sentence guessing: the teacher writes a future time on the board and students guess the plan.
lp.pres: Write three sentences on the board: "I'm going to study for my exam." (plan), "I'm meeting my manager at 4 o'clock." (arrangement with a time), "Oh, I forgot my keys. I'll go back and get them." (decision at the moment). Elicit the differences from a diary page and a phone conversation. Teach the structure and the key phrases for making arrangements: Are you free on...? How about...? Shall we meet at...? That suits me.
presAlt: Show a week diary with some days filled and elicit sentences with present continuous; then add intentions without times for going to.
Read a short dialogue of two colleagues arranging a lunch and underline the future forms.
lp.prac: Diary swap: each student gets a different half-empty week diary (appointments, a doctor's visit, a family event, a class). In pairs, students find a time to meet by asking and answering ("Are you free on Thursday afternoon?" "No, I'm seeing the dentist. How about Friday?"). Then three quick pair roles where one person asks for help and the other responds with I'll...
pracAlt: Sentence halves: match a plan, an arrangement and a decision to the correct form.
Put in will or be going to worksheet from the kit, completed in pairs.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a phone call twice where two friends arrange to go to a concert and change the plan (day, time and meeting place). Students complete a diary page with times and places. For a recording instead, use Listening 735 or the Business English video on scheduling an appointment from the kit.
lp.re: Spot the future form: the teacher reads twelve short sentences and students hold up a card marked plan, arrangement or decision. Then they say one real example of each about next week.
lp.prod: Plan a day trip: in groups of four, students plan a day trip from Oujda (Saidia, Berkane, Taza, the Beni Snassen) and decide where they are going to go, what they are doing at each time, and who will bring what. Each group presents their plan in two minutes and the class asks questions.
lp.rw: Read three short messages (an invitation, a change of plan, a decision about where to eat) and label each future form. Then write a message of 40 to 60 words inviting a friend to do something this weekend and suggesting a time and place.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one plan, one arrangement with a time and one decision ("I'll call you tonight.") and hand them in at the door.
g: Ask classmates about their plans and report.
Find a time to meet using diary cards.
Respond to problems with I'll... and plans with I'm going to...
Plan a trip from Oujda in groups.
Write the best short invitation in three minutes.
diff: Fast finishers: write a four-line voicemail changing an arrangement and apologising.
Support: give a table showing the three forms with one example each and a diary template.
hw: Write a message of 40 to 60 words to a friend arranging to meet this weekend.
Write six sentences about your plans and arrangements for next month.
Listen to a short recording from the Listening folder and write down two plans you hear.
lp.tip: Choose local contexts (Berkane, Saidia, a cafe in Oujda, a work meeting) so the future forms feel useful. Many adults say will for everything; keep the three-way contrast visible and do quick concept checks.

occ.act: Halloween falls this weekend (31 Oct). Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students say what shops, cafes and families are going to do for Halloween ("Shops are going to sell costumes.") and what they are going to do this weekend. Then they compare with a Moroccan occasion: "At Eid, people are going to visit family."

weeks.obj: talk about experiences with the present perfect and follow up with past simple details
weeks.lang: present perfect (have/has + past participle); ever, never, already, yet, just; present perfect for experience vs past simple for details; common irregular participles (been, seen, eaten, done, gone)
weeks.res: Ever and never worksheet; Lesson plan: Present perfect simple
weeks.act: Bucket list mingle; Have you ever...? interviews with follow-up questions; yet and already to-do list
weeks.hw: write 8 sentences about experiences you have and have not had

skills.L: Listen to two people talk about their experiences and note what they have and have not done
skills.S: Ask and answer Have you ever...? and give past simple details
skills.R: Read a short travel profile and find present perfect and past simple verbs
skills.W: Write 8 sentences about my experiences

lp.wu: Bucket list mingle: each student writes five things they would like to do before they are 40. They mingle and ask "Have you ever...?" to find who has already done each thing, then tell one new fact to the group.
wuAlt: Two truths and a lie with have/never: students write three sentences ("I have never eaten sushi.") and the group guesses which is false.
Class poll: the teacher asks "Who has been to Spain? Who has driven in a big city?" and students raise a hand and say "I have / I haven't".
lp.pres: Draw a timeline from birth to now. Show "I have been to Casablanca" with no time marker and "I went there in 2019" with a marker. Elicit that the present perfect talks about experience up to now and past simple gives details. Write the forms (have/has + participle) and teach ever, never, already, yet and just with a to-do list on the board. Give the participles of ten common verbs on cards, focusing on the irregular ones.
presAlt: Show five photos of the teacher's experiences and elicit "She has climbed Toubkal." Then ask follow-ups in the past simple.
Read a short profile and underline each verb, asking "Do we know when?".
lp.prac: Have you ever...? cards: pairs take turns drawing a card (eat something unusual, work abroad, meet a famous person, break a bone, live in another city). The partner asks "Have you ever...?" and, if yes, asks two past simple follow-up questions ("When did you do it?" "What was it like?"). Then a controlled exercise: choose between present perfect and past simple in ten sentences.
pracAlt: To-do list pairs: students decide what they have already done and what they have not done yet this week and write six sentences with already and yet.
Participle sorting: sort twelve verbs into regular and irregular and give the participle of each.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short interviews twice (a woman who has worked in three countries and a man who has never travelled by plane). Students tick what each person has and has not done on a checklist and note one past simple detail. If a recording is available, use a travel-experience recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Experience bingo: students get a card of nine experiences (ride a camel, speak at a conference, make a cake, miss a flight). They ask questions to match each square to a classmate; the first with a line wins and tells the class one detail.
lp.prod: Interview and report: students work in pairs to prepare a short interview with a classmate about travel, work or food. They ask at least six Have you ever...? questions and two follow-up questions for every yes. Then each student reports one interesting experience to the class ("Ilham has been to Turkey. She went last summer and she loved it.").
lp.rw: Read the Present Perfect textbook pages (Learn English 2026, in the kit) and underline all present perfect and past simple examples, writing P or S above each. Then write 8 sentences about your own life: four with have/never and four with a past simple detail.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one experience you have had with a past simple detail and one experience you have never had ("I have never been to Egypt, but I would like to go.") and hand them in.
g: Find classmates who have done each thing on your list.
Ask a question and follow up with past details.
Match bingo squares to classmates with questions.
Use already and yet to talk about this week.
Sort verbs into regular and irregular participles.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short profile of a classmate using present perfect and past simple.
Support: give a table of irregular participles and a sentence frame ("I have never ___, but I have ___.").
hw: Write 8 sentences about experiences you have and have not had.
Interview a family member with five Have you ever...? questions and write the answers.
Learn 12 irregular participles with flashcards and write one sentence for each.
lp.tip: Present perfect is hard because Arabic and French use different tenses for experience, so keep the timeline and the with-time or without-time contrast visible. Teach irregular participles in small groups of five or six and recycle them every week.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students use Have you ever...? to talk about national-day experiences ("Have you ever watched the Green March speech with your family?") and add one past simple detail.

weeks.theme: How long? Duration and recent changes
weeks.obj: say how long something has lasted using for and since, and choose between present perfect and past simple
weeks.lang: present perfect with for/since; How long have you...?; present perfect continuous for activities (I've been learning); present perfect vs past simple (ago, in 2019, last year)
weeks.res: For vs since worksheet; Learn English 2026: Present Perfect Continuous textbook (PDF)
weeks.act: Timeline interviews; for or since sorting; How long have you been...? survey
weeks.hw: write 8 sentences about how long things have been part of your life

skills.L: Listen to people say how long they have lived, worked or studied somewhere and complete a table
skills.S: Ask and answer How long have you...? with for and since
skills.R: Read a short biography and find how long events have lasted
skills.W: Write about how long things have been part of my life

lp.wu: Timeline: each student draws a timeline with four dates (moved to a city, started a job or course, met a friend, bought something important). In pairs they ask "When did you...?" and "How long have you...?" and note the answers.
wuAlt: Number dictation: the teacher says five years or periods ("since 2018", "for six months") and students write them and make a sentence.
Quick circle: "I have lived in ___ for ___ years."
lp.pres: Put "I live in Oujda" and "I moved here in 2015" on the board. Elicit "I have lived in Oujda for eleven years" and "since 2015". Show that for takes a period (two years, a long time) and since takes a starting point (2015, Monday, I was a child). Compare "I've worked here for two years" (still true) with "I worked there for two years" (finished). Introduce I've been learning English for... as an activity that continues.
presAlt: Show a short blog post with five life events and ask students to complete a table: when it started, how long.
Teacher tells a short story about their own life and students write the for and since sentences.
lp.prac: For or since? Sorting race: pairs sort 20 time expressions into for and since. Then information-gap pairs: Student A has a card about Hanane (lives in Fes since 2012, works at a bank for four years) and Student B asks "How long has she lived in Fes?" Next they swap and write three true sentences about their partner.
pracAlt: Present perfect or past simple? A mixed gap-fill with ago, in 2019 and since.
Dominoes: match a question to its answer with for or since.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short biographies twice (a chef, a nurse, a student) with details like how long each has had the job. Students write for or since and the time in a table. If a recording is available, use a "work or home" recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Two minute stories: students speak for one minute about one long-term thing in their life (a hobby, a job, a friendship) while a partner counts for and since phrases. Swap and then report.
lp.prod: How long have you...? survey and profile: students write six survey questions (live here, speak English, have a phone, know your best friend, work or study) and ask five classmates. In groups they build a profile of a classmate and present it using for and since and one past simple sentence.
lp.rw: Read the short biography of Nelson Mandela (Reading task in the kit) and underline every for, since and ago, and the dates. Then write 8 sentences about how long things have been part of your own life, with at least three using since.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence with for, one with since and one with a past simple ago ("I have lived here for ten years. I moved here ten years ago.") and hand them in.
g: Draw and describe your own life events.
Sort time expressions into for and since.
Ask questions to complete a profile.
Choose the right tense in short texts.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short biography of someone you admire with for, since and past details.
Support: give a time-expression chart and sentence frames ("I have lived in ___ since ___.").
hw: Write 8 sentences about how long things have been part of your life.
Interview a colleague or neighbour about how long they have lived or worked in their place and write three sentences.
Write a short biography of a friend or relative using for, since and ago.
lp.tip: Many learners say "I am living here since 2015". Give a quick test: is it still true? If yes, present perfect. Keep for/since on a visible poster all week and correct gently every time.

weeks.obj: compare places, products and options and say which is best, using comparatives, superlatives, as...as and too/enough
weeks.lang: comparatives (-er, more...than, much/a bit/far); superlatives (the -est, the most...); as...as / not as...as; too and enough; superlatives with ever and the present perfect (the best meal I've ever had)
weeks.res: Comparatives (PowerPoint lesson); Comparatives + not as + as
weeks.act: Choose a flat or a phone decision matrix; city debate; as...as role cards
weeks.hw: write 8 sentences comparing two places or products and choosing the best

skills.L: Listen to two people compare options and note which one each person chooses and why
skills.S: Compare options and justify a choice with comparatives and superlatives
skills.R: Read two short reviews and find the comparatives and superlatives
skills.W: Write a short comparison of two products or places

lp.wu: Compare and guess: the teacher writes pairs on the board (bus and train, Oujda and Rabat, tea and coffee, a laptop and a phone). Students make one sentence per pair with a comparative; the group guesses the pair from the sentences ("It is cheaper but slower.").
wuAlt: Superlative round: each student says "the best ___ I've ever ___" for a topic card (meal, film, trip).
Quick quiz: "What is the longest river in Africa?" with superlative general knowledge questions.
lp.pres: Show two real adverts for flats (price, size, distance from the centre) and elicit comparisons. Build a table of forms: short adjectives (cheaper, the cheapest), long adjectives (more comfortable, the most comfortable) and irregular forms (better, worse, further). Teach modifiers (much, a bit, far) and as...as / not as...as, then too and enough with the same flats ("It's too small." "It isn't big enough."). Add the superlative with ever and the present perfect.
presAlt: Use the Student Book comparatives and superlatives page from the kit and let students find the rules in the examples.
Show three phones in a table; elicit sentences about price, size and battery.
lp.prac: Decision matrix: pairs get three options (three flats, three phones, three study courses) with data. They write six comparisons with a comparative, a superlative, as...as, too or enough, then agree on the best choice for a given person. Next, error correction: pairs fix eight sentences with common errors (more cheaper, the most big).
pracAlt: Comparative or superlative? Choose the right form in 12 sentences.
Changing partners: each student has a card with three facts about a city and compares with a partner, then changes partner.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a conversation twice between two friends choosing between two courses (cost, distance, teacher, timetable) and students note which option each prefers and why. If a recording is available, use a city or choice recording named in the Listening folder in the kit.
lp.re: Quick auction of sentences: teams get twelve sentences on cards (some correct, some wrong). They bid fake dirhams on the ones they think are correct and the teacher reveals the answers.
lp.prod: Choosing for a friend: in groups of three, each student has a different person profile (a student with little money, a family with two children, a manager who travels a lot). Groups compare three city or apartment options and decide which is best for each profile, giving reasons with comparatives and as...as. Each group presents one decision.
lp.rw: Read the comparatives and superlatives reading task in the kit and list the comparatives and superlatives. Then write 8 sentences comparing two places or products you know, ending with "The best choice is... because...".
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one comparative, one superlative with ever and one sentence with too or enough ("It is too expensive for me.") and hand them in.
g: Write comparisons so others guess the pair.
Compare options and choose the best for a person.
Answer general knowledge questions with superlatives.
Choose the best option for a person in the group.
diff: Fast finishers: write a mini review comparing three cafes in town.
Support: give a form table (adjective, comparative, superlative) and sentence frames with than and as...as.
hw: Write 8 sentences comparing two places or products and choosing the best.
Compare two services you use (two buses, two banks, two mobile plans) in a short paragraph.
Find an English review online and underline all comparatives and superlatives.
lp.tip: Use real local comparisons (apartments in Oujda, buses and trains, university courses) so the language has a purpose. Watch for double comparatives (more cheaper), missing than, and the wrong article with superlatives.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students compare life in Morocco then and now ("Travel is much easier than it was in 1956. Phones are cheaper than before.") using comparatives.

weeks.obj: make predictions and talk about possibilities with will, won't and might, and give reasons
weeks.lang: will/won't for predictions; might/may (not); probably, definitely, perhaps; I think + will; first impressions
weeks.res: Will: Predicting the Future; Life in the Year 2050 (might, may, will)
weeks.act: Predictions about 2040; chance scale cards; prediction panel
weeks.hw: write a paragraph of predictions about your city in 20 years

skills.L: Listen to experts or ordinary people make predictions and note the strength of each one
skills.S: Make and justify predictions and discuss how sure you are
skills.R: Read a short article of predictions and mark which ones came true
skills.W: Write a paragraph of predictions about my city

lp.wu: Fortune-telling in pairs: students look at a small object of a partner's (a key, a pen, a bag) and make three funny predictions with will and might. The partner says whether each is "definitely", "probably", "possibly" or "no way".
wuAlt: Prediction of the day: students predict three things for the next week (weather, news, class) and compare.
Quick chain: "In ten years' time, I will..." each adds a new prediction.
lp.pres: Show a chance line on the board from 0 to 100% with: won't, probably won't, might not, might, probably will, will. Give sentences about the near future ("It will rain this evening." "I might get a promotion.") and elicit the forms. Teach I think + will and I don't think + will, plus the adverbs probably, definitely and perhaps with their positions in the sentence. Compare with going to when there is evidence now ("Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.").
presAlt: Show a headline "Robots will clean our streets by 2035" and ask students whether it is certain, probable or possible.
Use the Student Book will/won't page from the kit for the rule box and examples.
lp.prac: Chance scale cards: pairs get ten prediction cards about work, technology, health and the environment and place each one on a line from certain to impossible, giving a sentence ("Cars will definitely be electric.", "Teachers might not exist."). Then pairs write six predictions of their own with probably and definitely in the correct position.
pracAlt: Will or going to? Choose the right form in twelve sentences, some with evidence and some with opinion.
Tennis: one pair says a prediction, the next adds a reason with because.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a two-minute talk twice where three people make predictions about life in 2040 (jobs, transport, food). Students write each person's prediction and how sure they are. For a recording instead, use the video "7 amazing technologies we'll see by 2030" or Listening 763 from the kit.
lp.re: Agree or disagree? The teacher reads a prediction and students write on a slip I think so, I'm not sure or I don't think so, plus one reason. They compare in threes.
lp.prod: Prediction panel: groups of four prepare a two-minute panel on one topic (jobs, transport, education, health in Oujda in 2040). Each person gives two predictions with a reason and says how sure they are. The class asks questions and votes on the most likely prediction.
lp.rw: Read the article "Ten 100-year predictions that came true" (Reading task in the kit) and mark which predictions used will and which used might. Then write a 6-8 sentence paragraph of predictions about your city in 20 years.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two predictions for your city, one certain and one uncertain, and one reason ("The tram will probably change traffic.") and hand them in.
g: Make funny predictions about a partner and rate them.
Place predictions on a scale from certain to impossible.
Add a new prediction with a reason.
Choose the right future form from evidence or opinion.
Present and vote on future scenarios.
diff: Fast finishers: write predictions about three technologies and rank them by how likely they are.
Support: give a chance scale poster with example sentences and word order for probably and definitely.
hw: Write a paragraph of 8 to 10 predictions about your city in 20 years.
Read a short article about the future and underline the predictions.
Ask a family member for two predictions about the future and write them with will or might.
lp.tip: Link predictions to issues adults care about: jobs, cost of living, climate and technology. Check the position of probably and definitely and the difference between will and going to with evidence.

occ.act: Thanksgiving (26 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students predict what an American family will cook and talk about on Thanksgiving ("They will probably eat turkey.") and compare with a Moroccan family meal.

weeks.obj: talk about rules, obligations, advice and ability in work, travel and daily life
weeks.lang: must/mustn't; have to/don't have to; should/shouldn't; can, could, be able to; rules at work, at airports, on the road and in public places
weeks.res: Modal Auxiliaries Explained (grammar sheet); Should vs shouldn't worksheet
weeks.act: Sign and rule matching; workplace rules debate; advice clinic; Welcome to Morocco guide
weeks.hw: write 8 rules or pieces of advice for a new colleague or a visitor to Oujda

skills.L: Listen to a short talk about rules at a new job and note what is a must and what is optional
skills.S: Give advice and explain rules using the correct modal
skills.R: Read a short set of workplace or travel rules and sort them by obligation, prohibition and permission
skills.W: Write 8 rules or pieces of advice for a new colleague or visitor

lp.wu: What is this sign? The teacher shows six real signs (No parking, Keep right, Staff only, Wet floor, Please queue here, Mobile phones off). Pairs say what each sign means with must, mustn't or can.
wuAlt: Quick rules for a library or a gym: students write three rules each and compare.
Two-minute list: the rules at your workplace or school.
lp.pres: Show a short airport and a short workplace rule list. Elicit: must (strong obligation from the rule maker), have to (outside rules), mustn't (prohibition), don't have to (no need), should (advice), can/can't (permission). Build a table and emphasise the key contrast: mustn't and don't have to. Add ability: can/could/be able to (I couldn't open the account online, but I was able to do it at the bank).
presAlt: Use the Student Book obligation and ability pages from the kit to read examples in context.
Use the Should vs shouldn't worksheet from the kit to practise advice, then add must and have to.
lp.prac: Rule makers: pairs get a situation card (new job in a clinic, a language school, a hotel, driving in a foreign country) and write eight rules or pieces of advice, then read them aloud so the class can guess the situation. Controlled practice follows: choose must/mustn't/don't have to/should in twelve sentences and check with a partner.
pracAlt: Sort the rules: place twelve cards under Must, Mustn't, Don't have to and Should.
Correct the mistakes in eight sentences (You mustn't to go; She don't have to).
lp.ls: Teacher reads a first-day induction at a clinic or a hotel twice (what staff must do, mustn't do, don't have to do, should do). Students tick or write the rule types. If a recording is available, use a rules or signs recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Advice clinic: students write a problem on a slip (I can't sleep. I have a job interview tomorrow. My neighbour is very noisy.) and pass it on. The partner writes advice with should and a reason, then they discuss.
lp.prod: Welcome to Morocco guide: in groups of three, students prepare a 90-second guide for a visitor to Oujda or Morocco about what to do, what not to do, what is necessary and what is optional (dress, tea, visiting a home, bargaining, public transport). Groups present and the class adds one more piece of advice.
lp.rw: Read a short text of rules for a language centre or travel advice for a foreign country (about 120 words) and underline the modals, then say whether each is obligation, prohibition, permission or advice. Then write 8 sentences of rules or advice for a new colleague.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one must, one mustn't, one don't have to and one should for your own workplace or home ("At home, we don't have to take our shoes off in the kitchen.") and hand them in.
g: Explain what each sign means with a modal.
Write rules for a situation and others guess it.
Place rule cards under the correct modal.
Pass problem slips and give advice.
Present dos and don'ts for visitors.
diff: Fast finishers: write a staff handbook page with ten rules using five different modal forms.
Support: give a table with must, mustn't, have to, don't have to and should and a sentence frame for each.
hw: Write 8 rules or pieces of advice for a new colleague or a visitor to Oujda.
Take photos of three signs or rules in town and write what each means with a modal.
Ask a person who has moved to a new place what they had to learn and write three sentences.
lp.tip: Teach mustn't vs don't have to with a real example every lesson. Include real adult contexts: a visa office, a workplace, driving rules. Make sure students do not add to after modals.
