weeks.theme: Problems and solutions: zero and first conditional
weeks.obj: describe general truths and likely future results with zero and first conditionals, and negotiate solutions
weeks.lang: zero conditional (If you heat ice, it melts); first conditional (If it rains, we'll stay home); when/as soon as/until/unless; if + present simple, will + base
weeks.res: Zero conditional worksheet; First conditional (grammar sheet)
weeks.act: If-chain; problem scenarios; negotiation role-play; weather and travel disruption plans
weeks.hw: write 8 first conditional sentences about real plans and problems

skills.L: Listen to a short phone call about a delayed trip and note the conditions and results
skills.S: Describe likely results and negotiate with if, unless and when
skills.R: Read a short advice article and find the conditionals
skills.W: Write 8 first conditional sentences about real plans and problems

lp.wu: Chain story: the teacher starts "If I win a prize, I'll buy a car." The next student says "If I buy a car, I'll drive to Marrakech" and so on, building a chain of five or six links.
wuAlt: Quick facts: students complete "If you mix red and blue, you get..." with general truths.
Pairs write two worries about the week and the possible results.
lp.pres: Write two sets on the board: general truths (If you don't eat, you feel tired. Water boils if you heat it.) and a real future possibility (If the bus is late, I'll take a taxi.). Elicit that both talk about real situations, one general and one specific. Teach the structure (if + present simple, will + base), the alternative if the result is advice (If you feel sick, you should rest) and the words when, as soon as, until, unless. Stress that we never use will in the if clause.
presAlt: Read a short problem page letter and underline the conditionals.
Student Book Unit 8B conditionals page from the kit as the rule box and examples.
lp.prac: If-chain pairs: each pair gets four situations (a delayed flight, a broken phone, a late payment, bad weather) and writes two zero and two first conditional sentences for each. They read them aloud and others decide which is a general truth and which is a specific plan. Then a controlled gap-fill with if, when, until and unless.
pracAlt: Sentence halves: match each if clause to the best result.
Error correction: fix eight sentences with will in the if clause.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a phone call twice between a traveller and a travel agent about a cancelled bus (the conditions and what the agent will do). Students write the condition and result in a two-column table. If a recording is available, use a travel recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: What happens if...? One student draws a problem card (I lose my passport abroad; my boss is angry; my internet stops during an exam) and the others take turns giving one first conditional response until someone has a better solution.
lp.prod: Negotiation role-play: in pairs, a tenant and a landlord (or an employee and a manager) negotiate three issues (rent, working hours, repair). Each uses at least five conditional sentences ("If you reduce the rent, I'll pay on time. Unless you fix the heating, I won't renew."). The class guesses which agreement is fairest.
lp.rw: Read the explanation sheet with exercises in the kit and underline the conditionals, then do the exercises. Then write 8 first conditional sentences about your own real plans and problems, with at least two using unless or when.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one zero conditional and one first conditional about your week ("If I don't sleep, I can't think. If I finish early, I'll call my friend.") and hand them in.
g: Build a chain of if sentences.
Reach an agreement with if and unless.
Correct will in the if clause.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue where two people negotiate with five conditionals.
Support: give a table (If + present, will + base) and half-sentence starters.
hw: Write 8 first conditional sentences about real plans and problems.
Write a short email to a landlord or colleague asking for a change and giving two conditions.
Read a problem page letter online and underline the conditionals.
lp.tip: Keep the if clause in present simple and watch for the typical error "If it will rain". Use authentic scenarios (travel, rent, jobs) so the grammar solves a real problem. Practise unless as a natural alternative.

weeks.obj: talk about unreal or unlikely situations, give advice with If I were you, and justify choices
weeks.lang: second conditional (If I won, I would travel); If I were you, I'd...; wish + past simple (introduction); dilemmas and choices
weeks.res: Second conditional worksheet; What would you do if... (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: What would you do? cards; dilemma discussions; agony aunt replies
weeks.hw: write an advice reply to a problem letter using the second conditional

skills.L: Listen to people answer What would you do? and note each person's choice
skills.S: Talk about imaginary situations and give advice with If I were you
skills.R: Read two short problem letters and the advice given
skills.W: Write a reply to a problem letter

lp.wu: Lottery question: "If you won one million dirhams tomorrow, what would you do first?" Students write one sentence, then mingle to find someone with the same answer and one with the most surprising answer.
wuAlt: If I could be anywhere: students write a place and a reason and share it.
Wish list: each student completes "I wish I had...".
lp.pres: Contrast the first and second conditional with two examples on the board: "If I get a raise, I'll buy a car." (possible) and "If I won the lottery, I would buy an island." (unlikely). Elicit the structure (if + past simple, would + base) and the use of were for all persons (If I were you). Teach the shorter forms (I'd, wouldn't) and the polite advice "If I were you, I'd talk to him." Compare with should for advice.
presAlt: Use the Student Book second conditional page from the kit as the example source and let students find the pattern.
Read two short dilemmas and elicit what each person would do.
lp.prac: What would you do? Pairs take turns drawing dilemma cards (you find a wallet with 500 dirhams; your best friend lies to you; you are offered a job abroad). They answer with the second conditional and explain why, and the partner asks "Why would you do that?". Then a controlled exercise: put verbs into the correct form in ten sentences.
pracAlt: Pass the question: one student asks "What would you do if...?" and passes to the next with a new question.
Sentence completion: finish ten if clauses with a logical result.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three people answering the question "What would you do if you could change jobs?" twice and students write each person's answer and reason. If a recording is available, use a dream-job or choices recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Quick advice: the teacher reads a problem ("I'm always tired at work." "My neighbour plays loud music at night.") and students give advice starting If I were you, I'd... Then pairs choose the best advice.
lp.prod: Agony aunt panel: groups receive one problem letter (work, family, money, study). They discuss the situation, then each person gives advice with If I were you and the group writes one reply. The class listens to each reply and votes for the most helpful.
lp.rw: Read two problem letters from the Agony aunt writing prompts in the kit and underline the problem in each. Then write your own reply of 80 words to one of them that gives advice with If I were you and two more second conditionals.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two sentences, one dream ("If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.") and one piece of advice ("If I were you, I'd ask for help.") and hand them in.
g: Say what you would do with a million dirhams.
Give advice for real problem letters.
Ask a new second conditional question.
Match unreal conditions to logical results.
diff: Fast finishers: write the dream-life paragraph "If I could live anywhere, I would...".
Support: give a table comparing the first and second conditional with one example for each.
hw: Write an advice reply of 80 words to a problem letter using the second conditional.
Write five sentences about what you would do if you lived in another country.
Listen to a short recording from the Listening folder and note what the speaker would do.
lp.tip: Use dilemmas adults can discuss without private information (a found wallet, a job offer, a noisy neighbour). Check that learners use the past simple in the if clause and would in the result clause, and teach were for all persons.

weeks.obj: describe jobs, skills and experience, answer interview questions and read a job advertisement
weeks.lang: work vocabulary (qualified, responsible for, deadline, salary, contract); skills and qualities; I'm good at/interested in + -ing; present perfect for experience and past simple for details; interview questions
weeks.res: Lesson plan: Jobs, lesson 2; Business English video 3: The Job Interview
weeks.act: Job advert analysis; mock interviews in pairs; strengths and weaknesses; CV profile writing
weeks.hw: write a short profile of yourself for a CV or a LinkedIn page

skills.L: Listen to a short job interview and note the questions and the strong answers
skills.S: Answer interview questions with experience, skills and a plan
skills.R: Read a short job advertisement and underline the requirements
skills.W: Write a short professional profile

lp.wu: Dream job guessing: one student thinks of a job and the group asks yes/no questions ("Do you work indoors?" "Do you need a degree?") until they guess. Winner chooses the next job.
wuAlt: Word association: the teacher writes "work" and students add words (boss, salary, shift, colleague).
Quick pairs: say three things you like and dislike about your job or studies.
lp.pres: Show a short job advertisement (a customer service assistant at a bank or a nurse at a clinic) and ask what the employer wants. Teach the key language: qualified, experienced, responsible for, team player, to apply for, deadline. Model typical interview answers: "I have worked in sales for three years." "I'm good at organising my time." "My biggest weakness is that I take on too much." Show how to answer with the present perfect for experience, the past simple for a specific example and will for plans.
presAlt: Play a short interview clip (Business English videos in the kit, a good vs a poor interview) and ask students to note what the candidate does well or badly.
Present a CV with a typical profile paragraph and highlight the verbs.
lp.prac: Job advert analysis: pairs get one advertisement (a receptionist, a mechanic, a teacher, an IT assistant). They list the requirements and write three questions an interviewer might ask. Then they match each of eight skills to a typical answer and practise saying "I'm good at -ing" and "I've worked as...".
pracAlt: Interview question race: teams write the most likely questions for a given job.
Vocabulary matching: match job words to definitions.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short interview twice (about two minutes: questions about experience, a weakness, why this job, plans) and students tick what the candidate says on a checklist. If a recording is available, use the Business English interview video or a work recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: One-minute answer: students draw a question card (Tell me about yourself. Why do you want this job?) and speak for one minute while a partner times and notes one thing to improve. Swap.
lp.prod: Mock interviews in pairs: each student prepares a job advertisement for the partner's real or chosen job. Student A interviews student B for six minutes, then they swap. The observers use a checklist (eye contact, past and present perfect used correctly, example given). The class gives feedback on the strongest answers.
lp.rw: Read a short job advertisement (or the employment text in the kit) and underline the requirements. Then write a four-sentence profile for a CV or LinkedIn page (I am a qualified..., I have worked..., I am good at..., I am looking for...).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one strength and one weakness in a full sentence for an interview ("I am good at solving problems. I sometimes take on too much.") and hand them in.
g: Ask yes/no questions to guess a job.
Find requirements and write interview questions.
Write likely questions for a job.
Answer one interview question for a minute.
Read a partner's CV profile and suggest one improvement.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short cover letter paragraph linking your experience to the job ad.
Support: give interview question frames and a skills word bank (organised, flexible, reliable).
hw: Write a short profile of yourself for a CV or LinkedIn page (4 to 6 sentences).
Find one job advert in English online and list the requirements.
Practise answering "Tell me about yourself" aloud and record one minute.
lp.tip: Many students use this vocabulary in real applications, so use real job adverts and invite them to bring their CV. Practise the present perfect for experience and past simple for examples. Keep the focus on speaking confidently rather than on perfect English.

occ.act: Christmas (25 December) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: a colleague invites you to an office party or a friend invites you to a Christmas meal. Pairs practise polite accepting and declining: "Thank you for inviting me. I'd love to come." and "I'm afraid I can't make it, but thank you for asking."
occ.hw: Write a short polite reply to an invitation.

weeks.obj: write clear emails of about 100 words that request, apologise, confirm and reply, in a suitable formal or informal register
weeks.lang: register (formal, neutral, informal); I'm writing to...; Could you...? Would you mind...? I would be grateful if...; Please find attached; apologising and explaining; Best regards / Best wishes; polite modals
weeks.res: Business Writing (PowerPoint); Writing guide: E-mail writing
weeks.act: Register transformation; email triage and reply; guided formal email; peer editing with a checklist
weeks.hw: write a send-ready formal email of about 100 words about a real request

skills.L: Listen to a short voicemail and write the key points of the message for an email reply
skills.S: Explain a request or a problem aloud before writing it
skills.R: Read three emails and decide which register each one uses
skills.W: Write a formal email of about 100 words

lp.wu: Same message, different person: the teacher writes "I can't come to the meeting" on the board and students say it to a friend, a manager and a client in the right register. They notice how the words change.
wuAlt: Email word race: teams write as many email phrases as they can in two minutes (Dear, Hi, Best regards, Please find attached...) and sort them into formal and informal.
Pairs rank four emails from most formal to least formal.
lp.pres: Show two emails about the same request (an informal one to a friend and a formal one to a manager). Students list the differences: greeting, length, polite forms, contractions, closing. Build a language bank: opening (Dear Mr/Ms..., Hi...), purpose (I'm writing to..., I'm writing about...), request (Could you...? Would you mind...? I would be grateful if...), apology (I'm sorry for..., Please accept my apologies), closing (I look forward to hearing from you. Best regards). Teach the structure: greeting, reason, details, request, closing.
presAlt: Use the Writing guides "E-mail writing" resource from the kit as the model.
Show a real email with jumbled paragraphs and students order them.
lp.prac: Register transformation: pairs receive six informal sentences ("Can you send me the report?" "Sorry I missed the call.") and rewrite them formally, then do the reverse with six formal sentences. Next, email triage: pairs read three short incoming emails (a request for information, a complaint about a delivery, an invitation) and decide the purpose and the right register for each reply.
pracAlt: Matching: match request, apology and complaint phrases to the correct register.
Sentence ordering: put the parts of an email in a logical order.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short voicemail twice (a client changing a delivery date and asking for a call back). Students note who, what, when and the request, and then write the first two lines of an email reply. For a recording instead, use the Business English audio "Communication at work" in the kit.
lp.re: Fix the email: the teacher shows a short email with eight errors of register, spelling and punctuation. Pairs find and fix them and read the improved version aloud.
lp.prod: Guided formal email: each student gets a situation card (ask your landlord to repair the heating, apply for a course, apologise to a client, ask a manager for leave). They plan four content points with a partner and then write a draft of 80 to 100 words using the language bank. In the last ten minutes pairs swap drafts and use a checklist (greeting, purpose, four points, polite request, closing, punctuation) to give two pieces of feedback.
lp.rw: Reading and editing: students read a partner's email and mark one strong sentence and one sentence to improve. Then they write a final improved version of the first and last paragraphs.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the opening line and the closing line of your email ("I am writing to ask about... I look forward to hearing from you.") and hand it in.
g: Say one message to three different people.
Sort phrases into formal and informal.
Find and fix mistakes in a short email.
Decide the purpose and register of incoming emails.
Check a partner's email with a checklist.
diff: Fast finishers: write a polite complaint email of 120 words with a request for a refund.
Support: give an email skeleton with the opening, purpose, request and closing phrases.
hw: Write a send-ready formal email of about 100 words about a real request.
Find a real work email in English (from a friend or a template) and label its parts.
Rewrite an informal message you sent recently in a more formal register.
lp.tip: Students need to see that register is a choice, not a rule: ask who is reading and why. Use real tasks such as a visa, a course application or a work request. Keep emails short and structured; reward clear paragraphing and polite modals.

occ.act: New Year week. Optional 10-minute task: students write three resolutions with I'm going to and one promise to a colleague or friend with I will ("I will send the report by Friday."), then tell a partner how they will keep them.
occ.hw: Write your three resolutions and how you will keep them.

weeks.obj: show progress in reading, writing, listening and speaking at A2-B1 level in a PET-style progress check
weeks.lang: all Semester 1 outcomes: tenses, comparatives, future forms, modals, conditionals, work and email language
weeks.res: PET (B1) Reading Test 01; Reading exam (A2-B1)
weeks.act: Reading and writing papers; short listening paper; paired speaking interviews with a rubric; self-assessment
weeks.hw: write three sentences about what went well in the progress check and what you want to improve

skills.L: Listen to short recordings and answer multiple-choice questions
skills.S: Complete a paired speaking interview
skills.R: Read short texts and answer matching and multiple-choice questions
skills.W: Write an email of about 100 words

lp.wu: Exam strategies review: the teacher shows five PET-style task types on cards (notice, matching, long text, gap fill, email) and students say in one sentence what they need to do for each. Remind students about timing, answering every question and reading the instructions.
wuAlt: Pairs quiz on Semester 1 grammar: each pair writes three quick questions for another pair.
Quick circle: each student names one thing they learned and one thing they find difficult.
lp.pres: Distribute the reading paper (20 minutes): short notices and messages, a matching task, one longer text with multiple choice, and a gapped text. Read the instructions aloud, model the first question on the board, then students work silently.
presAlt: Alternative paper: use PET Reading Test 01 from the kit (Parts 1 to 3 only).
For a shorter paper, use the Reading and Writing sample paper in the kit and select five tasks.
lp.prac: Writing paper (20 minutes): students write an email of about 100 words in response to a given email (for example, a friend asks about your new job and invites you for a weekend). They include all four content points and check for errors at the end.
pracAlt: Use a task from the Writing Part 1 resources in the PET folder of the kit.
Alternative: a short article of 100 words on a familiar topic.
lp.ls: Listening paper (about 10 minutes): the teacher reads or plays five short recordings (a voicemail, a travel announcement, a conversation about a plan, a talk about a job, a dialogue about shopping). Students answer multiple-choice questions and the teacher plays each twice. Use the PET Listening tasks from the Listening folder or the teacher's script in the kit.
lp.re: Grammar and vocabulary paper (10 minutes): students complete a short cloze of 10 gaps using the Semester 1 grammar (past, present perfect, will, comparatives, conditionals).
lp.prod: Paired speaking interviews (about 5 minutes per pair): the teacher acts as examiner with two candidates, using the PET Part 1 and Part 2 style: personal questions, then a simple situation where the pair makes suggestions. While waiting, other students read a text and answer comprehension questions in rw.
lp.rw: While the other pairs are examined, students read a short article on a familiar topic and answer five questions. Pairs that finish speaking join in for the last few minutes.
lp.st: Closing: the teacher thanks the class and tells them when feedback and marks will be returned. Each student writes one sentence about which part felt easiest and which part felt hardest and hands it in at the door.
g: Match each task type to the best strategy.
Write three grammar questions for another pair.
Complete a short cloze against the clock.
Check an email draft against a list of common errors.
Practise PET speaking questions with a partner.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second short text of 80 words on the same topic as the email.
Support: allow a word bank of linkers and give a template for the email layout.
hw: Write three sentences about what went well in the progress check and what you want to improve.
Choose three grammar points from Semester 1 and write one sentence for each.
Read a short English text and list five words you want to learn.
lp.tip: Frame this as a progress check, not a test, to reduce anxiety. Use the same descriptors as the PET writing and speaking scales so students understand their results. Record the semester marks and prepare feedback sheets for the next week.
checklist: I can write a 70-word email with a clear purpose and closing.
I can answer 5 multiple-choice listening questions.
I can speak for 1 minute about my life in Morocco.
I can match headings to reading paragraphs.
I can identify PET exam parts and their tasks.
I can use present perfect for experience (e.g., 'I have visited Casablanca').
I can use comparatives (e.g., 'Oujda is more beautiful than...').

occ.act: New Year recap (4 January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year using the past simple and one thing they are going to do this semester.

weeks.obj: learn from Semester 1 results, understand the PET format, and set personal targets for Semester 2
weeks.lang: PET format (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking); exam strategy language; correcting common errors; target setting (I need to improve my..., I will practise...)
weeks.res: Cambridge English PET Teacher's book; PET Advice: Do's and Don'ts
weeks.act: Error analysis from the assessment; PET format tour; mini diagnostic stations; target setting sheet
weeks.hw: choose two PET practice areas and complete one short task in each

skills.L: Listen to a short PET-style recording and identify what each part of the exam asks you to do
skills.S: Explain my target and practice plan to a partner
skills.R: Read the PET overview and map each paper to the skills needed
skills.W: Complete a target setting sheet

lp.wu: Common error carousel: the teacher posts eight anonymous sentences from the assessment on the walls (word order, present perfect, articles, prepositions). In pairs, students walk around, correct each sentence and tick the ones they think they have made themselves.
wuAlt: Quick quiz: students list the Semester 1 topics from memory in two minutes and compare lists.
Score share: each student says which paper they did best and which was hardest.
lp.pres: Return the assessment and show the class profile (without names): which areas were strong and which need work. Present a one-page overview of PET (B1 Preliminary): Reading (six parts), Writing (an email and an article or story of about 100 words), Listening (four parts), Speaking (face-to-face with a partner and an examiner). Explain that the course now aims at B1 Preliminary as the target for those who want a certificate, with Semester 2 including four PET skills weeks.
presAlt: Use the Useful Documents in the PET folder (PET Advice, Do's and Don'ts) as a short handout.
Show the interview questions sheet from the kit and let students try three PET Part 1 questions.
lp.prac: Mini diagnostic stations: students rotate in small groups through four stations (a notice reading task, a short listening, a two-minute speaking prompt, a six-sentence writing task) and note how confident they feel at each. The teacher moves between stations noting errors for the next few weeks.
pracAlt: Strategy match: match PET task types to the best strategies.
Pairs work through five questions from a past reading paper and discuss which clues helped.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short announcement and a conversation twice and students answer five PET-style questions. Discuss what the speaker's purpose is, which words help, and how students can tell the answer. For a recording instead, use the Listening tasks slideshow in the kit.
lp.re: Target setting in threes: students complete "For the writing paper, my biggest problem is... To improve, I will..." and then share one target with the group and agree on a way to support each other.
lp.prod: Speaking practice: pairs practise PET speaking Part 1 (answering personal questions about work, study, free time and plans) for three minutes, then a short Part 2-style task (a conversation about planning a day out with prompt cards). The partner uses a simple tick list (answers fully, uses linking words, keeps going).
lp.rw: Target setting sheet: students read the PET overview and complete a sheet with three targets (grammar, skill, exam) for Semester 2, plus the weekly practice they will do (for example, 20 minutes of reading and two short writings per week).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one specific target for Semester 2 and one action you will take this week ("I will write one email a week and ask for feedback.") and hand it in.
g: Correct anonymous sentences from the assessment.
Rotate through four short skills stations.
Write a target and share it.
diff: Fast finishers: write a one-week study plan with specific tasks and a reward.
Support: give a target sheet with sentence frames (I need to improve my ___ . I will ___).
hw: Choose two PET practice areas and complete one short task in each.
Write a study plan for the next four weeks.
Read a short English text (from the Reading tasks list) and write three questions about it.
lp.tip: Give adults control of their learning: let them choose the practice areas and track their own progress. Use anonymous error examples to avoid embarrassment. Record the semester marks and hand out the feedback sheets this week.
checklist: I can identify the 4 parts of the PET exam.
I can explain the timing for each section.
I can name 2 strategies for the reading test.
I can set a specific spring target for my speaking.
I can write a 80-word email using PET format.
I can understand a 3-minute PET listening audio.
I can describe my PET preparation plan to a partner.

occ.act: Yennayer (Amazigh New Year, 14 January) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students share how families celebrate it and what food is cooked, using the present simple, then say one thing they are going to do this year.
occ.hw: Write 5 sentences about how a festival is celebrated in your family.

weeks.theme: Customs, food and how things are made: the passive
weeks.obj: describe customs and processes using the present and past simple passive, and explain why they matter
weeks.lang: present simple passive (Mint tea is served to guests); past simple passive (The medina was built in...); by + agent; process sequencers (first, next, then, finally); agent not important
weeks.res: The Passive Voice worksheet; Active and passive voice (grammar sheets)
weeks.act: Process description (how is it made?); custom Q&A; culture quiz; passive transformation
weeks.hw: write 8 sentences describing how a traditional dish or custom is prepared or done

skills.L: Listen to a description of how a dish is made and put the steps in order
skills.S: Explain a custom or a process using the passive and sequencers
skills.R: Read a short text about a tradition and underline the passive verbs
skills.W: Write about how a traditional dish or custom is prepared

lp.wu: Guess the object: the teacher describes common things without naming them ("It is made of wood. It is used to stir the pot. It is found in every kitchen.") and the class guesses. Then pairs make their own two clues with is made of, is used for, is found in.
wuAlt: Quick quiz: "Where is argan oil produced? Where is the Mona Lisa kept?" with facts that need the passive.
Photo prompt: show a photo of mint tea and elicit what is done before it is served.
lp.pres: Show a process picture series for making mint tea in Morocco and elicit the steps in the active ("People put tea in the pot..."). Re-write them in the passive on the board ("Tea is put in the pot. Boiling water is added. Sugar is added. The tea is poured from a height."). Elicit that the object is more important than the person and teach the form: be + past participle, plus by when the agent matters. Compare present and past passive with a second example (The mosque was built in 1100 by...). Teach the sequencers first, next, then, finally.
presAlt: Use the Learn English 2026 Passive vs Active Voice video lessons in the kit to introduce the form.
Read a paragraph about argan oil or a local craft and underline the passive verbs.
lp.prac: Process cards: pairs get a card for a process (making bread, producing olive oil, preparing couscous, how coins are made, how a passport is issued). They write five passive sentences with sequencers, then read them to another pair who guess the process. Then a controlled exercise: change ten active sentences into the passive.
pracAlt: Passive or active? Choose the right form in ten sentences.
Sentence halves: match the object to the correct verb in the passive.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a description of how couscous or bread is prepared in a family, twice, as a process with six steps. Students number a mixed list of steps. If a recording is available, use a culture or food recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Custom stations: groups of three each take a card about a custom (a wedding, a birthday party, a family reunion, a first day at work). They say three things that are done, using the passive ("Gifts are given. A meal is served."). Then the groups rotate to a new card.
lp.prod: Present your process or custom: students prepare a two-minute explanation of a traditional dish, a craft or a custom for a guest from another country, using at least six passive sentences and four sequencers. The audience asks one question and gives one compliment.
lp.rw: Read the comfort food text (Reading task in the kit) and underline all passive verbs and any customs it describes. Then write 8 sentences about how a dish or custom from your family is prepared or done.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two passive sentences, one present and one past, about something in Morocco ("Mint tea is served to guests. The Karaouine library was founded in 859.") and hand them in.
g: Describe an object with the passive so others guess it.
Describe the steps of a process in the passive.
Change active sentences into the passive.
Rotate and say what is done at an occasion.
Answer questions about places and traditions using the passive.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short brochure paragraph about a local product (argan oil, pottery, Oujda's rai music) using the passive.
Support: give a model process text and a table of be + past participle for twelve verbs.
hw: Write 8 sentences describing how a traditional dish or custom is prepared or done.
Interview a family member about a process (making bread or preparing a feast) and write the steps.
Find a short description of how something is made and underline the passive verbs.
lp.tip: Choose processes learners know well, so the passive arrives with meaning. Watch for the missing be (The tea served) and the wrong past participle. Include customs from several backgrounds with respect, and do not ask students to explain private religious practices.

weeks.obj: define and describe people, places and things with relative clauses, and make guesses about people from clues
weeks.lang: defining relative clauses (who, which, that, where, whose); It's a person who...; a place where...; might/must/can't be for guessing from clues
weeks.res: Who, Which, When, Where worksheet; Learn English 2026: Adjective (relative) Clause (video lessons and textbook PDF)
weeks.act: Definition games; photo detective; describe and identify; place riddles
weeks.hw: write 8 definitions of people, places or things using who, which or where

skills.L: Listen to descriptions and match each one to a person or a place
skills.S: Define words and describe people and places to a partner
skills.R: Read short descriptions and find the relative clauses
skills.W: Write definitions with who, which and where

lp.wu: Taboo for adults: students describe a word on a card without saying it or the words below it ("It's a place where you wait for a train.") while their team guesses. Two minutes per team.
wuAlt: Quick riddles: the teacher gives three riddles with who, which and where for the class to solve.
Word association: say a job and a place where that person works.
lp.pres: Write four definitions on the board: "A baker is a person who makes bread." "A pharmacy is a place where you buy medicine." "A kettle is a thing which boils water." "A man whose car is old might take the bus." Elicit that who is for people, which for things, where for places and that can replace who or which, and show whose for possession. Show that we do not repeat the subject ("The man who he...") and that the clause gives essential information about the noun.
presAlt: Use the Student Book Unit 3C relative clauses page from the kit for the rule box and examples.
Show five photos and elicit one defining sentence for each.
lp.prac: Definition pairs: students make cards for ten words (a lawyer, a library, a nurse, a bakery, a keyboard, a neighbour, a passport) and define them in a full sentence using who, which, that or where. The partner guesses the word. Then a controlled exercise: combine two short sentences using a relative pronoun.
pracAlt: Gap-fill with who, which, where, whose in eight sentences.
Matching: match a person, place or thing to its definition.
lp.ls: Teacher reads three short descriptions twice (a famous person, a place in the city, an object) and students write the word and underline the clues. Then they say which clues helped. If a recording is available, use a places or people recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Photo detective: show five photos of unknown people. In groups students use might, must and can't to guess jobs and personalities ("He might be a doctor. She can't be a teacher.") and explain the clues with who or which.
lp.prod: Describe and identify: each student chooses a person, a place and an object that are important to them and writes three clues with relative clauses. In groups of four they read the clues and others guess. Then the group chooses the cleverest set of clues for the class.
lp.rw: Read the short text about Coca Cola (Reading task in the kit) and underline every relative clause and every place where who, which or that could be added. Then write 8 definitions of people, places or things using who, which, that or where.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write two definitions with relative clauses ("A librarian is a person who works with books. A cafe is a place where people meet.") and hand them in.
g: Describe words with relative clauses without saying them.
Guess people from photos with might and must.
Solve riddles with who, which and where.
Join two sentences with a relative pronoun.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short riddle about a place in Oujda using at least three relative clauses.
Support: give a chart for who, which, where and whose with a sentence for each.
hw: Write 8 definitions of people, places or things using who, which or where.
Find two English photos of unknown people and write what they might be and why.
Write a short description of your favourite place using where and which.
lp.tip: Relative clauses also feed PET writing, where students must describe things when they do not know a word, so teach "a thing that..." as a communication strategy. Check for the extra pronoun (the man who he works).

weeks.obj: tell and write a clear narrative with past simple, past continuous and past perfect, linked with time expressions
weeks.lang: narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect); linkers (suddenly, meanwhile, as soon as, after, by the time, in the end); building suspense; PET Part 2 story or article
weeks.res: Past perfect: Explanations; Past perfect simple worksheet
weeks.act: Story from six pictures; story train; anecdote exchange; story editing
weeks.hw: write a 100-word story that begins with a given sentence

skills.L: Listen to a short story and note the order of events
skills.S: Tell a short story with linkers and a surprise
skills.R: Read a story and find the three narrative tenses
skills.W: Write a story of about 100 words

lp.wu: Story dice (without dice): the teacher gives each pair three random words (key, rain, airport) and they have two minutes to make up a mini story and tell it to another pair.
wuAlt: Alibi recall: students retell the alibi story from Week 3 in two sentences.
One-word story: the group builds a story one word at a time.
lp.pres: Tell a short story with three tenses ("When I arrived at the station, the train had already left. It was raining and I was carrying two bags. Suddenly, a man offered me a lift...") and ask which tense gives the background, which the main events and which the earlier events. Build a story map on the board: setting (past continuous), problem (past simple), earlier event (past perfect), solution, ending. Teach linkers (suddenly, while, as soon as, by the time, in the end, luckily) and ways to add detail.
presAlt: Use the Student Book Unit 12A past perfect page from the kit as the source of examples.
Read a short story with the verbs in brackets and students choose the right tense.
lp.prac: Story from six pictures: in groups of three, students arrange six pictures of a journey (a missed train, an unexpected meeting, a lost bag, a taxi, a surprise at the hotel) and tell the story, using each tense at least twice. Then a controlled exercise with eight verbs to put into the correct narrative tense.
pracAlt: Past perfect or past simple? Choose in ten sentences with before, after and by the time.
Linker sort: put twelve linkers into categories (time, contrast, result).
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short story (about 150 words) twice with a surprise ending, for example a lost wallet returned by a taxi driver. Students number nine events in the correct order and say how the story ends. If a recording is available, use a storytelling recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Story train: pairs write the first sentence of a story and pass it on. The next pair adds a sentence with a different tense and a linker, and so on until each paper has six sentences. The pairs read the finished stories aloud.
lp.prod: Anecdote exchange: students prepare a two-minute true or invented story about a day they will not forget (a journey, a mistake, a surprise). They tell it in groups of three and the listeners ask two questions and note the tenses. The group chooses the best story to tell the class.
lp.rw: Read the true story "Aaron Ralston's story" (in the kit) and underline each narrative tense in a different colour. Then plan a story with the map from the board and write the first half (50 words) using a given opening sentence ("It was the worst day of my life, but it ended well.").
lp.st: Exit ticket: write three linked sentences from your story, with one past perfect ("I had left my wallet at home, so I...") and hand them in.
g: Make a story from three random words.
Order pictures and tell the story.
Add a sentence with a linker and pass on.
Tell a true story and answer two questions.
diff: Fast finishers: rewrite the story from the point of view of another character.
Support: give a story map with sentence starters and a list of ten linkers.
hw: Write a 100-word story that begins with a given sentence.
Read a short story or fable from the Reading tasks and underline the tenses.
Retell a story that someone told you this week using the past simple, continuous and perfect.
lp.tip: This is the PET Part 2 story task: look for a clear beginning, a problem, a solution and good linking. Do not push past perfect too hard; make sure students first control past simple and continuous. Do not ask for private stories.

weeks.obj: report what people said and asked, and pass on messages and news with a suitable backshift
weeks.lang: reported statements (He said he was tired; She told me she had a meeting); reported questions (He asked if I wanted... / where I lived); said/told/asked; time and place changes (today -> that day, here -> there)
weeks.res: Reported speech: statements (PowerPoint); Reported speech: yes/no questions (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Message relay; reporting an interview; news quote exchange; error clinic
weeks.hw: write a report of a short conversation using reported speech

skills.L: Listen to a short conversation and write what each person said as reported speech
skills.S: Report messages and questions accurately to a third person
skills.R: Read a short interview and rewrite quotes as reported speech
skills.W: Write a report of a conversation

lp.wu: Message relay in rows: the teacher whispers a message to the first student in each row ("The meeting is at ten tomorrow and bring your laptop."). Each student passes it on with "She said...". The last student writes it and the class compares.
wuAlt: Quick pairs: tell your partner something you said to someone today, and they report it to the group.
Memory test: students read five direct quotes and then say them as reported speech without looking.
lp.pres: Write three direct quotes on the board ("I'm tired." "I will call you." "Where do you work?") and then the reported forms ("She said she was tired. He said he would call me. She asked where I worked."). Elicit the backshift (present -> past, will -> would, can -> could, have -> had) and the word order in reported questions (no inversion, no do). Teach said vs told + person, and the changes to time words (today -> that day, tomorrow -> the next day, here -> there).
presAlt: Use the Reported Speech Explained resource (English Grammar folder in the kit) for the table of changes.
Use the Learn English 2026 Reported Speech introduction video from the kit and pause to write the changes.
lp.prac: Interview and report: pairs write five questions for an interview (work, plans, tech, free time) and take notes of the answers. They then report to a new partner ("Aya said she worked at a clinic. I asked her if she liked it."). Next, a controlled exercise: rewrite ten direct sentences and questions as reported speech.
pracAlt: Sentence transformation: pairs rewrite eight statements as reported speech and swap to check.
Tense changes table: complete a chart showing how each tense shifts.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short conversation between a manager and an employee about a schedule change twice. Students write four sentences using "He said..." and "She asked...". If a recording is available, use a work conversation from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Gossip chain: the teacher gives each group a short piece of news on a card ("My neighbour said the supermarket would open at 8."). Students pass it on, the last person writes it, and the groups compare how much the message changed.
lp.prod: News reporters: pairs interview a classmate about a topic (a recent trip, a change at work, a challenge), then write a news report with direct quotes and reported speech. They present it to the class as a short broadcast with "According to Karim..." and "He told us that...".
lp.rw: Read a short news article with direct quotes (Guardian: Facebook, intermediate, in the kit) and rewrite six of the quotes as reported speech. Then write a short report of a conversation from your week using said, told and asked.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one reported statement and one reported question about something someone said to you today ("My colleague said she was leaving early. He asked me if I wanted to join.") and hand them in.
g: Pass a message and compare it at the end.
See how a news item changes when it is reported.
Interview a partner and report to another.
Prepare a broadcast with reported speech.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short newspaper article with three reported quotes.
Support: give a table of backshift changes and a model reported question.
hw: Write a report of a short conversation using reported speech.
Report three things people said to you this week in writing.
Read a short English interview and underline the quotes.
lp.tip: Report real daily messages (work, family, phone) rather than abstract sentences. Teach the question word order carefully, because the typical error is "She asked me where do I live".

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students report what a family member said about their Ramadan plans ("My mother said she was going to cook harira. My brother told me he would fast for the first time.").
occ.hw: Write 5 sentences reporting what a family member said about their plans for Ramadan.

weeks.theme: Media, news and how things have changed
weeks.obj: talk about media habits then and now with used to, and give an opinion on a news story with a reason and an example
weeks.lang: used to / didn't use to / would for past habits; media vocabulary (headline, article, reporter, channel, platform, fake news); opinion + reason + example (I think... because... For example...)
weeks.res: Used to, get used to, be used to (worksheet); Did you use to...? (used to)
weeks.act: News panel discussion; headline matching; then and now interviews; listening with viewpoints
weeks.hw: write an opinion paragraph about a news topic

skills.L: Listen to people talk about how they get their news and note what has changed
skills.S: Compare media habits then and now and give an opinion with an example
skills.R: Read a short article about the history of television and find examples of used to
skills.W: Write an opinion paragraph on a news topic

lp.wu: Then and now: students think about how they got news and entertainment ten years ago. In pairs they say three sentences with "I used to..." ("I used to watch the news on TV at eight o'clock. Now I check my phone.").
wuAlt: Two truths and a lie about media habits with used to.
Quick quiz: what year was the first smartphone? Answer in a sentence with used to.
lp.pres: Show a photo of a family around a TV in the 1990s and a family on phones today. Elicit "People used to watch TV together. Now they use their phones." Teach used to + base for past states and habits that are no longer true, didn't use to + base, and Did you use to...? Contrast with the past simple (a single action) and with would for repeated habits. Teach media vocabulary: headline, article, reporter, channel, platform, source, fake news, subscribe.
presAlt: Use the Used to worksheets in the kit as the source of examples ("Then and Now", "What's changed").
Read a short text about how television has changed.
lp.prac: Then and now interviews: pairs receive a card about a topic (shopping, getting news, listening to music, communication, studying) and interview each other about how it was ten years ago and how it is now ("Did you use to...?"). Then a controlled exercise: choose used to or the past simple in ten sentences.
pracAlt: Sentence completion: finish ten sentences with used to and a real example.
Vocabulary match: match media words to definitions.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short monologues twice (a grandfather describing how he used to get news and a young person describing how she gets news now). Students note two differences and each person's opinion. If a recording is available, use a media recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Headline matching: students match six headlines to opening sentences of articles and say which headlines they would read and why.
lp.prod: News panel: groups of four choose one news topic from cards (a new law, a sports result, a technology launch, a local event) and hold a three-minute panel. Each person gives an opinion with a reason and an example ("I think the law is good because it protects workers. For example..."). Another group listens and asks one question.
lp.rw: Read a short article about the history of television or the media (about 130 words) and underline the examples of used to. Then write an opinion paragraph of 6-8 sentences about a news topic with a clear reason and an example.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence with used to about media and one opinion with a reason ("I used to read newspapers. I think social media is faster because...") and hand them in.
g: Compare habits ten years ago and now.
Choose the right form in short texts.
Match headlines to the first lines of articles.
Give opinions with a reason and an example.
Decide which headlines are likely to be false and why.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short blog post about how your habits have changed with five used to sentences.
Support: give sentence frames with used to and a media word bank.
hw: Write an opinion paragraph of 6 to 8 sentences about a news topic.
Interview an older relative about how they used to get news or entertainment and write three sentences.
Read a short news article in English and write the headline and two opinions about it.
lp.tip: Real news topics will naturally lead to strong opinions, so set simple rules for respectful discussion and keep sensitive subjects out of panel cards. Check the form didn't use to (not didn't used to).

weeks.obj: use skimming, scanning and careful reading strategies to answer PET-style reading tasks under time pressure
weeks.lang: reading strategies (skim for the gist, scan for names and numbers, read for detail, check distractors); reading texts: notices, messages, short profiles, articles; linking words and reference words
weeks.res: PET Advice: Do's and Don'ts; Objective PET Student's Book
weeks.act: Timed PET reading parts; strategy debrief; answer justification pairs; gapped text and cloze clinic
weeks.hw: complete one timed PET reading part and record your score

skills.L: Listen to a short reading strategy briefing and note three tips
skills.S: Justify an answer to a partner using evidence from the text
skills.R: Practise skimming, scanning and detailed reading in timed PET parts
skills.W: Write a short summary of a text in one or two sentences

lp.wu: Skim in thirty seconds: the teacher shows a short text for thirty seconds and then hides it. Students write what the text is (a notice, an email, an advert), who wrote it and the main message. They compare answers and then check.
wuAlt: Scanning race: the teacher projects a timetable or an advert and asks quick questions ("When does the last bus leave?" "How much is the family ticket?") for the pairs to find.
Word search for numbers and dates in a short article.
lp.pres: Present the six types of reading task in PET (short notices and messages, matching descriptions of people to short texts, a long text with multiple choice, a gapped text with sentences removed, a multiple-choice cloze, and an open cloze). For each give one strategy: read the question first, underline key words, find the part of the text, eliminate wrong options, check grammar and meaning for gaps. Model the process on one notice using a think-aloud.
presAlt: Use PET Advice: Do's and Don'ts in the kit as a handout and read it together.
Use the Objective PET Student's Book reading unit from the kit for another task example.
lp.prac: Timed practice, Parts 1 and 2: pairs of students do the first two parts of a PET reading test (the PET (B1) Reading Test files in the kit) with a timer of eight minutes, marking each other's answers. They then underline the text evidence for each answer and explain to their partner why a distractor is wrong.
pracAlt: Parts 3 and 4 for stronger groups: a longer text with five questions and a gapped text with sentences to put back.
Matching practice with an easier set from the Reading tasks.
lp.ls: Listening for strategy: the teacher reads aloud two short reading strategy tips as if they were a podcast ("Always read the question first. Underline one word in each question.") and students take notes and compare. Then they say which tip they will use first. Use the strategy list in the PET folder as a source.
lp.re: Gap fill clinic: students complete a short cloze of eight gaps in pairs. Before they write they decide whether each gap is a verb form, a preposition, a linker or a pronoun, then discuss and check.
lp.prod: Answer justification circles: in groups of four, each student takes one question from a PET reading part they have just done and explains in 30 seconds how they found the answer and why the other options are wrong. The group votes on the best explanation.
lp.rw: Read the article "The future of food" (Reading task in the kit) and write a summary in one or two sentences. Then answer five true/false questions you write for it and underline the text evidence for each.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the reading strategy you will use first in the exam and one question word you will underline ("I will read the question first and underline the key word.") and hand it in.
g: Name the text type and the message after a quick look.
Find facts in a timetable or advert.
Underline the proof for each answer.
Decide the grammar type of each gap before filling it.
Defend an answer to a group.
diff: Fast finishers: write three PET-style multiple-choice questions for a short text.
Support: give a strategy card (read the question, find the key word, scan, check) and an easier text first.
hw: Complete one timed PET reading part and record your score and time.
Read one short English article each day this week and write one-line summaries.
Write five new words from the article with a sentence for each.
lp.tip: Teach exam strategy as a skill, not a trick: for adults, anxiety is the main barrier. Keep timing realistic (about one minute per question) and always ask students to justify answers with the text. Record the timed scores this week.

Reading: How has technology improved healthcare

weeks.obj: use prediction and note-taking strategies to answer PET-style listening tasks
weeks.lang: listening strategies (read the questions first, predict, listen for key words, check distractors); note-taking symbols; numbers, prices, times and dates; paraphrase and distractors
weeks.res: PET Teacher's book (listening scripts and tasks); Objective PET Student's Book
weeks.act: Prediction before listening; two-stage listening tasks; transcript analysis; note-taking practice
weeks.hw: complete one PET-style listening task and record your score

skills.L: Listen to short PET-style recordings and answer multiple-choice questions
skills.S: Compare answers and justify choices in pairs
skills.R: Read a transcript and underline the words that give the answer
skills.W: Write notes from a short talk

lp.wu: Listening for numbers: the teacher reads ten numbers, prices and times at natural speed ("Ten forty-five." "Fourteen ninety-nine." "Five-fifteen.") and students write them as digits. Then pairs check and note which were hard.
wuAlt: Predict the word: the teacher reads a sentence with a gap ("The train leaves from platform ___.") and students say what kind of word could fit.
Dictation of three short travel announcements.
lp.pres: Introduce the four parts of PET Listening: short recordings with pictures, longer recordings with multiple choice, a gap-fill with notes, and a longer conversation. Show a sample question with options, read the question first and underline key words, and predict what you will hear. Show how distractors work with an example ("I'll take the bus, no, wait, I'll go by train."). Teach note symbols (arrows, ticks, abbreviations) for speed.
presAlt: Use the Listening tasks slideshow from the Listening folder as a model.
Show a sample recording script and underline the key words that give the answer.
lp.prac: Prediction before listening: in pairs, students read the questions and options for a multiple-choice task and write down what they expect to hear for each one. The teacher then reads or plays the recording (twice) and students check, marking correct predictions and distractors that appeared.
pracAlt: Cloze with gaps: students listen and fill the gaps in a transcript.
Matching task: match five speakers to five opinions.
lp.ls: Two-stage listening: first listening, students answer by instinct and compare with a partner; second listening, they check and change answers. The teacher uses a script from the PET Teacher's book in the kit, or a short podcast from the Podcasts folder in the kit. Then the class discusses which words gave the answer.
lp.re: Distractor hunt: the teacher reads five short dialogues where the speaker changes their mind (flight times, prices, meeting places). Students write the first and the final answer and underline the words that signal the change ("Actually...", "No, wait...").
lp.prod: Note-taking talk: in groups of three, one student gives a one-minute talk about a place or event and the others take notes on a grid (who, where, when, two details, opinion). They compare notes and decide which details were most important, then swap roles.
lp.rw: Read a transcript of a short listening (about 150 words) and underline the words that give each answer, marking each distractor with a cross. Then write a short set of notes from a one-minute talk the teacher reads aloud.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you will do before the recording starts and one thing you will do when you do not understand a word ("I will read the questions first. I will keep listening and not stop.") and hand it in.
g: Write numbers, prices and times from natural speech.
Guess the missing word type before listening.
Write notes from a one-minute talk.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue with two distractors for another pair.
Support: give a gapped transcript and a list of the missing words.
hw: Complete one PET-style listening task and record your score.
Listen to a two-minute English podcast (Podcasts folder) and write five notes.
Listen to a short recording from the Listening folder and write down three numbers or times.
lp.tip: Many students panic and try to catch every word. Teach them to listen for the answer, not for everything. Use the Listening folder for short mp3 practice and always give a second listening during practice. Record the listening scores this week.

Podcast: LearnEnglish Podcasts, Series 01 Episode 01 (British Council)

weeks.obj: take part in a conversation with a partner, agree and disagree politely, keep a conversation going, and describe a photo
weeks.lang: interaction language (What do you think? I agree up to a point; Why not...? Shall we...?); asking for repetition and clarification (Could you say that again?); indirect questions (Could you tell me where...?); question tags (It's nice, isn't it?)
weeks.res: Video: English conversation skills, how to give and ask for opinions; Speaking test: mock exam
weeks.act: PET speaking parts rehearsal; discussion cards with roles; photo description; peer rubric check
weeks.hw: record a two-minute speaking task and note two things to improve

skills.L: Listen to two speakers in a discussion and note the language they use to agree and disagree
skills.S: Interact with a partner by agreeing, disagreeing and asking follow-up questions
skills.R: Read a model dialogue and underline the interaction phrases
skills.W: Write four sentences using indirect questions and tags

lp.wu: Small talk speed round: students stand or sit in two rows facing each other and talk to a new partner every minute (the weather, weekend plans, the news, a recent film). They must ask at least one follow-up question each round.
wuAlt: Conversation question cards from the kit: each pair picks a card and asks all the questions.
Name five ways to start a conversation and then try one.
lp.pres: Present the four parts of PET Speaking: Part 1 personal questions with the examiner; Part 2 a simulated situation with a partner using pictures; Part 3 a one-minute photo description; Part 4 a conversation about a related topic. For each, model good interaction: asking your partner a question, giving a reason, agreeing or disagreeing, paraphrasing when you do not know a word. Teach useful language and polite indirect questions and tags.
presAlt: Use the mock speaking exam in the kit and read the examiner script with a volunteer.
Show a short dialogue that has no interaction and ask students to improve it.
lp.prac: Discussion cards with roles: groups of three take a discussion card (e.g., a school trip, a job, a city) and one student is the chair, one is the agree person and one is the disagree person. They hold a three-minute conversation and then switch roles. The teacher uses a checklist: interacts with the partner, develops ideas, uses polite language.
pracAlt: Suggest and decide: pairs decide on a gift using picture prompts, as in PET Part 2.
Photo description: one student describes a photo for one minute while the partner listens for two details.
lp.ls: Teacher reads or plays a short discussion between two speakers twice (about a weekend plan or a new phone) and students note the phrases used to agree, disagree and suggest. If a recording is available, use a speaking recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Photo challenge: students describe a photo for one minute using "In the picture I can see..., She looks..., I think they are..." while a partner times them and counts the number of descriptive words.
lp.prod: Retry rounds: pairs take a PET Part 2 task and complete it twice. After the first round, the observers give two pieces of feedback using the rubric (interaction, vocabulary, pronunciation, grammar) and the pair repeats the task and improves. Then the teacher asks a PET Part 4-style question to the whole group.
lp.rw: Write four sentences with indirect questions and tags ("Could you tell me where the post office is? It's a nice day, isn't it?") and read a short model dialogue, underlining all interaction phrases. Then write a short dialogue of six lines using five of them.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one phrase to agree and one phrase to disagree politely that you will use next time ("I see what you mean, but..." "That's true, and...") and hand them in.
g: Talk to a new partner every minute with follow-up questions.
Describe a photo for one minute.
Turn direct questions into indirect questions.
diff: Fast finishers: lead a four-minute discussion on a topic card with two prepared questions.
Support: give phrase cards for agreeing, disagreeing, asking for repetition and suggesting.
hw: Record a two-minute speaking task and note two things to improve.
Describe a photo from your phone aloud for one minute and ask a friend to give feedback.
Write six indirect questions for a hotel receptionist or an office.
lp.tip: Peer observation works best with a short rubric of four criteria and one specific comment per criterion. Always start with strengths. Many students speak in short answers: coach them to add a reason or example.

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: pairs tell each other about their best Eid memory and use follow-up questions to keep the conversation going ("Really? What happened next? Who was with you?").
occ.hw: Write a short paragraph about your best Eid memory.

weeks.obj: write an email and an article or story of about 100 words with a clear structure and linking, following PET conventions
weeks.lang: PET Writing Part 1 (email: answer all content points) and Part 2 (article or story); paragraphing; linkers (but, however, because, so, although, then); register (neutral and informal); self-checking
weeks.res: B1 Preliminary Writing Part 1: lesson plan; B1 Preliminary Writing: understanding the rubric (lesson plan)
weeks.act: Guided PET writing task; checklist peer review; model comparison; rewriting
weeks.hw: complete one PET writing task of about 100 words

skills.L: Listen to the teacher read a model email and note the content points
skills.S: Plan a text aloud with a partner before writing
skills.R: Read two model answers and compare their quality
skills.W: Write an email or article of about 100 words

lp.wu: Quick plan: the teacher gives a short email invitation ("Come to my cousin's wedding in Berkane. Can you come? What should I wear?") and pairs list the content points they must answer in 90 seconds.
wuAlt: Linker race: teams write sentences with because, so, but, however and although for one topic.
Unscramble the email: put the sentences of a short email in order.
lp.pres: Show a PET Part 1 task: an email from a friend with notes in the margin (about a school trip) and four content points to include. Elicit that students must answer all points in about 100 words, with a clear opening and closing. Compare a good answer and a weak one for content, organisation and language. Introduce the Part 2 choices (an article or a story) and show how the opening sentence and the ending help. Display a checklist: all points answered, 100 words, paragraphs, linkers, correct tenses, spelling.
presAlt: Use the PET writing lesson plan documents in the PET Useful Documents folder (kit).
Show the 2020 tips video for B1 Preliminary Writing Part 1 and pause for the main tips.
lp.prac: Guided writing: students plan a PET Part 1 email in pairs (four points, opening, closing) and then write alone for ten minutes. The teacher circulates to help with content and word count, and notes common errors for the whole class to see.
pracAlt: Sentence frames for each content point and a model first sentence.
Paragraph order: put a jumbled model email in order and label each content point.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a model PET email aloud twice (a friend replying about weekend plans) and students note the four content points and the closing line. They then compare with the written model. No recording is needed for this task.
lp.re: Error clinic: the teacher shows six anonymous sentences from the students' drafts. In pairs, students correct them and decide which error type each shows (tense, preposition, article, word order, spelling).
lp.prod: Checklist peer review: students swap emails and use the checklist (points answered, about 100 words, opening and closing, linking, tenses) to give two comments. The writer then improves the draft in class and reads one improved sentence to the group.
lp.rw: Read two model answers for the same PET task (one 3-band, one 5-band) and underline what makes the stronger answer better (linkers, variety, accurate tenses). Then rewrite one paragraph of your own text using at least two of those features.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one feature of a good PET email you will use next time and one error you will check for ("I will use linkers. I will check my verb tense.") and hand it in.
g: List the content points for a task in 90 seconds.
Write sentences using linkers within a time limit.
Put a jumbled email in order.
Give two comments using a checklist.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short article with a title, a hook and a conclusion on a topic of your choice.
Support: give a template for the email with sentence starters for each content point.
hw: Complete one PET writing task of about 100 words and hand it in.
Write a story that starts "I opened the door and..." in about 100 words.
Read a model PET article and underline the linkers.
lp.tip: Adults often write too much or too little: practise counting words and plan before writing. Ask them to answer all content points because missing a point costs marks. Return corrections as coded feedback (T for tense, P for preposition) so they correct themselves.

weeks.obj: talk and write about technology and digital habits, and use verb patterns correctly after common verbs
weeks.lang: verb patterns (enjoy/avoid/stop + -ing; want/decide/hope + to; remember/forget/try/stop + -ing or to with different meanings); technology vocabulary (device, app, password, update, privacy, online shopping); advantages and disadvantages
weeks.res: Gerund and Infinitive Master; Lesson plan: Technology, lesson 1
weeks.act: Tech debate (for and against); verb pattern sorting; digital habits survey and report
weeks.hw: write an 80-word email or post about your digital habits

skills.L: Listen to a short talk about technology and note the opinions
skills.S: Debate the advantages and disadvantages of a technology
skills.R: Read a short article about a digital detox and find verb patterns
skills.W: Write a short post about my digital habits

lp.wu: Phone survey: students rank their five most used apps on a slip and compare with a partner: "I spend a lot of time using...". Then groups of four count the top three apps in the group.
wuAlt: Tech word race: teams list as many technology words as possible in two minutes.
Two truths and a lie about your digital habits.
lp.pres: Write sentence pairs on the board: "I stopped smoking" / "I stopped to smoke", "I remember locking the door" / "I remember to lock the door". Elicit the verb patterns: some verbs take -ing (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest), some take to + base (want, decide, hope, plan, need, manage), and some change meaning (stop, remember, forget, try). Give a quick table and practise with technology examples ("I forgot to charge my phone." "I tried turning it off and on.").
presAlt: Use the Gerunds worksheet in the Worksheets folder (kit) to show common verb patterns.
Use the Student Book Unit 7A-B pages from the kit for the rule boxes.
lp.prac: Verb pattern sort: pairs sort twenty verbs into three columns (+ -ing, + to, both) and write one sentence for each. Then a controlled exercise: complete ten sentences about technology with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
pracAlt: Choose the correct form (ten sentences) and check with a partner.
Dominoes: match the beginning of each sentence to the correct verb pattern.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short talk twice by a person describing a digital detox (a week without social media) with benefits, difficulties and a plan. Students tick the benefits and difficulties on a grid and note one verb pattern each time they hear one. If a recording is available, use a technology recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Quick questions: pairs take turns asking each other questions that need a verb pattern ("Do you enjoy using social media? Have you ever forgotten to charge your phone?"). They note one answer to report back.
lp.prod: Tech debate: groups of four prepare a debate on a motion (Smartphones make us less social; Online shopping is better than shopping in a store; Children should not have phones until 14). Two students argue for and two against, using at least four verb patterns, and the class votes.
lp.rw: Read the article on screen-related eye damage (Reading task in the kit) and underline all verb patterns. Then write an 80-word email or post to a friend about your digital habits and one change you want to make.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence with a verb + -ing and one with a verb + to about technology ("I enjoy watching videos. I decided to delete the app.") and hand them in.
g: Rank apps and compare in groups.
Sort verbs by the pattern that follows.
Argue for or against a motion.
Ask questions with verb patterns and report the answer.
Plan a day without a phone and explain why.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short report on the group's digital habits with percentages.
Support: give a verb pattern table and sentence stems.
hw: Write an 80-word email or post about your digital habits.
Keep a screen-time diary for a day and write three sentences about what you found.
Read a short article about technology in English and list the verb patterns.
lp.tip: Verb patterns are learned by exposure: recycle the same lists each week. Keep debates respectful and prepare roles so that quieter students have a clear part. Focus on one or two meaning changes (stop, remember) rather than the whole list.

weeks.obj: explain environmental problems and their causes and effects, and propose solutions for the community
weeks.lang: cause and effect (because of, as a result, so, so that, in order to); quantifiers (too much/too many, enough, not enough, a few, a little); environment vocabulary (pollution, waste, recycling, drought, renewable energy); conditionals for solutions
weeks.res: Writing unit: cause and effect (PowerPoint); Too, Very, Enough (grammar sheets)
weeks.act: Cause-effect chains; problem-solution proposal in teams; recycling discussion; presentation
weeks.hw: write a proposal paragraph of 100 words for a community project

skills.L: Listen to a short talk about an environmental problem and note the cause and effect
skills.S: Present a problem and a solution to a group
skills.R: Read a short article about plastic and find causes, effects and solutions
skills.W: Write a proposal for a community project

lp.wu: Good or bad habit: the teacher reads ten habits (leaving the tap running, taking a bag to the market, buying bottled water, using a bike) and students decide in pairs whether each helps or harms the environment, then explain why.
wuAlt: Brainstorm: pairs write ten environment words in two minutes.
Quick quiz: how long does a plastic bottle take to break down?
lp.pres: Show a photo of a polluted beach or a drought-hit field and elicit the causes and effects. Put on the board: "There is too much plastic in the sea because people throw it away." "Because of drought, farmers have fewer crops." "We should recycle so that there is less waste." Teach cause and effect connectors (because, because of, so, as a result, so that, in order to), the quantifiers (too much/many, enough, not enough, a few, a little) and the pattern for solutions (If we reduce..., we will...; We could...; One solution is...).
presAlt: Use the quantifiers worksheets from the kit (Expressing Quantity) to present too much/too many/enough.
Read a short article about plastic and underline the causes and effects.
lp.prac: Cause-effect chains: pairs get a problem card (water shortage, plastic waste, traffic pollution, food waste) and build a chain of three links with so and as a result ("There is not enough water, so farmers use less. As a result, prices rise."). Then a controlled exercise on because / because of and the quantifiers.
pracAlt: Matching: match each cause with its effect and connect them with a linker.
Quantifier gap-fill: choose too much, too many, enough or not enough in ten sentences.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short talk twice about water or waste in a city (the problem, two causes and one solution). Students note them in a three-column table. If a recording is available, use an environment recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Solutions auction: teams get five solution ideas (a bottle deposit, free buses, tree planting, fines for littering, a school recycling club) and bid dirhams for the ones they think work best, defending their choice.
lp.prod: Community project proposal: in teams of four, students choose a problem in Oujda (waste, water, traffic, noise) and prepare a three-minute proposal: the problem, causes, effects, and a plan with who, what and when. Each team presents and the class asks one question and votes for the most realistic plan.
lp.rw: Read a short article about plastic or recycling (from the Reading tasks, The Environment folder) and underline causes, effects and solutions. Then write a proposal paragraph of about 100 words for a community project using at least four linkers.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one cause, one effect and one solution for an environmental problem in your city ("There is too much traffic, so the air is dirty. We should use buses.") and hand them in.
g: Decide whether habits help or harm and explain.
Build a chain with so and as a result.
Bid for the best ideas and defend them.
Choose the right quantifier in a short text.
Present a community plan and take questions.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short letter to the local council with a request and two reasons.
Support: give a table of linkers and a proposal template (problem, cause, effect, solution).
hw: Write a proposal paragraph of about 100 words for a community project.
Interview a neighbour about an environmental problem in your area and write three sentences.
Find one English article about an environmental topic and underline the cause and effect linkers.
lp.tip: Connect to local problems (water, waste, traffic) so that adults see themselves as part of the solution. Check the difference between too much and too many and the use of because of + noun. Avoid political arguments by focusing on practical steps.
