weeks.obj: complete a shortened PET-style test under timed conditions and reflect on strategies
weeks.lang: all A2-B1 skills: PET reading, writing, listening and speaking tasks
weeks.res: PET (B1) Reading Test 03; A2 English Reading Test 03
weeks.act: Mini test administration; self-marking; strategy reflection sheet; speaking pairs
weeks.hw: complete the strategy reflection sheet and choose one skill to improve

skills.L: Listen to short recordings and answer multiple-choice questions
skills.S: Complete a paired speaking task
skills.R: Read short texts and answer matching and multiple-choice questions
skills.W: Write an email of about 100 words

lp.wu: Exam routine warm-up: the teacher reviews the exam strategies from earlier weeks on cards (read the question first, underline key words, check the time, answer every question). Students choose their top three strategies and say when they will use them.
wuAlt: Pairs quickly test each other on exam vocabulary (task types, phrases).
Breathing and focus: one minute of quiet before the test starts.
lp.pres: Hand out the mini test (a shortened PET-style paper of the reading parts) and explain the format, the timing and the answer sheet. Read the instructions aloud and model the first question. Students then start the reading paper under timed conditions (20 minutes) using a mini test from the PET (B1) Reading Tests in the kit.
presAlt: Use a selected set of four tasks from the PET Reading and Writing paper in the kit.
Use a printed test from Tests/Reading tests for a lower-pressure paper.
lp.prac: Writing task: students write a PET Part 1 email of about 100 words (20 minutes), using a task from the PET folder and the checklist from Week 24. They count words and check tenses before handing in.
pracAlt: A PET Part 2 article or story as an alternative.
A short transformation exercise for students who finish early.
lp.ls: Listening test: the teacher reads or plays about eight short tasks (short recordings with a picture choice, a longer recording with multiple choice, a gap-fill) from the teacher's script in the kit, playing each twice. Students mark their answers on an answer sheet. If a recording is available, use a PET-style task from the PET folder or Listening tasks in the kit.
lp.re: Self-marking: the teacher gives the answers for the reading and listening papers. Students mark their own work, count their score and note the three questions they found hardest and why.
lp.prod: Speaking pairs: the teacher examines pairs for about five minutes (Part 1 personal questions, Part 2 a situation with picture prompts, Part 3 photo description, Part 4 discussion) while the other students complete the strategy sheet in rw. The teacher notes marks on the speaking scale.
lp.rw: Strategy reflection sheet: students record their scores, the strategies they used and what they would change, and set one target skill for the next three weeks.
lp.st: Closing: the teacher thanks the class, explains when feedback will be given and asks for a one-line comment on how they felt about the test. Collect the answer sheets and the reflection sheets.
g: Choose the three most useful exam strategies.
Mark your own paper and analyse errors.
diff: Fast finishers: write three extra PET reading questions for a short text.
Support: allow a word bank for the writing task and a checklist of content points.
hw: Complete the strategy reflection sheet and choose one skill to improve with two specific tasks.
Redo the three questions you found hardest and write why you got them wrong.
Read a short English text and answer five questions about it.
lp.tip: A mini test is a learning tool: use the results to plan the last weeks of the course and to decide who needs extra support for the final assessment. Record the practice test scores this week. Keep the atmosphere calm and supportive.

kit.l: B1 Preliminary Writing Part 1: answer sheet
PET Teacher's book (listening scripts and tasks)

weeks.obj: identify and correct their own most common errors, and use self-correction strategies in speaking and writing
weeks.lang: personal error patterns (verb tense, articles, prepositions, word order, subject-verb agreement, false friends); self-correction strategies; editing checklist
weeks.res: Verb tenses explained (grammar sheet); Simple Past or Present Perfect (grammar sheet)
weeks.act: Error auction from real class work; correction stations; personal error lists; speaking self-repair
weeks.hw: rewrite five corrected sentences and add them to your error log

skills.L: Listen to a short passage with errors and spot the mistakes while reading the text
skills.S: Self-correct during a short talk
skills.R: Read a text with errors and correct them
skills.W: Rewrite sentences and keep an error log

lp.wu: Spot the mistake: the teacher shows ten sentences from the class's real writing (anonymous) on the board, and students correct them in pairs in three minutes. The pair with the most corrections explains one.
wuAlt: Mistake bingo: bingo cards with error types; students tick off when the teacher shows an example.
Error confessions: each student writes the mistake they make most often and compares with a partner.
lp.pres: Present the five most common error types from the class (from the assessment and the mini test, sorted by frequency): tense (present perfect with a finished time), articles (the/a/no article), prepositions (in, on, at; depend on), word order (reported questions, adverbs), and false friends (assist/attend, actually, library). For each, show an example from the class and the correction, and the rule in one sentence. Introduce a code (T, A, P, WO, SP) to mark errors in writing.
presAlt: Use the English Grammar resources in the kit (Mixed Prepositions, Simple Past or Present Perfect) as extra models.
Show the Common English Grammar Mistakes folder (Learn English 2026) as a reference.
lp.prac: Error auction: teams get twenty sentences from class work (half correct, half wrong) and bid on the ones they think are correct. After the auction they fix the wrong ones and give the rule. Points for correct bids and corrections.
pracAlt: Correction stations: four stations (tenses, articles, prepositions, word order) with a short mixed exercise at each; groups rotate every five minutes.
Pairs rewrite a paragraph with ten errors.
lp.ls: Listen and read: the teacher reads aloud a short passage that contains five mistakes (for example, "She has gone there last year.") while students follow a printed copy and tick each error when they hear it. Then they correct it. No recording is needed for this task.
lp.re: Self-repair talk: in pairs, students talk for one minute about last weekend. The partner raises a hand only when the speaker makes a mistake, and the speaker tries to self-correct without help. Swap roles.
lp.prod: Personal error lists: each student looks through their last two written tasks and lists their five most common mistakes, with the correct form and a rule. In groups of three they compare lists and write one short paragraph that uses their corrections, then check each other's paragraphs.
lp.rw: Read a text about a trip with twelve errors and correct them using the code from the board. Then rewrite five of your own sentences with errors, and add them to your error log with the rule.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the error you will watch for this week and the correct form ("I will check: 'I have been there last year' -> 'I went there last year.'") and hand it in.
g: Correct real sentences from class work.
Bid on correct sentences and fix wrong ones.
Notice and fix your own errors.
Keep a personal list of mistakes and rules.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short quiz on the class's five common errors for another group.
Support: give a correction code chart and a rule card for each error type.
hw: Rewrite five corrected sentences and add them to your error log.
Find three of your own errors in last week's writing and correct them with the rule.
Write a short paragraph and underline the grammar you are unsure about.
lp.tip: Use anonymous examples from real student work so no one is embarrassed. Group errors by cause (first language, overgeneralisation) and teach one rule at a time. Good adults often make fossilised errors, so patience and repetition are essential. Include French and Arabic influences without judgement.

weeks.obj: review the year's grammar and skills through stations and speaking circles, and prepare for the final assessment
weeks.lang: all year outcomes: tenses, modals, conditionals, passive, reported speech, relative clauses, verb patterns, comparison, linking
weeks.res: Grammar revision: miscellaneous (tenses, comparatives, make or do); Verb tenses explained (grammar sheet)
weeks.act: Grammar station carousel; speaking circles with rotating topics; team quiz; checklist review
weeks.hw: complete the pre-assessment checklist and choose two areas to revise

skills.L: Listen to short clues at the quiz stations and write the answers
skills.S: Speak for two minutes on rotating topics with follow-up questions
skills.R: Read short texts at the stations and correct errors
skills.W: Write short answers and sentences at the stations

lp.wu: Grammar speed dating: students sit in two lines facing each other. The teacher puts a grammar prompt on the board (present perfect, conditionals, passive, reported speech, comparatives). Each pair has 90 seconds to say one sentence about their own life for the prompt, then one line moves.
wuAlt: Year in one minute: each student lists three things they can do now that they could not do in October.
Memory chain: recall the topic of each month in order.
lp.pres: Introduce the carousel: six stations (tenses, modals and advice, conditionals, passive and reported speech, relative clauses and verb patterns, comparison and linking) with a task card and an answer key. Explain the rotation (8 minutes per station), the roles (reader, writer, checker) and the points. Show a completed card as an example.
presAlt: Recap the year with a one-page map on the board listing each unit and the key grammar.
Pairs choose the three areas they most want to revise and begin there.
lp.prac: Grammar station carousel: groups of three rotate through six stations, each with a short mixed exercise (gap-fill, error correction, transformation, quick speaking task). They mark each station against the key and record their scores on a tracker.
pracAlt: Teams make a quiz question for each station for another team.
Self-check: students complete a short grammar test from the English Grammar folder and check it.
lp.ls: Listening quiz: the teacher reads ten short clues twice (about people, places, things from the year's topics) and students write the answers. If a recording is available, use a short recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Quick error race: the teacher shows five incorrect sentences and teams race to correct them. The first team with a correct answer gets a point.
lp.prod: Speaking circles: students sit in two circles of five or six with a topic card (work and careers, technology, travel experiences, the environment, customs, plans for the future). They speak for two minutes with follow-up questions from the group, then the circles rotate to a new topic. The teacher listens for tenses and linking, and notes strengths.
lp.rw: Review writing: students write a short paragraph of 80 to 100 words about what they have learned this year using at least five different structures (present perfect, a conditional, a passive, reported speech, a relative clause). Then they exchange paragraphs and tick the structures.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you are proud of and one area to revise before the final ("I can now write an email. I want to practise reported questions.") and hand it in.
g: Say a sentence for each prompt with a new partner.
Compete with questions from every unit.
Speak on rotating topics with follow-up questions.
Correct sentences before the other teams.
diff: Fast finishers: design a station task for a topic of your choice.
Support: give a one-page summary of the main grammar points with an example for each.
hw: Complete the pre-assessment checklist and choose two areas to revise.
Write a one-page summary of the grammar you find hardest and one example sentence for each.
Prepare a one-minute talk on a topic from the speaking circles.
lp.tip: Let the carousel results guide the last revision tasks. Balance the stations by difficulty so that no group is stuck. Provide the checklist for the final assessment this week and record who needs extra support.

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: groups plan a short Earth Day action for the American Space (a recycling corner, a clean-up, a plant swap) and present it with First we will..., If we..., and We should... (conditionals and modals already taught).
occ.hw: Write 3 sentences about one green habit you will start.

weeks.obj: show progress at A2-B1 in a final PET-style assessment, receive feedback and celebrate the year
weeks.lang: all year outcomes at A2-B1 level
weeks.res: PET (B1) Reading Test 02; Reading exam (A2-B1)
weeks.act: Final written paper; individual speaking interviews; course feedback; certificates
weeks.hw: write three goals for your English after the course

skills.L: Listen to short recordings and answer multiple-choice questions
skills.S: Complete a speaking interview with a partner
skills.R: Read texts and answer multiple-choice and matching questions
skills.W: Write an email or article of about 100 words

lp.wu: Calm start: the teacher reviews exam routines with the class (time, strategies, answer sheets) and students choose one strategy each from the exam strategy cards. Quick pair chat: "What was your best moment this year?"
wuAlt: Pairs test each other on five key grammar points.
Two minutes of quiet to review personal notes.
lp.pres: Hand out the final reading paper (a shortened PET-style paper with notices, a matching task, a long text and a gapped text). Explain the timing (20 minutes), read the instructions aloud and let students begin. Use a PET (B1) Reading Test from the kit or a teacher-prepared paper.
presAlt: Use a set of tasks from the PET Reading and Writing Paper in the kit.
A shorter paper made from Parts 1, 2 and 4 of a reading test.
lp.prac: Final writing paper: students write a PET Part 1 email and a short Part 2 article or story of about 100 words (20 minutes for both, split as 10 minutes each) using the checklist from the course. They count words and check tenses before handing in.
pracAlt: One longer piece of 100 words instead of two shorter ones.
A transformation exercise for early finishers.
lp.ls: Final listening paper: the teacher reads or plays eight short items (short recordings with a picture choice, a longer recording with multiple choice, a gap-fill) twice. Students answer on an answer sheet. If a recording is available, use a PET-style task from the PET folder or Listening tasks in the kit.
lp.re: Pair reflection: students tell a partner the three biggest improvements they have made since October, giving one example for each ("In October I could not write an email. Now I can.").
lp.prod: Speaking interviews: the teacher examines pairs for about five minutes in a PET-style test (personal questions, a situation task, a photo description, a short discussion) while other students complete the course feedback form and a short revision task.
lp.rw: Course feedback: students complete a short form (what helped, what to change, what they want next year) and write three goals for their English after the course. The teacher collects the forms.
lp.st: Closing ceremony: the teacher hands out certificates, thanks the class and gives a short message about next steps (the next level, the PET exam, practice resources). Students share one wish for the future.
g: Choose the best strategy for each task.
Complete a short cloze against the clock.
Write goals for after the course.
Present a short message to a classmate.
diff: Fast finishers: write a longer piece or a third content point for the writing task.
Support: allow a word bank and a checklist for the writing paper.
hw: Write three goals for your English after the course and one action for each.
Choose one English resource to use every week over the summer.
Write a short thank-you message to someone who helped you learn English this year.
lp.tip: Frame the assessment as a celebration of progress. Record the final marks and prepare report cards and certificates before the lesson; invite students to take a photo with their certificate. Share the next-level and PET options at the end.
checklist: I can give my opinion with 2 reasons in a short talk.
I can understand a short debate about work.
I can write an 80-word email applying for a job.
I can read a short text and answer multiple-choice questions.
I can use phrases like 'On one hand...' to present arguments.
I can talk about my dream job using future tense.
I can identify key values in the workplace (e.g., respect, fairness).

occ.act: Labour Day (1 May) is close. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students discuss "What makes a job worth doing?" and give two reasons with an example, using the present perfect for experience if they like.

kit.l: Optional (Labour Day): Jobs worksheet: Likes and Dislikes at Work

levels.desc: For adults aged 18+ at A2 moving into B1. The year covers present perfect, past continuous, comparatives, conditionals 0/1/2, modals, and reported speech basics through workplace, travel, citizenship, and digital-life themes, with extended speaking, short-article reading, and 80-100 word emails and reviews · PET task types rehearsed throughout S2.

levels.label: Adults · Advanced

weeks.obj: ask accurate and natural questions, give and defend an opinion, and plan how to learn English effectively this year
weeks.lang: question forms review (subject and object questions, indirect questions, question tags for checking); opinion phrases (As far as I'm concerned, I'd argue that, It seems to me that); learning-strategy vocabulary (revise, look up, guess from context, get the gist, keep a record)
weeks.res: How to improve your English (opinion discussion); I think that... (opinion phrases)
weeks.act: Two truths and a lie with follow-up questions; error-correction of question forms; speaking diagnostic in pairs; learning-strategy survey; goal contract
weeks.hw: write 120-150 words about your goals for the year and the three habits you will use to reach them

skills.L: Listen to two learners describe how they study and note which strategies work for them and why
skills.S: Hold a two-minute conversation using accurate questions and opinions with reasons
skills.R: Read the course outline and a short article on language-learning habits and underline useful strategy phrases
skills.W: Write 120-150 words about my goals and my study plan

lp.wu: Two truths and a lie, advanced edition: each student writes three sentences about their last holiday or an unusual experience (two true, one false). In groups of four they read them out and the others may ask three follow-up questions each, but only one of them can be indirect ("Could you tell me how long you stayed there?"). The group votes on the lie. The teacher listens for question order, tense choice and missing auxiliaries and keeps a private list for the diagnostic.
wuAlt: Find someone who: students mingle with a grid of unusual items (has lived in two cities, has used English at work, has failed an exam and passed it later) and must write the full question they asked for each name.

Name chain with a reason: each student says their name and why English matters to them in one sentence, and the next student must report it before adding their own ("Samira needs English because...").
lp.pres: Write six faulty questions on the board that come from typical errors ("What means this word?" "Do you know where is the post office?" "Who did come yesterday?" "You are a student, isn't it?"). In pairs students correct them and explain the rule. Elicit the four patterns: subject questions with no auxiliary (Who called you?), object questions with an auxiliary, indirect questions with statement order (Do you know where it is?), and question tags for checking. Then put opinion frames on cards, from neutral to strong (I tend to think..., As far as I'm concerned..., I'd argue that..., I'm not convinced that...), and ask for one real teacher example for each.
presAlt: Use the matching question and opinion pages of American English File 4 as the model; students then write one subject question, one object question and one indirect question about the same topic.
Dictate eight answers and students write the most natural question for each ("Since last March." "My cousin, I think." "Not really, no.").
lp.prac: Interview and report: pairs choose a topic card (study and work, technology, travel, family traditions, health, money) and write ten questions including at least two subject questions and two indirect questions. They interview each other for five minutes, then each student joins a new partner and reports what they learned using reporting phrases they already know ("She told me that..."). The teacher notes errors on the board without naming students, and the class corrects them at the end.
pracAlt: Opinion four corners: statements are read aloud ("Learning grammar rules is a waste of time.") and students stand in the corner that matches their view (strongly agree, agree, disagree, strongly disagree) and justify it with an opinion frame.
Mistake auction: teams bid on twelve questions, some correct and some faulty, and the team that buys the most correct ones wins.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short monologues twice, each about 100 words (a pharmacist who keeps a vocabulary notebook with example sentences and listens to podcasts on the bus, and an engineering student who only studies before exams and wants to change). Students complete a table: strategy, how often, result, and what the speaker would change. Check in pairs, then discuss which strategy they would copy. If audio is available, use one of the learning interviews from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Four corners revisited: the teacher reads five statements about learning (Mistakes are more useful than correct answers. Watching films with subtitles is a bad habit. You cannot improve without living abroad.) and students move to a corner and defend their position in one full sentence with an opinion frame. After each statement one student from each corner must answer a question from the opposite corner.
lp.prod: Speaking diagnostic: in pairs students talk for four minutes about "What has been the most useful way you have learned something, and what would you do differently now?" while the teacher circulates with a grid (range, accuracy, fluency, pronunciation, interaction) and listens to each student for about a minute. Then students swap partners, summarise what they heard in 30 seconds, and the listener asks one follow-up question.
lp.rw: Goal contract: students write 120 to 150 words headed "My English contract" with three specific goals, the habit for each (for example "learn five words a day and use them in an email") and one obstacle with a plan to overcome it. In the last five minutes they swap, underline one thing they like and circle one question form to check. The teacher keeps a copy of each contract to revisit in week 15.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence beginning "By the end of this course I will have..." using the future perfect if you can, or "I want to be able to..." if not, and hand it in at the door. The teacher uses the slips to form mixed-level groups for the next weeks.
g: Students ask questions to match bingo squares and write a name for each, with a real follow-up question.
Teams bid on correct and faulty questions and fix the faulty ones.
Groups ask three follow-up questions to find the false statement.
Students move to the corner that matches their view and defend it with an opinion frame.
Pairs swap one study tip each and rate it from 1 to 5 for how likely they are to try it.
diff: Fast finishers: write five indirect questions you would ask a person who has learned English in a different country, and predict their answers.
Support: give a question table (wh- word + auxiliary + subject + verb) with six examples, a card of three opinion starters and a model goal sentence.
hw: Write 120 to 150 words about your goals for the year and the three habits you will use to reach them.
Start a vocabulary notebook: record ten new words with a definition, an example sentence and a collocation.
Watch or listen to ten minutes of English on a topic you like and write three questions you would ask the speaker.
lp.tip: This first lesson sets the tone, so be warm and start from what each adult already knows and needs (work, visas, study, exams). Use the diagnostic only to place pairs and to choose two or three class-wide errors to recycle all term; do not correct every mistake today. Keep a one-page record of each student's goal and review it at the mid-point.

weeks.obj: tell a clear story with background, sequence and a surprise, and choose the right narrative tense for each part
weeks.lang: past simple, past continuous, past perfect simple and continuous; used to and would for past habits; sequencing and time words (as soon as, by the time, meanwhile, just as, eventually); story structure (setting, problem, climax, resolution)
weeks.res: Past perfect: explanations; Learn English 2026: Past Perfect and Continuous (Advanced)
weeks.act: Tense timeline and story structure; story chain with past perfect; recorded or live listening and sequence; story retell in groups; short narrative writing
weeks.hw: write a 150-word story that begins "I had never been so surprised..." using at least four different narrative tenses

skills.L: Listen to a short story and note which events came first, which were background and which was the surprise
skills.S: Tell a two-minute story using background and sequence markers
skills.R: Read a short narrative and underline the tense used for each part of the story
skills.W: Write a 150-word story with a setting, a problem and a resolution

lp.wu: Story in three words: in groups of five, the teacher gives an opening sentence ("It was raining when the phone rang.") and each student adds one sentence in turn, using a different tense each time (past continuous for background, past simple for the main event, past perfect for the cause). Groups read their story to another group. Anything that sounds wrong is written on a slip for the error-correction stage later.
wuAlt: Mini news: students tell a partner a true event from last week in four sentences, starting with background in the past continuous.
Odd one out: the teacher says four past sentences and the class finds the one with the wrong tense and fixes it.
lp.pres: Draw a timeline on the board for a story: "By the time I got to the station (past simple), the train had left (past perfect), and people were waiting for the next one (past continuous)." Elicit the job of each tense: past simple for the main events, past continuous for background or interrupted actions, past perfect for events before the main story, and past perfect continuous for causes ("I was exhausted because I had been waiting for two hours"). Then teach used to and would for past habits with the restriction that would cannot be used for states (I used to have a bike, not I would have a bike). Finish with sequencing words on strips (as soon as, by the time, just as, meanwhile, eventually).
presAlt: Show a three-line anecdote with the verbs removed and students choose the best form from two options for each gap, then explain their choices.
Use the matching narrative tenses unit of American English File 4 as the model text and the past perfect explanation sheet from the kit.
lp.prac: Story cards: each pair draws five cards with story ingredients (a delayed flight, a lost wallet, a stranger, an old photograph, a broken phone) and builds a story on a storyboard with three scenes: before, during, after. They must use at least one past perfect, one past continuous and one used to or would. Pairs then tell the story to another pair, who ask two questions and note one tense error. The teacher listens and writes three typical errors on the board, and the class corrects them together.
pracAlt: Past perfect worksheet from the kit: pairs complete the sentences, then change them to invent a new story with the same grammar.
Tense race: teams get a story with eight gaps and a choice of tenses; the first team with all correct answers wins.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a story of about 150 words twice (a woman who had saved for years to open a small bakery, went to sign the lease, found the owner had already rented the shop to someone else, and then met a stranger who offered her a better place). Students number the events in the order they happened, mark which ones were background, and write down the surprise. Check in pairs, then ask: "What had happened before the story began?" If audio is available, play one of the storytelling recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Past perfect Fact or Fiction: each student writes a short true or false sentence about their past using the past perfect ("By the time I was twenty I had already lived in three cities."). Others ask two questions to decide if it is fact or fiction, then vote. The student reveals the answer and the class says one sentence about what had happened before.
lp.prod: Story retell in groups of four: each student gets a story outline from the kit, a famous short story, or a moment from their own life (an exam, a journey, a mistake). They prepare for three minutes with no writing except key words, then tell the story for two minutes, with the group listening for tense accuracy, a clear opening and a surprise. The group gives one thing they liked and one question; the speaker then retells the story in one minute using different words.
lp.rw: Read a short narrative (for example the story of Virginia Hall) and underline in two colours: background verbs and main-event verbs. Then students write the opening paragraph of their own story in 80 to 100 words, starting with a setting in the past continuous, and swap with a partner who corrects tenses with a coloured pen. Finish by reading the best opening aloud.
lp.st: Story exit: in one sentence, each student finishes "The strangest thing that had ever happened to me was..." with a past perfect clause, and reads it to the class on the way out.
g: Students roll for a character, place and problem and tell a story in two minutes.
Students decide whether a classmate's past perfect statement is true.
Teams choose the right narrative tense for eight gaps in a story.
Students tell three short stories and the class guesses which is false.
Groups reorder cut-up sentences from a story using time words.
diff: Fast finishers: write a story in exactly fifty words using the past perfect continuous at least once.
Support: give a story map (when, where, who, what went wrong, what happened first) and a card with three tense jobs and one example each.
hw: Write a 150-word story that begins "I had never been so surprised..." using at least four different narrative tenses.
Retell a film or book plot in 120 words using past simple for events and past perfect for what happened earlier.
Record a two-minute voice message telling a real story from your life and listen to it once for tense mistakes.
lp.tip: Mistakes in past perfect usually come from overuse (using it for every past action) or from avoiding it. Insist that students always have two past events in mind, one earlier than the other. Let them tell the story first and clean up grammar afterwards.

weeks.theme: Present perfect: life experience and projects
weeks.obj: talk about experiences, news and projects in progress using the present perfect simple and continuous, and contrast them with the past simple
weeks.lang: present perfect simple vs continuous; for, since, already, yet, just, recently, so far, ever, never; present perfect vs past simple (finished vs unfinished time); news report language (has been announced, has risen)
weeks.res: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous: what is the difference; Learn English 2026: Present Perfect and Continuous (Advanced)
weeks.act: Experience interviews; news and results report; time-expression error hunt; mini-presentation of a project in progress
weeks.hw: write 150 words about a project you have been working on and what you have achieved so far

skills.L: Listen to a person describe a job or project and note what has been done, what is still in progress and for how long
skills.S: Interview a classmate about experiences and projects and report the main points
skills.R: Read a short biography and underline all present perfect and past simple verbs
skills.W: Write about a project in progress and what has been done so far

lp.wu: Find someone who has: students receive a grid of unusual experiences (has never been on a plane, has met a famous person, has changed a career, has started a business, has learned a skill online) and must find a different classmate for each, asking "Have you ever...?" and one follow-up question in the past simple. They report two of the most surprising answers to the class.
wuAlt: Chain news: each student says one piece of news about themselves from this week ("I've just finished a report.") and the next must ask a question with how long, what or why.
Quick mingle: students ask "How long have you...?" about five items (live in Oujda, study English, know your best friend, have your phone).
lp.pres: Write on the board: "I've lived here for ten years." "I lived there in 2015." "I've been waiting for an hour!" "I've read three chapters." Elicit the contrast: present perfect for unfinished time or present results, past simple for finished time. Teach present perfect continuous for activities in progress and for recent activities with visible results ("I've been running, so I'm tired") and the contrast with simple when you count what is completed (I've read three chapters; I've been reading all day). Build a time-expression map on the board: for/since, already/yet/just, so far, recently, lately, ever/never, this week/this year.
presAlt: Give students two short texts, one with a finished past and one with an unfinished state, and ask them to mark which verbs have a time link to now.
Use the matching present perfect unit of American English File 4 as the model and the present perfect vs continuous sheet from the kit for concept checks.
lp.prac: Project interviews: each student writes three lines about a real project (learning a skill, building a house, writing a CV, organising an event) with what they have done, what they have been doing and what they have not done yet. In pairs they interview each other with how long, how many and what have you been doing questions. Then the pair writes a two-sentence summary using for and since. In the end the teacher chooses six sentences from the board and the class corrects them.
pracAlt: Present perfect continuous guided practice from the Learn English 2026 folder, done in pairs with a short speaking follow-up.
Choose the best tense: a worksheet with ten sentences where students decide between simple, continuous and past simple and justify the choice.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short descriptions twice (a young man who has been working as a delivery rider for two years and has just bought his own moped, and a woman who has been studying for a nursing degree since September and has already passed three exams). Students fill in a table: what has been completed, what is still happening, for how long, and what is next. Check in pairs, then discuss which verbs showed whether the action was finished or still in progress. If audio is available, play one of the life or trip recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Time expression tennis: the teacher says a sentence stem (I've been learning English...) and the class throws back time expressions (for three years, since 2022, recently, lately) while a student writes the correct sentence. Then pairs invent a short dialogue using three of them. The game ends with a speed round: the teacher says a time expression and students respond with a full true sentence in 10 seconds.
lp.prod: Mini-presentation: each student prepares a one-minute update on a real project in progress (for example "my English course", "my new job", "my cousin's wedding") using at least three present perfect forms. They present to a group of three, who each ask one question using how long or what have you been doing. The group chooses the clearest update and that student presents again to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short biography and mark each verb as present perfect or past simple and say why. Then students write a 100-word update about a project using this structure: where I am now (present perfect), what I did to start (past simple), what I will do next. Pairs swap and underline one tense choice that they would like to discuss.
lp.st: Exit slip: complete "So far this year I have..." and "Next month I will have..." and drop it in a box. The teacher reads a few aloud next week.
g: Students find different classmates for each experience on the grid.
Teams respond to a sentence stem with the right time expression.
A student is accused of the wrong tense and the class defends or corrects it.
Groups write three sentences of news about the class with the present perfect.
Pairs retell a news story using past simple for events and present perfect for results.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short interview with a famous person, using at least five questions in the present perfect continuous and the likely answers.
Support: give a table with finished/unfinished time columns and 8 sentences to sort, plus a card with for/since examples.
hw: Write 150 words about a project you have been working on and what you have achieved so far.
Find a news article from this week and write five sentences about what has happened using the present perfect.
Interview a family member about what they have been doing recently and write six sentences about their answers.
lp.tip: Students often say "I am living here since 2015" or "I have seen him yesterday". Do not stop speaking to fix this; collect examples on the board and correct together. Use real life as the content, since adults enjoy talking about their own projects.

weeks.theme: Habits, change and getting used to things
weeks.obj: describe how life has changed, how you adapted to something new, and compare then and now with nuance
weeks.lang: used to, would, be used to, get used to; comparatives of degree (much, far, slightly, a bit, considerably, not nearly as); describing change (increase, decrease, improve, rise, fall); contrasting then and now
weeks.res: Used to, get used to, be used to; Then and Now
weeks.act: Life then and now interviews; adaptation stories; change graph description; short talk on a life change
weeks.hw: write 150 words comparing life in Morocco now with ten or twenty years ago

skills.L: Listen to someone describe moving to a new country and note what they used to do, what they got used to and what they still find difficult
skills.S: Give a short talk on a change in my life or city, comparing then and now with degree words
skills.R: Read a short article about a change and underline the words for increase, decrease and comparison
skills.W: Write about how something has changed

lp.wu: Then and now line-up: the teacher reads statements about life ("In my childhood I used to walk to school.", "I'm now used to getting up early.") and students decide whether they are true for them and stand on one side of the room. They explain to a neighbour in two sentences and ask one question. The teacher notes which structures cause problems.
wuAlt: Draw and guess: a student draws something that has changed in Oujda (a new tramway, a shopping mall, a phone shop) and the class guesses with "Did there use to be...?"
Word map: groups list verbs and nouns for change (grow, drop, spread, decline, trend, shift).
lp.pres: Put four sentences on the board: "I used to live in a village." "I'm used to the noise." "I'm getting used to the heat." "Every Sunday we would visit my grandmother." Elicit the difference: used to + verb for finished habits and states; be used to + noun or -ing for something familiar; get used to + noun or -ing for becoming familiar; would for repeated past actions but never for states. Then introduce degree words on a scale on the board (far more, considerably, much, a bit, slightly, not nearly as) with examples about Morocco: "Public transport is far more reliable than it used to be." "Prices are slightly higher than last year."
presAlt: Read a short text about a person who moved to another city and let students underline all forms of used to, would and get used to and say what each shows.
Use the matching habits and change unit of American English File 4 and the used to, get used to, be used to sheet from the kit.
lp.prac: Then and now interviews: pairs interview each other with prompts (How did you use to get to school? What were you used to eating as a child? Which things have you got used to since you started working or studying?). They then write six sentences for each other with used to, would, be used to and get used to and compare differences with degree words. The teacher listens for mistakes between used to + verb and be used to + -ing and notes them on the board.
pracAlt: Usually, used to, get used to board game from the kit played in groups of four with a short explanation for each correct answer.
Error hunt: ten sentences from learners' writing with mixed structures; students find and fix them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a story of about 150 words twice (a Moroccan student who moved to Canada: at first he missed his family and was not used to the cold, then he got used to cooking for himself, and now he accepts the snow although he still cannot get used to the food). Students note two things he used to do, two things he got used to and one thing he cannot get used to. Check in pairs, then discuss which experiences they share. If audio is available, play a recording about culture shock or school days from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Growing Up board game from the kit, adapted: groups answer questions with used to, would and get used to about school, food and technology; every correct answer scores one point, and a sentence with a degree word scores two.
lp.prod: Life then and now talk: each student prepares a one-minute talk on a change that affected their life or their neighbourhood (a new job, a new city, a change of habit, new technology) with at least two uses of used to or be used to, two degree words and one example with would. Students deliver the talk in groups of three, who then ask one question each and give one piece of feedback on accuracy.
lp.rw: Read a short text about how some aspect of life has changed (for example This week in history) and underline the words for change. Students then write 120 to 150 words comparing a place in Oujda five or ten years ago and now, using at least four degree words and two structures with used to or get used to. Pairs exchange and mark with symbols (T for tense, WW for wrong word).
lp.st: Story: "The change I am proudest of" in one sentence each, read aloud with a degree word. Optional: the history of Halloween reading.
g: Students ask classmates about their past habits and find similarities.
Teams correct wrong sentences with used to, be used to and get used to.
Groups place statements on a scale of change and defend their choice.
Students describe a childhood memory in detail and others ask questions with did you use to.
A student mimes a change and the class describes it with the right structure.
diff: Fast finishers: write a paragraph comparing two generations in your family using at least five degree words.
Support: give a table with the four structures, one example each and a model sentence about Morocco to adapt.
hw: Write 150 words comparing life in Morocco now with ten or twenty years ago.
Interview a grandparent about what life used to be like and write six sentences.
Write about a time when you had to get used to something new and how long it took.
lp.tip: Learners at this level often mix up used to and be used to. Write the pairs in two columns on the board and keep them up for the whole lesson. Keep the topic personal and let students choose what to talk about.

occ.act: Halloween falls this weekend (31 October). Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students discuss how Halloween has changed in Morocco and abroad in the last ten years and how people used to celebrate it, using used to, would and degree words ("It's far more commercial than it used to be."). Then they compare with how a Moroccan occasion like Eid has stayed the same or changed.

weeks.theme: Future plans, predictions and degrees of certainty
weeks.obj: talk about plans, arrangements and predictions with the right future form and the right degree of certainty
weeks.lang: will, going to, present continuous for arrangements, present simple for timetables; future continuous and future perfect; certainty adverbs (definitely, probably, possibly, might well, is bound to, is unlikely to)
weeks.res: Future continuous (PowerPoint); Future perfect (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Future forms sorting; future diary and arrangements; prediction poster; future perfect "by 2040" talk
weeks.hw: write a 150-word prediction essay about your city in 2040 using at least three future forms and four certainty words

skills.L: Listen to people make predictions and arrangements and note the future form and certainty level
skills.S: Make and defend predictions about technology or work in 2040
skills.R: Read a short prediction article and underline the certainty words
skills.W: Write a prediction paragraph with certainty language

lp.wu: Future in 20 seconds: each student writes the ending of two sentences on slips ("By this time next year I will have..." "Next Saturday at 10 I'll be...") and mingles to read them to three classmates, who must say whether the plan is a prediction, an arrangement or an intention. Then the teacher collects slips with errors for the correction stage.
wuAlt: Crystal ball: pairs take turns predicting a classmate's next week with definitely, probably and might.
Calendar swap: students show a page of their calendar and ask what they will be doing at specific times.
lp.pres: Write six sentences on the board and ask students to sort them by meaning: "I'm meeting Sara at eight." "It's going to rain; look at those clouds." "I'll call you tonight (promise)." "The train leaves at six." "This time next week I'll be flying to Paris." "By 2030 most cars will have become electric." Elicit the rule for each form: arrangement (present continuous), evidence-based prediction (going to), spontaneous decision or opinion (will), timetable (present simple), action in progress at a future time (future continuous), result by a future time (future perfect). Add a certainty scale on the board: definitely, almost certainly, probably, might well, could, is unlikely to, definitely won't.
presAlt: Play a short video or read a short text about future technology and ask students to mark all future forms with a different colour.
Use the matching future forms unit in American English File 4 and the future perfect and continuous PowerPoints from the kit.
lp.prac: Future diary: each student gets a fictional busy diary of a week (a doctor, a student, a farmer, a wedding planner) and writes eight sentences, one in each future form, then reads them to a partner, who has to say which form it is. After that pairs create a prediction poster for 2040 (jobs, transport, education, health) with a certainty word for each prediction, and present it to the class with two reasons.
pracAlt: Future perfect guided practice from the Learn English 2026 folder, with a speaking follow-up about "by the time I am 40".
Sort the sentences: cut-up sentences in five future forms that groups sort and justify.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a conversation twice (two friends planning a week: one has an exam on Thursday so she will be studying all evening, one is going to start a new job on Monday, and they agree to meet on Saturday at six). Students complete a diary page showing arrangements, plans and predictions, and tick the certainty words they hear. Check in pairs, then discuss which statements were arrangements and which were intentions. If audio is available, play a recording about future plans from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Predictor game: the teacher reads a topic (Moroccan football in 2030, the price of fuel, online schools) and teams write three predictions each with a different certainty word. Another team challenges one prediction with "I don't think that's likely because..." and both teams score for good reasons.
lp.prod: Prediction talk: each student gets a topic card (work, health, cities, communication, environment) and prepares a two-minute talk on "Life in 2040" with at least one future continuous, one future perfect and three certainty words. The listeners agree or disagree in one sentence. After each talk the speaker answers one challenge question.
lp.rw: Read a short article on predictions that came true and underline the verbs and certainty words used. Then students write a 150-word paragraph predicting how their city will look in 2040, using three different future forms and four certainty expressions. In the last five minutes they swap, mark the future forms with F and the certainty words with C, and give one comment.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence beginning "By the end of this year I will definitely have..." and one starting "I might well..." and read one to the class on the way out.
g: Groups sort sentences into arrangements, predictions and plans.
Teams write predictions with certainty words and challenge another team.
Students write a note to be opened in six months, using future perfect.
Pairs find a time that fits two busy diaries using future continuous.
Students place a prediction on a scale from impossible to certain and defend it.
diff: Fast finishers: write a dialogue between two friends arguing about whether robots will take their jobs, using at least five different future forms.
Support: give a table with each future form, its meaning and one example, and a card with certainty words in order.
hw: Write a 150-word prediction essay about your city in 2040 using at least three future forms and four certainty words.
Write your diary for next Saturday hour by hour using present continuous and future continuous.
Make a list of ten things you will have done by the end of the year and say how sure you are about each.
lp.tip: Do not try to teach every shade of future in one go. Focus on the three or four forms your students actually need and keep the certainty scale on the board for the whole lesson. Ask students to react to each other's predictions, because that makes the language real.

occ.act: The Green March (6 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students predict how the national day will be remembered in 2050 and what will have changed in Morocco by then, using future perfect and certainty language ("By 2050 the country will probably have invested much more in renewable energy.").

weeks.theme: Speculation and deduction: mysteries and clues
weeks.obj: speculate about present and past situations from evidence, and justify a conclusion with the right modal and clue
weeks.lang: modals of deduction in the present (must, might, may, could, can't + infinitive); in the past (must have, might have, could have, can't have + past participle); continuous forms (must be working, might have been sleeping); evidence phrases (judging by, it looks as if, there's no way)
weeks.res: Modal verbs of deduction in the present (joke worksheet); Present perfect speculation
weeks.act: Mystery pictures and clue cards; lost-and-found stories; deduction role-play; crime-scene report writing
weeks.hw: write a 150-word report on a mystery with three theories, ranked by likelihood

skills.L: Listen to a short description of a mystery and decide which conclusions are possible, probable or impossible
skills.S: Speculate about a mystery with a partner, defending a theory with evidence
skills.R: Read a short mystery article and underline the modal verbs used for speculation
skills.W: Write a short report on a mystery with several theories

lp.wu: What's in the bag? The teacher shows a closed bag and gives clues one by one ("It's heavy." "It rattles." "It smells of oranges."). Students speculate with must, might, could and can't, and the teacher accepts only answers with a clear reason ("It can't be a book because it rattles."). Then students bring a bag or an object from their own pockets and run the same game in groups of four.
wuAlt: Photo clues: show a photo of an unknown person's desk (a coffee cup, a passport, a map, a wedding ring) and the class speculates about the owner.
Guess my job: a student mimes a work action and the class speculates "You must be a mechanic, you might be a driver."
lp.pres: Put three sentences on the board: "She must be at work; her car is outside." "He might have missed the bus." "They can't have left; the lights are on." Elicit the scale of certainty: must (almost certain), may or might or could (possible), can't (almost certain it is not true), and show the structure for the present (modal + infinitive) and the past (modal + have + past participle). Add the continuous form (He must be sleeping; she can't have been waiting long) and the difference between could have (possible) and couldn't have (impossible). Finish with evidence phrases written on strips (judging by, it looks as if, there's no way).
presAlt: Show a photo of an empty office (coat on the chair, cup still warm, computer on) and elicit as many sentences as possible.
Use the matching deduction unit of American English File 4 and the modal verbs of deduction sheet from the kit.
lp.prac: Lost and found: each group of three gets a card with a lost item and clues about the owner (a wallet with a bus ticket from Nador, a dental appointment card, a half-eaten sandwich). Groups write six speculations (three present, three past) with a modal and a clue, then read to another group, who say whether they agree. The teacher listens for a common error: must have + infinitive, and writes examples on the board for the class to fix.
pracAlt: What's that noise? worksheet from the kit: pairs guess the cause of each noise with the past or present deduction forms.
Sentence swap: students write a sentence with a modal on a card, pass it to a partner who rewrites it with a different degree of certainty.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short story twice (a woman comes home to find the door open, a window broken, nothing stolen, and a cup of tea on the table that is still warm). Students write down three possible explanations using must, might and can't, and mark each as likely, possible or unlikely. Check in pairs, then ask the class to vote on the most likely theory. If audio is available, use a crime-related recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Who is the burglar? The teacher gives each group a set of conversation cards about suspects. Groups take turns to read clues, speculate with must have, can't have and might have, and finally vote on the culprit. The first group to give a correct reason for the culprit wins.
lp.prod: Mystery role-play: groups of four have a mystery card (a missing painting at a museum, a stolen bicycle, a student who has not arrived, a ghost light in an old house). Two students are detectives and two are witnesses. The witnesses give statements, and the detectives have five minutes to question them and then tell the class their theory using at least three past modals of deduction, with evidence. The class decides who has the best theory.
lp.rw: Read a short mystery article (Skeleton Lake or Otzi the Iceman) and underline the verbs used for speculation. Then students write a 150-word report with three theories, ranked from most to least likely, using at least five modals and two evidence phrases. They finish with a recommendation for what an investigator should do next, and swap texts for a quick peer check.
lp.st: Short story: the teacher reads the first two sentences of a mystery and each student writes one sentence of explanation with a past modal on a slip. The teacher reads out the best.
g: Groups guess the contents of a bag from clues using must, might and can't.
Groups use clues to decide who did it and justify with past modals.
Students place sentences on a scale from impossible to certain.
Students speculate about the lives of people in a photo.
Pairs invent two different theories for the same mystery and argue for one.
diff: Fast finishers: write a one-paragraph mystery and three questions with clues for another pair to solve.
Support: give a table with modals on a certainty scale and 8 clue sentences to complete.
hw: Write a 150-word report on a mystery with three theories, ranked by likelihood.
Find a photo or a short news story and write six deduction sentences about it using present and past modals.
Watch a short mystery video and write what you think the explanation is and why.
lp.tip: The most common error is mixing up can't and mustn't, and using the infinitive instead of have + past participle for the past. Keep a certainty scale on the board and point to it when students make errors. Encourage playful guesses: students use the language more when they are curious.

weeks.obj: talk about real and unreal situations, express regrets and wishes, and give advice using all four conditionals
weeks.lang: zero and first conditionals; second conditional for imaginary present; third conditional for past regrets; mixed conditionals light; wish and if only (wish + past simple, wish + past perfect, wish + would); unless, as long as, provided that
weeks.res: Conditionals review (mixed); Wish about the present (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Dilemma discussions; regrets and wishes; advice column roleplay; moral dilemma debate
weeks.hw: write an advice reply of 150 words to a letter from a person with a difficult decision

skills.L: Listen to people describing difficult decisions and note the conditionals and wishes they use
skills.S: Discuss a dilemma, give advice and defend a decision
skills.R: Read a short advice letter and underline all conditional structures
skills.W: Write an advice reply using several conditionals

lp.wu: What would you do? The teacher reads a short dilemma ("You find a wallet with 2,000 dirhams and an ID card in a cafe.") and students write what they would do on a slip. In groups they compare answers and use "If I were you..." to advise each other. The teacher listens for the verb form after if.
wuAlt: Chain conditional: one student says "If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house" and the next continues with the result "If I bought a house, I'd..."
Wish line: students complete "I wish..." for three things in their life and read one aloud.
lp.pres: Put four sentences on the board: "If you heat ice, it melts." "If it rains, I'll stay home." "If I had more time, I would learn the guitar." "If I had studied harder, I would have passed." Elicit the form and meaning of each: zero (facts), first (real future), second (imaginary present), third (imaginary past). Then show wish and if only: "I wish I had more time" (present regret), "I wish I had studied" (past regret), "I wish he would listen" (annoyance). Teach the replacements for if: unless, as long as, provided that, supposing, and give one sentence each about Moroccan life.
presAlt: Use the matching conditionals unit in American English File 4 and the conditionals review sheet from the kit as the model.
Show a PowerPoint on wish and if only and ask students to match each sentence to present or past regret.
lp.prac: Regrets and wishes: each student writes four sentences about their life, two regrets with the third conditional ("If I had learned English earlier, I would have studied abroad.") and two wishes with wish + past simple or past perfect. Pairs read them aloud, ask each other why, and suggest a first conditional for the future ("If you start now, you'll be fluent in two years."). The teacher monitors for the common mistake of using would after if.
pracAlt: Third conditional chain from the kit: groups build a chain of consequences ("If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met you.").
Conditional completion: pairs complete ten half-sentences and classify them as zero, first, second or third.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a conversation twice (a woman asks her friend whether to accept a job in another city: if she goes, she will earn more but she will miss her family; if she had taken the other job last year, she would have been promoted; she wishes she were braver). Students note the conditionals and wishes they hear and write the decision the friend makes. Check in pairs, then ask: "What would you advise her to do?" If audio is available, play the choices recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Conditional chain game from the kit: students sit in a circle, the first says a sentence with if, and the next uses the result as the start of a new sentence in a different conditional type. A student who hesitates for more than five seconds or uses the wrong structure is out.
lp.prod: Ethical dilemma debate: groups of four have a dilemma card (a doctor who can save one of two patients, a manager who must decide whom to dismiss, a friend who cheated in an exam, a person who finds a mistake in their own favour). They discuss for ten minutes, using all four conditionals and wish at least once each, and prepare a two-minute justification. One student from each group presents the group's decision, and the class challenges it with a question starting with "What if...?"
lp.rw: Read a short advice column letter and underline all conditionals and wishes. Students then write a 150-word reply to a letter from a person torn between two choices (staying in Morocco or emigrating, working or studying), using at least one of each conditional and one wish. Pairs swap, mark the conditional types with Z, 1, 2, 3 and give one suggestion.
lp.st: Exit: "If I could change one decision from my past, I would..." written in one sentence with a third conditional clause.
g: Students link sentences and change the conditional type each time.
Students match wish sentences to their meaning (regret, annoyance, desire).
Groups discuss and justify their decisions with conditionals.
A student draws a topic and states a regret in a third conditional.
Teams bid on sentences giving advice and the best form scores.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 120-word story that ends "If I hadn't opened that letter, none of this would have happened."
Support: give a table with the four conditionals, the verb forms and one model sentence for each, and a card with wish sentence starters.
hw: Write an advice reply of 150 words to a letter from a person with a difficult decision.
Write a list of eight regrets and wishes (four each) from your own life in full sentences.
Interview a friend about a difficult decision and write what they would do differently using conditionals.
lp.tip: Learners often use would in the if clause or mix up forms. Show the structure as two boxes on the board, an if box and a result box, and let students point to the box where the error is. Choose dilemmas that are close to your students' lives, such as work, studies and migration, but avoid very sensitive personal topics.

occ.act: Independence Day (18 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students discuss what might have happened if Morocco had not gained independence when it did, and what they wish had been different, using second and third conditionals and wish ("If the country had become independent earlier, it might have developed faster." "I wish I could have heard the stories first-hand.").

weeks.theme: The passive: processes, reports and services
weeks.obj: describe how things are made and how systems work, report facts and events with the passive, and talk about services you have done for you
weeks.lang: passive in present, past, perfect, future and with modals (is made, was built, has been announced, will be delivered, must be checked); agent with by; have/get something done; passive reporting verbs (is said to be, is believed to have been)
weeks.res: Passive: Processes; Video: Causative verbs (let, make, have, get, help)
weeks.act: Process descriptions; science and technology reading; news headlines in the passive; "have something done" role-play
weeks.hw: write a 150-word description of a process (making bread, producing olive oil, building a house) using at least six passive forms

skills.L: Listen to a description of a process and put the stages in order
skills.S: Explain a process clearly to a partner using passive structures
skills.R: Read a short article on technology in healthcare and underline all passive forms
skills.W: Describe a process in writing

lp.wu: What am I describing? The teacher describes a product without naming it in the passive ("It is grown in the mountains. It is picked by hand. It is dried in the sun. It is sold in markets.") and students guess (saffron, argan, dates). Then groups of three write their own three-sentence description of a Moroccan product and read it for others to guess.
wuAlt: Passive headlines: show three headlines with the passive ("New tramway line to be opened") and ask students what the sentences mean.
Chain: one student says an active sentence and the next changes it to the passive.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "Argan oil is produced in the south-west." "The new library was built last year." "The road has been repaired." "The results will be announced on Friday." "The machine must be checked every week." Elicit be + past participle and the tense of be, and when we use the passive: when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or when we want to focus on the result. Teach by + agent only when it adds information, then add have/get something done ("I had my phone repaired") and passive reporting verbs ("He is believed to have left").
presAlt: Show a flow chart of how olive oil or paper is made and ask the class to describe each step aloud in the passive.
Use the matching passive unit in American English File 4 and the processes sheet from the kit.
lp.prac: Process cards: groups get a set of jumbled stages of a process (producing bread, recycling plastic, issuing a passport, making a mobile phone) and put them in order with sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally), then write each stage in the passive. They explain the process to another group without notes. Next, a short role-play at a service centre: pairs practise "I'd like to have my laptop repaired." / "It'll be ready by Friday." using have something done.
pracAlt: Newspaper headlines from the kit: students expand each headline into a full passive sentence in three tenses.
Passive snap: pairs match active and passive cards in different tenses.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a text twice about how tea is produced and served in Morocco (leaves are grown, picked, dried, imported, mixed with mint, and poured from a height). Students number the stages and write the passive verb heard for each. Check in pairs, then ask: "Who does each step?" If audio is available, play the technology recording or the nanotechnology mini lesson named in the kit and ask students to note two passives.
lp.re: Heads and Tails from the kit: half the class has the first half of a passive sentence and the other half has the end. They mingle and match, then read the full sentence and say the active version.
lp.prod: Process presentation: each pair chooses a process they know well (making couscous, getting a driving licence, how a festival is organised, how a mobile network works), prepares a flow chart and gives a two-minute explanation using at least six passives, including two with modals. The audience asks two questions each, and the speakers answer using the passive when possible.
lp.rw: Read a short article on technology and healthcare and underline all passive forms, then label each with its tense. Students then write 150 words describing a process or a service in their country, using at least six passives, one passive with a modal and one have/get something done. A partner marks the passives with a coloured pen and checks the use of by.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence in the passive about the school or the city ("A new classroom will be opened next year.") and one about something you had done recently.
g: Students describe a product with passives and others guess.
Pairs match active and passive cards.
Groups order the stages of a process and describe them.
Teams turn headlines into full passive sentences.
Students role-play a service request using have something done.
diff: Fast finishers: write a news report of 100 words about an event using at least six passives, including two reporting passives (is said to, is reported to).
Support: give a table of passive forms in five tenses with one example each and a flow chart template with the stage words.
hw: Write a 150-word description of a process (making bread, producing olive oil, building a house) using at least six passive forms.
Collect five news headlines in English and rewrite each as a full passive sentence in two tenses.
Describe three things you had done for you this year (a haircut, a repair, a delivery) using have or get.
lp.tip: Students tend to overuse the passive after they learn it. Remind them that the passive is for processes, formal writing and when the doer is not important. Let them speak about familiar processes so they can concentrate on form.

occ.act: Thanksgiving (26 November) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students describe how a Thanksgiving dinner is prepared and served in the United States using the passive ("The turkey is roasted for several hours. The pies are baked the day before."), and compare it with how a festive Moroccan meal is prepared.

weeks.obj: report what people said, asked and promised accurately, and choose a suitable reporting verb to show attitude
weeks.lang: say, tell, ask; backshift of tenses and when it is not needed; reported questions and imperatives; reporting verbs with patterns (suggest + -ing, admit + -ing, deny + -ing, promise to, warn someone not to, refuse to, insist on); reporting words and place changes (that day, the following week, there)
weeks.res: Reported speech: statements (PowerPoint); Reported speech: yes/no questions (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Gossip chain; interview report; reporting verbs matching; news report role-play
weeks.hw: write a 150-word news report of an interview using at least six different reporting verbs

skills.L: Listen to an interview and note what each speaker said, admitted, denied or promised
skills.S: Report a conversation orally and choose a reporting verb to show attitude
skills.R: Read a short news report and underline the reporting verbs
skills.W: Write a news report of an interview

lp.wu: Telephone gossip: in lines of five, the first student whispers a message of 20 words to the next ("The manager said that he would send the contract on Monday, but he hasn't called me yet"), and the last student writes down what he heard. The teacher shows the original and the class compares. In the second round the first student reports the message back in reported speech when he passes it on ("He said that...").
wuAlt: Who said it? The teacher reads famous quotes and students turn them into reported speech ("She said she had a dream").
Quick quiz: say, tell or ask? Ten sentence stems with the verb removed.
lp.pres: Write on the board: "I'm tired," she said. / She said (that) she was tired. Then add "I will call you." / He promised to call me. Elicit the changes: backshift (present to past, past to past perfect, will to would), pronouns, time and place words (now to then, tomorrow to the next day, here to there). Teach that tenses do not always change when the situation is still true or the reporting verb is in the present ("The doctor says that you need rest."). Show reported questions with statement order (She asked where I lived) and the three reporting patterns: verb + that, verb + object + infinitive (told me to wait), and verb + -ing (suggested going).
presAlt: Show a short video on reported speech and ask students to note the rules.
Use the matching reported speech unit in American English File 4 and the PowerPoints on reported statements and questions from the kit.
lp.prac: Interview and report: students interview a partner using six questions (What did you do last weekend? Are you planning to travel? Why did you choose this job?), take notes and then report the answers to a third person using reporting verbs ("She told me that she had gone to Nador and said she was planning to visit her cousin."). The teacher gives each pair a list of 10 reporting verbs and asks them to use at least six. Then pairs take a short worksheet where they transform direct statements into reported speech and choose the best reporting verb.
pracAlt: Reporting verbs matching: pairs match direct speech with the correct reporting verb (admit, deny, warn, suggest, refuse, promise, insist) and form the sentence.
You said...: from the kit, pairs argue about who said what in a dialogue and practise correcting each other.
lp.ls: Teacher reads an interview twice between a journalist and a football coach after a lost match (he admitted that the team had played badly, denied blaming the referee, promised to change the tactics and refused to resign). Students note what the coach said in his own words and write a report of three sentences with reporting verbs. Check in pairs and compare reporting verbs. If audio is available, play one of the interview recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Why did you say that? from the kit: pairs have dialogues and must report them with the right verb and tense change, justify their choice and challenge each other's reports. The group with the most correct reports in five minutes wins.
lp.prod: News report role-play: groups of four act as a TV news team. One student plays the reporter who interviews three people about a local event (a market fire, a school sports day, a new road), taking notes. Then the reporter writes a one-minute news report using at least five reporting verbs and presents it to the class, with the interviewees checking that the report is accurate and not exaggerated.
lp.rw: Read a short news report and underline all reporting verbs and tense changes. Students then write a 150-word news report based on an interview (a class interview recorded earlier or a short teacher-supplied dialogue) using at least six different reporting verbs and two reported questions. In the last five minutes pairs check each other's reports against the original and fix any change that alters the meaning.
lp.st: Exit gossip: write one sentence of something someone said to you today and report it on the slip ("My neighbour told me that..."). The teacher reads out three without names.
g: Students pass a message down a line and compare the final version.
Pairs match direct speech to the right reporting verb.
Groups report a dialogue from memory.
Teams change direct sentences into reported speech as fast as possible.
Students invent a rumour and the class reports it using is said to.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 100-word dialogue between a customer and a manager and then report it using ten different reporting verbs.
Support: give a backshift table (present simple to past simple, will to would, etc.) and a card with the ten reporting verbs and their patterns.
hw: Write a 150-word news report of an interview using at least six different reporting verbs.
Record a short conversation with a friend in English and report it in writing in one paragraph.
Find a quote from an interview in a newspaper or video and report it three different ways.
lp.tip: Do not insist on the full set of backshift rules for every sentence. Focus on the changes that cause meaning problems (will to would, now to then) and the reporting verbs that sound natural at B2. Use real news and conversations so that reporting has a real purpose.
