weeks.theme: Relative clauses and describing with precision
weeks.obj: describe people, places and things with defining and non-defining relative clauses, and join ideas in a compact way using reduced clauses and participles
weeks.lang: defining and non-defining relative clauses (who, which, that, whose, where, when); omitting the relative pronoun; prepositions in relative clauses (the person I was talking to, the house in which); reduced relative clauses and participle clauses (the man standing there, the book written by...); commas and register
weeks.res: Relative clauses: test and information; Grammar Sense Book 3: relative clauses exercises
weeks.act: Guess who or what; sentence-combining; place description; short descriptive writing
weeks.hw: write a 150-word description of a person who has influenced you using at least six relative clauses

skills.L: Listen to a description of a person and a place and identify who or what is being described
skills.S: Give a precise description of a person, place or object so that a partner can guess it
skills.R: Read a short descriptive text and underline the relative clauses
skills.W: Write a descriptive paragraph with relative clauses

lp.wu: Describe it: students receive a card with a person, a place or an object (a pharmacist, the medina, an umbrella) and give a definition with a relative clause ("It is a place where people buy medicine."). The group guesses the word and the best definition wins. The teacher notes which relative pronouns are used wrongly.
wuAlt: Who is it? A student describes a famous person without naming them, using who, whose and where.
Sentence stretch: start with "The man" and add relative clauses to make it as long as possible while still logical.
lp.pres: Put on the board: "The woman who lives next door is a doctor." "The book that I bought is excellent." "My brother, who lives in Spain, is a chef." "That's the shop where I bought my phone." Elicit the difference between defining (essential information, no commas) and non-defining (extra information, with commas, no that). Show when the pronoun can be left out (when it is the object) and the use of whose and prepositions at the end (the colleague I work with). Then introduce reduced clauses: "the man who is standing there" becomes "the man standing there", "the book which was written by..." becomes "the book written by...".
presAlt: Give students two short descriptions, one with commas and one without, and ask them to explain the difference in meaning.
Use the matching relative clauses unit in American English File 4 and the relative clauses information sheet from the kit.
lp.prac: Sentence combining: pairs get ten pairs of short sentences ("My cousin lives in Tangier. He sells carpets.") and combine them into one sentence with a relative clause, deciding if commas are needed. Then, in groups of three, one student describes a place or person in the classroom using at least three relative clauses and the others guess. The teacher listens for the misuse of that in non-defining clauses and for the omitted pronoun errors.
pracAlt: Describe and draw from the kit: one student describes a picture with relative clauses and a partner draws it.
Error correction: ten sentences with wrong pronouns, missing commas or extra pronouns; groups correct them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a description of a person and a place twice (a grandmother who sells bread in the old market, whose recipe has been used for forty years, and the street where she lives, which is narrow and always crowded). Students tick the details they hear and write the relative pronoun used for each. Check in pairs. If audio is available, play a recording about a famous person from the Listening folder named in the kit and ask students to note how the speaker describes them.
lp.re: Matchmaker from the kit: students receive cards describing the ideal flatmate, colleague or friend with relative clauses. They must find the card that fits a partner's description, rephrasing in their own words using who, which or whose.
lp.prod: Place and person portraits: each student prepares a two-minute description of a person who has influenced them and a place they love, using at least six relative clauses, two non-defining clauses and two reduced clauses. They present in groups of three, and the listeners must draw or note three details and ask a follow-up question. The best description is read to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short descriptive text (for example about the Eiffel Tower) and underline all relative clauses, labelling them as defining or non-defining. Then students write 150 words about a person or place that is important to them, using at least six relative clauses with correct punctuation and one participle clause. Pairs swap, circle every relative pronoun and check commas.
lp.st: Story: in one sentence, each student describes the person who taught them the most, using a relative clause, and reads it aloud on the way out.
g: Students define words with relative clauses.
Groups build the longest logical sentence with relative clauses.
Pairs join two sentences into one with the right pronoun.
Teams decide if a clause is defining or non-defining.
Groups find and fix errors in relative clause sentences.
diff: Fast finishers: write a one-paragraph description of your ideal city using at least eight relative clauses, including two with prepositions.
Support: give a table with who, which, that, whose and where, a model sentence for each and a comma rule card.
hw: Write a 150-word description of a person who has influenced you using at least six relative clauses.
Find a paragraph in an English article and underline all relative clauses, then rewrite two of them as reduced clauses.
Describe your neighbourhood to a friend in six sentences with where and which.
lp.tip: Many students leave the pronoun in the clause (the man who he called) or overuse that. Show the rule as a cut-and-paste exercise: they must cut one element and paste in the pronoun. Participle clauses are an introduction only, so aim for recognition and a few good examples rather than perfect use.

weeks.obj: give and defend an opinion, agree and disagree politely, make concessions and structure a short argument in a group discussion
weeks.lang: giving opinions (In my view..., As far as I'm concerned..., I'm convinced that...); polite disagreement (I see what you mean, but..., I'm not sure I'd go that far); concession (although, even though, however, despite, in spite of, while); structuring an argument (my main point is..., for example, what is more, in conclusion)
weeks.res: Although vs Even though (commonly confused words); Linking words and their functions (grammar sheet)
weeks.act: Four Corners opinion game; concession sentence building; structured group debate with roles; argument paragraph
weeks.hw: write a 120-word paragraph arguing for or against a statement, using at least three concession structures

skills.L: Listen to a short radio-style debate and note each speaker's position, reason and concession
skills.S: Defend a position for one minute and respond politely to a counter-argument
skills.R: Read a short opinion text and underline the claim, the reasons and the concessions
skills.W: Write a 120-word argument paragraph with a concession and a conclusion

lp.wu: Four Corners: the teacher reads a statement ("Social media does more harm than good", "Young people should live with their parents until they marry") and students walk to a corner (strongly agree, agree, disagree, strongly disagree). In each corner they have two minutes to prepare one reason, then one person speaks for the group and a student from another corner answers with "I see your point, but...".
wuAlt: Do you agree? Pairs get five opinion cards and must respond with a different phrase each time (I couldn't agree more, That's partly true, but..., I'm afraid I see it differently).
One-minute talk: each student speaks for sixty seconds on "the best way to learn a language" while the partner counts how many opinion phrases they use.
lp.pres: Write two short extracts on the board, one that only states opinions ("Homework is bad. Teachers give too much.") and one that argues with concession ("Although homework can be stressful, it helps students build good study habits. However, too much of it leaves no time for family."). Elicit the difference and build a language bank in three columns: giving an opinion, agreeing and disagreeing politely, conceding a point. Teach the grammar of concession: although / even though / while + clause, despite / in spite of + noun or -ing, however + comma at the start of a new sentence. Check with a quick sentence-combining drill: "The course was expensive. It was worth it." becomes "Although the course was expensive, it was worth it. / Despite being expensive, the course was worth it."
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on opinions or debate from the kit for model dialogues.
Use the Although vs Even though sheet from the kit, then the linking words grammar sheet to compare however, whereas and despite.
lp.prac: Concession ladder: pairs get six pairs of contrasting ideas (cheap but unreliable, modern but noisy) and write each one in three ways (although, despite, however). Then a controlled error hunt in which pairs correct eight sentences such as "Despite he was tired, he came" and "Although it was cold, but we went out". Finally, Disagree with me: in pairs, A states a strong opinion on a card and B must disagree politely using a different phrase each turn, for three rounds each.
pracAlt: Opinion cards with mixed statements; students agree or disagree with a reason and one concession.
Rewrite blunt replies ("No, that's wrong") as polite ones with a softener and a reason.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short radio-style debate twice (two speakers on whether cities should ban cars from the centre). First listening: who is for and who is against. Second listening: students complete a table with each speaker's main reason, one concession and the phrase used to disagree. If a recording is available, use the debate recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Explain yourself: one student picks an opinion card ("Learning English is more useful than learning a third language") and gives an opinion with a reason and an example. The next student must either add a reason or disagree politely and concede one point before giving a counter-reason. The chain continues round the class for five minutes.
lp.prod: Structured group debate: groups of six split into two teams of three and receive a motion (for example "Mobile phones should be banned in school", "Working from home is better than working in an office"). Each team prepares for ten minutes, with roles: opening speaker, rebuttal speaker, closing speaker. The debate lasts 12 minutes (90 seconds per speech, then free exchange), while the other group acts as judges and scores structure, politeness and use of concession on a simple tick sheet. Swap roles with a new motion if time allows.
lp.rw: Read a 150-word opinion article on a familiar topic from the kit and underline the claim, each reason and each concession in three colours. Then write a 120-word paragraph for or against a statement of your choice with a clear opening opinion, two reasons, one concession with although or despite, and a one-sentence conclusion. Swap with a partner, who marks one strong sentence and one to improve.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence that gives your opinion on today's motion and one that concedes a point against it ("Although I believe phones help learning, I accept that they distract many students.") and hand it in.
g: Move to a corner and defend an opinion.
Pass a ball and respond with a new softener each time.
Two teams hit arguments back and lose a point for repeating a reason.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 150-word balanced paragraph that presents both sides of a topic without giving a final opinion. Support: give a language bank card with six opinion phrases, four softeners and a gapped model paragraph (Although..., However..., In conclusion...).
hw: Write a 120-word paragraph arguing for or against a statement, using at least three concession structures.
Listen to or watch a short debate in English online and note three phrases speakers use to disagree politely.
Ask two people their opinion on a local issue (traffic, prices, school hours) and write four sentences reporting their views with although and however.
lp.tip: Opinions in Morocco are often strong and quick, so teach the softeners first: students enjoy the debate, but you must stop interruptions by giving each speaker a fixed time. Correct concession grammar after the speaking, not during it, with three or four examples on the board. Choose motions that matter to the class (work, school, social media) and keep politics and religion out of the motions.

weeks.obj: handle a job interview, talk about skills and experience, write a short CV profile and use modal verbs for obligation, permission and ability in a workplace
weeks.lang: job interview questions and answers (Tell me about yourself; What are your strengths?; Where do you see yourself in five years?); CV and cover letter language (responsible for, managed, I am writing to apply for); workplace modals (must, have to, don't have to, mustn't, be allowed to, can, be able to, needn't); skills and qualities vocabulary
weeks.res: Job Descriptions (must, have to, can); Business English video 3: The Job Interview
weeks.act: Job preference mingle; mock interview with feedback; CV profile writing; workplace rules role-play
weeks.hw: write a 100-word CV profile or a short cover-letter paragraph for a real or imaginary job

skills.L: Listen to a good and a poor job interview and list what makes each one effective or weak
skills.S: Answer interview questions in full, confident turns of 30 to 45 seconds
skills.R: Read a short job advertisement and a CV and match the requirements to the candidate
skills.W: Write a 100-word CV profile or cover-letter paragraph

lp.wu: Job preference mingle: each student gets a role card with a likes and dislikes list (prefers working in a team, hates routine, loves numbers, speaks three languages) and mingles to find the two classmates with whom they would work best, and the one job they would be good at. They report: "I think Samira would be a great translator because she's fluent in three languages."
wuAlt: Ranking: pairs rank eight qualities (reliable, creative, punctual, good with people, ambitious, flexible, organised, confident) for the best employee and defend the order.
One-minute talk: describe the best boss or teacher you have had.
lp.pres: Show the job advertisement for a receptionist or a customer adviser at a language centre. Elicit what the employer wants and build the language of requirements and abilities (must have, is required to, need to be able to, you will be allowed to work from home, you don't have to wear a uniform, you mustn't share client data). Contrast obligation (must / have to), absence of obligation (don't have to / needn't), prohibition (mustn't / not allowed to) and permission (can / be allowed to). Then watch or read two short interview extracts (good and poor) and list the differences: answer length, examples, eye contact, questions to the interviewer.
presAlt: Use the Job Descriptions worksheet from the kit to practise workplace modals.
Show the Business English video 3, The Job Interview, from the kit and have students compare it with the good and poor example videos.
lp.prac: Interview question builder: students write three answers to each of three standard questions (strengths, a difficult situation at work or study, goals), each built around a specific example in two sentences instead of a bare adjective such as "I'm hard-working". Then in pairs they practise the answers aloud, with the partner giving one tip on length and detail. Controlled modal practice follows: pairs describe the rules and expectations of their ideal job in eight sentences with must, have to, don't have to, mustn't and be allowed to.
pracAlt: Necessary Skills worksheet from the kit: decide what is necessary, useful or not needed for different jobs.
Careers Advice worksheet from the kit: give advice to people choosing a career.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short interview extracts (one good, one poor) of about 60 seconds each, twice. Students tick a checklist (gives an example, speaks clearly, asks a question, answers too briefly, criticises a past employer) and decide which candidate they would hire and why. If a recording or video is available, use the good and poor job interview videos from the Business English folder in the kit.
lp.re: Likes and dislikes at work: students complete a quick survey about their ideal working day, then pair up to find out whether they would be good colleagues, using "I'd rather...", "I don't mind...", "I can't stand...".
lp.prod: Mock job interview: in groups of three (interviewer, candidate, observer), the candidate gets a job advertisement (hotel receptionist, English tutor, call-centre agent, shop manager) and a short CV card. The interviewer asks six questions, including one unexpected one (Why should we hire you?), and the observer notes strong phrases, length of answers and one thing to improve. Rotate roles so everyone is interviewed.
lp.rw: Read a model CV profile (about 80 words) and a cover-letter paragraph. Underline the verbs of achievement (managed, organised, improved, trained) and the formal phrases (I am writing to apply for..., I would welcome the opportunity to...). Then write a 100-word CV profile or a cover-letter paragraph for a job from the interview task, using at least four achievement verbs.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you must do and one thing you don't have to do in your current or future job, and one thing you can do really well ("In a hospital, you mustn't share patient information. I can work well under pressure.") and hand it in.
g: Find the best colleague from role cards.
Ask and answer fast interview questions with a ball.
Teams write achievement verbs and use them in sentences.
diff: Fast finishers: write the full cover letter (150 words) for the job in the mock interview. Support: give an answer frame (I'm good at... For example, last year I... As a result...) and a list of 12 achievement verbs.
hw: Write a 100-word CV profile or a short cover-letter paragraph for a real or imaginary job.
Find a job advertisement in English online and write down five requirements and five modal structures you notice.
Practise answering "Tell me about yourself" in 45 seconds and record it on your phone, then listen and note two improvements.
lp.tip: Many adults are afraid of interview practice, so start with pair work before groups and praise detail ("you gave a real example"). Avoid asking personal questions about salary or family; keep the roles fictional if needed. Stress that a good answer is a short story with an example, not a list of adjectives.

occ.act: Christmas (25 December) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: a colleague invites you to a company party and a client sends a seasonal greeting. Pairs write and role-play a polite acceptance, a polite refusal and a thank-you reply using semi-formal language ("It's very kind of you to invite me. I would love to come, but unfortunately I have a prior commitment.").
occ.hw: Write a short polite reply to an invitation, with a reason if you decline.

weeks.obj: write a formal letter or email of 120 to 150 words (complaint, enquiry or application), choosing the right register, linking ideas and organising paragraphs
weeks.lang: register shifts (informal, neutral, formal); opening and closing (Dear Sir or Madam / Yours faithfully; Dear Ms Alami / Yours sincerely); I am writing to complain about / enquire about / apply for; I would be grateful if you could...; I was disappointed to find that...; linking (furthermore, as a result, nevertheless, in addition, consequently); softening and indirect questions
weeks.res: Writing guide: E-mail writing; Writing paragraphs, essays, emails and letters
weeks.act: Register transformation; complaint analysis; guided formal letter; peer editing with a checklist
weeks.hw: write a send-ready formal letter or email of 120 to 150 words about a real situation

skills.L: Listen to a customer complaint on the phone and note the problem, the cause and the action requested
skills.S: Explain a problem clearly and politely to a customer service officer
skills.R: Read three messages and decide the register, the purpose and which phrases show politeness
skills.W: Write a formal complaint or enquiry letter of 120 to 150 words

lp.wu: Polite requests: the teacher shows a blunt message ("Send me the document. Now.") and students make it more polite in three steps (neutral, polite, very formal): "Could you send me the document?" / "I would be grateful if you could send me the document at your earliest convenience." They discuss how register changes the relationship.
wuAlt: Register sort: cards with phrases (Hi there, I look forward to hearing from you, Cheers, Please find attached, Yours faithfully, Get back to me) are sorted into informal, neutral and formal.
Pairs improve a rude complaint ("Your service is terrible!") into a firm but polite one.
lp.pres: Show a badly written complaint (aggressive, messy, no paragraphs) and a good one (clear problem, evidence, request). Students compare them and build a structure: opening (reason for writing), the problem with dates and facts, the effect on you, what you expect, closing. Present the language bank for each part, with softening ("I was rather surprised to find that...", "I would appreciate it if you could...") and linking words (furthermore, as a result, nevertheless). Teach the greeting and closing pairs (Sir or Madam / faithfully; name / sincerely) and the rule that formal writing avoids contractions and phrasal verbs (find out becomes discover).
presAlt: Use the Writing guide on e-mail writing from the kit as the model, and compare it with the IELTS video on how to write a formal letter.
Use the Business Writing PowerPoint from the kit to review layout and tone.
lp.prac: Register transformation: pairs rewrite eight informal sentences formally ("Sorry for not turning up" becomes "I apologise for my absence") and then go the other way. Then in complaint analysis, pairs get a business complaint worksheet from the kit and find the problem, the evidence and the request. Finally, a controlled linking task: students join short sentences using furthermore, as a result and nevertheless.
pracAlt: Softening Complaints worksheet from the kit: rewrite harsh complaints so they stay firm but polite.
Indirect questions: change eight direct questions into polite ones (Do you accept returns? becomes Could you tell me whether you accept returns?).
lp.ls: Teacher reads a phone complaint twice (a customer says an online order of a laptop arrived a week late and damaged, and asks for a refund or a replacement). Students note the problem, the dates, the effect and what the customer wants. Then they write the two opening sentences of a follow-up email. If a recording is available, use the complaints recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Auction: the teacher shows 12 sentences, some correct and some with register or linking errors ("Dear Sir, I want my money back." "Furthermore, I am happy with the service."). Teams have a budget of 1,000 dirhams to buy only the correct sentences, then explain the errors in the rest.
lp.prod: Guided formal letter: each student chooses a situation card (a damaged parcel, a wrong hotel booking, an enquiry about an evening course, an application for a volunteer position). Pairs plan four content points together, then write alone for 15 minutes (120 to 150 words) using the structure and language bank. In the last ten minutes partners swap and use a checklist (greeting and closing match, reason for writing, facts, polite request, linking words, no contractions) to give two pieces of feedback.
lp.rw: Read a model letter in the kit (for example the IELTS General Training letter task) and compare it with the student drafts. Underline the formal phrases and the linking words. Then each student writes a final improved version of the first and last paragraph of their own letter.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the opening sentence and the closing sentence of your letter ("I am writing to complain about... I look forward to receiving your reply at your earliest convenience.") and hand it in.
g: Rewrite blunt sentences in three registers.
Teams add the right linker to a gapped letter.
Check a partner's letter against the criteria.
diff: Fast finishers: write the reply of the company (100 words) accepting part of the complaint and offering a solution. Support: give a letter skeleton with the opening, problem, request and closing phrases, and a list of eight linkers.
hw: Write a send-ready formal letter or email of 120 to 150 words about a real situation (a service, an enquiry, a course).
Find a real formal email in English (from a bank, an airline or a school) and label its parts.
Rewrite an informal message you sent in a formal register and underline all the changes.
lp.tip: Remind students that formal does not mean long and complicated: the best letters are short, clear and polite. Keep a classroom list of 'send-ready' phrases on the wall. When marking, correct only register and layout errors on the first draft and give one grammar point per student.

occ.act: New Year week. Optional 10-minute task: students write a short semi-formal email to a colleague or teacher wishing them a good new year and mentioning two plans for the coming months ("I hope you've had a restful break. This year I'm hoping to... and I will have finished my course by June.").

weeks.obj: show progress in reading, use of English, listening, writing and speaking at B1+/B2 level in a Cambridge B2 First-style progress check
weeks.lang: all Semester 1 outcomes: narrative tenses, present perfect, future forms, speculation, conditionals, passive, reported speech, relative clauses, opinions, work and formal writing
weeks.res: Grammar test (general); Cambridge Grammar for First Certificate (use-of-English practice)
weeks.act: Reading and use of English papers; listening paper; writing paper; paired speaking task with a rubric; self-assessment
weeks.hw: write three sentences about what went well in the progress check and two targets for Semester 2

skills.L: Listen to short recordings and answer multiple-choice and note-completion questions
skills.S: Complete a paired speaking task (photos, collaborative task and discussion)
skills.R: Read a text and answer multiple-choice and gapped-text questions
skills.W: Write a formal email or an opinion essay of about 140 words

lp.wu: Exam strategy briefing: the teacher shows six task types on cards (multiple-choice cloze, word formation, gapped text, multiple matching, note completion, email/essay) and students say in one sentence what the task asks them to do and one tip. Remind everyone about timing, never leaving a blank, and reading the instructions twice.
wuAlt: Pairs quiz: each pair writes three grammar questions on Semester 1 and swaps them with another pair.
Circle: each student names one thing they can now do better than in September.
lp.pres: Distribute the reading and use of English paper (about 30 minutes): a multiple-choice cloze of eight gaps, a word-formation task of eight gaps, one text with four multiple-choice questions and a short gapped text. Read the instructions aloud, model the first item on the board, then students work in silence. Collect the papers on time.
presAlt: Use a reading and use of English test from the Ready for B2 First Student Book in the kit (choose three parts).
Use the grammar tests in the kit for a shorter use-of-English paper of 20 items.
lp.prac: Use of English and writing paper (30 minutes): first a key-word transformation of six sentences (for example "I haven't seen him since 2022" becomes "I last saw him in 2022"), then a writing task of about 140 words: a formal email (to a hotel about a booking problem) or a short essay (Should children use smartphones in school?). Students plan for three minutes, write and check for five minutes.
pracAlt: Writing task from the Ready for B2 First Workbook in the kit, with a clear question and four content points.
Writing Task 1 style letter from the IELTS General Training samples in the kit.
lp.ls: Listening paper (about 15 minutes): the teacher reads or plays four short recordings twice (a phone message, a conversation between colleagues about a new project, a short talk on a historic place, a radio interview about sleep). Students answer multiple-choice questions and complete short notes. Use the audioscripts of the Ready for B2 First Student Book or the IELTS listening materials in the kit if a recording is wanted.
lp.re: Error check and consolidation (10 minutes): students receive an anonymous text with 12 common errors from Semester 1 (tenses, articles, prepositions, word order) and correct it. They compare with a partner and then with the key.
lp.prod: Paired speaking tasks (about 8 minutes per pair): the teacher acts as examiner with two candidates. Part 1: personal questions (3 minutes). Part 2: each candidate compares two photographs for one minute and answers one short question about the partner's photos. Part 3: a collaborative task with a decision (choose the best way to spend a small budget for a community project). Part 4: two discussion questions. While waiting, other students complete the reading task in rw.
lp.rw: While other pairs are examined, students read a 300-word article from the kit and answer eight questions (multiple choice and matching). Pairs that finish speaking join in for the last few minutes.
lp.st: Closing: the teacher thanks the class and says when feedback and marks will be returned. Each student writes one sentence about which part felt easiest, which part felt hardest and one target for the next semester and hands it in at the door.
g: Match each task type to its best strategy.
Write three grammar questions for another pair.
Complete key-word transformations against the clock.
Find and fix errors in a short text.
Compare two photos for a minute with a partner.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second text of 100 words on the same topic with a different register. Support: allow a word bank of linkers and give a layout for the email or essay.
hw: Write three sentences about what went well in the progress check and two targets for Semester 2.
Choose three grammar areas from Semester 1 and write two sentences for each.
Read a short article in English and note ten words you want to learn, with a collocation for each.
lp.tip: Present this as a progress check, not an exam, and give clear timings. Use the same criteria (content, communication, organisation, language) in the speaking and writing feedback so students understand their results. Record marks and prepare feedback sheets for the next week, and do not mark with red pen only: note two strengths for each student.
checklist: I can answer personal and opinion questions in a paired speaking task with extended answers.
I can follow a recorded conversation and answer multiple-choice and note-completion questions.
I can read a longer text and answer gist and detail questions.
I can write a 120-150 word email or article with paragraphs and linking words.
I can use narrative tenses and the perfect forms accurately.
I can use future forms, conditionals and the passive in context.
I can interact with a partner, agree and disagree politely, and reach a decision.

occ.act: New Year recap (4 January). Optional 10-minute task: students tell a partner three things they did over Christmas and New Year using narrative tenses, then one thing they are going to try this semester ("I had been planning to visit my cousin for months, so I finally went to Nador.").

weeks.theme: Mid-year review and B2 First orientation
weeks.obj: learn from Semester 1 results, understand the B2 First format and set personal targets for Semester 2 using an error log
weeks.lang: B2 First format (Reading and Use of English, Writing, Listening, Speaking); strategy language (skim, scan, paraphrase, eliminate); correcting recurring errors; target setting (My weakest area is..., I intend to..., By June I would like to be able to...)
weeks.res: Conditionals Review (mixed); Phrasal Verbs Race
weeks.act: Error analysis from the assessment; B2 First format tour; mini diagnostic stations; target setting and error log
weeks.hw: choose two practice areas and complete one B2 First-style task in each

skills.L: Listen to a short B2 First-style recording and identify what each part of the Listening paper asks you to do
skills.S: Explain a target and a practice plan to a partner in a one-minute turn
skills.R: Read the B2 First overview and map each paper to the skills needed
skills.W: Complete a personal error log and target sheet

lp.wu: Error carousel: the teacher posts ten anonymous sentences from the assessment on the walls (tense, articles, prepositions, word order, register). In pairs, students walk round, correct each sentence, name the error type and tick any they think they might have made.
wuAlt: Memory challenge: in two minutes, students list all the Semester 1 topics and grammar points they can remember and compare lists.
Score share: each student says which paper went best and which was hardest.
lp.pres: Return the assessment and show the class profile without names: which areas are strong and which need work. Present a one-page overview of the B2 First exam: Reading and Use of English (seven parts, 75 minutes), Writing (two tasks of 140 to 190 words: an essay and a choice such as an email, article, report or review), Listening (four parts, about 40 minutes), Speaking (about 14 minutes with a partner and two examiners). Explain that Semester 2 includes four skills weeks and a mock exam, and that each student chooses whether to aim at the certificate or just at B2 skills.
presAlt: Use the Ready for B2 First Teacher's Book from the kit for the exam overview and the marking criteria.
Use the Ready for B2 First Student Book exam overview pages as a short handout.
lp.prac: Mini diagnostic stations: students rotate through four stations (a short gapped text, a short listening with note completion, a one-minute photo comparison, a 60-word writing opener) and rate their confidence after each one. The teacher notes common errors at each station for later weeks and gives a one-line comment to each student.
pracAlt: Strategy match: match each exam task to the best strategy (skim first, underline key words, eliminate wrong options, check word class).
Review questions: pairs choose five items from the conditionals and phrasal verb review sheets in the kit and swap.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short monologue and a conversation twice (a person describing a first job; two friends discussing a weekend trip). Students answer five B2 First-style questions (multiple choice and sentence completion) and then discuss in pairs what clues told them the answer (paraphrase, tone, a word that changed the meaning). If a recording is available, use the audioscripts from the Ready for B2 First Student Book or a listening task in the kit.
lp.re: Target setting in threes: students complete "In Reading, my biggest problem is... To improve I will..." and share one target with the group. The group agrees on a way to support each other (a weekly vocabulary swap, a writing exchange, a speaking partner call).
lp.prod: Speaking practice: pairs practise a B2 First-style long turn (compare two photographs for one minute, then answer a short question) and a collaborative task (decide together which of five options is the best for a given situation, with two minutes of discussion). The partner uses a simple tick list (answers fully, develops ideas, uses linking words, invites the partner to speak) and gives one tip.
lp.rw: Personal error log and target sheet: students read the exam overview and fill in three columns (my recurring errors, the rule, a corrected example) with at least five entries from the assessment. Then they write three targets (grammar, skill, exam) for Semester 2 and the weekly practice plan (for example, one written task, 30 minutes of listening and ten new collocations per week).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one specific target for Semester 2 and one action you will take this week ("By March I want to stop dropping the third-person -s, so I will check it in every piece of writing.") and hand it in.
g: Rotate through four short skill tasks.
Write a target and share it.
Review phrasal verbs from Semester 1 in a quiz.
diff: Fast finishers: write a four-week study plan with times, resources and a reward. Support: give a target sheet with sentence frames (My weakest area is... I will practise by... I will check my progress by...).
hw: Choose two practice areas and complete one B2 First-style task in each.
Write a four-week study plan and share it with a partner.
Read a short English article, write three questions about it and summarise it in 60 words.
lp.tip: Give adults control of their learning: let them choose their targets and keep their own error log, since this is more effective than corrections from the teacher alone. Use anonymous errors to avoid embarrassment. Be honest that B2 is a stretch for some students, and praise progress in small steps.

occ.act: Yennayer (Amazigh New Year, 14 January) falls this week. Optional 10-minute task: students describe how their family celebrates it and what is cooked, then explain why traditions like this matter, using at least two linking words (because, whereas, although).
occ.hw: Write 6 sentences about a festival in your family and why it is important.

weeks.obj: compare cultures, discuss stereotypes with tact, and use gerund and infinitive patterns accurately in conversation
weeks.lang: verbs followed by -ing (enjoy, avoid, suggest, keep, mind, can't stand); verbs followed by to (decide, hope, manage, refuse, afford); verbs followed by both with a change of meaning (stop doing / stop to do, remember, try, forget, regret); prefer, would rather, used to; comparing cultures (in my culture it is customary to..., people tend to..., it is considered rude to...); polite disagreement
weeks.res: Gerund and Infinitive Master; Gerunds (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Culture quiz; gerund and infinitive card game; culture shock stories; stereotype discussion
weeks.hw: write a 120-word guide to the customs of your city for a foreign visitor, using at least six gerund or infinitive patterns

skills.L: Listen to two speakers describe culture shock and note what surprised them and what they did about it
skills.S: Compare customs in two countries and discuss a stereotype in a balanced way
skills.R: Read a short text on customs around the world and underline the gerund and infinitive patterns
skills.W: Write a 120-word guide to the customs of your city for a visitor

lp.wu: Culture quiz: groups of four get ten statements about customs ("In Japan, it is polite to slurp noodles." "In Morocco, it is usual to take a gift when visiting a home.") and decide whether they are true, false or depends. They must say "I think it's true, as far as I know..." and give an example. The teacher reveals the answers and groups share any custom that surprised them.
wuAlt: Brainstorm: in two minutes, pairs list everything a visitor should know before staying with a Moroccan family.
Postcard talk: students describe the strangest custom they have seen abroad or on television.
lp.pres: Write on the board three pairs of sentences that show meaning change: "I stopped smoking" / "I stopped to smoke"; "I remember meeting him" / "I must remember to call him"; "I tried opening the window" / "I tried to open the window, but it was stuck". Elicit the meanings and build a table: verbs + -ing (enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind, keep, finish), verbs + to (decide, hope, manage, refuse, afford, plan), verbs with both (stop, remember, forget, try, regret). Add structures for comparing cultures: "It is considered rude to...", "People tend to...", "In my family, we're expected to...". Check with ten quick sentence completions.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on gerunds and infinitives from the kit.
Use the Gerund and Infinitive Master worksheet and the Verb + infinitive sheet from the kit as a rule reference.
lp.prac: Gerund or infinitive card game in groups of four: players put down a verb card and a sentence card and the others decide if the pattern is correct, with the winner of each round explaining the rule. After ten minutes, controlled practice: students complete 15 sentences with the right form (She refused ___ (pay). I regret ___ (not study) harder.) and correct four errors in a short paragraph.
pracAlt: Gerund and Infinitive Dominoes from the kit: match the verbs to the correct pattern.
Board game from the kit: move around the board and make a sentence with the correct verb pattern at each square.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short monologues twice (a student from Morocco describing the first month in France or Canada; a visitor describing a first week in Morocco). Students note what surprised each speaker, what they found difficult and what they decided to do, and then underline the gerund and infinitive patterns in the teacher's script. If a recording is available, use the culture or culture shock recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: True or False: each student writes three sentences about their own habits and customs using gerunds and infinitives, one of them false (I can't stand eating alone. I never forget to call my mother on Fridays). Partners guess the false sentence and ask two follow-up questions.
lp.prod: Culture swap and stereotype discussion: in groups of four, each student chooses a country or region they know (or their own) and prepares a 90-second turn on three customs: one they enjoy, one that outsiders often misunderstand and one that is changing. Then groups discuss the question "Why do stereotypes exist and are they ever useful?" for six minutes, with a rule that every disagreement must start with a polite phrase (That's one way of looking at it, but...). Each group reports one conclusion to the class.
lp.rw: Read a short text about customs around the world (about 200 words) from the kit and underline the gerund and infinitive patterns. Then write a 120-word guide for a foreign visitor to Oujda using at least six patterns (remember to take off your shoes, avoid arriving empty-handed, expect to be offered tea).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one custom you enjoy doing and one you would like to stop doing, or a stereotype about your city that you want to change ("People in my city tend to avoid talking about money, but I'd like to see this change.") and hand it in.
g: Decide if a statement about customs is true or false.
Play a verb pattern card game.
Explain meaning changes with mime and sentences.
Find someone who has experienced a custom on the card.
Give evidence for or against a stereotype in 30 seconds.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short dialogue of 12 lines between a host and a guest from another culture who misunderstand a custom, using eight verb patterns. Support: give a verb-pattern table with a model sentence for each group.
hw: Write a 120-word guide to the customs of your city for a visitor, using at least six gerund or infinitive patterns.
Interview someone who has lived abroad about culture shock and write five sentences about what they told you.
Watch a short video about a country's customs in English and write down three useful expressions for comparing cultures.
lp.tip: Teach stereotypes with care: ask students to discuss ideas about groups, not to criticise real people. Keep the focus on tact and evidence. For gerunds and infinitives, avoid long lists; teach three groups and add verbs gradually, correcting with a rule and an example sentence.

weeks.obj: talk about money and shopping, understand persuasion in advertising, use quantifiers and articles accurately and write a short product review
weeks.lang: quantifiers (a great deal of, a large number of, plenty of, hardly any, few / a few, little / a little, several); articles review (a / an / the / zero article, generalisations and unique things); persuasion language (superlatives, rhetorical questions, imperatives, power words such as free, new, proven, limited); consumer language (refund, receipt, guarantee, faulty, complaint); review phrases (it's worth the money, I would recommend, the only drawback is)
weeks.res: Articles Practice; Learn English 2026: Pre-determiners (advanced lessons)
weeks.act: Quantifier race; advert analysis; consumer rights role-play; product review writing
weeks.hw: write a 120-word review of a product or service you bought recently

skills.L: Listen to two people talk about a purchase or an advertisement and note what persuaded them
skills.S: Persuade a partner to buy a product and deal with a complaint politely
skills.R: Read a short text about advertising and underline the persuasion techniques
skills.W: Write a 120-word product review with a recommendation

lp.wu: Quantifier race: teams stand in lines; the teacher says a topic ("people in your town who ride bicycles", "free time students have", "money teachers earn") and the first team member runs to the board and writes a sentence with the correct quantifier (a few, hardly any, plenty of). The class votes on correct and incorrect answers.
wuAlt: Guess the advert: the teacher reads slogans from well-known brands without naming them and teams guess the product.
Quick debate: is it better to save money or enjoy it now?
lp.pres: Show three short adverts or slogans (a mobile phone, a soft drink, a bank) and elicit the persuasion techniques: superlatives, rhetorical questions, imperatives, emotional images, 'free' and 'new'. Then present quantifiers by countable and uncountable (many / much / a large number of / a great deal of; few / little / hardly any) and the meaning difference between few and a few, little and a little. Review articles with a short text where students fill a / the / zero and explain the choice (generalisations with zero article, the for unique things, the for something already mentioned).
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on quantifiers and articles from the kit.
Use the Pre-determiners lesson from the Learn English 2026 advanced folder in the kit.
lp.prac: Article story: pairs get a short anecdote with 12 missing articles and complete it, then explain two choices to another pair. Next, quantifier cards: students make true sentences about their town and about shopping habits ("There are hardly any bookshops left in our neighbourhood. A great deal of people buy clothes online."). Finish with an advert analysis: in groups, students identify the persuasion technique in six slogans.
pracAlt: Determiners exercise from the kit for extra controlled practice.
Make It Count worksheet from the kit: choose the correct quantifier in context.
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short monologues twice (a woman who bought a second-hand laptop online and regrets it; a man who bought a pair of shoes because of an advert). Students note what the speaker bought, what persuaded them and whether they are satisfied, and then write which technique worked. If a recording is available, use the commercial and credit recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Articles pelmanism: pairs match sentence halves and decide which article is correct for each (the, a, zero) before keeping a card. The pair with the most correct matches wins.
lp.prod: Consumer rights role-play and advert: in groups of three, students play a customer, a shop assistant and a manager. The customer has a faulty product (a phone that stops working after two weeks) and a receipt, and wants a refund; the assistant offers a repair; the manager decides. Switch roles for a second situation (a hotel room that does not match the photos). Then groups design a 60-second advert for a made-up product and present it, using at least three persuasion techniques and four quantifiers.
lp.rw: Read a short article about advertising or product placement (about 250 words) from the kit and underline the persuasion techniques. Then write a 120-word review of a product or service you bought (what it is, what is good, the only drawback, who would like it, your recommendation) using at least four quantifiers and correct articles.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one sentence about a product you would recommend and one about an advert that tried to persuade you ("A large number of people in my town use this app, and I would recommend it because it saves time.") and hand it in.
g: Write sentences with the correct quantifier.
Identify the persuasion technique in a slogan.
Match sentence halves and justify the article.
Persuade a partner to buy a strange object in 45 seconds.
Exchange complaints and solutions in role play.
diff: Fast finishers: write a persuasive 100-word advert for a local business using three techniques and a call to action. Support: give a table of quantifiers by countable and uncountable and an article decision flowchart.
hw: Write a 120-word review of a product or service you bought recently.
Find two adverts (print or online) and write what technique each uses and whether it works on you.
Keep a note of all the money you spend in a week and write five sentences about your habits using quantifiers.
lp.tip: Money can be a sensitive topic, so keep the focus on shopping habits and prices rather than salaries. Articles are a stubborn area; do a short article correction in every lesson from now on. Use real Moroccan brands, markets and online shops as examples, and let students bring a product to the lesson.

weeks.obj: give advice and talk about regrets and hypothetical situations in health contexts, use medical vocabulary and give a short talk of two minutes
weeks.lang: advice and criticism (should / shouldn't have, ought to, had better, if I were you, why don't you, you'd be better off); hypothetical language (if I had slept more, I would feel better; if I hadn't eaten so much, I wouldn't be ill now; mixed conditionals light); health vocabulary (symptoms, remedy, prescription, check-up, stress, diet, fitness); talk structure (opening, three points, closing)
weeks.res: Advice + If I were you; Learn English 2026: Conditionals Mixed Type (advanced lessons)
weeks.act: Advice clinic; mixed conditionals; health talk; doctor-patient role-play
weeks.hw: write a 120-word reply to a letter from a person with a health or lifestyle problem

skills.L: Listen to two speakers discuss a health problem and a remedy and note the advice given
skills.S: Describe symptoms, give advice with should and if I were you and deliver a two-minute talk
skills.R: Read a short article on lifestyle and health and match the advice to the problem
skills.W: Write a 120-word advice reply to a letter

lp.wu: Idiom quiz: the teacher writes six health idioms on the board (under the weather, as fit as a fiddle, a pain in the neck, back on your feet, a clean bill of health, burn the candle at both ends). Pairs guess the meaning and then use two of them in a short exchange.
wuAlt: Healthy habits circle: each student says one habit that helps and one that harms, and the next person gives advice with "You'd be better off...".
Pairs rank six lifestyle factors (sleep, exercise, diet, stress, friends, screen time) from most to least important for health and defend the order.
lp.pres: Write on the board a short situation: "Karim has a headache and feels exhausted. He worked until 2 a.m. for a week, drank six coffees a day and skipped lunch." Elicit advice (He should sleep more. If I were him, I'd cut down on coffee.) and criticism about the past (He shouldn't have worked so late. He ought to have taken breaks.). Build a language bank of present advice (should, ought to, had better, if I were you, why don't you) and past criticism (should have, shouldn't have, ought to have). Add mixed conditionals light: "If he hadn't worked so late, he wouldn't feel so tired now." Check meaning with concept questions.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on health or advice from the kit.
Use the Learn English 2026 mixed conditionals advanced lesson from the kit for further examples.
lp.prac: Advice clinic: students write a short health or lifestyle problem on a slip. Slips are passed round and each student writes advice with a different structure (should, if I were you, had better). Then pairs match each problem with two pieces of advice and one criticism about the past. Controlled practice: 12 sentences with should have / shouldn't have / if + past perfect, with a quick correction round.
pracAlt: Advice for Aches and Pains worksheet from the kit: give advice for physical problems.
Should Survey from the kit: find out classmates' views on healthy habits and report them.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a radio phone-in twice (a listener explains she sleeps four hours a night and has constant headaches; an expert gives advice). Students note the problem, three pieces of advice and one criticism, and then discuss which advice they would follow. If a recording is available, use the health recordings from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Advice game: groups roll a dice or draw a card to receive a problem and a structure (should have / if I were you / why don't you). Each player gives advice with the structure and the group gives a point for the most helpful and natural answer.
lp.prod: Health talk: students prepare a two-minute talk on a health or lifestyle topic of their choice (how to sleep better, managing exam stress, healthy eating on a budget, giving up smoking). They plan with a three-point outline, use at least two advice structures and one hypothetical sentence, and give the talk to a partner and then to a group of four. Listeners complete a feedback card (clear opening, three points, useful advice, eye contact). In the last ten minutes, pairs role-play a doctor and a patient with symptoms and advice.
lp.rw: Read a 250-word magazine article on lifestyle and health from the kit and match five problems with the advice. Underline structures of advice and regret. Then write a 120-word reply to a letter from a person who has a problem (for example, a student who cannot sleep before exams), using at least four advice structures and one hypothetical sentence.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you should have done for your health this year and one piece of advice you would give yourself ("I should have started walking earlier. If I were you, I'd go for a walk every evening.") and hand it in.
g: Guess the meaning of health idioms.
Pass problem slips and give advice.
Make past criticism sentences from picture cards.
Role-play a consultation in two minutes.
Add a hypothetical sentence to the chain.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short health blog post of 150 words giving five pieces of advice and one personal regret. Support: give a table of advice structures with example sentences and a three-point talk planner.
hw: Write a 120-word reply to a letter from a person with a health or lifestyle problem.
Prepare a two-minute talk on a health topic and practise it aloud twice.
Find a medical or health website in English and write down ten useful words with a short definition.
lp.tip: Do not ask students to share private medical information; use fictional characters or general topics. Remember that should have is a common weak point, so give three or four model sentences on the board. Practise the talk structure slowly, and give feedback on content before grammar.

weeks.obj: read news critically, spot bias and fake news, summarise an article and use passive reporting verbs and news language
weeks.lang: headlines (short forms, present tense for past events, passive without be); passive reporting verbs (is said to, is believed to, is thought to, is reported to, is expected to; it is said that...); news vocabulary (source, headline, bias, misleading, evidence, claim); summarising (the article argues that..., according to the writer, in brief); media habits
weeks.res: Video: How news feed algorithms supercharge confirmation bias; Learn English 2026: Passive vs Active Voice (advanced lessons)
weeks.act: Headline decoding; fake news detective; summary writing; media habits survey
weeks.hw: write a 100-word summary of a news article you read in English, using at least two passive reporting verbs

skills.L: Listen to two short news items and decide which source is reliable and why
skills.S: Discuss media habits and explain whether a news story is reliable
skills.R: Read an article and identify the claim, the evidence and any bias
skills.W: Write a 100-word summary of an article

lp.wu: Headline decoding: the teacher writes six short headlines on the board (MINISTER QUITS AFTER SCANDAL, CITY TO BAN CARS FROM CENTRE, SCHOOL CLOSURES EXPECTED) and pairs expand them into full sentences. They notice what is missing (articles, auxiliary verbs) and what time the headline describes.
wuAlt: Which source? Students rank where they get their news (social media, TV, newspapers, friends, radio) and say how much they trust each one.
Rumour chain: the teacher whispers a rumour and the class passes it on; the last student says the final version and the class discusses how it changed.
lp.pres: Show a real-style news report with the sentence "The company is said to be planning to close 200 shops." Elicit the structure and write the pattern on the board: subject + is/are said / believed / thought / reported / expected + to-infinitive, and the alternative It is said that the company is planning to close 200 shops. Add the perfect infinitive for the past (The driver is believed to have left the country) and the continuous (He is thought to be living abroad). Practise with five facts about a famous place or person ("Marrakech is believed to have been founded in 1070.").
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on news or reporting verbs from the kit.
Use the Passive vs Active Voice lesson from the Learn English 2026 advanced folder in the kit.
lp.prac: Sentence transformation: pairs change 10 active news sentences into passive reporting structures (People believe the minister resigned because of illness becomes The minister is believed to have resigned because of illness). Then critical reading: pairs read two short accounts of the same event (one balanced, one emotional) and list the differences in word choice, evidence and sources. They note three words that signal bias (shocking, disaster, claimed).
pracAlt: Read a Guardian article from the kit with the advanced task sheet and underline the passive reporting verbs.
Newspaper article lesson plan from the kit: students identify the parts of a news story (headline, lead, details, quote).
lp.ls: Teacher reads two short news items twice about the same event (a fire in a market): one factual with a named source, the other with exaggeration and no source. Students tick which statements are facts and which are opinions, note three bias words and decide which item they trust. If a recording is available, use the media recording from the Listening folder named in the kit.
lp.re: Fake or fact: the teacher shows eight short claims on slips (some true, some false) and pairs decide in 20 seconds each whether they would share them, saying what they would check first. Give a point for each good reason (check the date, look for another source, look at the photo).
lp.prod: Fake news detective: groups of four receive a package of three short stories or social media posts (one true, one half-true, one false) and use a checklist (source, date, evidence, emotion, other reports) to decide which is which. Each group presents its conclusion in 90 seconds, using passive reporting verbs ("The post claims..., it is said to have been shared a million times..."). Then the class discusses: how can we protect ourselves from misleading information?
lp.rw: Read a 300-word article from the kit and underline the claim, the evidence and any emotive language. Then write a 100-word summary using the pattern "The article argues that... According to the writer,... It is believed that..." with no personal opinion. Swap and check that the summary uses the writer's ideas in new words.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one headline from your day and a passive reporting sentence about it ("The new tram line is expected to open next year.") and one question you would ask to check a news story. Hand it in.
g: Decide whether to share a claim and why.
Rewrite active sentences with is said to.
Replace emotive words with neutral ones.
Rank sources from least to most reliable.
diff: Fast finishers: write a balanced 120-word news report on a local event with a quote from two sources. Support: give a summary frame (The article is about... The writer says that... According to the article...) and a passive reporting table.
hw: Write a 100-word summary of a news article you read in English, using at least two passive reporting verbs.
Keep a media diary for three days and write 80 words about your habits and one change you want to make.
Choose a viral claim you have seen and check it using two reliable sources, then write what you found.
lp.tip: Choose examples from sources students recognise, but avoid sensitive political topics: the aim is to teach how to check, not what to believe. Passive reporting verbs are formal, so give many short examples and correct the infinitive form carefully (is believed to have left, not is believed that he left to). During Ramadan, shorten the production task if students are tired.

occ.act: Ramadan begins around this week. Optional 10-minute task: students discuss how media habits change in Ramadan (television series, social media, news) and report what they have heard with passive reporting verbs ("Ramadan series are said to attract millions of viewers. It is believed that people spend more time on their phones at night.").
occ.hw: Write 5 sentences with passive reporting verbs about how Ramadan is changing in your city.

weeks.obj: present for and against arguments about technology and AI, predict the future with future perfect and future continuous, and express cause and result clearly
weeks.lang: future perfect and future continuous (By 2040, robots will have replaced..., This time next year I'll be working...); cause and result (so, such... that, therefore, as a result, consequently, due to, because of, lead to, result in); AI and technology vocabulary (algorithm, automation, privacy, data, bias, surveillance); presenting for and against (On the one hand..., On the other hand..., a further drawback, the main benefit)
weeks.res: Learn English 2026: Future Perfect (advanced lessons); Future perfect (PowerPoint)
weeks.act: Future predictions; cause and effect chains; AI ethical debate; for-and-against presentation
weeks.hw: write a 150-word for-and-against paragraph on a technology issue

skills.L: Listen to a short talk on automation and jobs and note the predictions and their causes
skills.S: Present the advantages and disadvantages of a technology and make predictions
skills.R: Read an article on technology or AI and identify cause and effect links
skills.W: Write a 150-word for-and-against paragraph

lp.wu: Future snapshot: the teacher writes on the board "By 2040..." and "This time in 10 years..." Pairs make five predictions about work, health, transport, school and daily life, using future perfect and future continuous ("By 2040, most of us will have stopped carrying cash. In ten years' time, I'll be working remotely."). Pairs read their best prediction and the class votes on the most likely.
wuAlt: Technology timeline: students put six inventions (printing press, telephone, internet, smartphone, social media, AI chatbots) in order and say which changed life most.
One-minute talk: what technology could you not live without?
lp.pres: Show a short text on a job of the future and elicit the verb forms. Teach future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action in progress at a future time and for polite plans, and future perfect (will have + past participle) for an action finished before a future time. Contrast: "In 2035, I'll be working in Rabat" and "By 2035, I'll have finished my studies". Then present cause and result: so / such... that (The program was so fast that it replaced ten jobs), therefore / as a result / consequently (new sentence), because of / due to + noun, lead to / result in. Practise with a cause and effect chain on the board: more data, better algorithms, faster decisions, fewer human jobs.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 on the future or technology from the kit.
Use the future perfect and future continuous PowerPoints from the kit, followed by the cause and effect writing guide.
lp.prac: Prediction table: pairs get a table of six areas (work, health, school, money, transport, privacy) and write one future perfect and one future continuous sentence for each, then join two ideas with a cause and result link. Controlled practice: gap-fill of 12 sentences with future perfect or continuous and a short exercise turning pairs of sentences into one with so... that, as a result or because of.
pracAlt: Automation and jobs exercises from the IELTS activities in the kit: work through the vocabulary and comprehension tasks.
Sentence combining: join 10 cause and effect pairs in two different ways.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a short talk twice (about 90 seconds) on how machines will change jobs: which jobs will disappear, which will remain, and why. Students complete a table with three jobs, the prediction (will have disappeared, will still be needed) and the cause. If a video is available, use the talk on automation and jobs from the IELTS activities in the kit.
lp.re: Cause and effect writing: pairs write a three-link chain on a card (Phones are cheaper, so more people have them. As a result, many shops have closed. Consequently, ...) and swap. Another pair must add a fourth link and read the chain aloud.
lp.prod: AI ethical debate and presentation: groups of four choose a motion (Schools should allow students to use AI to write essays; Self-driving cars should replace human drivers; Companies should not use AI to decide who to hire). Each group splits into two sides, prepares for ten minutes (two arguments with cause and result, one prediction with future perfect, one concession) and holds a four-minute debate. Then each student gives a one-minute for-and-against summary to a new group using On the one hand... On the other hand....
lp.rw: Read a short article on technology from the kit (for example the robotic bees reading or the quantum computers video script) and underline the cause and effect words and the future forms. Then write a 150-word for-and-against paragraph on a technology issue (social media for teenagers, remote work, AI in schools), with at least two cause and result links, one future perfect or continuous sentence and a recommendation at the end.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one prediction about technology in your life ("By 2035, I'll have stopped using paper maps.") and one sentence with so... that or as a result about a technology you use. Hand it in.
g: Add a prediction to the chain using future perfect.
Match causes to results and link them.
Defend a side picked from a card in 60 seconds.
Interview a partner as a person from 2040.
Replace one linking word with another and keep the meaning.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 200-word essay for or against AI in education, with a conclusion that recommends a policy. Support: give a table of cause and result linkers with example sentences and a for-and-against paragraph frame.
hw: Write a 150-word for-and-against paragraph on a technology issue.
Watch a short video about artificial intelligence in English and write five sentences about it using future forms.
Interview someone about how technology has changed their job or studies in the last ten years and write a summary of 80 words.
lp.tip: Students often have strong feelings about technology, so enforce time limits and give every speaker a turn. Check that the future perfect is used for completed actions with a time marker (by 2040), since many students confuse it with the future simple. Do not assume every student has a smartphone or fast internet; allow printed alternatives for research tasks.

weeks.obj: use skimming, scanning and text-attack strategies on gapped text, multiple matching and multiple choice tasks, and infer unknown vocabulary from context
weeks.lang: reading strategies (skim for structure, scan for specific detail, read for inference and attitude); text cohesion (reference words such as this, that, such, the latter; linkers such as nevertheless, whereas, as a result); inferring word meaning from context, word class and word parts; paraphrase between question and text
weeks.res: Ready for B2 First SB: Reading and Use of English (Parts 5-7); Ready for B2 First TB: exam tips and keys
weeks.act: Timed text attack; gapped text sentence-removal clinic; multiple-matching speed round; vocabulary inference stations; answer-justification pairs
weeks.hw: complete one timed gapped text or multiple-matching task and write a justification note for each answer

skills.L: Listen to the teacher think aloud while solving a reading question and note the strategy words
skills.S: Justify an answer to a partner by quoting the text and naming the distractor
skills.R: Practise skimming, scanning and reading for inference on B2 First-style texts
skills.W: Write a 40-word summary of a text and a paraphrase of one sentence

lp.wu: Sixty-second skim: the teacher shows an article for sixty seconds (headline, first and last paragraph, one sentence per paragraph) and then hides it. Students write the text type, the writer's purpose and the attitude in one line, then compare in pairs and check. Repeat once with a different text so that students see how much the first and last sentences give away.
wuAlt: Headline match: the teacher gives six headlines and six first sentences from different articles and pairs match them, explaining which words helped.
Reference chase: pairs underline every this, that, such, one and the latter in a paragraph and draw an arrow to what each refers to.
lp.pres: Present the three reading tasks in B2 First that need the most strategy: Part 5 (long text, multiple choice, questions follow the order of the text), Part 6 (gapped text, six sentences removed, one extra) and Part 7 (multiple matching, ten statements, four or five short texts or one text in sections). For each give a routine: Part 5, read the question stem first and find the paragraph, then predict before looking at options; Part 6, read the text around each gap and look for reference words, linkers and tense clues that the missing sentence must match; Part 7, underline key words in the statements and scan for paraphrase, not for the same words. Model Part 6 with a think-aloud on one gap, pointing to "this", "However" and a time reference as clues.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in Ready for B2 First (Student's Book) for the format of Parts 5 to 7 and read its exam-tips box together.
Use the Guessing words from context reading task to teach the three steps for unknown words: decide the word class, look for a definition or contrast in the sentence, check against the word parts.
lp.prac: Part 6 clinic: pairs get a short article with four gaps and six sentences (one extra) cut into strips. Before moving any strip they write beside each gap the clue they can see (a pronoun, a linker, a date, a repeated noun), then place the strips and check with the answer key. Then they swap with another pair and defend one choice using the words "The word this in the sentence refers to..." and "It cannot go in gap 3 because...".
pracAlt: Part 7 speed round for stronger groups: four short profiles and eight statements, five minutes, with the rule that every answer needs a paraphrase pair written next to it.
A Part 5 task with a lower-level article from The Guardian folder (Intermediate versions) for students who need an easier first step.
lp.ls: Think-aloud listening: the teacher reads a Part 5 question and a paragraph aloud twice, then talks through the decision process out loud ("The question asks about the writer's attitude, so I look for words like unfortunately, surprisingly... Option B says 'angry' but the text only says 'disappointed'"). Students note down five strategy phrases they hear. Then a second text is read and pairs do the same think-aloud for a different question. If a recording is available, use a Reading-skills podcast or a short talk from the Podcasts folder, but the activity works with the teacher's voice alone.
lp.re: Distractor hunt: the teacher shows a multiple-choice question with four options and the paragraph it comes from. In pairs, students label each wrong option with the distractor type: too extreme, true but not answering the question, from a different part of the text, or reversed meaning. Repeat with three questions and compare labels as a class.
lp.prod: Answer-justification circles: in groups of four each student takes a question from the texts done today and explains in forty seconds, with a sentence from the text, why the right answer is right and which distractor was most tempting and why. The group rates the explanation for evidence, clarity and use of paraphrase words (the writer implies, the text suggests, this rules out). Rotate until everyone has explained twice.
lp.rw: Read the article "The future of food" or "Ten 100-year predictions that came true" (Reading tasks in the kit) and write a 40-word summary, then paraphrase three sentences using different grammar (for example, active to passive, noun to verb). Underline two unknown words, write the word class and a guess of the meaning before checking in a dictionary.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the strategy that helped you most today and the reading task you will practise at home ("I will look for reference words around each gap. I will practise Part 6 twice this week.") and hand it in.
g: Decide text type, purpose and attitude from a quick look.
Draw arrows from pronouns and reference words to the ideas they replace.
Reassemble a gapped text from cut-up sentences using clues.
Name why each wrong option looks right.
Match a question phrase to the text phrase that means the same.
Guess an unknown word from context and defend the guess to the group.
diff: Fast finishers: write a Part 7 style statement for each paragraph of an article and swap with another pair to find the paragraph.
Support: give a strategy card (read the question, find the paragraph, predict, check options) and a gapped text with only three gaps and four sentences.
hw: Complete one timed gapped text or multiple-matching task from Ready for B2 First and mark a justification note (clue word plus reason) next to each answer.
Read one English article of 500 words and write a 40-word summary and three vocabulary guesses.
Take three sentences from an article and rewrite each with a different structure, keeping the meaning.
lp.tip: Adults at this level often read word by word and run out of time. Teach them to ask what the question wants before reading the whole text, and time every task, about 1 minute 15 seconds per Part 5 question. Always insist on the text evidence for each answer, even when it is correct, and note the average timed score this week for the mock exam.
