weeks.obj: use prediction, paraphrase awareness and note-taking to answer sentence completion, multiple matching and multiple choice listening tasks, and understand fast connected speech
weeks.lang: listening strategies (read and predict, listen for paraphrase, ignore distractors); connected speech (weak forms, linking, elision, contractions such as would've, could've, gonna, wanna); signposting language in talks (what I'd like to do first, to cut a long story short); note completion with numbers, names and spelling
weeks.res: Ready for B2 First SB: Listening units (Parts 1-4); Ready for B2 First SB: audio and audioscripts (rar)
weeks.act: Prediction and paraphrase work; connected-speech dictation; two-pass task cycle; distractor analysis with transcripts; extended listening with notes
weeks.hw: complete one B2 First listening task and bring a list of five phrases you misheard

skills.L: Understand B2 First-style extracts with multiple-choice, sentence completion and multiple matching tasks
skills.S: Compare answers and explain why the distractor is wrong
skills.R: Read a transcript and underline the words that give each answer
skills.W: Complete notes and write the sentences they heard in full

lp.wu: Reduced speech dictation: the teacher reads eight sentences at natural speed with weak forms and linking ("I should've told her." "What d'you want to do?" "Could you pass me the salt?") and students write what they hear. Pairs compare, then the teacher writes the full forms and models the natural versions. Students notice which words are stressed and which almost disappear.
wuAlt: Gist before detail: the teacher reads a thirty-second announcement once and students write the situation (who, where, why) only.
Number and name check: students spell names and write numbers dictated at normal speed (phone numbers, a postcode, a price with decimals).
lp.pres: Present the four parts of B2 First Listening: Part 1 (eight short extracts, multiple choice), Part 2 (monologue, sentence completion, 1 to 3 words), Part 3 (five speakers, multiple matching) and Part 4 (interview or conversation, multiple choice, seven questions). Teach the routine: read the question and underline key words, predict the type of word or the likely paraphrase, listen the first time for the answer and the second time to check. Show with a short example how distractors work: a speaker says "I was going to take the bus, but my brother offered me a lift", so "bus" is a distractor and "car" is the answer. Teach the three connected-speech features (weak forms, linking, elision) with examples on the board.
presAlt: Use the matching unit in Ready for B2 First (Student's Book and the Workbook) for the format and the exam-tips box.
Use the Listening tasks slideshow from the Listening folder for a visual model of prediction.
lp.prac: Prediction and paraphrase: pairs get the questions of a Part 3 multiple-matching task (five speakers, eight options) without the recording and write the paraphrases they expect (for example "I could never have afforded it" = money problem). The teacher reads or plays the recording twice, with pairs marking where their prediction matched, which options were distractors and which words gave the answer. Then pairs read the transcript and underline the key phrases.
pracAlt: Part 2 sentence completion with a short talk from the Listening folder (a Jeff, Tini or Tim recording named in the kit) and a gapped note sheet.
A Part 1 set with six short extracts read by the teacher, one question each.
lp.ls: Extended listening with notes: the teacher plays a recording of about three minutes (a Cambridge IELTS Section 3 or 4 recording, or a podcast from the Podcasts folder) or reads a prepared text aloud twice, a speed slightly faster than normal. Students take notes in a two-column grid (main ideas / details and numbers) and use the second listening to complete what they missed. They then compare notes in threes and decide together which three notes would answer an exam question.
lp.re: Mis-heard game: the teacher reads ten phrases that are often mis-heard in fast speech ("I'd've", "should've been", "a lot of them", "not at all", "going to be") and students write what they hear. Teams score a point for each correct written form and a bonus for repeating it with the right linking.
lp.prod: Podcast summary pairs: Student A listens to a one-minute section read by the teacher (or played) and takes notes, Student B listens to a different one-minute section. They then tell each other what they heard in two minutes using their notes and signposting phrases ("The main point was..., apparently..., what surprised me was..."). The listener asks two questions to check detail. Teacher listens for accurate reporting and fluent linking.
lp.rw: Read the transcript of today's extended listening and underline the paraphrase pairs (question words and the matching words in the transcript). Then write a 60-word summary of the talk from your notes, using at least two reporting verbs (suggested, pointed out, argued).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one thing you will do before the recording starts and one thing you will do when you miss an answer ("I will predict the word type. I will stop thinking about the missed answer and keep listening.") and hand it in.
g: Write what you hear in fast natural speech.
Guess how the recording will rephrase the question.
Find the word that changed the speaker's answer.
Answer on the first pass and check on the second.
Decode fast phrases before the other team.
Compare note grids and decide whose notes are most useful.
diff: Fast finishers: write a 100-word script for a Part 3 style monologue with one distractor in each sentence and read it to another pair.
Support: give a gapped transcript with the missing words listed on the board, then give the same task without the list.
hw: Complete one B2 First listening task from Ready for B2 First (audio and audioscripts rar are in the Drive folder) or a task from the Listening folder, and record your score.
Listen to a three-minute podcast and write five reduced-speech phrases you heard, with their full forms.
Watch a short TED-style talk in the Videos folder and write ten notes in a two-column grid.
lp.tip: Students try to catch every word and give up when they miss one, so train them to let it go. Always play or read twice during practice, and check after the second listening using the transcript. If audio is not available, read the script yourself at a natural pace and look at the students, not the page, so they hear real intonation.

weeks.obj: perform the individual long turn, the collaborative task and the discussion with natural discourse markers, balanced turn-taking and developed answers
weeks.lang: discourse markers and fillers (well, actually, to be honest, as far as I'm concerned, what I mean is, let me think); reacting and developing (That's an interesting point, because..., Not necessarily, in my experience...); comparing and speculating about photos (it could be, he looks as if, whereas); negotiating (Shall we start with...? How about you? Let's agree on...); peer feedback with a rubric
weeks.res: Ready for B2 First SB: Speaking units (Parts 1-4); Speaking test: mock exam
weeks.act: Photo comparison long turns; collaborative decision task with timing; rubric-based peer feedback; discussion extension; filler and discourse marker practice
weeks.hw: record a one-minute long turn comparing two photos and note two things to improve using the rubric

skills.L: Listen to a model long turn and note the discourse markers and the comparing language
skills.S: Compare two photos for one minute, negotiate a decision with a partner and extend a discussion
skills.R: Read a speaking transcript and mark examples of developing an answer
skills.W: Write six sentences using discourse markers and speculation

lp.wu: Speed talk with development: students stand in two rows and answer a question in 30 seconds each (What was the best advice you ever received? Which skill would you most like to have?). Their partner must ask one follow-up question that begins with Why or How. After three rounds, ask the class which answers were easiest to develop and why.
wuAlt: Filler bank: pairs list ten phrases they can use to buy thinking time and use five of them in a one-minute chat.
Two photos, one minute: the teacher shows two contrasting photos and students compare them in pairs for forty-five seconds.
lp.pres: Present the four parts of B2 First Speaking: Part 1 interview (personal questions), Part 2 long turn (compare two photos and answer a short question, about 1 minute), Part 3 collaborative task (discuss options with a partner, then reach a decision), and Part 4 discussion (the examiner asks both candidates abstract questions). For each part show one marked answer: a weak version (short, repeated vocabulary) and a developed version with reasons, examples, speculation and a discourse marker. Teach and board the useful language: comparing (whereas, similarly, in contrast), speculating (it might be, she could be feeling), negotiating, and giving an opinion with balance (On the one hand, on the other...).
presAlt: Use the IELTS Speaking sample recordings (Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 prompts, recordings and transcripts in the IELTS folder) as examples of developed answers.
Use the Speaking test mock exam and the Speaking about photographs resources from the Tests folder for photo prompts.
lp.prac: Long turn rotation: in groups of three, one student speaks for one minute comparing two photos from a set (for example two ways of studying, two types of holiday), the second is the examiner and asks the follow-up question, and the third observes with a tick sheet (compares, speculates, uses markers, no long pauses). Rotate roles three times so everyone gets feedback. The teacher listens to one group each round and writes one strong phrase and one error on the board.
pracAlt: Collaborative task for pairs: a card with five options (ways to reduce plastic waste in Oujda) and the instructions "Talk to each other about how useful these would be and choose the best one" with a two-minute timer.
Part 4 discussion cards for threes: abstract questions such as "Do you think social media makes people more or less honest?"
lp.ls: Model listening: the teacher reads or plays two versions of the same Part 2 long turn, one weak and one strong (the IELTS speaking recordings and transcripts can be used if available). Students listen twice, note the discourse markers and the comparing language in the strong version, and decide on three differences that would raise the score. Then they say aloud the best sentence they heard.
lp.re: Interrupt and develop: in pairs, Student A states an opinion in one sentence ("I think remote work is better.") and Student B responds with a challenge, a question or an example for thirty seconds before they swap. The target is three turns on one point without using yes or no alone.
lp.prod: Mock speaking test in fours: two candidates do Parts 2 to 4 with a printed task set (long turn each, a collaborative task and a short discussion) while two students act as assessors with a rubric (grammar and vocabulary, discourse management, pronunciation, interactive communication) scored from 1 to 5. After each pair finishes, the assessors give one strength and one target, and the pairs swap roles. The teacher moves between groups and notes patterns for feedback.
lp.rw: Read a transcript of a Part 3 discussion (from the IELTS sample transcripts or the mock exam) and mark every phrase that develops an answer, balances an opinion or invites the partner. Then write six sentences using discourse markers and speculation ("To be honest, I think it could be too expensive, whereas...").
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one phrase you will add to your answers and one habit to reduce ("I will use 'To be honest' and 'for example'. I will stop saying 'yes' with no explanation.") and hand it in.
g: Answer and develop questions in short timed rounds.
Compare two images for one minute without stopping.
Use thinking-time phrases without losing fluency.
Keep one topic going for three turns.
Score a classmate on a four-criteria rubric.
Reach a decision from five options in two minutes.
diff: Fast finishers: prepare two Part 4 discussion questions for the class and lead a four-minute discussion.
Support: give phrase cards (comparing, speculating, agreeing, disagreeing) and a sentence frame for each long turn: "Both photos show... whereas... I think..."
hw: Record a one-minute long turn comparing two photos and note two things to improve from the rubric.
Practise a collaborative task with a friend on a message call for two minutes and note three phrases you used.
Write six sentences with discourse markers about a topic from today.
lp.tip: Many Moroccan learners give short, correct answers and stop. Coach them to add a reason, an example and a comparison every time. Keep rubric feedback specific (one strength, one target) and never correct grammar during a speaking turn. Use stopwatches so students feel the length of a real long turn.

occ.act: Eid al-Fitr falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: in pairs, students compare how their family celebrates Eid now with how they celebrated when they were children, using the long-turn structure ("In the past we used to..., whereas nowadays...") and invite two follow-up questions.

weeks.obj: plan and write an essay, an article and a report or proposal with a clear structure, appropriate register and linking, then edit with a checklist
weeks.lang: text types (essay: for and against, opinion; article: engaging opening, direct address; report and proposal: headings, impersonal language, recommendations; review); linking devices (furthermore, in addition, nevertheless, consequently, as a result, whereas, in spite of); paragraphing; register choice; self-editing codes
weeks.res: Ready for B2 First SB: Writing units (essay, article, report); Writing guide: argumentative essay
weeks.act: Five-minute planning drill; model analysis by text type; guided essay writing; code-based self-editing; peer review against the band descriptors
weeks.hw: write a 140 to 190 word essay or article in 40 minutes and edit it with the checklist

skills.L: Listen to the teacher read a model essay and note the paragraph topics
skills.S: Plan aloud with a partner and defend choices of structure and register
skills.R: Read two model answers and compare their quality against the checklist
skills.W: Write and edit an essay or an article of 140 to 190 words

lp.wu: Five-minute plan: the teacher gives a B2 First essay question ("Some people believe that young people today spend too much time online. What is your opinion?") and pairs plan it on paper in five minutes: three paragraph topics, one example for each and a conclusion sentence. Pairs then swap plans and say what is missing. This is repeated with an article question the next time the class meets.
wuAlt: Linker sort: teams sort twenty linking words under contrast, addition, cause, result and concession, then write one sentence with the hardest one.
Register switch: students turn a casual message into a formal sentence ("Can't make it, sorry" to "I regret that I will be unable to attend").
lp.pres: Compare the four B2 First writing text types (Part 1 is always an essay, Part 2 offers an article, an email or letter, a report, a review or a story). Show a model of each for 30 seconds and ask what features make it that type: essay (introduction, two main ideas, a conclusion, formal register), article (a title, a hook, rhetorical questions, personal opinion), report (headings, bullet points, impersonal verbs such as it is recommended that), review (description, evaluation, recommendation). Teach the checklist: content (all points), communicative achievement (right register), organisation (paragraphs, linkers) and language (range and accuracy). Underline the linking devices in the essay model and teach three new ones each time.
presAlt: Use the Writing guides (Writing an article, writing a report, argumentative essay and Helpful Guide to Essay Writing) in the kit as printable models.
Use the IELTS Writing task samples (Task 2) in the IELTS folder for a longer model that students can shorten to B2 First length.
lp.prac: Guided essay: students write the introduction and one body paragraph of the essay they planned in the warm-up, in fifteen minutes, with the checklist on the board. The teacher walks around, marks only one error code in each paragraph (T for tense, WW for wrong word, P for punctuation, ^ for missing word, Reg for register) and asks writers to correct from the code. Pairs then read each other's paragraph and say which linker works best.
pracAlt: Paragraph builder: students are given a topic sentence and three jumbled supporting sentences to order and link with appropriate linkers.
Register rewrite: students rewrite a 60-word informal email as a formal letter of complaint.
lp.ls: Dictated model: the teacher reads aloud a short model article of 100 words twice at a natural pace and students write down the hook, the three main points, and the closing line in note form. Then they compare with the printed model. No audio is needed.
lp.re: Error clinic: the teacher displays six anonymous sentences from the students' guided drafts. In teams, they identify the error type with the code (T, WW, P, ^, Reg) and correct it. A team gets a point for the correct code and a bonus for a better alternative wording.
lp.prod: Timed writing and peer review: students write the second body paragraph and a conclusion in fifteen minutes, then swap texts with a partner and review it against a four-criteria checklist (content, organisation, language range, register). The reviewer writes two comments and one question for the writer. The writer rewrites one sentence with a better linker or stronger vocabulary and reads it to the group.
lp.rw: Read two model answers for the same task (one at band 3 and one at band 5, from the Writing guides or Ready for B2 First) and underline what makes the stronger answer stronger (range, accuracy, linking, tone). Then finish the essay at home or in class and edit it with the code list before handing it in.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write the error code you make most often and one linker you will use next time ("I often forget articles (^). I will use 'consequently' once.") and hand it in.
g: Plan an essay in five minutes with three paragraph topics.
Sort linking words by function and use the hard ones.
Rewrite informal sentences in formal register.
Correct anonymous mistakes using the code.
Write the best opening line for an article in one minute.
Mark two sample answers against a checklist and justify the band.
diff: Fast finishers: write a second version of the same text type (an article instead of an essay) using different linking and register.
Support: give a paragraph template with sentence starters for each paragraph and a bank of ten linkers.
hw: Write a 140 to 190 word essay or article in 40 minutes and edit it with the checklist (mark the errors with codes).
Choose a report or review task and write a plan with headings only.
Collect five linking devices from an English article you read and write one sentence for each.
lp.tip: Adults under time pressure skip the plan and write too much. Train a five-minute plan on every task. Return corrections as codes so that students edit their own work, and always give a word range (140 to 190) so they practise counting. Collect the first drafts to use anonymously in Week 28.

weeks.obj: talk and write about education and learning habits using nuanced comparison and emphasis
weeks.lang: comparison (the more... the more; as... as; not nearly as... as; by far the most; a great deal more; considerably less); emphasis (cleft sentences: What I find hardest is..., It was my teacher who...; inversion for emphasis, Never have I...); education and skills vocabulary (curriculum, assessment, dropout, tuition, vocational, lifelong learning, soft skills)
weeks.res: American English File 4 SB (unit on comparison and emphasis); American English File 4 Workbook (matching unit)
weeks.act: Cline of comparison; cleft sentence workshop; learning habits survey and report; roundtable on education reform; short opinion paragraph
weeks.hw: write 150 words on the best way to learn a skill using comparison and emphasis structures

skills.L: Listen to speakers talk about their studies and note comparisons and emphasis
skills.S: Discuss education options and defend an opinion with comparison and emphasis
skills.R: Read an article about universities or learning and underline comparative and emphatic structures
skills.W: Write a short opinion paragraph using at least four target structures

lp.wu: Learning habits line-up: the teacher reads statements (I learn best by listening. I prefer studying alone. I find grammar easier than speaking.) and students stand along a line from "totally agree" to "totally disagree", then justify their position to the person next to them using "far more" or "not nearly as". After each statement students compare who stands where and why.
wuAlt: Skill auction: pairs list five skills they think matter most in the future and rank them.
Memory test: students recall a lesson they remember from school and say why it stuck.
lp.pres: Write on the board a sentence at the A2 level and upgrade it in steps: "Online learning is better than classroom learning." becomes "Online learning is far more flexible than classroom learning." and then "The more flexible the course is, the more students enrol." Teach the nuance in the cline: slightly, a bit, considerably, far, by far the most; not as... as, not nearly as... as, twice as... as. Then introduce emphasis with cleft sentences: "It is motivation that matters most." "What I find hardest is listening." "The person who changed my attitude was my teacher." Show and drill with three learning-related prompts. Mention (without drilling) inversion for emphasis ("Rarely have I felt so nervous before a test.").
presAlt: Use the matching unit in American English File 4 (Student Book and Workbook) for comparison and emphasis exercises, choosing the unit that matches the grammar.
Use the Comparative Expressions and Comparatives with not as... as worksheets from the Worksheets folder.
lp.prac: Comparison and cleft transformations: pairs complete ten sentence transformations, for example "Learning in a group is more motivating than learning alone." to "The more students work together, the more motivated they become." and "I love their enthusiasm." to "What I love is their enthusiasm." They check with another pair and mark which version sounds more natural. Then each pair writes three sentences about their own school years using at least one cleft and one nuance of comparison.
pracAlt: Match-the-halves cards for emphasis structures, then a short gap-fill on comparative modifiers (slightly, nowhere near, by far).
Error correction: a paragraph on education with eight faulty comparisons and clefts.
lp.ls: Teacher reads or plays a student talking about their university experience (a Fred, Tini or Jeff recording named in the kit, such as Tini student life or Fred Uni) or reads a prepared 150-word monologue twice. Students listen for three comparisons and two emphasis structures and write them down in a table. They then decide in pairs whether the speaker would recommend the university and give a reason.
lp.re: Which is the best? Teams get a card with three learning options (a traditional university, an online course, learning on the job) and prepare a ninety-second pitch to persuade the class that theirs is "by far the most useful". The class votes after each pitch and gives one reason using a comparative structure.
lp.prod: Education roundtable: in groups of four, students discuss "How should schools in Morocco change to prepare students better for work?" using at least four target structures, with roles (chair who keeps time, reporter, devil's advocate, note-taker). They reach three recommendations in ten minutes and the reporter presents them to the class in sixty seconds. The teacher notes comparison and emphasis errors on the board for the end.
lp.rw: Read the Guardian article on universities (Advanced) or "The best Asian universities" (Reading tasks) and underline every comparative or emphatic structure. Then write 150 words about the best way to learn a skill (languages, coding, a craft) using at least two comparatives with modifiers, two cleft sentences and a the-more-the-more sentence.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one cleft sentence and one the-more-the-more sentence about learning English ("What helps me most is speaking. The more I practise, the more confident I feel.") and hand them in.
g: Stand on a line to show how strongly you agree and justify it.
Place comparison modifiers on a scale from slightly to by far.
Turn plain sentences into cleft sentences against the clock.
Persuade the class that your learning option is the most useful.
Chair a discussion and summarise it in sixty seconds.
Choose between two nuanced comparisons and explain the difference.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short letter to the Ministry of Education suggesting one change, using three emphatic structures.
Support: give a card with the structures and one model sentence for each and let the student fill the slots.
hw: Write 150 words on the best way to learn a skill using comparison and emphasis.
Interview a classmate or friend about the best teacher they have had and write six sentences with clefts and comparatives.
Read a short article about education in English and underline all comparison structures.
lp.tip: Clefts and the-more-the-more are easy to drill and hard to use freely, so keep the practice personal and frequent. Check that students do not overuse emphasis, which sounds unnatural if it is in every sentence. Make sure quieter learners get a role in the roundtable and record the participation notes.

weeks.obj: describe environmental problems, propose and evaluate solutions, and write a proposal or opinion essay with recommendations
weeks.lang: expressing purpose (so that, in order to, so as not to, with a view to); so/such/too/enough (so much waste that..., such a serious problem that..., too polluted to swim, not clean enough); modals for recommendation (should, ought to, could, it would be advisable to); conditionals for solutions; vocabulary (carbon footprint, landfill, renewable, deforestation, overfishing, single-use, drought, sustainable)
weeks.res: Writing unit: cause and effect (PowerPoint); Too, very, enough (grammar sheets)
weeks.act: Problem and cause analysis; so/such/too/enough transformations; solutions auction; proposal writing with recommendations; mini presentation to a "local council"
weeks.hw: write a 150-word proposal to a local organisation with recommendations

skills.L: Listen to a talk about an environmental issue and note problems, causes and solutions
skills.S: Present a proposal and respond to challenges
skills.R: Read an article about plastic or sustainable fashion and underline purpose clauses and recommendations
skills.W: Write a proposal with headings and recommendations

lp.wu: Footprint check: each student ticks a list of fifteen daily habits (I take a bag to the market. I leave the tap running. I use single-use plastic bottles.) and counts their "green score". Then they compare with a partner and argue for the habit that makes the biggest difference. Ask: which of these is hardest in Oujda and why?
wuAlt: Environment word web: pairs build a web around "waste" with at least fifteen words in five minutes.
Quick quiz: how long does plastic take to break down? How much food is wasted in the world each year? (Use the Earth Day ice-breaker cards.)
lp.pres: Put on the board three sentences about one problem: "There is so much plastic in the sea that fish are dying." "It is such a serious problem that governments must act." "The sea is too polluted to swim in." Elicit and teach so/such/too/enough (with a table: so + adjective/adverb, such + (a/an) + adjective + noun, too + adjective + (for) + to, adjective + enough) and purpose structures (in order to, so as not to, so that + modal). Then give a model recommendation set: "It would be advisable to introduce a deposit on bottles." "The council should install more recycling bins so that residents can sort waste easily." Teach headings for a proposal (Introduction, Current situation, Suggestions, Conclusion).
presAlt: Use the Writing unit on cause and effect PowerPoint and the Too, Very, Enough grammar sheets from the kit as handouts.
Use the matching unit in American English File 4 (Student Book and Workbook) for so/such/too/enough exercises.
lp.prac: Transformations and use: pairs complete eight sentences with so, such, too and enough from the problem list ("The beach is so dirty that..." "It is too hot to..."), then link pairs of sentences with purpose structures ("People should recycle. There will be less waste." becomes "People should recycle so that there will be less waste."). They write three real sentences about their own neighbourhood and share them with the class.
pracAlt: Gap-fill on so/such/too/enough with ten sentences from environmental news.
Speaking pairs: Student A states a problem; Student B must reply with an effect using so that or such...that.
lp.ls: Teacher reads or plays a talk on an environment topic about 2 minutes long (Tim Global Warming, Tim Energy or Keiko Trash Facts recordings in the kit, or the teacher reads a prepared script on plastic in the Mediterranean). Students listen twice and complete a three-column table: problem / cause / solution. In the second round, they note the purpose structure or modal used for each solution. Pairs then decide which solution is most realistic and why.
lp.re: Solutions auction: teams receive 10,000 dirhams of "budget" and a list of eight solutions (bottle deposit scheme, free public buses, a ban on plastic bags, school recycling club, tree planting, fines for littering, solar panels on public buildings, water-saving taps) with costs. They bid, defend the choices in 30 seconds and justify with purpose clauses ("We chose this so that...").
lp.prod: Council proposal: groups of four prepare a three-minute proposal for the Oujda municipality on one problem (waste collection, water use, traffic and air quality, noise). Each group presents: the problem and evidence, two causes, three recommendations with purpose, and an expected result. The rest of the class acts as councillors and asks one challenging question each ("Who will pay for this? Why would people follow it?"). The group answers using conditionals and modals of possibility.
lp.rw: Read "Saving the planet", "Sustainable fashion" or "Turning waste plastic into packaging" in the Reading tasks and underline the purpose structures and the recommendations. Then write a 150-word proposal with headings (Introduction, Suggestions, Conclusion) on a problem in your area.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one so... that or such... that sentence and one purpose sentence about an environmental problem in Oujda ("There is so much litter that the beach is unsafe. We should install bins so that visitors can use them.") and hand it in.
g: Count your daily green habits and argue for the biggest impact.
Complete and transform sentences against another team.
Bid for solutions and defend choices with purpose clauses.
Answer tough questions from a mock council.
Build a chain of at least four links using different linkers.
Describe an environment word without saying it.
diff: Fast finishers: write a one-paragraph letter to a local newspaper on an environmental issue, using three purpose structures and a rhetorical question.
Support: give a table with sentence frames for problem, cause and solution plus a word bank.
hw: Write a 150-word proposal to a local organisation (a school, a cafe, the municipality) with recommendations.
Interview a family member about how the environment in their neighbourhood has changed and write six sentences.
Read or listen to a short English item about the environment and write five new words with examples.
lp.tip: Local topics (water saving, plastic bags, traffic) work better than global ones because students can offer real evidence. Keep the discussion practical and avoid political arguments. Check that students can distinguish so (adjective) and such (noun phrase) and that they use "in order to + base verb" correctly.

weeks.obj: complete an adapted B2 First mock exam under timed conditions, apply strategies and plan for the final weeks
weeks.lang: all B2 First skills at B1+/B2 level: reading and use of English, listening, writing, speaking
weeks.res: Ready for B2 First SB: practice test papers; Ready for B2 First TB: keys and marking guidance
weeks.act: Timed reading and use of English paper; listening paper; writing task; speaking pairs; self-marking and target setting
weeks.hw: complete the exam reflection sheet and set two targets for the final assessment

skills.L: Complete a B2 First-style listening paper with multiple choice and sentence completion
skills.S: Complete a speaking test with a partner (long turn, collaborative task, discussion)
skills.R: Complete reading and use of English tasks (multiple-choice cloze, open cloze, word formation, key word transformation, gapped text)
skills.W: Write a 140 to 190 word essay or article

lp.wu: Exam routine briefing: the teacher gives out strategy cards (read the instruction twice, check the time every ten minutes, answer every question, use the five-minute plan for writing) and each student chooses three to follow. Pairs say when they will use each one. One minute of silent breathing before the paper begins.
wuAlt: Quick vocabulary check: pairs give each other ten exam instruction words (underline, tick, complete, paraphrase) and explain them.
Mock exam rules: students read the rules aloud and ask questions.
lp.pres: Hand out the use of English and reading paper: an adapted B2 First paper with multiple-choice cloze (8 gaps), open cloze (8 gaps), word formation (8 gaps), four key word transformations and a gapped text (4 gaps) taken from the Ready for B2 First tests and sample tasks in the kit. Explain the format and time (about 50 minutes for the full set, or shorter if you reduce the number of items), read the instructions aloud and model the first item of each part. Students work in silence and mark the answer sheet.
presAlt: Use a shorter selection of tasks (one cloze, one transformation, one gapped text) when time is limited.
Use sample tasks from the Ready for B2 First Workbook and the IELTS Reading Practice 1 for the reading part if the class prefers different text types.
lp.prac: Writing paper: students choose one task from a pair (an essay or an article, as in B2 First Part 1 and Part 2) and write 140 to 190 words in 40 minutes. They use the checklist from Week 24, count words and check codes before handing in.
pracAlt: Report or review task if the class prepared it in Week 24.
A shorter 100-word task for students at the lower end who are not yet ready for the full length.
lp.ls: Listening paper: the teacher plays or reads aloud a B2 First-style paper in four parts: three short extracts with multiple choice, a monologue with eight sentence-completion gaps, a five-speaker matching task and an interview with six multiple-choice questions. Each part is played twice. Use the Ready for B2 First audio and audioscripts in the kit, or, if no audio is available, a prepared script read aloud at natural speed. Students mark answers on a sheet.
lp.re: Self-marking: the teacher gives out answer keys for the reading, use of English and listening papers. Students mark their own work, count their scores and write three questions they got wrong with the reason (language, strategy or time). Pairs compare and guess how a distractor fooled them.
lp.prod: Speaking pairs: the teacher examines pairs for about 10 to 12 minutes in the B2 First format (Part 1 interview questions, Part 2 long turn with two photos, Part 3 collaborative task with prompts, Part 4 discussion) while the others complete the writing (if not finished) or the self-reflection sheet. Use the mock exam and Speaking about photographs resources and the IELTS speaking cards for prompts. The teacher scores each candidate on four criteria from 1 to 5 and writes one strength and one target.
lp.rw: Exam reflection sheet: students record their scores in each paper, list the strategies they used, the one strategy they forgot, and set two targets for the final assessment in Week 30. In the last 10 minutes, they exchange writing papers with a partner and highlight one sentence they liked and one they would change.
lp.st: Closing: the teacher thanks the class, explains when feedback will be given, and asks each student to write one line on how they felt during each paper. Collect the answer sheets and the reflection sheets.
g: Choose the three strategies you will use in the exam.
Mark your own paper and analyse each error.
Discuss the three hardest questions with a partner.
Plan an essay in five minutes under a timer.
Write two SMART targets for the final weeks.
diff: Fast finishers: write three extra word formation items for another pair.
Support: allow a word bank of connectors for the writing task and extra time for the cloze.
hw: Complete the exam reflection sheet and set two targets with a specific practice task each.
Redo the five questions you found hardest and write why you were wrong.
Write one essay paragraph that improves a weak part of your exam writing.
lp.tip: Treat the mock as a diagnostic: record every score by skill and use it to plan Weeks 28 to 30. Keep the room silent and calm, and explain that scoring a low result is useful information, not a failure. If you cannot run all four papers in two hours, run the use of English and listening papers in class and ask students to do speaking pairs in the break or in the first twenty minutes of Week 28.
checklist: I can manage my time across a reading and use of English paper.
I can follow an extended listening and choose the best answer.
I can write a 140-190 word essay, article or report with a clear plan.
I can speak for one minute on a photo or topic with few pauses.
I can interact in a collaborative task and give reasons.
I can correct my own errors using a checklist.
I can name my three main targets for the final weeks.

weeks.obj: improve range and accuracy with collocations, phrasal verbs, word formation, fixed expressions and prepositions, and fix their own recurring errors
weeks.lang: collocations (make a decision, take a risk, heavy rain, strongly recommend); phrasal verbs (carry out, come up with, put up with, turn out, look into, bring about); word formation (prefixes un-/im-/dis-, suffixes -ment/-ness/-ity/-able, noun-verb-adjective families); fixed expressions and idioms (in the long run, on the whole, by and large); dependent prepositions (depend on, responsible for, interested in, approve of); error correction (fossilised errors from class writing)
weeks.res: Check Your English Vocabulary for FCE; Check Your English Vocabulary for Phrasal Verbs and Idioms
weeks.act: Collocation matching; phrasal verb story; word formation family tree; preposition auction; error clinic from the students' own drafts
weeks.hw: rewrite your corrected sentences and add five collocations to your personal vocabulary log

skills.L: Listen to a short talk with collocations and phrasal verbs and note them
skills.S: Use new collocations and phrasal verbs in a short talk
skills.R: Read a text and underline collocations, phrasal verbs and fixed expressions
skills.W: Rewrite sentences with error corrections and write new sentences with target vocabulary

lp.wu: Collocation snap: the teacher says the first word of a collocation (make, take, do, heavy, strongly) and students shout out partners (a decision, a risk, a favour, rain, recommend). After three rounds, pairs write five sentences using collocations they were surprised by. Quick ask: which collocation did you not know?
wuAlt: Odd one out: the teacher writes four words (make / do / take / have) and one noun (progress) and students decide which verb fits.
Preposition quick fire: the teacher says the adjective or verb (interested, depend, responsible) and the class shouts the preposition.
lp.pres: Present four vocabulary systems quickly with examples taken from students' own earlier writing: collocations (verbs with nouns: make progress, take advantage, do research), phrasal verbs (come up with, put up with, look into, carry out; separable and inseparable), word formation (decide, decision, decisive, decisively; un- im- dis- prefixes; -ment -ness -ity -able suffixes), and dependent prepositions (depend on, consist of, approve of). Give a one-page handout with 20 items per system and ask students to underline the five they will adopt. Teach how to store items: record the whole phrase with an example sentence and a translation, not the single word.
presAlt: Use the Collocations Go, play or do? sheet, the Make or Do sheet and the English Phrasal Verbs in Use book from the kit.
Use the Check Your English Vocabulary for FCE book (Coursebooks by Subject) or Phrasal Verbs and Idioms in the kit for printed exercises.
lp.prac: Four-station clinic: groups rotate every eight minutes through four stations: Station 1 collocation matching (verbs with nouns), Station 2 phrasal verb gap fill with a short story, Station 3 word formation (complete a table of noun / verb / adjective / adverb for ten roots), and Station 4 dependent preposition quiz. Each station has a key at the side. At each station they write two original sentences. The teacher monitors the stations that cause the most errors.
pracAlt: Collocation ladder game: students climb a ladder by supplying a collocation partner.
Phrasal verb Jeopardy game from the Worksheets folder for teams.
lp.ls: Teacher reads a 150-word anecdote twice with ten embedded target items (collocations and phrasal verbs, for example "I came up with an idea. We had to put up with the noise. It turned out to be a risk worth taking."). Students listen for the target items from a list of twenty and tick them as they hear them. On the second listening they write the full phrase. Pairs retell the anecdote using at least five of the items. If a recording is available, use a Podcast from the Podcasts folder as a second text.
lp.re: Error auction: teams get twenty sentences from the class's own writing from Weeks 24 and 27 (anonymous, with errors in collocation, preposition, word form and tense). They bid dirhams on the sentences they believe are correct. After the auction they correct the wrong sentences and name the type of error. Points are awarded for each correct bid and each correct repair.
lp.prod: Mini-talk with target language: students prepare for three minutes and then speak for ninety seconds on a topic (the biggest change in my city, a risk I took, a project I would like to carry out), using at least six items from their personal vocabulary list. A partner ticks the items used and writes down one error. They swap roles. Volunteers give their talk to the whole class.
lp.rw: Read a short text about travel or work (from the Reading tasks or a Guardian article) and underline all collocations, phrasal verbs and fixed expressions. Then take five of your own sentences with errors from the earlier tasks, correct them using the rule, and add them to your error log with the correct form and a note.
lp.st: Exit ticket: write three new items you will actively use (one collocation, one phrasal verb, one word family) and one error you will watch for ("make a decision, put up with, development / developing; I will check 'depend on'.") and hand it in.
g: Shout out the best partners for a key word.
Retell a short story using target phrasal verbs.
Complete noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms.
Bid on correct sentences and repair the wrong ones.
Climb up by supplying a partner word.
Judge a sentence guilty or not guilty and give the rule.
diff: Fast finishers: write a short quiz of ten items on today's topics for another team.
Support: give a table with the collocation and preposition lists and a worked example for each station.
hw: Rewrite your corrected sentences and add five collocations and two phrasal verbs, each with an example, to your vocabulary log.
Choose a short English text and underline ten fixed phrases, then write new sentences using them.
Write a 120-word paragraph about your last holiday using six target items.
lp.tip: Group errors by cause (first language transfer from Arabic or French, over-generalising a rule) and teach one rule at a time. Use anonymous sentences from the students' own writing so no one is embarrassed, and make the log personal and visible. Remind students that vocabulary that is recorded in a sentence is far easier to recall than a word list.

weeks.theme: Review carousel, presentations and speaking circles
weeks.obj: review the year's key grammar and skills through stations, give a three-minute talk on a topic of choice and run a short Q&A
weeks.lang: year review (tenses, conditionals, passive, reported speech, relative clauses, gerund and infinitive, comparison, linking); presentation language (Today I'd like to talk about, to begin with, this brings me to, to sum up); handling questions (That's a good question, let me think; I'm afraid I'm not sure, but I'd say...)
weeks.res: Preparing EFL learners for oral presentations; Talk: There's more to life than being happy (model talk)
weeks.act: Rapid grammar review carousel; presentation planning; three-minute talks; audience feedback; speaking circles
weeks.hw: prepare a final goal sheet and complete the practice checklist for the final assessment

skills.L: Listen to presentations and note two good points and one question for each
skills.S: Give a three-minute talk and respond to questions
skills.R: Read a short text at a carousel station and correct errors
skills.W: Write the outline of a talk and a feedback note

lp.wu: Year in one sentence: students stand and share one thing they can do now in English that they could not do in September, using the present perfect or a comparison ("I've learned how to... I'm much more confident at..."). Then they pass the ball to someone who adds a follow-up question. The teacher notes a few examples on the board.
wuAlt: Grammar speed dating: two rows talk for ninety seconds on a grammar prompt (the third conditional, reported speech, relative clauses) and then one row moves.
Group memory chain: recall the topic of each month in order.
lp.pres: Present the structure of a three-minute talk: opening hook, three main points with examples, a transition between points (this brings me to..., on top of that), a conclusion and an invitation for questions. Demonstrate by giving a 60-second talk yourself on a familiar topic (such as "Why I love tea in Oujda" or "My first week at the school") and ask students to tick the structural moves as they hear them. Hand out the feedback form (content, organisation, language, delivery) and a card with question-handling phrases. Take sign-ups for the talk order.
presAlt: Use the Preparing EFL Learners for Oral Presentations sheet and the Opinions sheets from the Speaking folder for models and phrases.
Show a short TED-style talk from the Videos folder (Educational Talks) and have students tick the presentation moves.
lp.prac: Rapid carousel: six stations (tenses, conditionals and wishes, passive and reported speech, relative clauses and participles, gerund and infinitive, comparison and linking) with a short task card, a ten-minute rotation and a key. Groups of three score each station and note their weakest. After the carousel, each student chooses one weak area and writes a sentence in that area that they will use in their talk.
pracAlt: Talk preparation clinic: students write an outline with three points on a card and rehearse the opening in pairs.
Self-check: complete a grammar test from the Tests folder and mark it.
lp.ls: Listening for feedback: during the first three talks, the audience listens with a form: one good point, one question, one language item they noticed. After each talk the speaker listens to two pieces of feedback. If no talks are ready yet, the teacher gives a 2-minute talk twice and the class completes the form.
lp.re: Quick error race: the teacher puts six incorrect sentences from the year's writing on the board and teams race to correct them and name the grammar point. The first team with the right answer gets a point; a bonus for a second correct version.
lp.prod: Three-minute talks and Q&A: in two groups of six (or one whole class if small), students give a prepared three-minute talk on a topic of choice (a place, a skill, a social issue, a person who influenced them) with a two-minute Q&A. The audience completes the feedback form. The teacher scores confidence, structure and language and collects one strength and one target for each speaker. Students who do not speak this week speak at the start of Week 30.
lp.rw: Write a one-page reflection: what you did well in your talk, what you would change, two grammar points you still need to revise and one goal for the final assessment. Use at least four different structures from the year (a conditional, a passive, a relative clause and a reporting verb).
lp.st: Exit ticket: write one compliment for a classmate's talk and one personal goal for the last session ("Your talk was clear and full of examples. I want to use more linking words.") and hand it in.
g: Share one proud moment with a structure from the year.
Say a sentence for each prompt with a new partner.
Rotate through six stations and score your group.
Answer a surprise question for thirty seconds without hesitating.
Correct sentences before the other teams.
Give a compliment, a suggestion and a compliment.
diff: Fast finishers: prepare a second, shorter talk (90 seconds) on a different topic.
Support: give a talk outline template with sentence starters and an opening and closing sentence to adapt.
hw: Prepare a final goal sheet and complete the practice checklist for the final assessment.
Practise your talk once more and record yourself, noting two filler words to reduce.
Write a one-page summary of the grammar you find hardest with one example for each.
lp.tip: Anxiety is highest before talks. Offer a rehearsal in pairs, a clear time limit, and the option of speaking from notes (not a full script). Give feedback that is specific and kind, and track who still needs to speak next week. Use results to decide who needs extra support in the final assessment.

occ.act: Earth Day (22 April) falls around this week. Optional 10-minute task: groups plan a short action for the American Space or their neighbourhood (a clean-up, a recycling corner, a plant swap) and pitch it in sixty seconds, using purpose clauses and recommendations from Week 26 ("We should organise a clean-up so that the beach is safe for families.").

weeks.lang: all year outcomes at B1+/B2 level

skills.L: Complete a B2 First-style listening paper
skills.S: Complete a speaking test in pairs and take part in a feedback conference
skills.R: Complete reading and use of English tasks
skills.W: Write an essay, article, report or review of 140 to 190 words

lp.wu: Calm start: the teacher reviews the exam routine (time, answer sheets, strategies) and each student chooses one strategy from the exam strategy cards. Pair chat: "What is the biggest change in your English since September?" for one minute, with a follow-up question from the partner.
wuAlt: Quiet review: two minutes of silent review of personal notes and the error log.
Pairs test each other on five collocations and five phrasal verbs.
lp.pres: Final reading and use of English paper: hand out an adapted B2 First paper (multiple-choice cloze, open cloze, word formation, key word transformations and a gapped text or multiple-matching task) from the Ready for B2 First books in the kit or from a teacher-prepared selection. Explain the timing, read the instructions aloud and let students begin in silence. Collect the papers at the end.
presAlt: Use a shorter set of tasks (one cloze, one transformation and one gapped text) if time is short.
Use the IELTS Reading Practice 1 sample as an alternative reading text.
lp.prac: Final writing task: students choose one of two tasks (an essay or an article) and write 140 to 190 words in 40 minutes with the planning time included. They count words, use the checklist from Week 24 and edit with the code list before handing in.
pracAlt: A report or review task for students who prepared those text types.
A shorter 120-word task for lower-level students.
lp.ls: Final listening paper: the teacher plays or reads aloud a B2 First-style paper in four parts (short extracts with multiple choice, a monologue with sentence completion, a five-speaker matching task and an interview with multiple choice) twice each. Use the audio and audioscripts of Ready for B2 First, or a Cambridge IELTS listening in the kit, or, if audio is not available, the teacher's script read aloud at natural speed. Students answer on an answer sheet.
lp.re: Pair reflection: students tell a partner the three biggest improvements since September and give an example for each ("In September I couldn't give a long answer. Now I can talk for a minute about a photo."). Each partner reports one improvement back to the class in a sentence using reported speech.
lp.prod: Speaking pairs: the teacher examines pairs for 10 to 12 minutes in the B2 First format (interview, long turn, collaborative task, discussion) while the other students complete the course feedback form and a short vocabulary task. The teacher scores each candidate on grammar and vocabulary, discourse management, pronunciation and interactive communication, and writes one strength and one target. Include a short individual feedback conference of two minutes after each pair if time allows.
lp.rw: Course feedback and goals: students complete a feedback form (what helped, what to change, what they want next year) and write three goals for their English with one action for each. The teacher collects the forms. Students who finished early write a thank-you note to a classmate.
lp.st: Closing ceremony: the teacher hands out certificates, thanks the class and gives a short message about next steps (the next level, the Cambridge B2 First exam, free practice resources, an English-speaking club or conversation partners). Students share one wish for the future and take a group photo.
g: Choose the best strategy for each task.
Complete a short cloze against the clock.
Write three goals with an action for each.
Give a classmate a short spoken message of thanks.
Describe your English year in one word and explain it.
diff: Fast finishers: add a third task (a short review or report paragraph) or write an extra key word transformation.
Support: allow a word bank of connectors and a checklist for the writing paper.
hw: Write three goals for your English for next year with one action for each.
Choose one English resource to use every week over the summer and write why.
Write a thank-you message to someone who helped you learn English this year.
lp.tip: Frame the assessment as a celebration of progress, not as a test of worth. Record the marks by skill, prepare the certificates and the report cards before the lesson, and use the feedback forms to plan the next course. If a student is close to B2 level, show them the Cambridge B2 First options and the free practice tasks in the Drive.
checklist: I can talk about the topics of the year with range and detail.
I can follow authentic-style recordings and note key information.
I can read a text of about 400 words and answer questions on opinion and detail.
I can write a well-organised text of 150-190 words for a stated purpose.
I can use conditionals, reported speech, relative clauses and the passive accurately.
I can give and receive feedback and set my goals for next year.
I can take part in a discussion and keep it going with questions.

levels.desc: For adults aged 18+ at a secure B1 who are moving towards B2. Semester 1 builds accuracy and range: narrative tenses, perfect forms, future forms, deduction, all four conditionals, the passive, reported speech and relative clauses, with longer speaking turns and formal writing. Semester 2 trains B2 First-style reading, listening, speaking and writing, with debates on culture, media, technology and the environment, a mock exam, a vocabulary and accuracy clinic and student presentations. The course book is American English File 4, with Ready for B2 First for exam tasks.
